Lecture 1: Introduction to Spring Framework

Source: "Spring Boot & Spring Framework Full Course | Spring Boot Full Course #1" · 43 min · Code Army · First lecture of the series

Why learn more than Spring Boot

Learning only Spring Boot means learning its syntax without knowing how anything works inside. Underneath, every Spring Boot app runs on:

  • Spring Core (IoC / DI).
  • Spring MVC, if it is a web app.
  • Other modules such as Spring Data and Spring Security.

A Java full-stack engineer needs all of these. The series covers the whole architecture: Spring Core, Spring MVC and the full Spring Framework, plus practical industry experience. The aim is to handle any Spring interview and to build your own projects.

How a user reaches a website: client–server architecture

Before using Spring for development, answer the basic question: how does visiting a website give you a response?

  1. You type a URL such as www.amazon.in in a browser.
  2. Somewhere, Amazon has a server. That is just a computer where Amazon's application is hosted.
  3. The server entertains the request and sends back a response.
  4. The browser displays the response as a web page.

At the most basic level this is the client–server architecture. Whoever requests is the client, and whoever responds is the server. The request travels as an HTTP request (or HTTPS), and the server answers with an HTTP response.

Who can be a client, and what a server does

A client is anything that sends a request to a server, not only a user or a browser:

  • A browser.
  • A mobile app (Android or iOS). You can open Amazon from its app.
  • A frontend app, for example one built in React.
  • Postman, a tool for calling APIs on a backend server.
  • Another server. In a microservice architecture there are many servers. When an Order service calls the Payment or Notification service over HTTP, the Order service is the client for that call.

A client's job is simply to send an HTTP request, whether to store, fetch, update or delete information.

A server is any entity that entertains the request: it receives it, does some processing and returns a response. Processing can mean:

  • Storing data in a database.
  • Fetching information.
  • Updating or deleting records.
  • Authenticating the user, for example on a login request to a site.
In one line:
The client asks for information and the server responds. Who is the client and who is the server depends on who starts the request, not on the kind of machine.

HTTP: the rulebook between client and server

HTTP = HyperText Transfer Protocol. Client and server need an agreed language and format to talk; they can't just throw random data at each other. A protocol is a rulebook of the internet. HTTP defines:

  • The structure of a request.
  • The structure of a response.
  • Which method was called, i.e. what kind of operation is wanted.
  • How data is sent: encrypted or not.
MethodPurposeHas body?SafeIdempotent
GETOnly retrieves informationNormally noYesYes
POSTStores / creates information (e.g. login, signup)YesNoNo
PUTUpdates information, replacing the whole resourceYesNoYes
PATCHUpdates specific fields onlyYesNoNot guaranteed
DELETEDeletes informationUsually noNoYes
Worth adding: safe vs idempotent (not in the lecture; commonly asked):
Safe means the method doesn't change server state. Idempotent means sending the same request many times leaves the server in the same state as sending it once. Calling DELETE /users/5 twice still leaves user 5 deleted, while calling POST /orders twice creates two orders. HTTP is also stateless: every request stands alone, and login state is carried by cookies, sessions or tokens.

Structure of an HTTP request

Say the client is fetching the courses from a course site. The request says which method (GET, to retrieve data), which host (www.example.com) and which endpoint (/courses). The full URL is www.example.com/courses. When it arrives, the server may authenticate you, fetch all the courses from the database and send a response.

A complete request has four parts:

  1. Method name: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH.
  2. URL, also called the path or endpoint.
  3. Headers: key–value pairs carrying extra metadata. For example, Accept: application/json says "I accept a JSON response". Credentials or tokens also go in a header.
  4. Request body: detailed data you want the server to store. A GET has no body, because it only fetches.
GET /courses HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Accept: application/json

A login is a POST to /login on the same host. Content-Type: application/json says the body I'm sending is JSON, and the body carries the email and password:

POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 51

{"email":"user@example.com","password":"secret123"}

The server sees it is a login request, reads the email and password from the body, authenticates you and, if they're correct, sends back a response.

Accept vs Content-Type:
Accept says what format you want back. Content-Type describes the body of the message it is on. A blank line separates headers from body. Credentials in a body must only travel over HTTPS.

Structure of an HTTP response

The response also follows HTTP's guidelines and has three parts:

  1. Status code, the most important part. It decides whether the response is a success, a failure or some other issue.
  2. Headers: optional key–value pairs, e.g. Content-Type.
  3. Body: the information returned.
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"message":"Login successful"}
Common status codes
ClassMeaningExamples
1xxInformational100 Continue
2xxSuccess200 OK, 201 Created (a resource was created), 204 No Content
3xxRedirection301 Moved Permanently, 304 Not Modified
4xxClient error400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (not authenticated), 403 Forbidden (authenticated but not allowed), 404 Not Found (resource not found)
5xxServer error500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable

HTTP vs HTTPS

  • By default, HTTP data is not encrypted, so anyone in between could read it. That is why sites moved from HTTP to HTTPS.
  • HTTPS is the same protocol; the S means secure. Both the request and the response are encrypted, so nobody in the middle can listen in.
  • Technically, HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. Beyond encryption, the server's TLS certificate also proves its identity (added).
  • Default ports are 80 for HTTP and 443 for HTTPS.
Transcript slips to ignore:
  • "2001" for a created resource is 201 Created.
  • 503 was called "internal server error". 503 is Service Unavailable; Internal Server Error is 500.
  • The header carrying credentials or tokens is Authorization (e.g. Authorization: Bearer <token>), not "Authentication".

What core Java gives us: code that runs once

With core Java we write a class such as public class Main with public static void main, and put our code inside it. Then:

  1. Save it as Main.java, named after the class.
  2. Compile it: javac Main.java produces bytecode, Main.class. Bytecode is platform-independent and runs on any OS ("Write Once, Run Anywhere").
  3. Run it on the JVM, which provides a sandbox for your code. Your code does not run natively on the OS; it runs inside the JVM, and the JVM is a process on the OS.

When a request hits a server running a Java application, we are really interacting with Java code on that server's JVM. That code was compiled from a file and runs there.

Code flow vs website flow

A Java program is a set of instructions: start → run → stop → exit. A website never behaves like that. You can hit instagram.com at any time of day and get a response. It is always active.

Could core Java run forever? A hack like while (true) { … } keeps a program alive and mimics a website. But even then the real question stays open: how do you map an incoming HTTP request to a method?

An endpoint is just a method call

Apply first-principles thinking. Java is object-oriented, so whatever runs on the server is a method inside some class. Hitting an endpoint should run a particular piece of work:

  • GET /courses → a courses() method that fetches all courses (perhaps from the database) and returns them.
  • /signup → a signup() method that registers the user.

Hitting the endpoint over the internet is the method call. Core Java already covers classes, objects, inheritance and OOP principles. What it doesn't cover:

  • How to read an HTTP request: the URL, headers and body.
  • Who calls the method, i.e. how the endpoint → method mapping happens.
  • How to send an HTTP response.

Can core Java do networking? Yes: java.net

The internet is a network, and Java has been able to listen to one since Java 1, through the java.net package. It offers classes like Socket and ServerSocket:

ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(8080);   // listen on port 8080
  • Port. A computer runs many applications at once (WhatsApp, Chrome, Spotify). An incoming request carries the machine's IP address, but the port number decides which application it is for. Each application listens on its own port, and your Java server can listen on 8080.
  • localhost means your own computer; its loopback IP is 127.0.0.1. So localhost:8080 means "send the request to port 8080 on my own machine".

So if Java can listen to a network, why do we need any framework? This is where the lecture's "no" answer comes in.

Why java.net isn't enough: the boilerplate problem

Java code does not understand the HTTP format. To the JVM, GET /courses Host: … is just an incoming stream of bytes. It can read it "dumbly", as it is, but it cannot interpret what it means. So you would have to do all of this by hand:

  1. Read the input stream. Use a BufferedReader, which turns the byte stream into characters, as with any Java input.
  2. Parse the request manually, to work out what GET, /courses and the host are.
  3. Map a method to an endpoint manually: if (endpoint.equals("/courses")) callThisMethod(); else if (…) …, one condition per endpoint.
  4. Build the HTTP response manually from whatever the method returned. You must follow the protocol, and java.net doesn't understand HTTP responses either.
  5. Implement multithreading manually. With only the main thread busy doing all this, any other request to the server gets stuck. You need multiple threads so that many users are handled concurrently.

That is a lot of boilerplate and manual effort for the developer, before writing any business logic.

Worked example: GET /courses with plain java.net

An illustration (added; the lecture only lists the steps). Each manual step from above is marked in the comments:

import java.io.*;
import java.net.*;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

public class RawHttpServer {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        try (ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(8080)) {
            System.out.println("Listening on http://localhost:8080");
            while (true) {                                   // stay up forever
                Socket client = server.accept();             // blocks until someone connects
                new Thread(() -> handle(client)).start();    // manual multithreading
            }
        }
    }

    private static void handle(Socket client) {
        try (client;
             BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(
                     new InputStreamReader(client.getInputStream(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
             OutputStream out = client.getOutputStream()) {

            String requestLine = in.readLine();              // "GET /courses HTTP/1.1"
            if (requestLine == null) return;
            String[] parts = requestLine.split(" ");         // manual parsing
            if (parts.length < 2) return;
            String method = parts[0], path = parts[1];
            String line;                                     // skip headers until blank line
            while ((line = in.readLine()) != null && !line.isEmpty()) { }

            int status;
            String body;
            if (method.equals("GET") && path.equals("/courses")) {  // manual routing
                status = 200;
                body = getCourses();
            } else {
                status = 404;
                body = "{\"error\":\"Not Found\"}";
            }

            byte[] bytes = body.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            String head = "HTTP/1.1 " + status + (status == 200 ? " OK" : " Not Found") + "\r\n"
                    + "Content-Type: application/json\r\n"
                    + "Content-Length: " + bytes.length + "\r\n"
                    + "Connection: close\r\n\r\n";           // manual response building
            out.write(head.getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII));
            out.write(bytes);
        } catch (IOException e) {
            e.printStackTrace();
        }
    }

    private static String getCourses() {                     // the only business logic
        return "[\"Java\",\"Spring Boot\",\"LLD\"]";
    }
}

To run it (Java 9 or later, because of try (client; …)): javac RawHttpServer.java, then java RawHttpServer, then curl -i http://localhost:8080/courses.

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 28
Connection: close

["Java","Spring Boot","LLD"]
Why this doesn't scale:
About 50 lines, and only getCourses() is business logic. The code still ignores request bodies, query strings, keep-alive, chunked encoding and malformed input, and it starts an unbounded number of threads. Every endpoint adds another if.

Servlets and the Servlet container (1997)

To remove this manual effort, Servlets and the Servlet container arrived in 1997. It was the first Java package designed specifically for web applications and web development.

  • Servlet. A Java class that runs inside a servlet container. Doesn't everything in Java run inside the JVM? Yes: the container itself runs inside the JVM, and the servlet runs inside the container.
  • Servlet container. Usually just called "the server". Well-known ones:
    • Tomcat, the most famous and most used.
    • Jetty.
    • Undertow.

Why Tomcat is special: it does all the boilerplate you were doing by hand.

  • Opens the port.
  • Reads the incoming bytes and deciphers them into HTTP.
  • Works out which URL was hit and calls the servlet mapped to that URL.
  • Builds the HTTP response from what the servlet returns.
  • Implements multithreading internally.

You write your code inside servlets and focus on business logic. The method you used to call for /courses now lives inside a servlet.

  • Tomcat is a server, so it stays up like any other website, listening for clients. That solves the "always running" problem too.
  • There can be many servlets, and the one called depends on which request arrived.
  • This is the first time Java solved the problem of building web applications.

The same endpoint as a servlet (added; servlet syntax is covered later in the series):

import jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebServlet;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServlet;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import java.io.IOException;

@WebServlet("/courses")                        // URL → servlet mapping
public class CoursesServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        resp.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_OK);
        resp.setContentType("application/json");
        resp.getWriter().write("[\"Java\",\"Spring Boot\",\"LLD\"]");
    }
}

This is deployed as a WAR file to Tomcat 10.1 or later. @WebServlet needs Servlet 3.0+; before that, mappings lived in web.xml. The container also manages each servlet's lifecycle: init() → service() → destroy().

Why the Spring Framework came

If servlets worked, why Spring? Because servlet-oriented code, scaled up to an enterprise-level application, becomes tightly coupled. Many objects end up interlinked, which makes the application very hard to scale.

Spring presented its own ideology and introduced core concepts, Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control. These make applications loosely coupled, so they are easy to scale. Both get dedicated lectures later; here is the shape of the idea (added):

// Tightly coupled: the service builds its own dependency
class CourseService {
    private final MySqlCourseRepository repo = new MySqlCourseRepository();
}

// Loosely coupled: the dependency is handed in (Spring's IoC container does this)
class CourseService {
    private final CourseRepository repo;          // interface
    CourseService(CourseRepository repo) {        // constructor injection
        this.repo = repo;
    }
}
Why this matters:
In the second version, switching from MySQL to Postgres, or to a fake repository in a unit test, doesn't touch CourseService. The container creates the objects (called beans) and wires them together.

Spring is an ecosystem, not one framework

Calling Spring "a framework" is inaccurate, because it contains many frameworks. It is an ecosystem, and it is not only for web apps. According to spring.io ("What Spring can do"), you can build:

  • GenAI applications.
  • Microservices.
  • Reactive applications.
  • Cloud applications.
  • Event-driven systems.
  • Web apps, the focus of this series.
  • Serverless architectures.
  • Batch processing jobs.

Spring's own tagline is that it makes Java simple, modern and productive.

The Spring ecosystem, layer by layer

LayerWhat it gives you
Spring CoreThe ideology Spring introduced: dependency injection, inversion of control, beans. The goal is loosely coupled systems. Every module rests on it.
Spring MVCBuilding web applications. Uses Servlets internally, so you no longer use servlets directly, but you still need to understand them to go deep and debug issues.
Spring DataConnecting the application to a database.
Spring AOPAspect-Oriented Programming. Explained when it is introduced later in the series.
Spring SecurityLogging users in and authenticating them.
Spring AIThe modern addition. It extends the core stack for GenAI apps (1.0 GA in 2025).
Spring BootAn automation layer on top of all of these.
Precision note (added):
Spring MVC (spring-webmvc) and Spring AOP are modules inside the Spring Framework itself. Spring Data, Security, Boot, Cloud and AI are separate projects built on the Framework.

Spring Boot: the opinionated automation layer

A common confusion is that Spring Boot made the Spring Framework obsolete, or replaced it. Not at all. The lecture's point:

  • Spring Boot isn't even a skill. The skills are the modules in the middle: MVC, Data, AOP and Security.
  • Spring Boot is an automation layer on top of them. Its ideology is to let you start application development very quickly, hence the name: you "boot up" fast.
  • It is an opinionated framework. It has its own opinions and sets up the project by assuming configurations. If the defaults suit you, start writing APIs; if not, change them.
  • With plain Spring MVC you have to write many configurations manually, so the manual effort goes up. Spring Boot removes that.
  • To change its defaults you must know the internal architecture: how MVC, Data, AOP and Security work. You can never learn only Spring Boot and skip these, because the core technology is the same, and Spring Core underneath is shared by all.

Main features (expanded beyond the lecture):

  • Auto-configuration based on what is on the classpath.
  • Starter dependencies, e.g. spring-boot-starter-web.
  • An embedded server, Tomcat by default, so the app runs as java -jar app.jar.
  • External configuration in application.properties or application.yml.
  • Production features through Actuator.

The same endpoint in Spring Boot, as a preview (added; the next lecture writes the first real code):

import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@SpringBootApplication                         // auto-configuration + component scanning
public class DemoApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);   // starts embedded Tomcat on 8080
    }
}

@RestController
class CourseController {
    @GetMapping("/courses")                    // GET /courses → this method
    public List<String> getCourses() {
        return List.of("Java", "Spring Boot", "LLD");        // converted to JSON automatically
    }
}

This needs spring-boot-starter-web, and Spring Boot 3.x requires Java 17 or later. curl http://localhost:8080/courses returns ["Java","Spring Boot","LLD"].

Spring Data: JDBC → JPA → Hibernate → Spring Data JPA

Spring Data is about how a Java application connects to a database. Understanding it means following the history:

  1. JDBC (Java Database Connectivity). The earlier approach. Inside Demo.java you write the exact SQL queries (SELECT … FROM table …), and the database returns the result.
  2. JPA (Java Persistence API). The next step: "we don't want to write SQL by hand". You call methods, and internally they talk to the database. But it isn't magic: the database still only understands SQL, so JDBC is used underneath. JPA isn't an implementation either; it is an idea, a rulebook.
  3. Hibernate implements JPA, and Hibernate uses JDBC internally.
  4. Spring Data JPA sits on top and brings this idea into Spring. Hibernate implements it underneath.
The lecture's learning order:
To understand Spring Data and Spring Data JPA you must understand Hibernate. To understand Hibernate you must understand JDBC. The series covers the whole chain. 
// JDBC: SQL and mapping by hand
String sql = "SELECT id, title FROM courses WHERE id = ?";
try (Connection con = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass);
     PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    ps.setLong(1, 42L);
    try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
        if (rs.next()) {
            course = new Course(rs.getLong("id"), rs.getString("title"));
        }
    }
}

// Spring Data JPA: declare an interface; the SQL is generated
public interface CourseRepository extends JpaRepository<Course, Long> {
    List<Course> findByTitleContaining(String keyword);   // query derived from the method name
}

JDBC vs JPA vs Hibernate vs Spring Data JPA

JDBCJPAHibernateSpring Data JPA
TypeLow-level APISpecificationORM, JPA implementationAbstraction over JPA
You writeSQL + row mappingEntities, JPQLEntities (SQL generated)Repository interfaces
Uses underneathDB driverNeeds a providerJDBCA JPA provider (Hibernate by default in Boot)
BoilerplateMostLessLessLeast

The complete Spring architecture

The full picture:

  • The client sends a request to a Spring Boot application.
  • Internally the app is built from modules (MVC, Security, AOP, Data), and all of them share Spring Core.
  • To reach the database, it goes through Spring Data JPA → Hibernate → JDBC.
  • Spring MVC itself uses servlets.

The order of one request (added; the lecture shows only the blocks, and DispatcherServlet comes in later lectures):

  1. Tomcat accepts the request, parses it and assigns a thread.
  2. The Security filters authenticate the request.
  3. DispatcherServlet, Spring MVC's single front-controller servlet, routes it to the matching controller method.
  4. The controller calls the service.
  5. The service calls the repository, which goes through Hibernate and JDBC to the database.
  6. The return value is turned into JSON by Jackson and written as the response.

Monolith vs microservices

A common doubt: what are microservices? "Spring microservices" is not a separate module. It is an architecture design, a way of building your web application. A Spring Boot app can be built in two ways:

  • Monolithic architecture. One complete application handles all the endpoints.
  • Microservice architecture. Many small services (Order, Payment, User…) that call each other. How to split and distribute them is covered later in the series.
MonolithMicroservices
DeploymentOne unitMany independent units
CommunicationIn-process method callsNetwork calls (HTTP, messaging)
ScalingScale the whole appScale each service separately
ComplexitySimpler to build, test and debug at firstDistributed-system problems: latency, partial failures, tracing
FitsSmall teams, early productsLarge systems or teams that need independent releases

Spring Cloud provides the tooling for microservices, such as service discovery, an API gateway and centralized config (added).

Spring Framework vs Spring Boot

AspectSpring FrameworkSpring Boot
What it isCore framework: IoC/DI plus modules (MVC, AOP, …)Opinionated automation layer on top of Spring
ConfigurationMostly manual (Java config / XML)Auto-configuration with sensible defaults, overridable
DependenciesPick and version-match each oneStarters with managed, compatible versions
ServerDeploy a WAR to an external serverEmbedded Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow, run with java -jar
Setup timeSlowerFast; that's the whole point

Anticipated question: "Does Spring Boot replace Spring?"

No. Spring Boot is built on Spring Core and the modules. It only automates configuration. Every Spring Boot app is a Spring app underneath. You override its defaults with properties (server.port=9090), your own bean definitions, or by excluding an auto-configuration, and doing that well requires knowing the modules.

Anticipated question: "Why was Spring needed if Servlets already worked?"

Servlets solved networking and HTTP. They didn't solve application structure. Large servlet apps, along with the heavyweight EJB 2.x model of J2EE at the time, became tightly coupled and hard to test. Spring's IoC container and DI made them modular and loosely coupled. Spring came from Rod Johnson's 2002 book on J2EE design, and Spring 1.0 shipped in 2004 (added).

Anticipated question: "Can a server be a client?"

Yes. Client and server are roles per request. An Order service is a server to the frontend and a client to the Payment service.

Anticipated question: "How does a servlet container serve many users at once?"

With a thread-per-request model backed by a pool. Tomcat's default maximum is 200 threads (server.tomcat.threads.max). A servlet is usually a single instance shared across threads, so its instance fields must be thread-safe. On Java 21 with Spring Boot 3.2+, spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true makes Tomcat use virtual threads.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Servlets predate the J2EE brand. The lecture says servlets came in 1997 "as a Java Enterprise Edition package". Servlet 1.0 did appear in 1997. J2EE 1.2 (1999) came later and included servlets. Today it is Jakarta EE.
  • javax.* → jakarta.*. Since Jakarta EE 9 (Servlet 5.0), and therefore in Spring Boot 3+, Spring Framework 6+ and Tomcat 10+, the packages are jakarta.servlet and jakarta.persistence. Mixing in old javax.servlet code causes compile errors or ClassNotFoundException.
  • "Spring JPA" is called Spring Data JPA. JPA itself has been renamed Jakarta Persistence. Hibernate is Spring Boot's default JPA provider; EclipseLink is an alternative.
  • Spring Boot isn't tied to Spring MVC. The lecture says Boot "is based on Spring MVC". Boot configures MVC only when spring-boot-starter-web is present. It works equally for non-web apps (batch, CLI) and for reactive apps with Spring WebFlux, which doesn't need the Servlet API and runs on Netty by default.
  • Tomcat is not a full application server. There are three kinds of server:
    • A web server (Nginx) serves static content and proxies requests.
    • A servlet container (Tomcat, Jetty, Undertow) runs servlets.
    • An application server (WildFly, WebLogic) implements the whole Jakarta EE platform, including EJB, JMS and JTA.
    Spring apps get those extra capabilities from libraries and run fine on Tomcat.
  • POST retries. Because POST isn't idempotent, a retried payment could charge twice. APIs use an idempotency key: the client sends a unique key and the server ignores duplicates.
  • Other JDK options exist. JDK 6+ ships a lightweight com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer, and JDK 18 added jwebserver for static files. Neither is used for production web apps, and neither was mentioned in the lecture.
  • HTTP versions. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 run over TCP; HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (UDP). The request and response concepts stay the same.

Lecture 2: Your First Spring Boot Application (Hello World)

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #2 · 31 min · Code Army · First hands-on lecture

The goal: "Hello World" in the browser

Build a tiny Spring Boot app: type a URL in the browser and see Hello World. No Spring syntax has been taught yet, so the code won't make full sense, and that's intentional. The point of this lecture is to feel how simple starting a Spring Boot app is, and how it configures everything automatically so you can start straight on business logic. How Spring Boot does all this is explained in the coming lectures.

  • Client: your own browser (Chrome).
  • Server: your own Spring Boot application, running on the same computer.
  • Because both are on one machine, the browser hits localhost, i.e. your own computer's address, on port 8080.
  • The request is GET /hello, and the server should respond with the string Hello World, which the browser displays.

IP addresses and the real client–server flow

Every device on a network has an IP address. You can see yours by searching "what is my IP" (e.g. whatismyip.com), which shows an IPv4 and an IPv6 address. For a client anywhere in the world to send data to a machine, it must send it to that machine's IP address.

So the Lecture 1 picture, where a request went "directly to www.example.com", was simplified. The network knows nothing about a name like example.com; it only routes to IP addresses. The real flow:

  1. The client asks DNS (Domain Name System) for the IP address of the domain. DNS's job is to resolve a domain name to an IP address.
  2. DNS returns the server's IP.
  3. The client calls the server using that IP, e.g. GET /hello with the IP as the host.
  4. The request reaches the server, which sends back a response.

localhost and 127.0.0.1

When the client (your browser) and the server (your Spring Boot app) are on the same computer, the host is 127.0.0.1. It is a fixed IP that means "send this request to myself". The word localhost can replace it. So in localhost:8080/hello, the host is localhost, the port is 8080 and the endpoint is /hello.

Port numbers: which application gets the data

An IP address gets a packet to the right machine. But that machine runs many applications at once: Chrome, WhatsApp, Spotify, your Spring Boot app… How does the OS know which one the data is for?

Definition:
Besides the IP address there is one more identifier, the port number. One IP address has many ports, and each listening application is bound to its own port. A Spring Boot app listens on 8080 by default. That's why the URL carries a port along with localhost: it tells the client which port on the server to hit.

Anticipated question: "We never type a port for real websites. How does the server know which port?"

Earlier we found the server's IP through DNS and sent the request to that IP, with no port. Some ports are defined by standard:

ProtocolDefault port
HTTP80
HTTPS443

All HTTP traffic goes to port 80 and all HTTPS traffic to 443. Typing https://www.example.com makes the browser attach port 443 automatically.

Reverse proxy: mapping 443 to 8080

If the site's backend is Spring Boot, it probably runs on 8080 by default. You can change the port, but suppose you don't. The client sent the request to 443, yet the app listens on 8080. Between client and app sits a reverse proxy:

  • It receives incoming requests on the public port, 443.
  • It maps them to port 8080, so every HTTPS request ends up at the Spring Boot app.
  • It is part of the server side. You can think of the proxy and the app together as "the server".
Worth knowing: what a reverse proxy really does (added):
It forwards (proxies) the request to the app. That isn't an HTTP redirect: the browser never sees port 8080. Typical reverse proxies are Nginx, HAProxy and cloud load balancers. They usually also terminate TLS (decrypt HTTPS, then talk plain HTTP to the app), load-balance across several app instances, and serve static files. Keeping the app on 8080 also means it doesn't need the admin rights that ports below 1024 require on Linux.

Before any code: "This site can't be reached"

Opening localhost:8080/hello now gives "This site can't be reached", because nothing is listening on port 8080 yet. The goal is to make "Hello World" appear there.

Requirements

  • An IDE. The lecture uses IntelliJ IDEA, the most popular IDE for Java. Eclipse or NetBeans work the same way.
  • Java installed. Any recent version. Spring Boot 3 and 4 need Java 17 or later.

The problem: building a Java web app from scratch

Before writing a single line of business code, i.e. the logic your app exists for, a from-scratch Java web app needs:

  1. A folder structure. Loose files anywhere won't do once a web app has many classes.
  2. Lots of configuration.
  3. Downloading dependencies.
  4. Configuring the Spring Boot version.
  5. Configuring the Java version.
  6. A package structure.

All of that is just playing with configuration. That's why the Spring team built Spring Initializr.

What a dependency (library) is

Say your Java code must connect to a MySQL database. You won't write your own connector from scratch; you use a MySQL connector. That is a library: ready-made code someone already wrote for you to use. When your code uses an external library, the library becomes a dependency, because your code depends on it.

The official MySQL driver is called MySQL Connector/J (added). Maven, which downloads dependencies, is covered in the next lecture.

Spring Initializr: a ready-made project skeleton

At start.spring.io you pick options and click Generate. A zip downloads, and unzipping it gives the skeleton of the whole project, with Spring Boot configuration, Java version, Spring Boot version and folder structure already set up. You go straight to business logic. The series uses it for every project.

The options chosen in the lecture
OptionChoicesPickedWhy / what it means
ProjectGradle - Groovy, Gradle - Kotlin, MavenMavenThese are project management / build tools. Maven is the most popular and is used throughout the series. Why a build tool is needed comes next lecture.
LanguageJava, Kotlin, GroovyJava—
Spring BootSeveral versions, some marked SNAPSHOT or RC4.0.6Take the latest stable one (see the table below). The series uses Spring Boot 4; a later version would change a little, but most things stay the same.
Project metadataGroup, Artifact, Package nameLeft as defaultExplained with Maven in the next lecture.
PackagingJar, WarJarJAR = Java ARchive, WAR = Web ARchive. Older Java web apps used WAR; modern Spring Boot apps use JAR.
ConfigurationProperties, YAMLPropertiesEither works.
Java17, 21, 25, 2621Not the very newest, not old. Java 17, 21 and 25 are the LTS (long-term support) releases (added).
Dependencies—Spring WebSo the code can talk to the web and listen on a port. Its description reads: "Build web, including RESTful, applications using Spring MVC. Uses Apache Tomcat as the default embedded container."
Why the Spring Web description matters:
Tomcat, the servlet container from Lecture 1, comes embedded inside the app. You don't download or install a server separately.

SNAPSHOT vs RC vs stable

LabelMeaningUse it?
SNAPSHOTWork in progress, not finalized, can change dailyNo: bugs are likely
M1, M2… (added)Milestone: an early preview of the next versionNo
RCRelease Candidate: almost final, a candidate for release, but not released yetNo: don't take the risk
No suffix (e.g. 4.0.6)GA / stable releaseYes, the newest stable one

JAR vs WAR

JAR (Java ARchive)WAR (Web ARchive)
ServerEmbedded inside the app (Tomcat by default)External: you install Tomcat and deploy the WAR into it
How to runjava -jar app.jarCopy into the server's deploy folder
Used byModern Spring Boot apps, containers / cloudOlder Java web apps, shared app servers

The JAR vs WAR detail is covered later in the series. The "embedded server" column is exactly the Lecture 1 point that Spring Boot ships its own Tomcat.

The generated project

Click Generate, which downloads demo.zip. Unzip it, then in IntelliJ choose Open and select the demo folder. The first import takes a moment.

demo/
├── .mvn/                       Maven wrapper files
├── mvnw, mvnw.cmd              Maven wrapper scripts (no global Maven install needed)
├── pom.xml                     Maven config: dependencies, versions, build
└── src/
    ├── main/
    │   ├── java/
    │   │   └── com/example/demo/
    │   │       └── DemoApplication.java      ← entry point (main method)
    │   └── resources/
    │       └── application.properties        ← configuration (e.g. server.port)
    └── test/
        └── java/com/example/demo/
            └── DemoApplicationTests.java

Most of this makes no sense yet (.mvn? pom.xml?). Inside src/main/java/com/example/demo is DemoApplication.java, and it contains something familiar, public static void main. Java execution starts from main.

package com.example.demo;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
public class DemoApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);
    }
}

What @SpringBootApplication is and what SpringApplication.run does aren't clear yet, and nothing else is written. That's fine for now; the point is that the template and skeleton are ready.

Step 1: print "Hello World" on the console

Add System.out.println("Hello World"); in main and click Run DemoApplication. Some logs appear, and Hello World is printed. So far this is just a plain Java application printing to the console, but it proves the project runs.

Tomcat is already running: the Whitelabel Error Page

Now localhost:8080/hello, or even plain localhost:8080, shows something, though not Hello World. The logs explain why: running the app started the embedded server.

Tomcat initialized with port 8080 (http)
Starting service [Tomcat]
Tomcat started on port 8080 (http) with context path '/'

(Abridged: only the message part of each log line is shown, because logger names differ between versions.) Tomcat, the servlet container, got port 8080, started its service and is now listening for network calls. The browser therefore shows:

Whitelabel Error Page
This application has no explicit mapping for /error, so you are seeing this as a fallback.
... There was an unexpected error (type=Not Found, status=404).

Nobody has mapped this endpoint, so an error page appears. Since there is no custom error fallback, you see Spring Boot's default one. That doesn't matter now. The living proof that the server runs is "Tomcat started on port 8080".

Step 2: the first endpoint, HelloController

In the com.example.demo package, create a new Java class HelloController and annotate it with @RestController.

What a controller is (for now):
Think of it as the gateway where you write API endpoints. Inside it you declare which method runs when someone hits /hello, /orders, and so on. This is exactly the Lecture 1 problem: mapping a URL / endpoint to a Java method.

First, a plain Java method: public void hello() won't do, because it has to return a string. So it becomes public String hello() { return "Hello World"; }. Nothing new here, just Java syntax.

Who calls this method? You could call it yourself from main:

HelloController controller = new HelloController();
String s = controller.hello();
System.out.println(s);          // Hello World

Rerunning prints Hello World on the console, because you called hello() yourself. That's how Java has worked so far. But the goal is for the method to run when a browser hits /hello. For that, add one more annotation, @GetMapping("/hello"): it's a GET method, and this is its endpoint. Then remove the manual call from main.

package com.example.demo;

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController                          // "this class holds API endpoints"
public class HelloController {

    @GetMapping("/hello")                // GET /hello  →  hello()
    public String hello() {
        return "Hello World";            // becomes the HTTP response body
    }
}

Rerun. Nothing prints on the console this time, and Tomcat starts on 8080. Now http://localhost:8080/hello shows Hello World, so the first Spring Boot application is built.

How little it took:
Download the skeleton from Initializr. Don't touch the folder structure. Write one class with one method and two annotations:
  • @RestController tells Spring Boot this class is a controller, a gateway for endpoints.
  • @GetMapping("/hello") maps GET /hello to hello().
Hitting /hello in the browser calls hello(), which returns "Hello World", and the browser shows it.
Worth knowing: the leading slash:
The lecture writes @GetMapping("hello") without the slash, and it works, because Spring adds a leading / if it is missing. Writing "/hello" is the usual convention.

Returning HTML instead of plain text

Change the return value to "<h1>Hello World</h1>", rerun, and the browser renders it as a big heading.

Why the browser renders it (added):
@RestController writes the returned String straight into the response body. When the request comes from a browser, which sends Accept: text/html,…, Spring responds with Content-Type: text/html, so the tags are rendered. Fine for a demo, but real HTML pages use a template engine such as Thymeleaf. REST APIs return JSON, which Spring produces automatically from returned objects.

Changing the port: application.properties

Open src/main/resources/application.properties and add:

server.port=9090

Rerun, and the log now says Tomcat started on port 9090. localhost:8080/hello gives "This site can't be reached", while localhost:9090/hello shows Hello World. The lecture's point: it's the Tomcat server that listens on the port, not "the Spring Boot app" by itself.

Precision (added): embedded Tomcat runs inside the same JVM process as your app, started by Spring Boot. From the OS's point of view, your app's process owns the port, and Tomcat is the component inside it that accepts the connections.

Step 3: a second endpoint, /bye

A controller can have many endpoints:

@GetMapping("/bye")
public String greetBye() {       // method name need not match the endpoint
    return "Bye";
}

Rerun; you have to rerun every time so the changes are deployed. /hello still shows Hello World, and /bye shows Bye. hello() and greetBye() are called based on the endpoint, and each returns a string that the browser displays. The method name and the endpoint are independent.

Worth knowing: no more manual restarts (added):
Adding the Spring Boot DevTools dependency restarts the app automatically when classes change. It's handy in development and is not included in production builds.

Questions still unanswered

A Spring Boot app printing Hello World was built in about 10 minutes, and that was the motive of the lecture: showing how fast Spring Boot is and how it sets up configuration so you can focus on business logic. But natural questions remain:

  • Who started the Tomcat server?
  • Did we even install Tomcat? Not separately. It came with the skeleton, through the Spring Web dependency ("uses Tomcat as the default embedded container").
  • How did /hello get mapped to hello()? Nothing in main calls it.
  • What are @RestController, @GetMapping, @SpringBootApplication? What does SpringApplication.run do inside?
A preview of the answer (added; each piece gets its own lecture):
  1. SpringApplication.run creates the Spring application context (the IoC container).
  2. Component scanning (part of @SpringBootApplication) finds classes like HelloController in the same package and its sub-packages, and creates them as beans.
  3. Auto-configuration sees Spring MVC and Tomcat on the classpath (thanks to Spring Web). It starts an embedded Tomcat and registers Spring MVC's DispatcherServlet in it.
  4. Spring MVC reads @GetMapping annotations and builds a URL → method table. On GET /hello, the DispatcherServlet looks it up and calls hello().

Anticipated question: "If Spring Boot configures everything, why learn Spring MVC and Spring Core?"

  • You can't understand Spring Boot on its own. Explaining it means explaining @GetMapping and @RestController (Spring MVC), and its ideology (Spring Core). You'd end up covering the whole architecture anyway.
  • Debugging. Suppose you write the /bye endpoint, run the app, and "Bye" doesn't appear. Without knowing what the annotations do, what controllers are and how an endpoint gets hit when main calls nothing, you can't go inside to debug it. Stepping into SpringApplication.run would make no sense to you.

That is why the series covers the full Spring architecture: to make you a good Java full-stack developer.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • "What is my IP" shows your public IP, usually your router's. Home devices sit behind NAT with private IPs (192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x). A request from the internet to that public IP reaches the router, not your laptop, unless port forwarding is set up. Your machine's local IP is shown by ipconfig (Windows) or ip addr (Linux).
  • Client apps don't "run on a port" the way servers do. The lecture says Chrome, WhatsApp and Spotify each run on a port. Servers listen on a fixed, known port (8080, 443, 3306). Clients like Chrome get a temporary ephemeral source port from the OS for each outgoing connection, and replies come back to that port. Either way, the IP + port pair identifies the application endpoint.
  • Only one process can listen on a given port at a time. Starting a second app on 8080 fails with "Port 8080 was already in use". Fix it with server.port, or stop the other process. server.port=0 picks a random free port.
  • The reverse proxy forwards; it doesn't redirect. The lecture says requests get "redirected" to 8080. An HTTP redirect would send the browser to a new URL. A proxy forwards the request internally, and the client never sees 8080.
  • DNS results are cached by the browser, the OS and resolvers, so a DNS lookup doesn't happen on every request. localhost resolves locally (via the hosts file) without asking DNS at all.
  • Spring Boot 4 and the web starter. Initializr still labels the dependency "Spring Web", but the generated Boot 4 pom.xml lists spring-boot-starter-webmvc (plus spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test) where Boot 3 used spring-boot-starter-web / spring-boot-starter-test, as confirmed in Lecture 3. Same behaviour: Spring MVC + embedded Tomcat.
  • Other ways to create the project. IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate has a built-in Spring Initializr wizard, VS Code has a Spring Initializr extension, and you can use curl https://start.spring.io/starter.zip -d dependencies=web -o demo.zip. All of them use the same service.
  • Running without an IDE. ./mvnw spring-boot:run (mvnw.cmd on Windows) runs the app. ./mvnw package then java -jar target/demo-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar builds and runs the JAR. The project's own version defaults to 0.0.1-SNAPSHOT, which is the same "work in progress" meaning as above.
  • Keep controllers under the main class's package. Component scanning starts from DemoApplication's package (com.example.demo). A controller placed in an unrelated package, e.g. com.other, isn't found, and its endpoints return 404. This is a classic "my endpoint doesn't work" bug.

Lecture 3: Maven in Depth

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #3 · 1h28m · Code Army · JARs, dependencies, pom.xml, repositories, lifecycle, archetypes

Why a build tool at all

A Java project needs a tool to manage it. The market has several, mainly Maven and Gradle. The series uses Maven because it is widely used in existing projects and easy to understand. This lecture covers what Maven is, what it does, and how it makes life easier. Understanding it starts with understanding JAR files.

The problem: sharing a project made of many class files

The normal flow: Demo.java → compiler → bytecode Demo.class → any JVM runs it. A real project, web or console, has many classes: Order.java, User.java, Payment.java, and so on. Compiling them one by one takes time. Even compiled together, you get one .class file per class.

Now share this project with a friend:

ApproachProblem
Email every .class fileTerrible. The friend downloads each one separately and runs them.
Zip a folder of classesTechnically works, but ugly. With hundreds of files, some get missed, the folder structure may not stay as intended (the friend may use a different one), and extra resources (images, static files, properties files) may be left out.

Java needed a standard way for developers to share projects made of many files. That gave birth to the JAR.

JAR: Java ARchive

Definition:
A JAR (Java ARchive) works like a zip file that acts as a package. It can contain:
  • Many compiled .class files.
  • Resources such as images and properties files.
  • The folder / package structure you created.
Your friend can integrate the JAR into their own application. A JAR always packages compiled code.

JARs give two big advantages:

  1. Share your own Java code easily. For example, you write a calculator library, package it as calculator.jar, and your friend calls its classes and methods from their app.
  2. Use external (third-party) libraries yourself. This is the more important one. To connect to MySQL you don't write a connector from scratch; you download the MySQL connector JAR and use it. Postgres has its own connector, and so on. Spring Boot and Spring MVC themselves arrive as JARs, i.e. dependencies.

Library vs application

LibraryApplication
Runnable?No. There may be no main method; it's packages and classes for others to useYes. It has a main method and runs as a whole
Used howPut inside an applicationRun directly
ExamplesJava's built-in libraries, MySQL connector, a calculator libraryYour Spring Boot app

A library used inside an application becomes a dependency of that application. That is the Maven / Spring Boot term.

Anticipated question: "When I build a JAR, are my third-party JARs inside it?"

It depends on whether you built a library or an application:

  • Library JAR (e.g. my-library.jar using MySQL connector): it contains only your code, not the external JARs. It is a non-executable JAR. Someone using it learns what else is needed from a special file that lists the further libraries required. With Maven that file is pom.xml. Maven then fetches those libraries automatically.
  • Application JAR (e.g. a Spring Boot my-application.jar with Main.java): it is an executable JAR that runs independently. When your friend runs it, dependencies like MySQL connector come along inside it; nothing needs downloading separately.
Precision note (added):
An application JAR isn't automatically a fat JAR. A plain Maven package of any project, application or library, produces a thin JAR with only your classes. It is runnable with java -jar only if its manifest names a Main-Class. Spring Boot's spring-boot-maven-plugin (in the Boot pom's <build>) repackages it into an executable "fat" JAR: dependencies go in BOOT-INF/lib and a launcher is set as the entry point. Published library JARs also carry a copy of their pom in META-INF/maven/…, and the repository stores the .pom next to the JAR, which is how Maven learns their dependencies.

The classpath: how the JVM finds a class

Your code consists of your own Java files plus third-party JARs. Only your code gets compiled; the JARs are already compiled. The compiled code then runs on the JVM. When your code calls a class or method from a third-party library, how does the JVM find it?

Definition:
The classpath is the list of places, directories and JARs, where the JVM searches for classes. The lecture's version: the JVM checks your own compiled code first; if the class isn't there, it looks inside the JARs' bytecode and uses it from there.

More precisely (added): classes are loaded by class loaders. JDK classes come first, from the bootstrap and platform loaders. Then the application classpath is searched in the order it's listed, and the first match wins. Maven puts target/classes before the dependency JARs, which is why your own code is found first.

Why manual dependency management breaks down

To connect to MySQL you need its connector JAR. You could search "mysql connector jar download", go to mysql.com, choose version 9.7.0 and your OS, and download it. Simple for one JAR, but not practical:

  1. Manual effort. Real apps need hundreds of third-party JARs, and you'd download each by hand.
  2. Version mismatch. Versions must be compatible. Spring Framework 7 works with Spring Boot 4; Spring 6 won't. Download Spring 7 but a Spring Boot 3 JAR and things break, and you'd have to manage that yourself.
  3. Transitive dependencies. Spring Boot's JAR itself depends on other JARs, and those on others. You'd have to know them all and download them too.
  4. Sharing a library. Your friend gets your JAR with no information about which JARs it needs. You'd add a text file listing every library, then exact versions too, and the friend still does all the manual work.

Maven: a project management tool

Maven's promise: "You focus on business logic. Just tell me which dependencies you need, and I'll download them. If they depend on other dependencies (transitive), I'll download those too, without you even telling me."

Definition:
Maven is a project management (and build) tool, an Apache project. It handles the complications of writing an application or library that uses many third-party libraries.

Roughly, it does four things:

  1. Maintains a standard folder structure. Maven fixes one layout and doesn't change it. In a team, if everyone used their own structure (main class here, config classes there), things would get complicated. Maven's structure is common to everyone.
  2. Compiles your Java code. One click compiles every class.
  3. Creates your JAR file. Compiling and packaging are both part of Maven's lifecycle, which has more phases too: clean, compile, test and so on.
  4. Downloads dependencies, i.e. external JARs, including transitive ones.

Getting Maven

  • Search "maven download" to reach the Apache Maven site. From there you can download it and install it on your system.
  • You don't need to for IDE work. IDEs like IntelliJ come with Maven preinstalled: you create Maven projects and it uses Maven internally.
Transcript slip to ignore:
The lecture says to install Maven by "setting up the classpath". For the command line you add Maven's bin folder to the PATH environment variable, with JAVA_HOME pointing to a JDK. The classpath is the JVM's class-search list, unrelated to installing tools.

Creating a Maven project in IntelliJ

  1. New Project, name maven-demo, choose a location.
  2. Build system: IntelliJ (built-in), Maven or Gradle. Choose Maven.
  3. JDK: 23 was preselected, so keep it. Tick Add sample code.
  4. Advanced settings asks for GroupId (org.example) and ArtifactId (maven-demo). Keep the defaults for now.
  5. Create.
Why not IntelliJ's built-in build system:
You'd be fine, but a teammate might use Maven and another Gradle. Everyone's folder structure and build system would differ. The build system decides how code is built, compiled and packaged; the folder structure and how dependencies are downloaded also differ between them. Choosing Maven as the standard means it doesn't matter who uses IntelliJ, Eclipse or NetBeans: everyone's build is Maven.

The generated sample code (a Main class) was deleted, keeping just a clean Main class with a main method.

Maven's standard folder structure

maven-demo/
├── .idea/                IntelliJ's internal files (ignore)
├── .mvn/                 Maven internal files (ignore)
├── .gitignore
├── pom.xml               ← the most important Maven file
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/         .java source files → org/example/Main.java
│   │   └── resources/    non-Java files: text files, images, properties
│   └── test/
│       └── java/         test classes, same package layout as main
└── (External Libraries)  IDE view of downloaded JARs; now only the JDK (OpenJDK 23)
  • src holds the whole application you build.
  • main is the real application code, your business logic. test holds test cases: unit tests with libraries like JUnit and Mockito, used later in the series.
  • main/java holds every .java file. main/resources holds every non-Java file.
  • External Libraries is where downloaded JARs appear. Now it shows only the JDK's libraries.
Don't be confused by the dots:
org.example under java is two folders: org, containing example. IntelliJ shows them on one line only because org has a single child. Create org.example2 and they split into org → example, example2. Your own files go under org.example (e.g. Demo.java, Demo2.java), and you can add packages such as org.example.controller for a HelloController. Spring Boot apps typically have a controller package.

The Spring Boot project's structure, side by side

If you don't have the Lecture 2 project, regenerate it from start.spring.io:

  • Maven, Java, any Spring Boot 4.x version that isn't a SNAPSHOT (4.0.7 or 4.1.0 now).
  • Defaults for the metadata, Jar, Properties, Java 21.
  • The Spring Web dependency.

Compared with the empty Maven project:

  • Same src/main/java, src/main/resources, src/test/java and pom.xml.
  • Packages com.example.demo: the folders com → example → demo, built from groupId com.example + artifactId demo. Inside: DemoApplication (generated) and HelloController (written last lecture).
  • resources isn't empty: Spring Boot gives static/ (images and other static resources), templates/ (templates) and application.properties (where the port was changed).
  • test/java mirrors the same packages and contains DemoApplicationTests. A test for HelloController goes in the same package under test as HelloControllerTest. How to write tests comes later.
  • An extra target/ folder appears for anyone who ran the app last lecture. It was deleted for now and explained next.

Note (added): Maven doesn't require package names to match groupId/artifactId. It's a convention the generators follow. IntelliJ's quickstart used the groupId alone (org.example), while Initializr uses groupId.artifactId.

Compiling: the target folder

With System.out.println("Hello World") in main, pressing Run compiles and then runs the code. In a Maven project, compiling is Maven's job, along with packaging and making JARs.

  1. Open the Maven tool window (the "m" icon; enable it in settings if hidden). It shows the project with Lifecycle, Plugins and Repositories.
  2. Under Lifecycle are phases such as clean, validate, compile and test. Click compile.
  3. You get BUILD SUCCESS, and a target/ folder appears containing classes/, generated-sources/ and maven-status/.
  4. target/classes mirrors the same package structure: org/example/controller, Demo.class, Demo2.class, Main.class.

Opening Main.class shows readable code only because the IDE decompiles bytecode back to source for display. Delete target, and compile or run again to bring it back.

Anticipated question: "Does the green Run button use Maven?"

No. Run uses IntelliJ's own build system to compile and run. But IntelliJ knows the project is a Maven project, so it puts compiled output in the same place Maven would: target/classes with the same folder structure. It looks identical, but internally it isn't Maven. (Added:) you can make IntelliJ really use Maven via Settings → Build Tools → Maven → Runner → "Delegate IDE build/run actions to Maven".

Creating a JAR: package

In the Maven tool window, click package. The log says "Building jar: …maven-demo-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar", and the JAR lands in target/ next to classes/. The file name matters; see the naming rule below. This one package holds everything you wrote and can be shared, though with Maven you won't share it manually. That covers three of Maven's jobs. The fourth, downloading dependencies, needs pom.xml.

pom.xml: Project Object Model

POM = Project Object Model. It gives Maven, and you, complete information about the project: its name, version, third-party libraries and plugins. It is Maven's most important file. An empty project's pom is small, and it grows as you add configuration and dependencies.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>org.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-demo</artifactId>
    <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.source>23</maven.compiler.source>
        <maven.compiler.target>23</maven.compiler.target>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
    </properties>
</project>
PartMeaning
<project>Root tag. Every pom starts with it.
xmlns, xsi, schemaLocationThe pom's schema: the rules for which tags are allowed. An invented <abc></abc> tag shows "invalid content was found", because you can't put just any tag.
<modelVersion>The version of the POM model (4.0.0), not Maven's version. Maven can be any version.
groupId, artifactId, versionThe GAV coordinates, which together uniquely identify the project worldwide.
<properties>Key–value pairs, where the tag name is the key and its content the value.

GAV: groupId, artifactId, version

  • groupId must be unique. If you upload your JAR to the internet, no other JAR may share its identity, so others can reference your library independently. How? The world's most unique names are domain names, so use yours reversed: codearmy.in → in.codearmy, optionally extended (in.codearmy.java, in.codearmy.spring). This is a Maven convention, not a Spring one. No domain? org.example is fine for practice.
  • artifactId is the project's name: maven-demo.
  • version defaults to 1.0-SNAPSHOT. SNAPSHOT means work in progress (as in Lecture 2), possibly buggy. When the project is complete and tested, you drop -SNAPSHOT to mark a proper release that others can safely use. This is a convention too.

Properties: custom keys and ${…}

  • Generated keys: maven.compiler.source = 23, maven.compiler.target = 23, project.build.sourceEncoding = UTF-8.
  • You can add any key, e.g. <java.version>23</java.version> or even <author.name>Aditya</author.name>, with no error.
  • Reuse a property anywhere in the pom with ${key}. Setting <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT-${author.name}</version> and running package produced maven-demo-1.0-SNAPSHOT-Aditya.jar.
Worth knowing (added):
  • Maven prints a warning for expressions in <version>. Only ${revision}, ${sha1} and ${changelist} are meant for that.
  • On Java 9+, <maven.compiler.release>23</maven.compiler.release> is preferred over source/target, because it also checks you only use APIs of that Java version.
  • java.version is special only in Spring Boot, whose parent pom maps it to the compiler release.

Another common tag is <packaging>, set to jar or war. It defaults to jar if omitted.

Downloading dependencies with Maven

The <dependencies> tag lists every external JAR the project needs. Each <dependency> has a groupId, an artifactId and a version: every library JAR has its own GAV, just like yours. But how do you learn a library's exact coordinates? You don't memorize them; use mvnrepository.com:

  1. Search "mysql connector" and open MySQL Connector/J.
  2. Pick a version. The lecture's rule: not the very latest, which is most likely to have bugs, is less tested and has few users. Going back increases the usage count (168, 193…), but don't go too far back, or versions mismatch. The lecture picks 9.5.0.
  3. Open that version, choose the Maven tab (among Gradle, SBT, Mill, Ivy, Grape…), copy the snippet and paste it into <dependencies>, removing the comment line.
  4. Nothing is downloaded yet: External Libraries still shows only OpenJDK. Click the Maven reload icon ("m" with arrows), or reload from the Maven tool window.
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
        <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
        <version>9.5.0</version>
        <scope>compile</scope>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

External Libraries now shows two JARs: mysql-connector-j and protobuf-java (Google Protocol Buffers). The Maven tool window's Dependencies node shows the hierarchy: protobuf-java sits under the connector. It's a transitive dependency that MySQL Connector needs, and Maven fetched it without being asked. The download was fast because these were already cached locally; the first time is slower.

Adding Hibernate the same way (org.hibernate.orm : hibernate-core, version 7.3.6.Final, again a little behind the newest) and syncing pulls in many JARs: Jakarta, GlassFish, Eclipse and more. The tree shows hibernate-core depending on those, and they on further ones, several levels deep. You only asked for Hibernate.

Dependency scope

<scope> is optional, and older snippets often omit it. It says in which phase the dependency is needed. The default is compile; sometimes it's test, meaning test phase only. The full list (added):

ScopeAvailable atIn the final app?Typical example
compile (default)Compile, test, runYesSpring, Hibernate
runtimeTest, run, not compileYesJDBC drivers such as mysql-connector-j. Initializr adds MySQL with this scope, because your code only uses the JDBC API.
testTest compile and run onlyNoJUnit, Mockito, spring-boot-starter-…-test
providedCompile and testNo: the server provides itServlet API when deploying a WAR to Tomcat, Lombok
system / importSpecial cases—import brings in a BOM inside dependencyManagement

The Spring Boot project's pom.xml

It's bigger because Spring Boot adds its own entries:

  • The same schema lines, modelVersion and GAV, plus a special <parent> tag (see below).
  • Some empty tags (url, licenses, developers, scm). You can ignore them.
  • <properties> with java.version, kept there so it can be reused elsewhere.
  • <dependencies> is not empty. Initializr added spring-boot-starter-webmvc (for building web apps with Spring MVC) and spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test (for test cases). Each has further transitive dependencies, visible in the Maven tool window.
  • <build><plugins>. Maven needs plugins to perform lifecycle work (compile, package, verify, install); they are declared here. Spring Boot's is spring-boot-maven-plugin. More on plugins later.

This is the value of Initializr's ready template: the needed dependencies are already there, Maven syncs them, and they appear under External Libraries.

Parent POM and the Super POM

POMs support inheritance. At the top is the Super POM, like Java's Object class, the parent of all classes. Every pom inherits from its parent. maven-demo declares no <parent>, so its parent is the Super POM by default, just as a Java class that extends nothing still extends Object.

Why inheritance? A pom needs far more configuration than you see. The Super POM holds it all, and your pom reuses it. Putting everything in your own pom would make it very heavy.

To see the full picture, right-click the pom → Maven → Show Effective POM, which opens maven-demo-effective-pom.xml. It contains:

  • Everything from your pom: GAV, properties, the MySQL and Hibernate dependencies.
  • Things you never wrote: <repositories>, <pluginRepositories>, <build> settings (source, output and resource directories, test resources), <pluginManagement> and more.

You keep your pom simple and write only what you directly need. To change an inherited setting, override it by declaring the same tag in your own pom (e.g. <repositories>), just as a subclass overrides a method.

The Spring Boot pom does declare a parent, org.springframework.boot : spring-boot-starter-parent. Ctrl/Cmd-click it: it has its own parent, spring-boot-dependencies, which declares no parent, so its parent is the Super POM. Multi-level inheritance exists for the same reason as in Java: each level declares some things and overrides some of its parent's.

Super POM vs effective POM

Super POMEffective POM
What it isThe built-in parent of all POMsThe final merged POM Maven actually uses to build
ContainsMaven's defaults: the central repository, standard directories, default plugin versionsYour pom + every parent + the Super POM (+ active profiles and settings), merged, with overrides applied
Where to see itInside Maven's own JARIntelliJ "Show Effective POM", or mvn help:effective-pom
Precision note:
The lecture opens the effective POM and calls it "the Super POM, the parent of my pom". It isn't the parent. It's the result of merging your pom with its parents, which is why your own MySQL and Hibernate dependencies appear in it. The lecture acknowledges the distinction afterwards: Super POM = parent of all; effective POM = what Maven finally uses.

Anticipated question: "Why does the Spring Boot pom have no dependency versions?"

(Added; it follows directly from the parent chain.) spring-boot-dependencies is a BOM (Bill of Materials). Its <dependencyManagement> section pins a tested, compatible version of hundreds of libraries: Spring, Jackson, Tomcat, Hibernate, MySQL Connector and more. Your pom inherits it, so you write only groupId and artifactId, and the version comes from the BOM. This solves exactly the "version mismatch" problem listed above. In a Boot project, don't hand-pick versions for managed libraries: the lecture's mvnrepository method is for plain Maven projects, and a hard-coded version in Boot can break the tested combination.

Repositories: where Maven downloads from

The effective POM's <repositories> tag names the central repository and its URL, https://repo.maven.apache.org/maven2. Maven Central is a huge repository holding thousands of JARs. You give the GAV, and Maven downloads the JAR from there.

Maven uses two kinds of repository:

  1. Maven Central, a remote repository.
  2. The local repository. Maven creates a hidden .m2 folder in your home directory (~/.m2 on Mac/Linux, C:\Users\<you>\.m2 on Windows). Inside it, repository/ stores everything downloaded from the internet.

The local repository serves two purposes:

  • Cache. For each dependency, Maven first checks ~/.m2/repository. If the JAR is there, it's used. If not, Maven downloads it from central, shows it under External Libraries, and stores it in .m2. The first build is slow; later builds are fast. With 100–200 dependencies the difference is noticeable.
  • Your own JARs. JARs you build and install (the install phase, below) are stored there too.

Naming rule: artifactId-version.jar

  • A JAR's file name is always artifactId-version.jar: maven-demo-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar, mysql-connector-j-9.5.0.jar.
  • Because library names start from the artifact, third-party libraries are often simply called artifacts ("downloading artifacts").
  • In .m2/repository, JARs sit in folders built from their coordinates. MySQL's is at com/mysql/mysql-connector-j/9.5.0/. On Mac, show hidden folders with Cmd+Shift+. or cd ~/.m2/repository.

Other remote repositories (company-wide)

A third kind: other remote repositories. Maven Central is itself remote. A company may run its own private remote repository (e.g. Sonatype Nexus or JFrog Artifactory, added), for two reasons:

  1. Private artifacts. Internal libraries built for the company aren't on Maven Central and shouldn't be public.
  2. Safety. Central is open, and some artifacts may be vulnerable, buggy or a security threat. A company repo holds only tried-and-tested artifacts.
<repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>company-repo</id>
        <url>https://repo.example.com/maven</url>
    </repository>
</repositories>

The lecture adds this to the pom and then comments it out, because the URL doesn't exist and the build would error.

Correction: adding a repository doesn't replace central:
The lecture says Maven will then fetch "from here instead of central". A <repository> with a new id is added. Maven still consults central, inherited from the Super POM with id central. To really route all downloads through a company repo, companies configure a <mirror> with <mirrorOf>*</mirrorOf> in ~/.m2/settings.xml, or redefine the repository with id central. Credentials also live in settings.xml, never in the pom.

Demo: deleting the local repository. Delete ~/.m2/repository and every project breaks: External Libraries is back to just OpenJDK in both projects. Syncing may leave "unresolved dependency" errors, so use Reload All Maven Projects, not just Sync. Everything is re-downloaded (slowly) and re-cached, and the repository folder fills up again.

The Maven lifecycle

Java code goes through many phases, compile and run among them, plus intermediate ones you don't normally see. Maven handles the project end to end: cleaning, validating, compiling, testing, packaging, all the way to deploying. The Maven tool window lists clean, validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, site, deploy.

Maven has three lifecycles:

LifecycleMain phasesPurpose
cleancleanDelete old build output (target/)
default (the important one)validate → compile → test → package → verify → install → deployBuild, test and publish
sitesiteGenerate documentation and reports
The key rule: phases run in order:
Running a phase runs every earlier phase in that lifecycle first. validate only validates. compile validates, then compiles. deploy runs validate → compile → test → package → verify → install → deploy. There are more hidden intermediate phases, but these are the main ones.
  • validate checks the project's structure: a pom must exist, be correct and readable, with all required details present.
  • compile converts .java to .class in target/classes.
  • test runs your test cases (JUnit, Mockito…) from src/test, e.g. the Spring Boot project's HelloControllerTest. It naturally comes after compile.
  • package builds the JAR into target/. The JAR is made from compiled code, and only after tests pass; with no tests written, it just builds.
  • verify runs further checks through plugins added to the pom's <plugins>: integration tests, code quality (extra spaces, variables declared but never used), code coverage. A team can make every member's build pass these checks before installing.
  • install puts your JAR into the local repository (~/.m2/repository). Because verify runs before it, only checked code gets there.
  • deploy uploads the installed JAR to a remote repository, usually the company-wide one, so other teams and members can download and use your artifact, the way you use Maven Central.
Don't confuse Maven deploy with deploying code:
git push to GitHub or GitLab sends your whole source code, which gets merged and goes to production. Maven deploy only publishes the JAR / artifact to an artifact repository so others can depend on it. It doesn't run your app anywhere.
  • clean is independent. It deletes the old builds in target/. Clicking it removed target and every locally built artifact in the project. JARs already installed in .m2 are not touched.
  • site builds documentation and reports. It ran for a long time, downloading plugins from central, and produced target/site with CSS, images and a dependency summary. It's rarely needed; clean it up again. Day to day you use the default and clean lifecycles.

Running Maven from the terminal

Instead of clicking, open a terminal and type mvn compile, which validates and then compiles. The first time you may get "mvn: command not found". Install Maven for the command line:

  • Mac: brew install maven.
  • Windows: choco install maven with Chocolatey.
  • Or download it from the Maven site and add it to PATH.

Then run commands like mvn compile, mvn install or mvn deploy.

Combining phases from different lifecycles:

  • mvn clean compile cleans old artifacts, then compiles afresh.
  • mvn clean install, the most famous command, used constantly. It deletes target, then runs validate → compile → test → package → verify → install. Here, test and verify have nothing to do, so they are effectively skipped.

Its output shows where it installed the JAR: ~/.m2/repository/org/example/maven-demo/1.0-SNAPSHOT/maven-demo-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar. The folder path is groupId (as folders) / artifactId / version /, and inside is artifactId-version.jar.

Clarification (the lecture got tangled here):
The lecture wonders why the path has org/example without a maven-demo package, and mixes up Java packages with repository folders. They're unrelated. The repository path is always groupId/artifactId/version/ (org/example/maven-demo/1.0-SNAPSHOT/), whatever your Java packages are called. Your classes' packages only matter inside the JAR.
Worth knowing (added):
  • Use the Maven Wrapper that Initializr generates: ./mvnw clean install (mvnw.cmd on Windows). It downloads the project's pinned Maven version automatically, so no global install is needed and everyone builds with the same Maven.
  • Phases run plugin goals. compile runs maven-compiler-plugin, test runs maven-surefire-plugin, package runs maven-jar-plugin, install runs maven-install-plugin and deploy runs maven-deploy-plugin. That is why a pom's <plugins> matters.
  • Useful flags: -DskipTests skips running tests; -o works offline; -U forces re-checking SNAPSHOTs. mvn dependency:tree prints the transitive tree.
  • Each lifecycle has more phases than the ones shown: clean has pre-clean and post-clean; site has pre-site, post-site and site-deploy; default has about 23, including process-resources and test-compile.

Maven archetypes: ready-made templates

New Project → Maven Archetype. An archetype is a ready-made template, so you don't write everything from scratch.

  • Catalogs. Internal is the small catalog built into the IDE. Maven Central is much larger, and includes Spring Boot ones such as a Spring Boot web starter and Spring JPA, the same kind of thing Initializr gives.
  • maven-archetype-quickstart (version 1.1 in the demo) generated:
    • A pom with a JUnit test dependency.
    • App.java printing Hello World.
    • AppTest.java with unit tests.
  • A Spring Boot starter archetype from Central generated:
    • A pom (with an Apache license header comment) containing Spring Boot starter dependencies and a Hibernate Validator dependency.
    • Some plugins.
    • Sample classes such as HelloConsumer and a hello implementation.
    Keep the dependencies you need and remove the rest. Its naming conventions differ from the series'.

You can use archetypes, but Spring Initializr remains the way to start Spring Boot projects. (Added:) the CLI equivalent is mvn archetype:generate.

Transcript slips to ignore:
The quickstart dependency is JUnit only; the lecture says "basically Mockito", but Mockito is a separate library. When describing the Spring archetype's plugins, the lecture ties plugins to the "validate stage", then corrects itself to "verify stage". In fact plugins can bind to any phase; compile, test and package all run through plugins.

Maven vs Gradle

MavenGradle
