Build filepom.xml (XML, declarative)build.gradle (Groovy) or build.gradle.kts (Kotlin DSL)
ModelFixed lifecycle and conventionsFlexible task graph
SpeedGoodOften faster (incremental builds, build cache, daemon)
Learning curveEasy and predictableSteeper; build scripts are code
Where usedMost enterprise Java / Spring projectsAndroid (default), large multi-module builds
SharedBoth use Maven repositories and GAV coordinates, and both are offered by Spring Initializr

Anticipated question: "What if two dependencies need different versions of the same library?"

(Added; a common interview follow-up to transitive dependencies.) Maven keeps one version per artifact and picks it by "nearest wins": the version closest to your project in the tree. At equal depth, the one declared first wins. This can silently pick a version that one library can't run with, causing NoSuchMethodError or ClassNotFoundException at runtime. Tools:

  • mvn dependency:tree to see what was picked.
  • <exclusions> to drop an unwanted transitive dependency.
  • Declare the version you want directly, or pin it in <dependencyManagement> or a BOM. In Spring Boot, its BOM already does this.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • .m2 lives in your home directory, not the "root level". The lecture says it sits at the root on Mac and "somewhere under Users" on Windows. It is ~/.m2 (/Users/<you>/.m2) on Mac and C:\Users\<you>\.m2 on Windows. The location can be changed with <localRepository> in settings.xml.
  • "Don't take the latest version" needs nuance. Avoid SNAPSHOT, milestone and RC versions. Among stable releases, newer patch versions usually carry security and bug fixes, so prefer the latest patch of a version line (e.g. the newest 9.5.x). Usage counts on mvnrepository show popularity, not quality.
  • Spring Boot 4 starters confirmed. The generated pom lists spring-boot-starter-webmvc and spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test, the Boot 4 names for Boot 3's spring-boot-starter-web and spring-boot-starter-test. This settles the open note in Lecture 2.
  • SNAPSHOT versions behave differently. Maven re-checks remote repositories for newer SNAPSHOT builds (daily by default), while release versions are immutable and downloaded once. Never depend on SNAPSHOTs in a release.
  • Don't commit target/. It's generated output, which is why Initializr's .gitignore excludes it. Do commit pom.xml, mvnw and .mvn/wrapper.
  • WAR packaging produces a web archive for an external servlet container; JAR is the Spring Boot default with its embedded server (Lecture 2).

Lecture 4: Dependency Injection & Inversion of Control (Plain Java)

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #4 · 39 min · Code Army · The Spring Core ideas, shown without Spring

Why Spring Core ideas at all?

Until now we built Java apps with classes, objects and OOP principles, and wrote reasonably clean code without Spring. So why do we need the Spring Core ideas, Dependency Injection (DI) and Inversion of Control (IoC)? This isn't about Spring MVC or web apps. These core ideas apply even to console applications, and they make Java code clean and loosely coupled.

Plan for this lecture: no Spring at all. First understand the problem and possible solutions in plain Java. The next lecture shows how Spring solves it.

Setup: a new Maven project core-demo (groupId in.codearmy, JDK 23, sample code). There are no dependencies and the pom stays untouched. The generated code is replaced with a quick "Hello" run to check the project works.

The problem: an OrderService that builds its own EmailService

The scenario is kept deliberately simple, because the ideas matter more than the logic. An order service places an order and then notifies the user.

public class EmailService {
    public void sendNotification() {
        System.out.println("Email notification sent");
    }
}

public class OrderService {
    EmailService notification = new EmailService();   // creates its own dependency

    public void placeOrder() {
        System.out.println("Order placed");           // stands in for real business logic
        notification.sendNotification();
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        OrderService order = new OrderService();
        order.placeOrder();
    }
}
Order placed
Email notification sent

It works. There are three classes: OrderService, EmailService, and Main, which calls OrderService.

What a dependency is (in code)

Definition:
OrderService creates an EmailService object and calls its method. placeOrder() can't do its job unless an EmailService object exists. So OrderService depends on EmailService, and EmailService is a dependency of OrderService.

This is a different use of "dependency" from the pom-file dependencies of Lecture 3, but it's the same idea. There, your code depends on a third-party library's JAR. Here, one class depends on another class's object.

Why this is tight coupling

The core problem is tight coupling. It has nothing to do with Spring; it's about the design of our Java code. In one line: OrderService is creating its own dependency.

Analogy from the lecture: tightly vs loosely coupled:
"I need to go from Delhi to Chandigarh, at this time, in this bus, with this driver, from this company." That's tightly coupled: I only needed to commute, yet I pinned every detail. Timing might matter, but which bus, which driver and which company shouldn't. Caring only that I get there is loosely coupled.

In code, OrderService only needed "send a notification". Instead it did two things:

  1. It bound itself to a concrete class. It can send nothing but email. Switching to SMS or pop-up notifications means editing OrderService to swap EmailService for the new class. (A concrete class is a non-abstract class with all methods implemented.)
  2. It creates the object itself. It both uses its dependency and builds it, so it juggles multiple jobs. The lecture comes back to this second point after fixing the first.

Step 1: code to an interface

General Java practice: program to interfaces, not concrete classes. Tomorrow we may want SmsService or PopupNotificationService instead of email. Editing OrderService each time breaks the Open/Closed Principle, the O in SOLID: extend a class with new behaviour, don't modify it. This is plain good design with no Spring involved, but Spring's whole ideology is built on it.

With several classes now, they are organized into a notification package: the interface, EmailService, SmsService and PopupNotificationService. OrderService and Main stay at the top level.

public interface NotificationService {
    void sendNotification();
}

public class EmailService implements NotificationService {
    @Override
    public void sendNotification() {
        System.out.println("Email notification sent");
    }
}

public class SmsService implements NotificationService {
    @Override
    public void sendNotification() {
        System.out.println("SMS notification sent");
    }
}

public class PopupNotificationService implements NotificationService {
    @Override
    public void sendNotification() {
        System.out.println("Popup notification sent");
    }
}

In OrderService: NotificationService notification = new EmailService();. Whatever object is created gets its method called through the interface reference. Change it to new SmsService() and the output becomes "SMS notification sent", and the same for the pop-up. That's basic polymorphism.

Why the interface alone doesn't fix it

The variable's type is now an interface, but the real object is still created concretely, right inside OrderService. Two things to keep straight:

  • Creating an object is not the problem. Where it's created is. OrderService's job is managing orders: placeOrder, add an order, delete an order. Why is it building notification objects? Why is it creating its own dependency?
  • SRP breaks (the S in SOLID: one reason to change). OrderService handles order logic and creates notification objects, which is a factory's job. Its job should be to use a notification (notification.sendNotification() once the order is placed), not to create one.
  • OCP still breaks. Every new notification type still means changing code inside OrderService.
Dependencies are normal; self-creating them is the problem:
One service depending on another always happens. A real project has hundreds, even hundreds of thousands, of Java files, and they depend on each other heavily. You get a whole dependency tree: A depends on B, and B on C. That's fine. The problem is depending on something and also constructing it yourself. Also, OrderService is business logic, and creating objects is not business logic. The lecture points to its LLD / clean-code playlist for more on this.

Step 2: Dependency Injection, where the dependency comes from outside

OrderService says: "I don't want to create this object. Someone else handle that. I just need to call its method, so hand me a ready-made object." The simplest way is to ask for it in the constructor:

public class OrderService {
    private NotificationService notification;             // instance variable, interface type

    public OrderService(NotificationService notification) {
        this.notification = notification;                 // whatever is passed in
    }

    public void placeOrder() {
        System.out.println("Order placed");
        notification.sendNotification();                  // calls the passed-in object's method
    }
}

Main now shows an error, because it was calling the no-argument constructor. Someone has to pass the object, and since Main creates OrderService, Main does it:

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        NotificationService notification = new EmailService();   // or new SmsService(), new PopupNotificationService()
        OrderService order = new OrderService(notification);    // inject it
        order.placeOrder();
    }
}
Order placed
Email notification sent

To switch to SMS, change only Main (new SmsService()) and the output becomes "SMS notification sent". OrderService isn't touched, and the notification classes aren't touched either, since they're an interface plus three implementations.

Why this fixes both principles:
  • OCP holds. A new notification type needs no change to OrderService.
  • SRP holds. OrderService's only responsibility is orders. It doesn't create notifications; it just calls one, delegating that work.
  • OrderService doesn't even know which notification it gets. It expects a NotificationService, and SMS, email and pop-up all are one. "Give me any notification and I'll call sendNotification." It cares only about its own logic.
Definition: Dependency Injection:
Before, OrderService created its dependency. Now the dependency is supplied from outside, here by Main. We took that responsibility away from it: "Don't create it; I'll inject it from somewhere else." Main creates a PopupNotificationService (or another type) and passes it through the constructor. OrderService stores it in its instance variable and calls it whenever placeOrder runs.
DI: don't let a class create what it depends on; provide it from outside. "Outside" can be anywhere; for now it's Main, which acts as the driver that wires everything, so the other classes stay independent.

Benefit: easy unit testing with a fake

Unit testing means testing one class in isolation. We want to test OrderService. Tests go in src/test/java under the same package, e.g. OrderServiceTest (Lecture 3).

  • Old design (new EmailService() inside OrderService). Testing placeOrder sends a real email, because OrderService is welded to EmailService. You're forced to work with EmailService even though you only wanted to test order logic. That's a terrible setup.
  • DI design. The dependency comes from outside, so pass a fake. It implements the same interface, so OrderService accepts it without any change. A parent-type (interface) reference can hold a child object: basic Java.
public class FakeEmailService implements NotificationService {
    @Override
    public void sendNotification() {
        System.out.println("Dummy email sent");   // no real email, no cost
    }
}

// in Main (for the demo)
OrderService order = new OrderService(new FakeEmailService());
order.placeOrder();
Order placed
Dummy email sent

In a real app, placeOrder runs real business logic and EmailService really sends notifications. Why spend money on real emails while testing? The fake lets you test OrderService alone.

Worth knowing (added):
The lecture puts FakeEmailService next to production code and wires it in Main, just for the demo. In a real project, fakes live in src/test/java and are passed in by the test. Usually a mocking library such as Mockito generates them: mock(NotificationService.class), then verify(mock).sendNotification() to check that placeOrder did notify. Fakes, stubs and mocks are collectively called test doubles, and all of them need DI to be pluggable.

The next problem: Main becomes a wiring nightmare

Every service could get its dependencies injected from Main. With UserService, PaymentService and dozens more, Main ends up creating and wiring every object one by one, and becomes very complicated. How do we make that easy?

That's what Spring Core provides. From the next lecture, Spring manages and injects dependencies for us, and even Main needs almost nothing. It will look magical at first.

The DI mantra

One-liners from the lecture:
  • "Don't create your own dependencies, get your dependencies."
  • "A class should ask for what it needs, and not build everything itself."

DI is not a Spring concept. Spring automates it, but DI exists independently. This whole lecture did DI without Spring.

Types of dependency injection

  1. Constructor injection, as above: the dependency is a constructor parameter.
  2. Setter injection: a setter assigns the dependency. In IntelliJ use Generate → Setter, choosing notification.
  3. Field injection: the framework sets the field directly. It's discussed once Spring is in use, because in plain Java it isn't really practical (see the note below).
public class OrderService {
    private NotificationService notification;

    public OrderService() { }                                     // overloaded empty constructor

    public OrderService(NotificationService notification) {       // constructor injection
        this.notification = notification;
    }

    public void setNotification(NotificationService notification) { // setter injection
        this.notification = notification;
    }

    public void placeOrder() {
        System.out.println("Order placed");
        notification.sendNotification();
    }
}

// Main, using setter injection
OrderService order = new OrderService();
order.setNotification(new EmailService());
order.placeOrder();          // Order placed / Email notification sent

Constructor vs setter injection

Not compared in the lecture (added), but a standard interview question
Constructor injectionSetter injection
Object always complete?Yes. It can't be created without its dependenciesNo. new OrderService() then placeOrder() without the setter gives a NullPointerException
ImmutabilityField can be finalField must be mutable
Best forMandatory dependenciesOptional dependencies, or ones changed later
Signals a problemA long constructor shows the class does too much (SRP)Hides how many dependencies a class has
Circular dependenciesFail fast at startupCan be resolved, which often hides a design flaw
Spring's recommendationPreferredFor optional dependencies
Precision note: field injection without Spring (added):
The lecture says field injection "isn't possible" without Spring. It is possible, since you could make the field public and assign it, or set a private field with reflection. It just isn't sensible. Frameworks such as Spring (@Autowired on a field) use reflection to write private fields. That's also why field injection is discouraged: the dependency is hidden, the field can't be final, and the class can't be built in a plain unit test without the framework.

Inversion of Control: what "control" means

IoC isn't a separate topic; it's tightly related to DI. People often use the terms interchangeably, but they mean different things. First, what is "control"? Here, it's who creates the dependency.

  • Initial design. Main creates OrderService, and OrderService creates EmailService. Control flows from OrderService to EmailService: OrderService was responsible for building its dependency, so control was inside it.
  • After DI. Main creates EmailService, Main creates OrderService, and Main provides EmailService to OrderService. Control now flows from outside into OrderService.
Definition: Inversion of Control:
The control of creating EmailService used to sit inside OrderService. With DI it moved outside: OrderService gets the object from outside. Control is inverted, hence "Inversion of Control".

IoC vs DI: the relationship

Inversion of ControlDependency Injection
What it isAn idea / principleAn approach / technique
Says"Don't control creation and flow yourself; let something outside do it""Pass a class its dependencies through the constructor, setter or field"
RelationDI is a way to achieve IoC. IoC is the goal, DI the implementation
Transcript slip: "dependency inversion" should be "dependency injection":
In this part the lecture says "dependency inversion" several times, meaning dependency injection. They are different things:
  • Dependency Injection is the technique shown here: supply dependencies from outside.
  • Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) is the D in SOLID: high-level modules shouldn't depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. Step 1 applied it, making OrderService depend on the NotificationService interface rather than on EmailService.
They work together: DIP says depend on an interface, and DI supplies the concrete object behind it. They aren't synonyms.
Worth knowing: IoC is broader than DI (added):
IoC means that the framework calls your code, not the other way round, often summed up as the "Hollywood Principle": don't call us, we'll call you. DI inverts control over object creation. Other forms invert control over flow:
  • Template Method, where a base class calls your overridden steps.
  • Event listeners and callbacks.
  • Servlets: Tomcat calls doGet (Lecture 1).
  • @GetMapping methods: Spring calls hello() (Lecture 2).
A Service Locator, where a class asks a registry for its dependencies, is another way to invert creation, though it hides dependencies, so DI is preferred.

Where Spring fits: the IoC container

So far Main injects every dependency and wires and configures everything. Even that is better than every class building its own dependencies, but Main gets complicated. That's where the Spring Framework comes in. It has an IoC container (Inversion of Control container) that does exactly what Main has been doing. Right now Main is our container.

JobNow, done by MainLater, done by the Spring IoC container
Create objectsnew EmailService(), new OrderService(…)Container instantiates them
Manage objectsImplicitly decides when they're created and destroyedContainer controls the lifecycle
Connect objects togetherPasses the notification into the constructor or setter (wiring)Container wires dependencies automatically
  • In Spring code you'll rarely see the new keyword; it becomes almost negligible. The Spring IoC container manages most objects, creating them and maintaining their relationships. Roughly 90% of the time you won't create objects or wire relationships yourself.
  • Spring isn't magic. Later lectures show how the container does this, and how we interact with it.
Definition: bean:
Inside the Spring IoC container, objects are called beans. A bean is simply an object whose lifecycle the Spring IoC container manages. Every bean is an object, but not every object is a bean. Only objects the container itself manages are beans.

Anticipated question: "Isn't Main wiring everything just moving the problem?"

Partly, and deliberately so. Putting all construction in one place (Main) is a known pattern called the composition root (added term). Every other class stays free of new for its collaborators, so there is exactly one place to change wiring. The cost is that the composition root grows with the app. Spring's container is essentially an automated composition root: you declare which classes are beans, and it builds the object graph from their constructors.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Make injected fields private final with constructor injection. The lecture's field is package-private and mutable. final guarantees the dependency is set exactly once and never null after construction.
  • DI removes new for collaborators, not everywhere. Creating value objects, collections or DTOs with new inside business methods is fine. The rule targets services a class depends on, the things you'd want to swap or fake.
  • Loose coupling has a cost. An interface with a single implementation that will never change adds indirection without benefit. Introduce the abstraction where variation or testing actually needs it. This is the LLD "gold plating / over-engineering" anti-pattern.
  • Factory vs DI. Moving new EmailService() into a NotificationFactory that OrderService calls still leaves OrderService pulling its dependency and coupled to the factory. DI pushes the dependency in, so OrderService knows nothing about how it was made.
  • Terminology. The lecture calls notification an instance variable: correct, since it's a per-object field. In Spring it's typically private final NotificationService notificationService with a single constructor, and Spring injects it without any annotation (Spring 4.3+).

Lecture 5: Spring Core — IoC Container, Beans & Annotation-Based Configuration

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #5 · 1h34m · Code Army · ApplicationContext, @Component, @Autowired, @Primary/@Qualifier, @Bean

From principle to framework

Lecture 4 covered DI and IoC as principles, without Spring. This lecture shows how Spring Core implements them: what the IoC container is and what beans are. The whole Spring Framework is based on Spring Core, which makes this lecture key to understanding everything that follows.

Setup: an empty Maven project spring-core-demo (groupId in.codearmy, JDK 23). The generated boilerplate is removed, and pom.xml starts with no dependencies.

Recap: manual DI with an OrderService and a PaymentService

An e-commerce flow: payment must happen before the order is placed.

public class PaymentService {
    public void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment done");
    }
}

public class OrderService {
    private PaymentService paymentService;

    public OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {   // dependency comes from outside
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }

    public void placeOrder() {
        paymentService.pay();
        System.out.println("Order placed");
    }
}

// Main: we create, wire and call everything ourselves
PaymentService service = new PaymentService();
OrderService order = new OrderService(service);
order.placeOrder();          // Payment done / Order placed
  • Declaring private PaymentService paymentService; and calling pay() without assigning an object would fail, because the reference is null.
  • Writing = new PaymentService() inside OrderService hard-codes the dependency and breaks SRP: OrderService should handle orders, not create payment objects.
  • So the dependency comes in through the constructor, and Main creates and injects it.

The goal now: stop doing this manually and let Spring's IoC container do it. The container will create the PaymentService object, create the OrderService object, and wire the first into the second. Right now Main plays the container.

The dependency you need: spring-context

Which dependency brings the IoC container?

  • Spring Boot? No. Boot is for easy auto-configuration.
  • Spring MVC? No. This isn't a web app; it's a console app.
  • Just spring-context, the Spring Core dependency that provides the IoC container that manages objects.

Search mvnrepository.com for "spring context". The series targets Spring Boot 4, which works with Spring Framework 7, so pick a 7.x version: not the very latest, but one a little older with many users. Copy the Maven snippet into <dependencies> and reload Maven.

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
        <version>7.0.0</version>   <!-- any stable 7.x release -->
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

External Libraries fills up with spring-core, spring-beans, spring-aop, spring-expression, spring-context, Commons Logging, Micrometer (observation), JSpecify and so on. Only spring-context was requested; the Maven tool window's Dependencies view shows that the rest are its transitive dependencies.

Beans, and the two ways to configure them

Definition: bean:
Inside the Spring IoC container, objects are called beans. The container creates them, wires and injects their dependencies, and is responsible for their whole lifecycle. Every bean is an object, but not every object is a bean. Objects we create and handle ourselves are not beans; only those Spring manages are.
ApproachWhere it appears
Annotation-based configuration (covered in this lecture)Modern code. It's what you'll mostly see.
XML-based configuration (next lecture)Older, mostly legacy code. More complicated, because you maintain XML files.

(Added:) there is also pure Java-based configuration, using @Configuration classes with @Bean methods. It appears later in this lecture as part of the "annotation" approach.

Prerequisite: Java Reflection and the Class object

Spring relies heavily on the Reflection API, which the Java series didn't cover. A full video is promised later; this is the minimum needed. Take a sample class:

class Student {
    private String name;
    private int age;

    public Student() { }

    public void getAttendance() { }
    public void print() { }
}

Student s1 = new Student();            // s1: a reference to a Student OBJECT
Class<Student> c1 = Student.class;     // c1: an object describing the Student CLASS
  • Just as Java has a class named Object, it has a special class named Class (generic: Class<Student>).
  • c1 is not a Student object; you can't do c1.name. It holds the class's metadata:
    • The class name (Student).
    • The fields (name, age) and their types.
    • The constructors.
    • The methods (getAttendance, print).
    • Which members are private or public.
    • Which annotations the class carries.
Why Spring needs this:
To create and manage an object by itself, Spring must know the class's blueprint: its constructors, fields and annotations. It gets that metadata through reflection. That's why you hand Spring things like AppConfig.class and OrderService.class.

Step 1: mark classes for Spring with @Component

First, tell Spring which classes to manage:

@Component
public class OrderService { ... }

@Component
public class PaymentService { ... }

@Component says: "Spring, you create and manage this class's objects (beans)." It acts as a marker. That alone isn't enough, though: the container must also be started.

Step 2: the IoC container is ApplicationContext

  • In Spring, the IoC container is represented by ApplicationContext, which is an interface (it has methods and extends other interfaces).
  • You can't write new ApplicationContext(); you need an implementation. The IoC container can be implemented in several ways.
  • For annotation-based configuration, the implementation is AnnotationConfigApplicationContext.
  • new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(...) means: start a Spring container using annotation-based configuration.

The container can't start until it knows the rules: which classes to monitor and how to configure them. Those rules go in a separate class, and that class's reflection (AppConfig.class) is passed to the constructor.

Step 3: the configuration class, @Configuration + @ComponentScan

@Configuration                          // "this is a configuration class"
@ComponentScan("in.codearmy")           // "scan this package for @Component classes"
public class AppConfig {
    // empty for now; @Bean methods come later
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ApplicationContext context =
                new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class);

        OrderService order = context.getBean(OrderService.class);   // no 'new'
        order.placeOrder();

        PaymentService payment = context.getBean(PaymentService.class);
        payment.pay();
    }
}
  • @Configuration marks AppConfig as a special configuration class.
  • @ComponentScan says: go through the project, find every class annotated @Component, and create and manage its beans. You pass the package to search: here in.codearmy, which holds OrderService, PaymentService, Main and AppConfig.
  • The class can be named anything. What matters is the @Configuration annotation on it.
  • In Main, the container reads AppConfig's metadata, sees its annotations, scans the package, and creates beans for both @Component classes.
  • context.getBean(OrderService.class) fetches the bean. No new is needed, because we don't want to create it, only use it.

For this first check, the constructor dependency was temporarily removed, so both classes are independent. The output confirms that both beans exist and the container is running:

Order placed
Payment done

How @ComponentScan searches

  • Sub-packages are included. Scanning in.codearmy also covers in.codearmy.random, in.codearmy.random.random2, and so on, at any depth.
  • Only @Component classes (for now; other stereotype annotations come later). Remove @Component from PaymentService and getBean(PaymentService.class) fails with "No qualifying bean of type PaymentService available". Spring was never allowed to manage it, so no bean exists.
  • No package given? @ComponentScan alone still works. It defaults to the package of the class carrying the annotation (AppConfig's package) and its sub-packages. A package outside it, such as a top-level random package, isn't scanned. To include it, name a common parent package.

Step 4: automatic wiring with @Autowired

Creating beans is only half the job. Restore the constructor dependency: OrderService needs a PaymentService. The container has both beans, so it can pass the PaymentService bean into the OrderService constructor, exactly what Main used to do by hand.

@Component
public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentService paymentService;

    @Autowired                                   // "inject this through the constructor"
    public OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }

    public void placeOrder() {
        paymentService.pay();
        System.out.println("Order placed");
    }
}

// Main
OrderService order = context.getBean(OrderService.class);
order.placeOrder();          // Payment done / Order placed

@Autowired means "wire this automatically". A constructor runs when an object is created. The container creates OrderService, so while calling the constructor it passes in the PaymentService bean.

Three types of injection in Spring

// 1. Constructor injection (recommended)
@Component
public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentService paymentService;
    public OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {   // @Autowired optional: single constructor
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }
}

// 2. Setter injection: called by Spring after the object is created
@Component
public class OrderService {
    private PaymentService paymentService;
    @Autowired
    public void setPaymentService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }
}

// 3. Field injection: Spring sets the field directly (via reflection)
@Component
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    private PaymentService paymentService;     // IntelliJ: "Field injection is not recommended"
}
  • Setter injection. The setter isn't called during construction. Spring first creates both objects, then calls the @Autowired setter to link them.
  • Field injection. Lecture 4 said this isn't possible in plain Java, but Spring can do it. It works, but IntelliJ warns "Field injection is not recommended".
  • Single constructor, so no @Autowired needed. In modern Spring, with exactly one constructor, Spring knows which constructor to call and injects automatically. With multiple constructors Spring can't tell which to use, so you mark one with @Autowired (covered later).
  • Setter and field injection always need @Autowired; without it the dependency is left null.

Why constructor injection is recommended

  1. Dependencies are wired at object creation. The object is never half-built, and linking doesn't happen later.
  2. The field can be final. Java allows a final instance variable to be initialized in the constructor, so nobody can swap the dependency later. With field or setter injection, final is impossible, because injection happens after construction.
  3. Easy to unit test. You can test OrderService without Spring: new OrderService(fakePayment).
    • With field injection on a private field, there's no constructor or setter to assign it. new OrderService().placeOrder() throws a NullPointerException at paymentService.pay().
    • A setter would allow it, but with more hassle.
    • For a fake payment, make PaymentService an interface with UPI, card and fake implementations, as in Lecture 4 with NotificationService.

What happens inside: the container's steps

  1. Start the container. new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class): Spring starts the application context using annotation config, with the rules taken from AppConfig's metadata.
  2. Spring reads AppConfig. It's a configuration class. It says which components to scan and in which package (in.codearmy), and later much more.
  3. Spring processes @ComponentScan.
  4. Spring finds the @Component classes: OrderService, PaymentService.
  5. Spring creates bean definitions before creating any object. For each class it stores metadata:
    • The bean name, e.g. paymentService.
    • The bean's class.
    • Its scope (a later lecture).
    • Its dependencies: none for PaymentService; PaymentService for OrderService.
    BeanDefinition is an actual Spring interface, used internally; we don't call it.
  6. Spring creates the objects. PaymentService is simple, so roughly new PaymentService(). OrderService needs a PaymentService in its constructor, so Spring passes the one it already made: roughly new OrderService(payment). The dependencies are now linked.
  7. The application uses the beans. context.getBean(OrderService.class).placeOrder() works because the dependency is already injected.

Anticipated question: "Why bean definitions first? Why not create objects directly?"

Spring doesn't just create objects; it manages them. It may need to wire one dependency, or several beans that depend on each other. To do any wiring correctly, it needs complete knowledge of every class before creating any object. So it collects all the metadata (bean definitions) first, then creates the objects.

(Added:) this is also why you can hook in before objects exist. A BeanFactoryPostProcessor can modify bean definitions (for example, resolving ${…} placeholders) before any bean is instantiated. Spring also works out the creation order from the dependencies: it doesn't rely on the order the classes were found, but creates a bean's dependencies first, on demand.

Anticipated question: "What errors can wiring produce?"

SituationResult
No wiring at all (no constructor, no @Autowired), then pay() is calledNullPointerException: paymentService is null
OrderService needs PaymentService, but PaymentService has no @ComponentFails at startup: IntelliJ shows "Could not autowire. No beans of 'PaymentService' type found". Running gives "No qualifying bean… expected at least 1 bean which qualifies as autowire candidate" (an UnsatisfiedDependencyException wrapping a NoSuchBeanDefinitionException)
Two beans match the needed type"expected single matching bean but found 2" (a NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException). See the next section.

Loose coupling with an interface: multiple candidate beans

OrderService is still tightly coupled to the concrete PaymentService, the same problem as Lecture 4. Payment could be by card or by UPI. So PaymentService becomes an interface in a new payment package. IntelliJ's Refactor → Move updates every import to in.codearmy.payment.

public interface PaymentService {
    void pay();
}

@Component
public class CardPayment implements PaymentService {
    @Override
    public void pay() { System.out.println("Paying via card"); }
}

@Component
public class UpiPayment implements PaymentService {
    @Override
    public void pay() { System.out.println("Paying via UPI"); }
}
  • @Component on the interface is meaningless. An interface can't be instantiated. With no @Component on any implementation, there is no PaymentService bean, and startup fails with "Could not autowire".
  • @Component only on CardPayment. Spring finds a PaymentService-type bean: CardPayment is a PaymentService. It injects it, and the output is "Paying via card / Order placed". Move @Component to UpiPayment and you get "Paying via UPI". OrderService doesn't change.
  • @Component on both. The container holds a cardPayment bean and a upiPayment bean. Creating OrderService needs one PaymentService, and Spring can't pass just anything, so it fails: "No qualifying bean of type PaymentService: expected single matching bean but found 2".

Resolving ambiguity: @Primary and @Qualifier

// Option 1: @Primary, the default winner
@Component
@Primary
public class UpiPayment implements PaymentService { ... }       // → "Paying via UPI"

// Option 2: @Qualifier at the injection point, naming the bean
@Component
public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentService paymentService;
    public OrderService(@Qualifier("cardPayment") PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;                   // → "Paying via card"
    }
}
  • @Primary goes on one of the candidates: "whenever you're confused, prefer this one".
  • @Qualifier("name") goes at the injection point: the constructor parameter, the setter parameter, or the field, depending on how you inject. It names the bean that wins.
  • Default bean name for a @Component class: the class name in camelCase. CardPayment becomes cardPayment, and UpiPayment becomes upiPayment.
  • Custom names. The lecture writes @Qualifier("cp") on CardPayment and @Qualifier("up") on UpiPayment, then injects with @Qualifier("up"), giving "Paying via UPI". This works, but see the precision note.
Precision note: qualifier vs bean name:
@Qualifier("cp") on a class doesn't rename the bean; it adds a qualifier value. The bean is still named cardPayment. At an injection point, @Qualifier("x") matches beans whose qualifier is x, and falls back to matching the bean name. That's why the lecture's plain @Qualifier (no value) on both classes wasn't needed: @Qualifier("cardPayment") at the constructor already works by bean name. To really rename a bean, use @Component("cp"), or @Bean("cp") / @Bean(name = "cp") for @Bean methods.
@Primary@Qualifier
Placed onThe bean (class or @Bean method)The injection point (plus optionally the bean, to give it a qualifier)
DecidesA global default for that typeThe choice for this specific injection
Precedence@Qualifier wins over @Primary when both apply
Use whenOne implementation is the usual choiceDifferent consumers need different implementations

(Added:) other options are injecting List<PaymentService> or Map<String, PaymentService> to get all implementations, which is handy for a Strategy-style lookup by name. Without any qualifier, Spring also tries to match the parameter name to a bean name as a last resort.

When @Component can't work

Can you hand any class to Spring by adding @Component? No. There are two cases where it fails.

Case 1: a class whose constructor needs values Spring can't know.

@Component                      // error straight away
public class User {
    private String name;
    private int age;

    public User(String name, int age) {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = age;
    }
    // getters and setters ...
}

Spring would have to call new User(?, ?), but which name and age? It won't invent random values. OrderService worked because its constructor needed another bean, and Spring had one. Plain values such as String and int aren't beans. So without @Component you can still create User yourself, but you can't simply hand it to Spring.

(Added:) @Value("Aditya") on constructor parameters, or values from properties files, can supply such values. That comes in later lectures.

Case 2: a class from a third-party library. A dependency's classes arrive as compiled .class files inside a JAR, and they are read-only. You can't add @Component to them. The demo:

  1. Create a separate plain Maven project, spring-core-demo-2 (groupId in.strikes), with no Spring at all. It has one class: 
    public class CartService {
    public void addToCart() {
        System.out.println("Added to cart");
    }
}
  2. Run Maven install. This runs validate, compile, test (none), package (the JAR goes to target/), verify (no plugins) and install, which puts the JAR in the local ~/.m2 repository (Lecture 3).
  3. In spring-core-demo's pom, add it as a dependency. Maven checks the local repository first and finds it there: 
    <dependency>
    <groupId>in.strikes</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-core-demo-2</artifactId>
    <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>
  4. After a reload, External Libraries shows spring-core-demo-2, and inside it in.strikes.CartService.class. The IDE decompiles it so it's readable, but it can't be edited.
  5. new CartService().addToCart() works in Main. But making Spring manage it with @Component is impossible, because you can't edit that file.

The fix: @Bean methods in the configuration class

Spring's offer: "If I can't create the object, you create it, give it to me, and I'll put it in my IoC container and manage it from then on." The failing step was only the first one, creation. You write a method in the @Configuration class that returns the object and annotate it with @Bean.

@Configuration
@ComponentScan("in.codearmy")
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public User createUser() {
        return new User("Aditya", 28);          // we supply the constructor values
    }

    @Bean
    public CartService createCartService() {    // third-party class: no annotation needed on it
        return new CartService();
    }
}

// Main
User user = context.getBean(User.class);
System.out.println(user.getName());             // Aditya

CartService cart = context.getBean(CartService.class);
cart.addToCart();                               // Added to cart
  • @Bean tells Spring: while reading the configuration rules, call every @Bean method, take the object it returns, and store it in the IoC container as a bean.
  • The method name can be anything.
  • Both beans are now managed. getBean returns them, and Spring can inject them anywhere they're needed as dependencies.

@Component vs @Bean

@Component@Bean
Placed onA class (class-level)A method (method-level), usually in a @Configuration class
Who creates the objectSpring (it calls the constructor)You write the creation code; Spring calls your method
Discovered by@ComponentScanProcessing the configuration class
Default bean nameThe class name in camelCase (cardPayment)The method name (createCardPayment)
Use whenYour own classes with simple, bean-only dependenciesYou can't annotate the class (third-party or read-only), or creation is complicated (constructor values, builders, conditional setup)

Both create beans, and you can use them together.

Dependencies between @Bean methods

@Bean works for your own classes too. With @Component removed from OrderService, CardPayment and UpiPayment, component scanning finds nothing, so all of them are declared as @Beans:

@Bean
public PaymentService createCardPayment() {          // return type can be the interface
    return new CardPayment();
}

@Bean
public OrderService createOrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
    return new OrderService(paymentService);         // Spring supplies the parameter
}

OrderService's constructor needs a PaymentService, so the @Bean method takes one as a parameter. When Spring calls the method, it passes a matching bean, here CardPayment. That's still constructor-style injection, so no @Autowired is needed. The container ends up holding user, cart, cardPayment and orderService, and running the app prints "Paying via card / Order placed".

If OrderService had no such constructor (say it used field injection), you couldn't pass the dependency in. There are two options:

// (a) wire it by hand inside the @Bean method: needs a setter
@Bean
public OrderService createOrderService() {
    PaymentService payment = createCardPayment();
    OrderService order = new OrderService();
    order.setPaymentService(payment);
    return order;
}

// (b) or put @Autowired on OrderService's setter and just return the object;
//     Spring still processes @Autowired on objects returned from @Bean methods
@Bean
public OrderService createOrderService() {
    return new OrderService();                  // Spring calls the @Autowired setter afterwards
}

Option (b) means "I create the object; you do the wiring." Afterwards the lecture goes back to the simpler constructor version.

@Primary and @Qualifier with @Bean

Add a second @Bean, createUpiPayment(), and the container has two PaymentService beans. Creating OrderService becomes ambiguous again: "Could not autowire. There is more than one bean". The same two fixes apply:

  • @Primary on the createCardPayment() method gives "Paying via card".
  • @Qualifier("createUpiPayment") on the createOrderService parameter gives "Paying via UPI". Here the bean name is the method name, not the class name.
  • Custom qualifiers work the same way, e.g. @Qualifier("cp") and @Qualifier("upi") on the methods, with @Qualifier("upi") at the parameter.

Anticipated question: "What if a class has both @Component and a @Bean method?"

The lecture re-enables @Component on CardPayment while keeping its @Bean method, and uses @Qualifier("cp"). The app prints "Paying via card" with no error. The lecture concludes that only one CardPayment bean is created, because @Bean "gets priority" over component scanning.

Correction: there are actually two beans here (verified on Spring 7.0.5):
Component scanning registers a bean named cardPayment. The @Bean method registers one named createCardPayment, the method name; @Qualifier("cp") adds a qualifier but doesn't rename it. Different names mean two separate CardPayment beans. There was no error only because the injection point said @Qualifier("cp"), which only the @Bean one matches. Without that qualifier you'd get "found 2".
Overriding happens only when both definitions have the same bean name (e.g. @Bean("cardPayment")). Then the later definition replaces the earlier one. Plain Spring allows that by default. Spring Boot disables bean-definition overriding by default (since Boot 2.1) and fails at startup instead, unless you set spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding=true. The idea that "what you build explicitly wins over what Spring builds" holds only in that same-name case.

Anticipated question: "Why a separate AppConfig instead of configuring in main?"

You could put all of this in main. Lecture 4 used main as the driver that injected everything, and that was exactly the problem: main got complicated. main is the program's entry point and should stay simple, so configuration lives in its own class. The name is up to you (AppConfig is just a choice); the @Configuration annotation is what marks it.

Correction: what removing @Configuration actually does (verified on Spring 7.0.5):
The lecture says that without @Configuration, @ComponentScan won't run, while @Bean methods still would. In fact, a class passed to new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class) is processed as a configuration class even without @Configuration, in what Spring calls "lite mode". Its @ComponentScan and @Bean methods are still honoured.
  • What @Configuration really adds is "full mode". Spring subclasses the config class (a CGLIB proxy), so when one @Bean method calls another, as in createCardPayment() inside createOrderService(), you get the same singleton bean back instead of a new object.
  • Lite mode has no proxy, so that call just runs the method again and creates a second, unmanaged instance.
Keep @Configuration on config classes.

ApplicationContext vs BeanFactory

Early Spring versions used BeanFactory, also an interface, to start and interact with the IoC container. Today we use ApplicationContext, which extends BeanFactory internally (via ListableBeanFactory and HierarchicalBeanFactory), so everything BeanFactory has, it has too.

Correction: super vs sub is inverted in the lecture:
The lecture calls ApplicationContext the "super interface" and BeanFactory the "sub interface". It's the reverse. BeanFactory is the root (super) interface, and ApplicationContext is a sub-interface that extends it and adds features. The lecture's own description, "ApplicationContext extends BeanFactory", is the correct part. Also, BeanFactory itself isn't deprecated. What was deprecated and then removed were old standalone implementations such as XmlBeanFactory.
What ApplicationContext adds (added)
BeanFactoryApplicationContext
Singleton creationLazy: on first getBeanEager: all singletons at startup, so wiring errors surface immediately
Post-processors (@Autowired handling, AOP)Must be registered manuallyDetected and registered automatically
ExtrasBasic DI onlyEvents (ApplicationEvent), i18n (MessageSource), resource loading, environment and profiles
UseLow-level / memory-constrained casesPractically always, and what Spring Boot creates for you

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Beans are singletons by default. getBean(OrderService.class) called twice returns the same object. The "scope" field in the bean definition controls this; scopes get their own lecture.
  • Close the context. AnnotationConfigApplicationContext implements AutoCloseable. Use try (var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class)) { … } so beans' destroy callbacks run when you're done.
  • Scanning doesn't load every class. @ComponentScan reads .class files' metadata with a bytecode reader (ASM) to find annotations, and only loads and reflects on the classes that actually become beans. That keeps startup fast.
  • Default-name edge case. The camelCase rule follows java.beans.Introspector.decapitalize: CardPayment becomes cardPayment, but a class starting with two capitals keeps its name (URLService stays URLService).
  • getBean(Type) with two matching beans throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException too. Use getBean("name", Type.class), or mark one @Primary.
  • You rarely call getBean in real apps. It's a "pull" (service-locator style) used here to peek into the container. In real code beans get each other injected, and only the entry point touches the context. In Spring Boot, even that is done for you by SpringApplication.run (Lecture 2).
  • Spring Boot's @SpringBootApplication bundles what this lecture wrote by hand: @Configuration (via @SpringBootConfiguration), @ComponentScan of its own package, and @EnableAutoConfiguration. That's why Lecture 2's controller had to be in the same package as the main class, or below it.

Lecture 6: Circular Dependency, Bean Scopes & Eager vs Lazy Initialization

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #6 · 1h22m · Code Army · Three linked Spring Core topics

Normal dependencies: Spring works out the order

Suppose OrderService can't be created without a PaymentService, and PaymentService needs a PaymentGateway. All three are @Components with @Autowired dependencies. The IoC container is smart enough to see the chain and create the beans in reverse: first the gateway, then the payment service (injecting the gateway), and last the order service (injecting the payment service).

The problem: circular dependency

Definition:
Class A needs B to be created, and B needs A. That is a circular dependency. There is no starting point, so which should Spring create first? For example, OrderService depends on PaymentService, and PaymentService depends back on OrderService.

Setup: a new project and a @Configuration fact

New Maven project circular-dependency-demo, with spring-context 7.0.7 from mvnrepository (Spring 7 pairs with Boot 4). Main starts an AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class). AppConfig has @Configuration plus a plain @ComponentScan; no package is needed because it's in the same package as the other classes.

Worth knowing: the configuration class is itself a bean:
Spring calls the @Bean methods in AppConfig. They aren't static, so Spring needs an AppConfig object, which we never created. Ctrl-click @Configuration and you'll see it is meta-annotated with @Component. So AppConfig is a component too: the container creates and manages its object. It's just a special one, because it declares beans and component-scanning rules. (Verified on Spring 7.0.5: the bean is actually a CGLIB subclass, AppConfig$$SpringCGLIB$$0, which is the "full mode" proxy from Lecture 5.)

Reproducing it with constructor injection

@Component
public class OrderService {
    private PaymentService paymentService;

    public OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }

    public void placeOrder() {
        paymentService.pay();
        System.out.println("Order placed");
    }

    public void getOrderDetails() {
        System.out.println("Order details");
    }
}

@Component
public class PaymentService {
    private OrderService orderService;

    public PaymentService(OrderService orderService) {   // now depends back on OrderService
        this.orderService = orderService;
    }

    public void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment done");
        orderService.getOrderDetails();                   // calls back into OrderService
    }
}

// Main
OrderService order = context.getBean(OrderService.class);
order.placeOrder();

The expected flow, if it could run: placeOrder calls pay, which prints "Payment done" and calls getOrderDetails ("Order details"); control then returns and prints "Order placed". But the beans can't even be created. Creating OrderService means calling its constructor, which needs a PaymentService. Creating that means calling its constructor, which needs an OrderService. The run fails:

BeanCurrentlyInCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'orderService':
Requested bean is currently in creation: Is there an unresolvable circular reference?
What "currently in creation" means:
Spring started creating orderService. To finish, it had to create paymentService. That in turn asked for orderService, which was already in the middle of being created. Spring detects this and even suggests the cause: an unresolvable circular reference.

It's a design problem, not a Spring problem

Circular dependencies come from badly designed code, not from Spring. You can cause one in plain Java. Two plain classes, A and B in a simple package, with no @Component:

  • With constructor parameters (A(B b) and B(A a)), you can't even write new A(new B(new A(…))). There is no way to start.
  • The "hack" of default constructors that build each other (A() { this.b = new B(); }, B() { this.a = new A(); }) makes new A() print "A created, B created, A created…" forever, until a StackOverflowError. The @Components on OrderService and PaymentService had to be removed for this demo, because otherwise the Spring error came first.

Spring's workaround: field or setter injection

The cycle is caused by the constructors: each needs the other's object at creation time. Switch both classes to field injection (or setter injection, which behaves the same) and it runs:

@Component
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    private PaymentService paymentService;
    ...
}

@Component
public class PaymentService {
    @Autowired
    private OrderService orderService;
    ...
}
Payment done
Order details
Order placed
Side question: how does Spring set a private field with no setter or constructor?
Through reflection. The container builds a bean definition first, so it has the class's full metadata. The Reflection API can write even private members, using Field.setAccessible(true). That's how field injection works at all, even without any cycle.

How field or setter injection breaks the cycle

Field and setter injection separate object creation from dependency injection. Every object is created by some constructor, the default one if you didn't write any. Here neither constructor needs the other bean. The dependencies are needed only after creation.

Spring's normal rule is: create A, inject A's dependencies, then create B, inject B's dependencies. Each bean is completed fully before moving on. With a cycle, it does this instead:

  1. Create the OrderService object, which is partial because its dependency isn't injected yet.
  2. Resolve its dependency: it needs PaymentService. Is there one in the container? No, so create it (also partial).
  3. Resolve PaymentService's dependency: it needs OrderService. One exists, only partially built, but Spring injects a reference to it anyway. PaymentService is now complete.
  4. Back in OrderService, inject the now-complete PaymentService. OrderService is complete too.
Terminology (added):
The lecture calls this the "reference concept". Spring's own term is an early singleton reference. DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry keeps a so-called three-level cache of singletons:
  1. singletonObjects: fully built beans.
  2. earlySingletonObjects: early references to partly built beans.
  3. singletonFactories: factories that can produce an early reference, possibly an AOP proxy.
It works only for singletons and non-constructor injection. With constructor injection there's no object to reference until the constructor finishes, so nothing can be exposed early.

Don't resolve a circular dependency, remove it

  • It isn't good practice. Making the cycle "work" hides a design flaw.
  • Spring Boot refuses it by default. Since Spring Boot 2.6, spring.main.allow-circular-references defaults to false. Boot then fails at startup even with field or setter injection, unless you set it to true. Plain Spring Core, as used here, still allows it.
  • There are other ways to "resolve" it too: a different scope, @Lazy (later in this lecture), and @PostConstruct (the bean-lifecycle lecture). But the right move is to refactor so the cycle never arises.
Transcript slip:
The lecture says 2.6 and later mentions "2.4". The version is Spring Boot 2.6, the release where circular references became prohibited by default.
Why the lecturer calls it bad design:
In an enterprise application you need to scale, circular dependencies should not exist. Why would OrderService and PaymentService be so entangled? It means their responsibilities weren't separated: the Single Responsibility Principle, the first SOLID principle, failed. Good applications follow design principles and patterns, so fix the design rather than hunt for ways to make the cycle work.

Refactoring the cycle away

Here, class A calls B, and B calls back into A, which is wrong.

  • OrderService manages orders. Placing an order requires payment first, so it delegates pay() to PaymentService and expects a result: in real code a success flag, then "Order placed". That's correct.
  • PaymentService handles payments: it talks to a gateway and logs "Payment done". But then it calls orderService.getOrderDetails(). Getting order details is not its responsibility.
  • So move that call into OrderService: after payment succeeds, it calls its own getOrderDetails().
@Component
public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentService paymentService;

    public OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }

    public void placeOrder() {
        paymentService.pay();
        getOrderDetails();                 // moved here: OrderService's own job
        System.out.println("Order placed");
    }

    public void getOrderDetails() {
        System.out.println("Order details");
    }
}

@Component
public class PaymentService {              // no OrderService field any more
    public void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment done");
    }
}

The output is identical (Payment done / Order details / Order placed), but the dependency is now linear. OrderService depends on PaymentService, and nothing depends back. Constructor injection works again.

(Added:) other standard refactors are:

  • Extract the shared logic into a third class that both depend on.
  • Invert one direction with an interface (DIP).
  • Replace the callback with an event: PaymentService publishes PaymentCompletedEvent and an order listener reacts.

Bean scopes: singleton

A new project, bean-scope-demo, with the same boilerplate. Its OrderService is a @Component with no dependencies, and its constructor prints "Order service created".

OrderService order  = context.getBean(OrderService.class);
OrderService order2 = context.getBean(OrderService.class);
System.out.println(order == order2);      // == compares references
Order service created
true

The constructor ran once, and both variables point to the same object. No matter how many times you ask, you get that one object.

Definition: singleton scope (the default):
One object per bean definition (per container). A class like OrderService produces one bean definition, and the container creates one object for it. Every getBean returns that object, and so does every injection. If classes A and B (both @Components) each take an OrderService in their constructors, Spring creates OrderService first, and A and B both receive the same instance.

Writing @Scope("singleton") on the class changes nothing, because it's the default.

Bean scopes: prototype

@Component
@Scope("prototype")          // or @Scope(ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE)
public class OrderService {
    public OrderService() { System.out.println("Order service created"); }
    public void placeOrder() { System.out.println("Order placed"); }
}
Definition: prototype scope:
A new object every time one is requested, whether through getBean or through injection. It's like writing new on each request.

With two getBean calls plus A and B both injecting it, the output shows "Order service created" four times, and order == order2 is false.

  • Prototype beans aren't fully managed by the container. It creates them and hands them over, but doesn't track their whole lifecycle. In particular, destroy callbacks are not called. Details come in the bean-lifecycle lecture.
  • Prototype beans are created lazily. With nobody requesting OrderService (no getBean, and A/B not depending on it), a singleton is still created at startup, printing "Order service created". A prototype isn't created at all: the context starts and nothing is printed. So the diagram above is slightly off in one way: prototype has no instance "waiting" in the container. Each is built only when asked for.
Singleton (default)Prototype
InstancesOne per bean definition per containerOne per request / injection
CreatedEagerly at startup (by default)Lazily, only when requested
Lifecycle managedFully, including destroy callbacksCreation and initialization only, no destroy
getBean == getBeantruefalse
SuitsStateless classes: services, managers, repositoriesStateful objects that each need their own data

Spring singleton is not the GoF Singleton

  • The Singleton design pattern (LLD) is strict: a class can ever have only one instance in the JVM (per class loader).
  • Spring's singleton only means one object per bean definition in this container:
    • You can still write new OrderService() yourself (order3). Spring just won't manage that one.
    • Two @Bean methods returning OrderService (getOrder() and getOrder2(), with @Component removed from the class) create two bean definitions, so "Order service created" prints twice. Each is a singleton within its own definition: getBean("getOrder") always returns the same one.

With two definitions, anything that asks for OrderService by type (A, B, getBean(OrderService.class)) now fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException: "expected 1, found 2: getOrder, getOrder2". You need @Primary or @Qualifier (Lecture 5).

The lecturer's emphasis:
"Singleton doesn't mean only one object exists in the IoC container. It means one object per bean definition." This depth point is often skipped in explanations of singleton scope, and it's a common interview trap.
Precision note (added):
For @Bean methods, the scope comes from @Scope on the method, not from @Scope on the returned class. In the lecture the class carried @Scope("singleton"). It made no difference only because singleton is the default anyway.

When to use which scope

  • Singleton for stateless classes, which hold no per-caller data. OrderService handles many orders but keeps no state itself; it just has methods. Service and manager classes (OrderManager, PaymentManager) are the best candidates.
  • Prototype for stateful classes. A User with name and age fields (its state) shouldn't be a singleton. If the container held one User named "Aditya", aged 28, every getBean would return that same user, and the app needs many users.
Worth knowing (added):
  • Singletons are shared across threads. In a web app, many requests use the same service bean at once, so mutable instance fields in a singleton cause race conditions. Keep singletons stateless, or make their state thread-safe.
  • Plain data objects usually aren't beans at all. Domain objects such as User or Order are normally created with new, deserialized from JSON, or loaded by JPA. They are not taken from the container. Prototype scope suits stateful helpers that need injection, such as a per-task builder or a non-thread-safe client.
  • The prototype-inside-singleton trap. Injecting a prototype into a singleton happens once, when the singleton is created, so the singleton keeps the same "prototype" forever. (In the lecture, A and B each got their own instance, but only one each.) To get a fresh one per use, inject an ObjectProvider<OrderService> and call getObject(), or use @Lookup methods or a scoped proxy.

Other scopes (web only)

ScopeOne instance per…
requestHTTP request
sessionUser HTTP session
applicationWeb application (ServletContext) while it runs
websocket (added)WebSocket session

These only matter in web apps (Spring MVC / Boot) and come later. application can look like singleton. (Added:) the difference is that it's per ServletContext, shared across all Spring contexts in that web app and exposed as a servlet-context attribute, while singleton is per ApplicationContext.

Bean initialization: eager

Project bean-initialization-demo. OrderService and PaymentService are both @Components whose constructors print "… created", and Main only starts the context. Running it prints both lines immediately.

Definition: eager initialization:
Beans are created as soon as the application context (IoC container) starts, whether or not anyone uses them. This is the default for singletons.

Bean initialization: lazy, with @Lazy

@Component
@Lazy                        // don't create at startup; create when first needed
public class OrderService { ... }
  • With @Lazy on both classes, starting the context prints nothing: the container is empty.
  • getBean(OrderService.class) prints "Order service created" at that moment, and the same goes for PaymentService.
Definition: lazy initialization:
The bean is created only when it's first needed: requested with getBean, or required as a dependency of a bean being created.

The rules: singleton can be lazy; prototype is always lazy

  • With no scope written, the scope is singleton, and singletons are eager by default. @Lazy changes a singleton to lazy.
  • Prototype is always lazy and can never be made eager. A prototype class without @Lazy still prints nothing at startup, and writing @Lazy on a prototype is redundant.
  • Why? Prototype hands out a new object on every request, so a pre-built object at startup would be useless: nobody would ever get it. Singleton returns the same object to everyone, so building it once up front makes sense.
ScopeDefault initCan change?
SingletonEagerYes: @Lazy makes it lazy
PrototypeLazyNo: always lazy

Lazy meets dependencies

Now OrderService depends on PaymentService through its constructor. With no annotations, both are eager: "Payment service created", then "Order service created", with payment first because order needs it.

@Lazy onWhat's created at startupWhy
OrderService class onlyOnly PaymentServiceNobody asks for OrderService. PaymentService is eager. On getBean(OrderService), Spring creates it and injects the existing PaymentService.
PaymentService class onlyBothOrderService is eager and needs PaymentService. Lazy only means "not until needed", and now it's needed.
Both classesNothingEverything waits for getBean.

@Lazy at the injection point: a proxy

@Lazy can also go where the dependency is injected, just like @Qualifier:

@Component
public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentService paymentService;

    public OrderService(@Lazy PaymentService paymentService) {   // inject a proxy, not the real bean
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
        System.out.println("Order service created");
    }

    public void placeOrder() {
        paymentService.pay();            // first real use: the real PaymentService is resolved now
        System.out.println("Order placed");
    }
}
  • This means: create OrderService, but don't create its dependency. Spring injects a proxy. The Proxy design pattern gives you an object that looks and behaves like a PaymentService but isn't the real one. OrderService thinks it got a PaymentService and is fully created.
  • When placeOrder() calls pay() on the proxy, Spring resolves the real PaymentService, creating it if it's lazy, and forwards the call.
  • If PaymentService is not lazy, it's still created at startup (it's eager). The proxy just points to it when first used.
  • With PaymentService also @Lazy, nothing needs it at startup, so only OrderService is created.

With @Lazy on PaymentService and at the injection point, Main calls getBean(OrderService), prints a marker, then calls placeOrder():

Order service created
Payment service not started yet
Payment service created
Payment successful
Order placed
Correction: the proxy is not swapped out (verified on Spring 7.0.5):
The lecture says that once placeOrder() runs, the proxy is "removed and the real object put in". In fact the field keeps holding the proxy for the bean's whole life. After the call, paymentService.getClass() is still PaymentService$$SpringCGLIB$$0. Each call on the proxy delegates to the target bean fetched from the container. The effect is the same, but it matters when debugging, since getClass() and == show the proxy, and when the target's scope changes.

Why is eager the default? Fail fast

Creating every bean at startup sounds heavy, so why does Spring make eager the default? Fail fast. If your wiring is broken (a missing bean, multiple candidates, a circular dependency), eager creation reports it at startup, before users arrive. With @Lazy, some beans are only created when needed, so the failure can happen in production, mid-request. Use @Lazy for a genuinely heavy bean you're confident is correct and don't want slowing startup. Either way, only singletons can be eager or lazy; prototypes are always lazy.

Global lazy mode:

# application.properties
spring.main.lazy-initialization=true     # default false: every bean becomes lazy
@Component
@Lazy(false)                 // opt this one bean back into eager creation
public class StartupCriticalService { ... }

@Lazy(false) (value = false) only makes sense when global lazy mode is on, because otherwise eager is already the default.

Correction:
spring.main.lazy-initialization is a Spring Boot property (Boot 2.2+), read by SpringApplication from application.properties. The lecture presents it as a Spring Framework property, but a plain Spring Core project like this lecture's has no application.properties processing for it. There, you'd set lazy defaults per bean with @Lazy, or via @ComponentScan(lazyInit = true).

Solving a circular dependency with @Lazy

Back to the constructor-injection cycle: OrderService(PaymentService) and PaymentService(OrderService), with pay() calling orderService.getOrderDetails(). It fails with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException, as before. The fix:

  1. @Lazy on the PaymentService class. Alone, this isn't enough: creating OrderService still needs it, and creating it still needs OrderService.
  2. Plus @Lazy at OrderService's constructor parameter. Now OrderService is created with a proxy instead of a real PaymentService, so the cycle is broken at startup.
  3. On placeOrder(), the proxy triggers creation of the real PaymentService. Its constructor needs OrderService, which already exists, so it's injected, and the call proceeds.
Payment successful
Order details
Order placed
Precision note (verified on Spring 7.0.5):
The @Lazy on the PaymentService class isn't what breaks the cycle. @Lazy on the one constructor parameter alone is enough. In the test, OrderService was built with a proxy, then PaymentService (eager) was built at startup with the real OrderService. The class-level @Lazy only defers when the real PaymentService gets created. And as the lecture stresses, this resolves the cycle but doesn't remove it; refactoring is still the real fix.

Ways to break a circular dependency

ApproachHowVerdict
Refactor (move responsibility, extract a class, use events)Remove the back-referencePreferred. Fixes the real SRP problem
Field or setter injectionSpring uses early singleton referencesWorks in plain Spring; blocked by default in Boot 2.6+
@Lazy at an injection pointInject a proxy, resolve on first useWorks with constructor injection; hides the flaw
ObjectProvider<T> / @PostConstruct wiringLook the bean up after constructionWorks; also a workaround
spring.main.allow-circular-references=trueRe-enable Boot's old behaviourLast resort for legacy code

Homework / suggested extensions

The lecturer will share practice questions: classes mixing @Lazy, singleton and prototype. Predict the output (what's created at startup, in what order, and how many instances) before running them.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Prototype beans don't participate in circular-reference resolution. Early references exist only for singletons. A cycle involving a prototype always fails, even with field injection.
  • @Scope("prototype") constants. Prefer ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE / SCOPE_SINGLETON over string literals to avoid typos. In web apps, use @RequestScope and @SessionScope.
  • @Lazy works on @Bean methods and @Configuration classes too. On a config class it applies to all its @Beans.
  • Lazy trades startup time for first-request latency. The first request that touches a lazy bean pays its creation cost. That's why global lazy mode suits development, tests and serverless cold starts, more than latency-sensitive production services.
  • A BeanFactory alone is lazy (Lecture 5). Eager singleton creation is an ApplicationContext behaviour.

Lecture 7: Spring Bean Lifecycle

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #7 · 1h27m · Code Army · From container start to bean destruction; aware interfaces, init/destroy callbacks

Why the lifecycle matters

The bean lifecycle is one of the most important topics in Spring, especially for interviews. It shows how the IoC container handles the beans it manages internally, and which processes each bean goes through. Earlier lectures touched parts of it. This lecture covers every phase in depth and ends with a summary.

  • Without Spring: you create objects, manage them, and garbage collection destroys them once nothing references them any more. You never call GC yourself.
  • With Spring: the container is responsible for creating, managing and destroying beans. "Destroying" means removing them from the IoC container. Creation and management (autowiring) came up before; destruction hasn't been covered yet.
  • The main walkthrough uses a singleton, eagerly initialized bean, the default. After that, the lecture covers what changes for lazy singletons and for prototypes. Once the singleton case is clear, those differences are small.

Setup

New Maven project bean-lifecycle-demo. The pieces:

  • spring-context 7.0.7.
  • AppConfig with @Configuration and a plain @ComponentScan, which scans its own package.
  • Main creating new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class). That passes AppConfig's metadata via reflection, not an AppConfig object.
  • OrderService, which depends on PaymentService through its constructor (no @Autowired needed with a single constructor). placeOrder() prints "Order placed" and calls pay(), which prints "Payment done".
OrderService order = context.getBean(OrderService.class);
order.placeOrder();          // Order placed / Payment done

Step 1: the IoC container starts

Nothing can be managed until the container is up. new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(…) starts it, and ApplicationContext is how we interact with it.

Step 2: read the configuration

The container needs information: which beans to manage and which packages to scan. That comes from the configuration class whose metadata was passed in. Through reflection, Spring learns:

  • @ComponentScan is present, and which package it names (the default is AppConfig's own package, in.strikes).
  • @Configuration is present, so this is a config class. It may also declare @Bean methods whose returned objects must be managed.
The config class is itself a managed bean:
To call a non-static @Bean method, Spring needs an AppConfig object. @Configuration is meta-annotated with @Component, so the container creates and manages an AppConfig bean, and this lifecycle applies to it too. Proof: add a plain method demo() (not a bean) to AppConfig. Then context.getBean(AppConfig.class).demo() prints "demo".

Component scanning then reflects over each class in the package (AppConfig, Main, OrderService, PaymentService) and picks those annotated @Component: here OrderService and PaymentService.

Step 3: read / create bean definitions

Spring could create objects straight away. But it works better when it first knows each bean's metadata, because then it can inject dependencies and manage beans properly. Take OrderService:

What a bean definition records
FieldExample for OrderService
Bean nameorderService by default (class name, first letter lower-case). @Component("orderBean") renames it.
Bean classOrderService
Scopesingleton (default)
Lazy?false (singletons are eager by default)
DependenciespaymentService
Anticipated question: "Does Spring build all definitions first, or one bean at a time?"
All bean definitions first (OrderService and PaymentService), and only then objects. The reason: definitions say which beans must be created now and which must wait.
