Prototype and lazy = true beans aren't created at startup, only when first used. Knowing this up front, the container instantiates only the eager singletons.

Step 4: instantiate objects

  • Creation isn't random. The container is dependency-aware. It starts with whichever class the scan produced first.
  • If it starts with PaymentService, which has no dependencies, it simply creates it.
  • If it starts with OrderService, calling the constructor reveals that it needs a PaymentService. So the container creates PaymentService first, then OrderService.

Step 5: inject dependencies

  • Constructor injection: steps 4 and 5 merge. OrderService can't exist without PaymentService, so the dependency is passed as the object is created.
  • Field or setter injection: separate steps. With @Autowired on the field (private is fine, since reflection is used), OrderService is created first without its dependency. While injecting, Spring finds it hasn't made PaymentService yet, creates it, and wires it in.

The container now holds AppConfig, OrderService and PaymentService, all wired. Could we start calling methods? Not yet: there are intermediate steps. Most material says "instantiate, inject, use", maybe mentioning @PostConstruct. The in-depth version comes next.

Step 6: Aware interfaces are called

Sometimes a bean needs information about itself or its container: its bean name, or which ApplicationContext it lives in. Spring provides special Aware interfaces. They're rarely used in business logic, but they are a lifecycle step.

@Component("userBean")
public class UserService implements BeanNameAware, ApplicationContextAware {

    public UserService() {
        System.out.println("User service constructor called");
    }

    @Override
    public void setBeanName(String name) {                       // from BeanNameAware
        System.out.println("Bean name is " + name);
    }

    @Override
    public void setApplicationContext(ApplicationContext ctx) throws BeansException {  // from ApplicationContextAware
        System.out.println("Application context name is " + ctx.getClass());
    }
}
User service constructor called
Bean name is userBean
Application context name is class org.springframework.context.annotation.AnnotationConfigApplicationContext
  • Each Aware interface is a functional interface with one method to override. In IntelliJ, hover over the error and choose Implement methods.
  • We never call these methods. Spring calls them after the bean is instantiated and its dependencies injected. Methods that Spring calls for you are callback methods ("the call comes back from Spring"). A bean that doesn't implement any Aware interface simply skips this step.
  • With XML configuration, the context class printed would be an XML-based one instead.
Why it's called setBeanName, not getBeanName:
A getter is something you call to read a value. Here Spring calls the method and sets (passes in) the name for you to keep. Calling userService.setBeanName("userBean2") yourself only prints "Bean name is userBean2". It does not rename the bean; inside the container it's still userBean. Calling a callback yourself changes nothing in Spring.

When are Aware interfaces useful? In about 99% of business logic, never. The niche cases:

  • Logging. Enterprise apps write leveled logs (info, error) to files through logging libraries. Including the bean name in each log line tells you which bean it came from.
  • More than one container in an app, for example XML- and annotation-configured ones side by side (uncommon). Knowing which container a bean belongs to helps you debug the right one.
Worth knowing (added):
Other Aware interfaces include BeanClassLoaderAware, BeanFactoryAware, EnvironmentAware, ResourceLoaderAware and ApplicationEventPublisherAware. In modern code, prefer injecting what you need instead, e.g. a constructor parameter ApplicationContext ctx or Environment env. Spring injects these like any bean, without tying the class to an Aware interface.

Step 7: initialization callbacks

This step matters a lot, unlike Aware interfaces. After a bean is created and its dependencies injected, but before you use it, Spring gives you a hook to initialize it. Example: a CartService @Component holding a Map<Integer, String>. Before addToCart() is ever called, you might want to:

  • Fill the map with initial values, or flush or clear it, perhaps because the map arrives pre-filled through an injected dependency.
  • Clear or invalidate a cache before the object starts working.
  • Pre-load an expensive resource, such as a large file, so it isn't loaded on the first method call.

There are three ways to get this callback.

1. InitializingBean (old style)

@Component
public class CartService implements InitializingBean {
    private Map<Integer, String> mp;

    public CartService() {
        mp = new HashMap<>();
        System.out.println("Cart service constructor called");
    }

    @Override
    public void afterPropertiesSet() {          // Spring calls this after DI (and after Aware callbacks)
        mp.put(1, "Aditya");
        mp.put(2, "Rohit");
        System.out.println("Bean is ready");
    }

    public String getValue(int key) { return mp.get(key); }
    public void addToCart() { System.out.println("Added to cart"); }
}

// Main
CartService cart = context.getBean(CartService.class);
System.out.println(cart.getValue(1));
Cart service constructor called
Bean is ready
Aditya

The @Component was removed from UserService to keep the output clean.

2. initMethod on @Bean

When the bean comes from an @Bean method instead of @Component, name a method of your own:

// AppConfig
@Bean(initMethod = "start")
public CartService getCartBean() {
    return new CartService();
}

// CartService: any public method; no interface, no annotation
public void start() {
    mp.put(1, "Aditya");
    mp.put(2, "Rohit");
    System.out.println("Bean is ready");
}

Without this, nothing fills the map, and getValue(1) prints null. Use InitializingBean or @PostConstruct for @Components; initMethod is still used for @Bean methods, especially for classes you can't edit.

3. @PostConstruct (the one used today)

@Component
public class CartService {
    ...
    @PostConstruct                               // jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct
    public void start2() {
        mp.put(1, "Aditya");
        mp.put(2, "Rohit");
        System.out.println("Bean is ready");
    }
}

This needs no interface, no method to override and no config: just an annotation on any method. But it shows an error at first. @PostConstruct isn't in spring-context; it comes from the Jakarta Annotations library. Spring Boot projects include it automatically. A bare Spring Core project must add it from mvnrepository:

<dependency>
    <groupId>jakarta.annotation</groupId>
    <artifactId>jakarta.annotation-api</artifactId>
    <version>3.0.0</version>
</dependency>

After the Maven reload, import jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct and run again: "Aditya" is printed.

Why @PostConstruct won (added reasoning):
It's a standard annotation from Jakarta Annotations (JSR-250), so your class isn't tied to a Spring API. InitializingBean ties your class to Spring. @PostConstruct is also easy to spot when reading a class.

With Aware interfaces and @PostConstruct together in CartService, the output is:

Cart service constructor called
Bean name is cartService
Application context name is class ...AnnotationConfigApplicationContext
Bean is ready
Aditya

Before the lecture removed the @PostConstruct, it had one in place and initMethod = "start", and "Bean is ready" printed twice. Both callbacks run if both are declared.

Anticipated question: "Why not do initialization in the constructor?"

A classic interview question. Filling the map in the constructor does work in this example. So why have @PostConstruct?

  1. Dependencies may not exist yet. The constructor runs at creation, before the dependency-injection and Aware steps. With field or setter injection, those dependencies are still null in the constructor. By @PostConstruct, every dependency is injected and the object is fully ready, so you can use them.
  2. Keep the constructor light. Loading an expensive file or warming a cache in the constructor slows object creation. Good practice: let the object be created cleanly, then do the heavy work in the init callback.
Constructor@PostConstruct
RunsAt instantiation (step 4)After DI and Aware callbacks (step 7)
Field / setter dependenciesNot yet injected (null)Injected
Good forAssigning fields, cheap setupValidation, cache warm-up, loading resources, using dependencies

Step 8: the bean is ready to use

Only now is the bean fully usable. Calls such as cart.getValue(1) or cart.addToCart() happen in this phase, for as long as the app needs the bean.

Step 9: destruction callbacks

Before destroying a bean, Spring gives one more callback: "I'm about to destroy this; do any last work." The destruction callbacks mirror the initialization ones:

InitializationDestructionStatus today
InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()DisposableBean.destroy()Old; couples the class to Spring
@Bean(initMethod = "…")@Bean(destroyMethod = "…")Used for @Bean-defined beans
@PostConstruct@PreDestroyThe usual choice

What to do in a destruction callback is the reverse of init:

  • Empty the map.
  • Clear or invalidate the cache.
  • Close the expensive resource, such as a file, connection or thread pool.
// 1. DisposableBean
@Component
public class CartService implements DisposableBean {
    @Override
    public void destroy() {
        mp.clear();
        System.out.println("Bean is getting destroyed");
    }
}

// 2. destroyMethod on @Bean
@Bean(initMethod = "start", destroyMethod = "stop")
public CartService getCartBean() { return new CartService(); }

// 3. @PreDestroy
@PreDestroy
public void stop() {
    mp.clear();
    System.out.println("Bean is getting destroyed");
}

How to trigger destruction: the program normally just exits ("Process finished with exit code 0") without the container shutting beans down. So close the context:

ConfigurableApplicationContext context =
        new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class);
CartService cart = context.getBean(CartService.class);
System.out.println(cart.getValue(1));
context.close();             // triggers destruction callbacks, then destroys singletons
  • ApplicationContext has no close() method. It lives on its child interface ConfigurableApplicationContext, which extends ApplicationContext.
  • The run now ends with "Bean is getting destroyed", whichever of the three styles is used.
Worth knowing (added):
  • context.registerShutdownHook() closes the context automatically when the JVM exits, including on Ctrl+C. Spring Boot does this for you.
  • try-with-resources (try (var ctx = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(…))) also closes it.
  • For @Bean methods, destroyMethod defaults to "(inferred)". A public no-arg close() or shutdown() method on the returned object is called automatically. That's why things like data sources get closed without configuration.

Step 10: the bean is destroyed

After the destruction callbacks, the bean is removed from the container, and nothing is left. With context.close(), the container shuts down.

The full singleton lifecycle

Worth adding: BeanPostProcessor and exact callback order (verified on Spring 7.0.5):
The lecture's steps leave out one piece every lifecycle interview expects: BeanPostProcessor. It's an extension point whose two methods wrap the init phase for every bean:
  • postProcessBeforeInitialization runs before the init callbacks. @PostConstruct is itself run by a built-in post-processor, CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor.
  • postProcessAfterInitialization runs after them. This is where Spring wraps beans in AOP proxies (@Transactional, @Async…).
A bean with every callback printed them in this order: 
constructor
setBeanName               (BeanNameAware)
setApplicationContext     (ApplicationContextAware)
postProcessBeforeInitialization
@PostConstruct
afterPropertiesSet        (InitializingBean)
initMethod
postProcessAfterInitialization
-- bean in use; context.close() --
@PreDestroy
destroy                   (DisposableBean)
destroyMethod
So when several styles are combined, the order is annotation, then interface, then custom method, both for init and for destroy. Singletons are destroyed in reverse dependency order, so a bean is destroyed before the beans it depends on.

What changes for a lazy singleton

With @Lazy on CartService, steps 1–3 are the same: the container starts, reads the config and creates the bean definition. Then everything stops until the bean is first needed, through getBean or as another bean's dependency. With no getBean call, nothing is printed at all; the lifecycle is stuck after "read bean definition". Once it's requested, steps 4–10 run exactly as for an eager singleton, and context.close() still triggers @PreDestroy.

What changes for a prototype

  • Prototypes are always lazy, so steps 4 onward happen only when the bean is requested.
  • Instantiation, DI, Aware callbacks and init callbacks all run normally for each new instance.
  • After that, the object is handed over to the client (the developer's code) and Spring stops managing it. It should now be called an object rather than a bean. It leaves the container, and handling it is your job.
  • So no destruction callbacks run for prototypes. With @Scope("prototype") on CartService, the run prints the constructor, Aware and "Bean is ready" lines, and @PreDestroy is never called, even with context.close().
Why Spring drops prototypes: to avoid memory leaks:
Every getBean creates a new prototype instance. If the container tracked them all so it could destroy them later, it would keep a reference to each one. Garbage collection could then never reclaim them, and repeated getBean calls would fill the heap. So Spring lets them go, and they're destroyed like any Java object: by garbage collection, once unreachable. context.close() does not destroy prototypes.
Consequence: if a prototype holds an expensive resource, you must release it, with the usual Java discipline of try-with-resources or finally. GC reclaims the object's memory, not the file handles or connections it holds.
Lifecycle stepEager singletonLazy singletonPrototype
Bean definition at startupYesYesYes
Instantiate / DI / Aware / initAt startupOn first requestOn every request
Kept in containerYesYesNo: handed to client
Destruction callbacks on close()YesYes (if created)No: GC only

Anticipated question: "Can @PostConstruct resolve a circular dependency?"

Yes. It's a trick question, and again it's a hack. Two @Components, where A's constructor takes a B and B's takes an A, fail with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException. The fix: B gets a plain setter instead of a constructor parameter (no @Autowired), and A hands itself over in @PostConstruct:

@Component
public class A {
    private B b;

    public A(B b) {                 // A still receives B via constructor
        this.b = b;
    }

    @PostConstruct
    public void setB() {
        b.setA(this);               // after A is fully built, give B a reference to A
    }
}

@Component
public class B {
    private A a;                    // no constructor dependency, no @Autowired

    public void setA(A a) {
        this.a = a;
    }
}

Spring creates B (it needs nothing), then A with B injected. Then A's @PostConstruct runs and wires A into B. The app starts with no error.

Why this trick matters in Spring Boot:
Plain Spring Core can already resolve such cycles with field injection. Since Spring Boot 2.6, circular references are prohibited even with field injection (Lecture 6). There you'd need @PostConstruct wiring or @Lazy. But the lecturer's point stands: don't resolve cycles, refactor them away.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Garbage collection uses reachability, not "is anyone referring to it". The lecture describes GC as scanning whether an object is referenced. More precisely, objects are collected when they're unreachable from GC roots (stack variables, static fields…). Two objects that reference only each other are still collected.
  • Init callbacks run for @Bean objects too. @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy inside a class returned from an @Bean method are honoured, so initMethod / destroyMethod are mainly needed for classes you can't annotate.
  • Exceptions in init callbacks fail startup (for eager beans). That's the fail-fast benefit from Lecture 6: a broken cache load or config validation in @PostConstruct stops the app before it serves traffic.
  • Don't rely on AOP inside @PostConstruct. The bean isn't wrapped in its AOP proxy until postProcessAfterInitialization, so @Transactional on a method called from @PostConstruct won't start a transaction. For work that needs a fully started app, listen for ContextRefreshedEvent / ApplicationReadyEvent (Boot), or use SmartInitializingSingleton.
  • Destroy callbacks run only on a graceful shutdown (close(), a shutdown hook, SIGTERM). A crash or kill -9 skips them, so never put critical persistence work only in @PreDestroy.

Lecture 8: XML-Based Configuration

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #8 · 1h11m · Code Army · The legacy way to configure the IoC container

Why look at XML at all?

So far, beans were created and dependencies managed with annotation-based configuration: @Component, @Bean, @ComponentScan, @Autowired. XML-based configuration is the older way, used heavily in legacy code and rarely today.

  • Is it essential? No. The rest of the series uses annotations only, and Spring Boot uses annotations.
  • When it helps: working on a legacy system, or a hybrid one that mixes XML and annotations, or simply understanding how Spring used to work.
  • Seeing how much configuration it once took to write a simple REST API makes it clearer why Spring Boot's auto-configuration matters.

Prerequisite: the annotation-config lectures (5–7). The lecturer isn't a big fan of XML either, since it can get complicated. The goal is to understand the concepts, not to memorize syntax.

The key idea: the container only needs configuration metadata

The IoC container's job doesn't change: create beans, inject dependencies, manage and destroy them (the lifecycle from Lecture 7). To do that it needs configuration metadata: which beans exist and how to build them. That metadata can come from two sources:

The lecture's emphasis:
Whatever the method, the IoC container ultimately has to create bean definitions and manage beans, and for that it needs just one thing: configuration metadata. It doesn't care whether that came from XML or annotations.

Recap: the annotation version

New project xml-based-config-demo, with spring-context 7.0.7. The annotation version, for comparison:

@Component
public class OrderService {
    public void placeOrder() { System.out.println("Order placed"); }
}

@Configuration
@ComponentScan
public class AppConfig { }

ApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class);
OrderService order = context.getBean(OrderService.class);
order.placeOrder();          // Order placed

To switch to XML, remove every annotation: @Component and the AppConfig class. OrderService becomes a plain Java class.

Step 1: ClassPathXmlApplicationContext and beans.xml

ApplicationContext context = new ClassPathXmlApplicationContext("beans.xml");
  • AnnotationConfigApplicationContext reads annotation config. ClassPathXmlApplicationContext reads XML config from the classpath.
  • Instead of an AppConfig class, you pass an XML file name. The name is up to you; beans.xml fits because it defines beans.
  • Where to put it? On the classpath. In a Maven project, anything in src/main/resources ends up there, so create src/main/resources/beans.xml.

The file needs a standard header (the XML declaration plus the <beans> root with its schema). Nobody writes this by hand. Search "XML metadata for Spring 7", open the official Spring docs, and copy the skeleton:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"
       xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
       xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans
           https://www.springframework.org/schema/beans/spring-beans.xsd">

    <!-- bean definitions here -->

</beans>

The schema lines define the rules: which tags you may write.

Step 2: define a bean with <bean>

<bean id="orderService" class="in.strikes.OrderService"/>
  • id is a unique identifier for the bean. It can be anything, but by convention it's the class name in camelCase.
  • class is the fully-qualified class name: the package plus the class (in.strikes.OrderService).
  • No body is needed, so a self-closing tag works.

This line is the XML equivalent of an @Bean method:

@Bean
public OrderService getOrderServiceBean() {
    return new OrderService();
}

An @Bean method needs no id (the method name becomes the bean name) and no class (Java already knows the type). XML has to spell both out.

Proof it works: give OrderService a constructor that prints "Order service created". Running Main prints it immediately, because beans are singleton and eager by default in XML too. The first run failed with FileNotFoundException, because the file was beans.xml but the code passed "bean.xml". The names must match exactly.

Three ways to fetch a bean

// 1. By type
OrderService o1 = context.getBean(OrderService.class);

// 2. By id (or name): returns Object, so a cast is needed
OrderService o2 = (OrderService) context.getBean("orderService");

// 3. By id AND type: no cast, no ambiguity  ← best
OrderService o3 = context.getBean("orderService", OrderService.class);
ApproachFails when
By typeTwo beans of the same class exist: NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
By idThe id is wrong: NoSuchBeanDefinitionException. It also needs a cast.
By id + typeOnly if that id doesn't exist. Recommended.
  • Two beans of one class are allowed: id="orderService" and id="orderService2", both of class OrderService. This is the XML twin of two @Bean methods returning the same type. The constructor prints twice, since two singletons are created, one per definition (Lecture 6). Fetching by type alone then fails.
  • Ids must be unique. Two beans with the same id get an IDE warning ("bean name duplicated") and a startup error.
Correction: beans without an id do get a name (verified on Spring 7.0.5):
The lecture removes the id, sees getBean("orderService") fail, and concludes XML generates no name at all, unlike annotations. In fact Spring generates one: the fully-qualified class name plus #0 (in.strikes.OrderService#0), with the plain class name (in.strikes.OrderService) registered as an alias for the first such bean. The test printed names=[demo.Order#0, …] aliases=[demo.Order], and getBean("demo.Order") worked. What's true is that there's no camelCase default like @Component gives. Always set an id anyway.

id vs name (aliases)

<bean id="orderService"
      name="orderServiceBean orderServiceBean2 orderServiceBean3"
      class="in.strikes.OrderService"/>

The bean can be fetched by orderService or by any of the names. The difference: a bean has exactly one id, but can have many names, called aliases. Separate them with spaces, commas or semicolons.

A second class, PaymentService with pay() printing "Payment done", is defined the same way (id="paymentService"). Fetching both beans and calling pay() then placeOrder() prints "Payment done / Order placed".

Dependency injection in XML

OrderService now depends on PaymentService. placeOrder() calls paymentService.pay() first, so Main only needs OrderService. With annotations, you'd mark both with @Component, and constructor injection needs no @Autowired. In XML, the injection is declared in the bean definition.

Only constructor and setter injection in XML:
XML config supports constructor and setter injection, not field injection. XML can only drive the constructor or call a public setter; it can't reach a private field. (Added:) once you turn on <context:annotation-config/> or component scanning in the XML, @Autowired on fields works again, but that's annotation processing, not XML injection.

Constructor injection: <constructor-arg ref>

public class OrderService {
    private PaymentService paymentService;

    public OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }

    public void placeOrder() {
        paymentService.pay();
        System.out.println("Order placed");
    }
}
<bean id="paymentService" class="in.strikes.PaymentService"/>

<bean id="orderService" class="in.strikes.OrderService">
    <constructor-arg ref="paymentService"/>      <!-- ref = id of another bean -->
</bean>

The container creates paymentService, which has no dependencies. For orderService it sees a constructor argument that references the bean with id paymentService. It finds that bean and effectively does new OrderService(paymentService). Output: "Payment done / Order placed". ref points to another bean; value supplies a literal.

Literal constructor values: value, index, name

public class PaymentService {
    private String type;
    private int retryCount;

    public PaymentService(String type, int retryCount) {
        this.type = type;
        this.retryCount = retryCount;
    }

    public void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment done. Type of payment is " + type
                + " with " + retryCount + " retry counts");
    }
}
<!-- by position (declaration order) -->
<bean id="paymentService" class="in.strikes.PaymentService">
    <constructor-arg value="UPI"/>
    <constructor-arg value="3"/>
</bean>

<!-- by index: tag order no longer matters -->
<constructor-arg index="1" value="3"/>
<constructor-arg index="0" value="UPI"/>

<!-- by parameter name -->
<constructor-arg name="type" value="UPI"/>
<constructor-arg name="retryCount" value="3"/>

Output: "Payment done. Type of payment is UPI with 3 retry counts". Spring converts the string "3" to int. IntelliJ may show a false warning, "Could not autowire. No beans of String type found", because it doesn't read the XML. Ignore it.

Worth knowing: name-based matching needs -parameters (verified on Spring 7.0.5):
Parameter names aren't in compiled bytecode unless you compile with -parameters. Spring 6.1 removed its old debug-info fallback. Without the flag, name="…" can't be matched, and Spring falls back to declaration order. In the test, listing retryCount before type failed with "Could not convert … 'UPI' to int". With <maven.compiler.parameters>true</maven.compiler.parameters> the same XML worked. Spring Boot's parent POM enables this flag, and IntelliJ may too, which can hide the issue. index always works.

Setter injection: <property>

public class OrderService {
    private PaymentService paymentService;

    public void setPaymentService(PaymentService paymentService) {   // no @Autowired
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }
    ...
}
<bean id="orderService" class="in.strikes.OrderService">
    <property name="paymentService" ref="paymentService"/>
</bean>
  • Setter injection works as in Lecture 7: beans are created first, then Spring calls the setter.
  • ref is the id of the bean to inject.
  • name is the property name, from which Spring derives the setter by convention: paymentService means calling setPaymentService(…).

Proof it's the setter, not the field: rename the setter to setPaymentServiceBean and the XML must say name="paymentServiceBean", even though the field is still called paymentService. Spring prefixes "set" itself. It's the JavaBeans property naming convention.

Multiple implementations: no @Primary needed

PaymentService becomes an interface in a payment package, with UpiPaymentService ("Paying via UPI") and CardPaymentService ("Paying via card"). OrderService takes a PaymentService in its constructor.

<bean id="upiPaymentService"  class="in.strikes.payment.UpiPaymentService"/>
<bean id="cardPaymentService" class="in.strikes.payment.CardPaymentService"/>

<bean id="orderService" class="in.strikes.OrderService">
    <constructor-arg ref="cardPaymentService"/>     <!-- → "Paying via card" -->
</bean>

With annotations, two PaymentService beans confuse the container and you need @Primary or @Qualifier. In XML the ref names the exact bean, so there's no ambiguity. Switch the ref to upiPaymentService and you get "Paying via UPI". The same works with <property ref>.

XML does have primary="true" on a <bean>. It isn't needed when you reference by id, and it matters only when wiring by type.

Worth knowing (added):
  • XML also supports autowiring without explicit refs: autowire="byType", "byName" or "constructor" on a <bean>, or default-autowire on <beans>. autowire-candidate="false" excludes a bean from by-type matching.
  • With autowiring, the same ambiguity as annotations reappears, and primary="true" becomes relevant.

Scope: scope="prototype"

<bean id="userService" class="in.strikes.UserService" scope="prototype"/>

With a UserService whose constructor prints "User service created": as a singleton (the default), it prints at startup. With scope="prototype", nothing prints until context.getBean(UserService.class). It's the equivalent of @Scope("prototype"), and all of Lecture 6's scope behaviour applies.

Precision note:
The lecture adds, in passing, that a prototype bean is also created at startup when a singleton depends on it. That holds only because the singleton is created eagerly and needs one prototype instance injected at that moment. The prototype itself is still created on demand.

Injecting collections: <list>, <set>, <map>

// String version first: <constructor-arg value="Aditya"/> → getUsername() prints Aditya
public class UserService {
    private List<String> userNames;
    public UserService(List<String> userNames) { this.userNames = userNames; }
    public List<String> getUserNames() { return userNames; }
}
<bean id="userService" class="in.strikes.UserService">
    <constructor-arg name="userNames">
        <list>
            <value>Aditya</value>
            <value>Rohit</value>
            <value>Rohan</value>
        </list>
    </constructor-arg>
</bean>

<!-- a Set: same shape with <set> -->
<!-- a Map: -->
<map>
    <entry key="1" value="Aditya"/>
    <entry key="2" value="Rohit"/>
</map>

getUserNames() prints [Aditya, Rohit, Rohan]. The first run failed because the getter's return type was still String; it must be List<String>. Java's collections framework has XML counterparts: <list>, <set>, <map> with <entry> (a map key–value pair is an "entry" in Java too), plus <props> for Properties (added). The Java parameter type must match: a <map> needs a Map parameter.

Lifecycle callbacks: init-method and destroy-method

public class UserService {
    public UserService() { System.out.println("User service created"); }
    public void init()    { System.out.println("Post construct phase"); }
    public void cleanUp() { System.out.println("Pre destroy phase"); }
}
<bean id="userService" class="in.strikes.UserService"
      init-method="init" destroy-method="cleanUp"/>
ClassPathXmlApplicationContext context = new ClassPathXmlApplicationContext("beans.xml");
UserService user = context.getBean(UserService.class);
context.close();       // ApplicationContext has no close(); use the concrete class (or ConfigurableApplicationContext)
User service created
Post construct phase
Pre destroy phase
  • The method names are up to you. The XML says which is the init (post-construct) method and which is the destroy (pre-destroy) method. It's the equivalent of @Bean(initMethod, destroyMethod) or @PostConstruct / @PreDestroy.
  • Without context.close(), the destroy method never runs.
  • With scope="prototype", cleanUp is not called, because the container doesn't manage prototypes after handing them out (Lecture 7).

Splitting XML across files: <import>

One XML file grows huge, so legacy projects split it. For example, beans.xml holds payment and order beans, beans2.xml holds user beans, and a parent appConfig.xml imports both. Each file needs the same header.

<!-- appConfig.xml -->
<beans ...same header...>
    <import resource="beans.xml"/>
    <import resource="beans2.xml"/>
</beans>

// Main
new ClassPathXmlApplicationContext("appConfig.xml");

Hybrid XML + annotations (migrations)

Old company projects are often pure XML, and migrations to annotations happen gradually, not all at once. So you'll meet hybrid setups. There's still one container, not two: you keep the XML context and add component scanning inside the XML. The container then builds beans from both the XML definitions and the @Component classes.

<!-- needs xmlns:context and the spring-context.xsd schema in the header -->
<context:component-scan base-package="in.strikes"/>

(Added:) the reverse direction exists too. From a Java config class, @ImportResource("classpath:beans.xml") loads legacy XML bean definitions into an annotation-based context, which is common in Spring Boot apps with old XML.

The IoC container doesn't care:
XML file or @Configuration class, it's all bean definitions to the container. Hybrid code looks complicated, but the same concepts run underneath.

Annotation vs XML: side by side

ConceptAnnotationXML
ContainerAnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class)ClassPathXmlApplicationContext("beans.xml")
Declare a bean@Component / @Bean<bean id="…" class="…"/>
Default namecamelCase class name / method nameFully-qualified class name + #0 (set id!)
Aliases@Bean({"a", "b"})name="a b"
Constructor DIConstructor parameter (@Autowired optional)<constructor-arg ref/value/index/name>
Setter DI@Autowired on the setter<property name ref/value>
Field DI@Autowired on the fieldNot possible in pure XML
Choosing among candidates@Primary / @QualifierReference the exact id (primary="true" exists)
Scope@Scope("prototype")scope="prototype"
Lazy@Lazylazy-init="true" (added)
Init / destroy@PostConstruct / @PreDestroyinit-method / destroy-method
Scanning@ComponentScan<context:component-scan/>
Split config@Import<import resource/>

Pros and cons of XML config

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Java classes stay plain, with no @Autowired or @Component clutter. All wiring lives in one place.One file grows very large and has to be split.
Wiring can change without recompiling Java (added).Verbose and harder to read.
Can wire third-party classes you can't annotate, like @Bean does.(Added:) no compile-time checking. A typo in a class name or property is found only at startup, and IDE refactors can miss string references.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Namespace shortcuts. The p: and c: namespaces shorten XML: <bean id="o" class="…" p:paymentService-ref="paymentService"/> or c:type="UPI". They're common in older codebases.
  • Other XML context classes. FileSystemXmlApplicationContext loads XML from a file path instead of the classpath. GenericXmlApplicationContext is the more flexible modern variant.
  • Inner beans. A <bean> nested inside <constructor-arg> or <property> is an anonymous bean used only there, so no id is needed.
  • Same lifecycle, same pitfalls. Circular constructor dependencies fail in XML too, prototype destroy callbacks aren't called, and singletons are per bean definition. Everything from Lectures 5–7 applies unchanged.

Lecture 9: How Spring Boot Manages Beans — @SpringBootApplication & Auto-Configuration

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #9 · 1h · Code Army · From Spring Core's manual setup to Spring Boot's auto-configuration

From Spring Core to Spring Boot

Lectures 5–8 used Spring Core only, with annotation config (@Component, @Bean, @Configuration) or XML, and no auto-configuration. This lecture shows how Spring Boot's IoC container manages beans and how it makes life easier with auto-configuration, so you can focus straight on business logic.

  • Boot still uses annotation-based configuration. The annotations (@Component, @Primary, @Qualifier…) and the bean lifecycle work exactly as before.
  • What disappears is the manual setup you did in Spring Core.

Prerequisite: how Spring Core manages beans (Lectures 5–7).

Recap: everything Spring Core made you do by hand

Project spring-core-demo, a Maven project with only spring-context. OrderService depends on PaymentService through its constructor (no @Autowired needed with a single constructor). placeOrder() calls pay(), which prints "Payment done", then prints "Order placed".

@Configuration
@ComponentScan("in.strikes")
public class AppConfig {
    @Bean
    public UserService getUserServiceBean() { return new UserService(); }
}

ApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class);
OrderService order = context.getBean(OrderService.class);
order.placeOrder();          // Payment done / Order placed

The first run failed with "no context", because the config class hadn't been passed to the constructor yet. The manual steps, every time:

  1. Create the IoC container yourself, choosing its type (annotation or XML), and keep a reference to it.
  2. Put @Component on every class Spring should manage.
  3. Write a config class with @Configuration + @ComponentScan and the package name, plus any @Bean methods.
  4. Pass that config class to the container.
  5. Call context.getBean(…) to reach a bean and call its method.

The container then holds OrderService, PaymentService and UserService, with the dependency autowired. These steps look simple for plain Spring Core, but Spring MVC web apps (built on servlets, covered later) need much more configuration. Spring Boot automates all of it.

Spring Boot does not mean "web app":
A common confusion is that Spring Boot is only for web applications. It isn't. Boot can build web apps by adding web dependencies, and it can sit on top of Spring MVC, but it's independent of Spring MVC. Its job is to automate the configuration of whatever Spring features you use. This lecture builds a plain console (non-web) Boot app with the same example.

Creating a Spring Boot project: two ways

1. A plain Maven project plus spring-boot-starter

Create a Maven project spring-boot-core-demo. Instead of spring-context, add the Boot starter from mvnrepository: "spring-boot-starter". Not -web, which is for web apps, and not -test. Pick a 4.x version, e.g. 4.0.5.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
    <version>4.0.5</version>
</dependency>
  • IntelliJ flagged a known vulnerability in that version. The lecture chose Ignore vulnerability, which is fine for a demo but not for production.
  • A starter is a bundle of dependencies. The Maven Dependencies view shows a whole tree underneath it: spring-boot-starter-logging, spring-boot-autoconfigure, spring-core, spring-context and more. They're all transitive, so you'd otherwise download each by hand.

2. Spring Initializr (preferred)

At start.spring.io (as in Lecture 2), choose:

  • Java, Maven, Spring Boot 4.1.0.
  • Group in.strikes, artifact spring-boot-core-demo-2.
  • Jar, Properties, Java 21.
  • No dependencies. The basic spring-boot-starter is always included.

Generate, unzip and open. The usual layout: src/main/java/in/strikes/springbootcoredemo2/SpringBootCoreDemo2Application.java (groupId + artifactId as the package) and src/test.

The generated pom.xml: why no versions?

  • It has two dependencies:
    • spring-boot-starter.
    • spring-boot-starter-test, for tests; not needed here.
  • Unlike the hand-made project, neither has a <version>.
  • The reason is a <parent> tag: spring-boot-starter-parent. Its parent is spring-boot-dependencies, whose parent is the Super POM (Lecture 3).
Why the parent POM matters:
A real Boot app uses many dependencies: starter-web, a MySQL driver, Hibernate, JDBC… Each has its own version, and only certain versions work together. Picked by hand from mvnrepository, you'd have to research which version of spring-boot-starter fits which version of Spring JDBC, and so on for 10–12 libraries, redoing it at every mismatch. That's hectic.
Boot solves it with spring-boot-starter-parent. It holds all the Boot-related configuration, including tested, compatible versions. Add spring-boot-starter-web or any Boot dependency without a version, and Maven takes the version from the parent. Whatever the child pom doesn't state comes from the parent.

The same works in a hand-made Maven project if you add the <parent> tag. (Added:) if your project already has another parent, import spring-boot-dependencies as a BOM instead, via <dependencyManagement> with <type>pom</type><scope>import</scope>. That gives the version management without the parent. The starter parent also sets defaults such as the Java version, -parameters compilation (Lecture 8) and plugin configuration.

The same app in Spring Boot: no config class, no container setup

Copy OrderService and PaymentService, both still @Component, into the Initializr project's package. The generated main class:

@SpringBootApplication
public class SpringBootCoreDemo2Application {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ApplicationContext context =
                SpringApplication.run(SpringBootCoreDemo2Application.class, args);

        OrderService orderService = context.getBean(OrderService.class);
        orderService.placeOrder();          // Payment done / Order placed
    }
}
  • No new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext. Step into SpringApplication.run and you'll see it returns a ConfigurableApplicationContext, a sub-interface of ApplicationContext. The IoC container is already started by that line; the original code simply didn't capture the return value.
  • No config class and no @ComponentScan. Yet both beans were created and the dependency was wired.
Don't use getBean like this in Spring Boot:
Pulling beans out of the container is the Spring Core way. In Boot, you let Boot drive everything. In a web app, placeOrder() would be triggered by an endpoint such as /order mapped to it (Lecture 2). For a non-web app there's another way to have Boot call your code at startup. That's in the next lecture; it's CommandLineRunner / ApplicationRunner.

Inside @SpringBootApplication: three annotations in one

Ctrl-click @SpringBootApplication. It's a composed annotation carrying:

  • Meta-annotations such as @Target, @Retention, @Documented and @Inherited. Ignore these for now; custom annotations get a separate Java video.
  • Three that matter:
    • @SpringBootConfiguration.
    • @EnableAutoConfiguration.
    • @ComponentScan (with some exclude filters).

Writing @SpringBootApplication is equivalent to writing those three yourself. It's a convenience parent annotation.

@SpringBootConfiguration: the main class is the config class

  • In Spring Core, a separate AppConfig with @Configuration told the container its rules. @SpringBootConfiguration is Boot's special version of @Configuration. It's meta-annotated with @Configuration and so is ultimately a @Component too.
  • It marks the primary configuration class. You can still create more @Configuration classes, but there's one main one.
  • It sits on the main class, so the main class itself is a configuration class. You can write @Bean methods right there:
@SpringBootApplication
public class SpringBootCoreDemo2Application {

    @Bean
    public UserService getUserServiceBean() {      // legal: the main class is a config class
        return new UserService();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) { ... }
}

@ComponentScan: Boot's package convention

  • It's already on the main class via @SpringBootApplication, so you never write it.
  • No package is given, so Boot uses its convention: scan the package of the main class (in.strikes.springbootcoredemo2) and all its sub-packages. OrderService and PaymentService are found because they live there.
  • A class in a sibling or outside package (e.g. in.strikes.newpackage) is not scanned, even with @Component. That's the classic "my bean / endpoint isn't found" bug from Lecture 2.
  • It's the same rule as Spring Core: keep your components in or under the config class's package.

Boot is an opinionated framework. Follow its conventions and everything works; disagree, and you override them:

@SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackages = "in.strikes")   // scan the parent package instead

@EnableAutoConfiguration: "look at my project and create what seems important"

So far there were two ways to put beans in the container:

  1. @Component on a class (class level), found by scanning.
  2. @Bean on a method in a configuration class (method level). This covers classes you can't annotate, like read-only third-party classes, or complex creation.

Either way, you tell Spring which objects to manage; without that, nothing is created. Spring Boot adds a third way: auto-configuration classes.

// written by Spring Boot (or a library author), not by you
@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnClass(WebClassA.class)          // only if this class is on the classpath
public class SomeAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean                 // only if the user didn't define one
    public WebClassA getWebClassA() {
        return new WebClassA();
    }
}
  • They look like ordinary config classes with @Bean methods, but they're marked @AutoConfiguration and ship inside Spring Boot, or inside a library. You normally don't write them; they're internal.
  • When the container starts, Boot creates their beans automatically, without being asked. They only take effect because @EnableAutoConfiguration is on, which it is by default via @SpringBootApplication.

Why Boot creates beans you didn't ask for

Adding a Maven dependency brings its classes (.class files) into External Libraries, but no beans are created from them automatically. For example, spring-boot-starter brings a JsonParser interface with implementations. To have the container manage one, you'd write it yourself:

@Bean
public JsonParser getJsonParserBean() {
    return new BasicJsonParser();          // an interface can't be instantiated; pick an implementation
}

That's fine for one class. But standard dependencies like spring-boot-starter-web bring many classes whose beans must exist for things to work: the embedded Tomcat, MVC infrastructure, JSON conversion. With plain Spring MVC you'd configure all of those by hand. Boot instead ships auto-configuration classes for standard libraries (web MVC, data/JDBC, Hibernate, Jackson, testing, Mockito…). Add the dependency, and the needed beans appear.

Demo: just adding the web starter starts Tomcat

  1. Run the console app: "Payment done / Order placed". The logs show "Starting SpringBootCoreDemo2Application… No active profile set… Started…", with no Tomcat, since no web dependency is present.
  2. Add only this dependency (no version, thanks to the parent) and reload Maven: 
    <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
    Its tree now includes Jackson and embedded Tomcat.
  3. Run again, without changing any code. The log now says "Tomcat started on port 8080".

Beans you never declared were created and managed behind the scenes. That's @EnableAutoConfiguration at work.

Version note (Spring Boot 4):
Boot 4's Initializr generates spring-boot-starter-webmvc (Lecture 3). The older spring-boot-starter-web used in this demo still resolved and worked with the Boot 4 parent, and it pulled in Tomcat. For new Boot 4 projects, prefer the webmvc name that Initializr uses.

Conditions: when an auto-configuration applies

AnnotationMeaning
@AutoConfiguration"Spring Boot, create the beans in this class yourself."
@ConditionalOnClass(X.class)Only if class X is on the classpath, i.e. the dependency that provides it is present. For example, web beans only when the web starter is added.
@ConditionalOnMissingBeanOnly if the container doesn't already have such a bean. If you defined your own (e.g. your own @Bean of that type), Boot backs off and uses yours.
@BeanThe bean to create when the conditions pass.

Library authors can ship their own auto-configurations too. If you build a "payment gateway" library, an @AutoConfiguration class inside it makes any Spring Boot app using your JAR create its beans automatically, with no setup from the user.

How auto-configuration is actually loaded (added)

Precision note: auto-configurations are not component-scanned:
The lecture's mental model ("Boot looks for classes annotated @AutoConfiguration") needs one correction. Boot does not find them by scanning. @SpringBootApplication's scan even excludes them, via AutoConfigurationExcludeFilter. Instead, @EnableAutoConfiguration reads a list from each JAR's
META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports
(Boot 2.7+/3+; older versions used META-INF/spring.factories). Every class listed there is a candidate, and its @Conditional… annotations decide whether it applies. So a library's auto-configuration only works if the library registers it in that file. Candidates are processed after your own configuration, which is why @ConditionalOnMissingBean can see your beans and back off.

Summary: what Spring Boot removed

Spring Core (manual)Spring Boot
new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class)SpringApplication.run(Main.class, args) starts and returns the context
Separate @Configuration classThe main class is the config class (@SpringBootConfiguration)
@ComponentScan("pkg")Built in: main class package and sub-packages
Hand-written beans for library infrastructureAuto-configured, conditionally
Hand-picked, version-matched dependenciesStarters + spring-boot-starter-parent manage versions
Deploy to an external server (web)Embedded Tomcat auto-configured

Everything else stays the same: @Component, @Bean, @Primary, @Qualifier, scopes and the lifecycle. From here the series prefers Spring Boot, since Spring Core is understood. Spring MVC comes next, learnt through Boot. Knowing the internals is the point: Boot is easy to use, but its depth is what matters. The next lecture covers application.properties and the proper way to run code at startup instead of getBean.

Anticipated question: "How does Spring Boot auto-configure everything?"

A favourite interview question. A good answer:

  1. @SpringBootApplication includes @EnableAutoConfiguration.
  2. That loads the auto-configuration classes listed in AutoConfiguration.imports in Boot's own JARs and any library JARs.
  3. Each is guarded by conditions such as @ConditionalOnClass (is the library on the classpath?), @ConditionalOnMissingBean (did the user already define one?) and @ConditionalOnProperty (is a property set?).
  4. Only matching configurations contribute beans, which is why adding a starter "just works" and why your own bean overrides Boot's default.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • See what was auto-configured. Run with --debug or set debug=true in application.properties to print the condition evaluation report: which auto-configurations matched, and why others didn't. It's the first tool for "why is/isn't this bean here?".
  • Turn an auto-configuration off. Use @SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class) or spring.autoconfigure.exclude=… in properties.
  • The context type depends on the classpath. SpringApplication detects the application type: plain (non-web), servlet web or reactive. It then creates the matching context. Without the web starter it's a plain annotation context; with it, a servlet web-server context that starts Tomcat. That's why the same code suddenly started Tomcat.
  • Only one @SpringBootConfiguration per application. Test support (@SpringBootTest) searches upward from the test's package to find it.
  • Hand-set versions override the parent. Writing a <version> on a Boot-managed dependency (as in the hand-made Maven project) takes precedence over the BOM and can break compatibility. Leave versions to the parent unless you have a specific reason.

Lecture 10: application.properties, @Value, @ConfigurationProperties & Startup Runners

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #10 · 36 min · Code Army · Externalized configuration and the right way to run code at startup

Two topics that finish the Boot core

This continues Lecture 9. It covers two things:

  1. application.properties: supplying values to your code from outside it.
  2. How to start your own logic in a Boot app. So far we pulled a bean from the context with getBean and called its method. That isn't good practice in Boot: Boot wants to be a black box driven by annotations and auto-configuration, not something you reach into. There's a proper hook instead.

Setup: a fresh Initializr project, demo, with the same choices as Lecture 9:

  • Java, Maven, Boot 4.1.0.
  • Package in.strikes.demo.
  • Jar, Properties, Java 21.
  • No dependencies, so the pom has just spring-boot-starter and -test.

Printing "Hello World" in main confirms it runs.

The starting point: hard-coded values

@Component
public class PaymentGateway {
    private String type;          // e.g. Paytm, Razorpay
    private int retryCount;
    // getters and setters
}

// main (the getBean way, for now)
ApplicationContext context = SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);
PaymentGateway paymentGateway = context.getBean(PaymentGateway.class);
paymentGateway.setType("Paytm");
paymentGateway.setRetryCount(5);
System.out.println(paymentGateway.getType());         // Paytm
System.out.println(paymentGateway.getRetryCount());   // 5

The problem: suppose this ships, and later the gateway switches from Paytm to Razorpay. You'd edit the Java code, recompile and redeploy. It's better not to hard-code such values, but to supply them from a configurable file outside the Java code.

What application.properties is

  • It lives in src/main/resources. Initializr already put one line in it: spring.application.name=demo.
  • It's a non-Java file of key=value pairs, much like a map.
  • It's a configuration file. Don't confuse it with a @Configuration class, which is Java code declaring @Beans. This is plain data.
  • It's special because it can supply values to your code from outside. Spring Boot loads it automatically, and its values can be injected anywhere.

Other external sources of configuration:

  • application.yml. Initializr offers "Properties" or "YAML".
  • Environment variables.
  • Command-line arguments.
  • Java system properties.

None of these are part of your Java code, and all of them can provide values to it.

# application.properties
spring.application.name=demo
payment-gateway.type=Paytm
payment-gateway.retry-count=5
Precision note: "change the file and the value changes":
The lecture says that if you edit the file, the new value is reflected, and that the file loads "whenever the code compiles". More precisely, Boot reads application.properties at application startup. A change takes effect on the next restart, not live. Also, a copy packaged inside the JAR still needs a rebuild. The real no-recompile benefit comes from overriding values from outside the JAR, with an external application.properties, an environment variable or a command-line argument (see precedence below). Or from keeping one build and changing only configuration per environment.

Injecting one value: @Value("${…}")

@Component
public class PaymentGateway {
    private String type;
    private int retryCount;

    public PaymentGateway(@Value("${payment-gateway.type}") String type,
                          @Value("${payment-gateway.retry-count}") int retryCount) {
        this.type = type;
        this.retryCount = retryCount;
    }
    // getters ...
}
  • The syntax is @Value("${key}"), with curly braces. The lecture first wrote parentheses and got UnsatisfiedDependencyException / TypeMismatchException / NumberFormatException. The error messages pointed straight at it.
  • The setType / setRetryCount calls in main are removed, and the output is still Paytm and 5. Spring converts "5" to int.
  • @Value works on constructor parameters, setters or fields, just like @Autowired. On fields: @Value("${payment-gateway.type}") private String type;.
  • It is dependency injection. PaymentGateway depends on these values, and the property file provides them instead of you. Where @Autowired would inject a bean (say an OrderService), @Value injects plain values such as String or int. The String isn't a primitive, as the lecture notes, but it's a plain value here.

Missing key: if payment-gateway.type isn't in any property source, bean creation fails: "Injection of autowired dependencies failed" (could not resolve placeholder). The error itself shows it's a form of autowiring. Fix it with a default after a colon:

@Value("${payment-gateway.type:Razorpay}")        // Razorpay if the key is absent
@Value("${payment-gateway.retry-count:3}")

If the key exists, its value wins; otherwise the default is used. @Value can also read YAML, environment variables and the other sources.

Many values: @ConfigurationProperties

A real config class may hold many settings: type, retry count, enabled or disabled, timeout… A separate @Value for each is tedious and error-prone, since it's easy to map a value to the wrong field. @ConfigurationProperties binds a whole group of keys by prefix onto a class's fields.

# application.properties
payment-property.type=Paytm
payment-property.retry-count=5
payment-property.enabled=true
payment-property.timeout=3000
@Component
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "payment-property")
public class PaymentProperties {
    private String type;
    private int retryCount;       // bound from retry-count
    private boolean enabled;
    private int timeout;
    // getters and setters (binding uses the setters)
}
  • Every key starting with payment-property. is matched to the field of the same name.
  • The prefix must be in canonical (kebab-case) form. paymentProperty was rejected ("prefix must be in canonical form"), and payment-property works.
  • Relaxed binding: retry-count in the file binds to the camelCase field retryCount. Write camelCase in Java and kebab-case in the file.
  • The lecture first named the boolean field isEnabled, which caused a mismatch. Renaming it to enabled (key enabled, getter isEnabled()) follows the JavaBeans convention for booleans.

The standard pattern: a properties class that only holds config, injected into the class that actually uses it. PaymentGateway exposes getters that delegate:

@Component
public class PaymentGateway {
    private final PaymentProperties paymentProperties;

    public PaymentGateway(PaymentProperties paymentProperties) {   // constructor injection
        this.paymentProperties = paymentProperties;
    }

    public String getType()      { return paymentProperties.getType(); }
    public int getRetryCount()   { return paymentProperties.getRetryCount(); }
    public boolean isEnabled()   { return paymentProperties.isEnabled(); }
    public int getTimeout()      { return paymentProperties.getTimeout(); }

    public void print() {
        System.out.println(getType());
        System.out.println(getRetryCount());
        System.out.println(isEnabled());
        System.out.println(getTimeout());
    }
}
Paytm
5
true
3000

You could read PaymentProperties directly. The lecture routes through PaymentGateway on purpose: business code talks to the class that uses the config, not to the raw properties holder. You'll see this pattern constantly in enterprise code.

@Value vs @ConfigurationProperties

@Value@ConfigurationProperties
BindsOne key per annotationAll keys under a prefix, onto a class
Best forOne or two valuesGroups of related settings
Defaults${key:default}Field initializers (private int timeout = 3000;)
Relaxed binding (kebab ↔ camel)Limited: write the key as it appearsYes
Type safety and validation (added)Per fieldWhole object; add @Validated + @NotNull, @Min…
SpEL (added)Yes: #{…} expressionsNo

Starting your code properly: ApplicationRunner / CommandLineRunner

So far main captured the context, called getBean(PaymentGateway.class) and called print(). That's interacting with the IoC container directly, which we want to avoid. In a web app, print() would be triggered by an endpoint (localhost:8080/print mapped to it, as in Lecture 2). In a console app you need a method that runs automatically when the app starts.

@Component
public class DemoRunner implements ApplicationRunner {
    private final PaymentGateway paymentGateway;

    public DemoRunner(PaymentGateway paymentGateway) {      // no @Autowired needed
        this.paymentGateway = paymentGateway;
    }

    @Override
    public void run(ApplicationArguments args) {
        paymentGateway.print();                             // runs automatically at startup
    }
}

@SpringBootApplication
public class DemoApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);   // no context, no getBean
    }
}
  • ApplicationRunner is a functional interface with one method, run. Implement it on a @Component, and Spring Boot calls run() automatically when the application starts.
  • main shrinks to one line, and the output is still Paytm 5 true 3000.

CommandLineRunner does the same job. Its run takes raw arguments instead:

@Component
public class DemoRunner implements CommandLineRunner {
    ...
    @Override
    public void run(String... args) {       // varargs: zero, one or many strings
        paymentGateway.print();
    }
}
ApplicationRunnerCommandLineRunner
run parameterApplicationArguments, parsedString... args, raw
Argument handlinggetOptionNames(), containsOption("x"), getOptionValues("x") for --x=value, plus getNonOptionArgs()You parse the strings yourself
When it runsAfter the context is fully started (all singletons created), before SpringApplication.run returns

The arguments are the same command-line arguments that main(String[] args) receives. They're rarely used in this series, since web apps come next.

Running from the terminal

mvn spring-boot:run

This builds and runs the app, and the same output appears after "BUILD SUCCESS". It needs Maven installed (Lecture 3) or the generated wrapper ./mvnw spring-boot:run. It works because Initializr's pom includes spring-boot-maven-plugin.

Worth knowing: passing values at launch (added): 
java -jar target/demo-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar --payment-property.type=Razorpay
./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.arguments="--payment-property.type=Razorpay"
PAYMENT_PROPERTY_TYPE=Razorpay java -jar target/demo-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar     # env var (relaxed binding)
Each of these overrides payment-property.type without touching the code or the packaged file. That's the real "configure without recompiling". The --x=value options also show up in ApplicationArguments.

Property source precedence (added)

The same key can be set in several places. Boot applies a fixed order, higher wins (simplified):

PrioritySource
1 (highest)Command-line arguments (--key=value)
2Java system properties (-Dkey=value)
3OS environment variables (KEY_NAME)
4Profile-specific files (application-prod.properties)
5application.properties / .yml outside the JAR (e.g. in the working directory or ./config/)
6 (lowest)application.properties / .yml packaged inside the JAR

Profiles (spring.profiles.active=prod) let one build carry dev, test and prod settings. Environment variables use relaxed binding: PAYMENT_PROPERTY_RETRY_COUNT maps to payment-property.retry-count.

The same config in YAML

# application.yml (equivalent to the properties above)
payment-property:
  type: Paytm
  retry-count: 5
  enabled: true
  timeout: 3000

YAML nests keys by indentation instead of repeating the prefix. It's handy for deep or list-valued config, but it's whitespace-sensitive. Use one format per project to avoid confusion. If both files exist, .properties takes precedence for the same key.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Registering @ConfigurationProperties without @Component. @EnableConfigurationProperties(PaymentProperties.class) on a config class, or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the main class, registers it. Many teams prefer that, so properties classes aren't treated like ordinary components.
  • Immutable properties with records. @ConfigurationProperties("payment-property") public record PaymentProperties(String type, int retryCount, boolean enabled, int timeout) {} binds through the constructor: no setters, and the object can't be changed afterwards.
  • IDE auto-complete for your own keys. Add the spring-boot-configuration-processor dependency (optional). It generates metadata so IntelliJ suggests and validates payment-property.* keys.
  • Several runners. If you have more than one ApplicationRunner / CommandLineRunner, order them with @Order(1), @Order(2)… An exception thrown from a runner fails startup.
  • Never put secrets in a committed application.properties. Passwords and API keys belong in environment variables or a secrets manager, referenced as ${DB_PASSWORD}.

Lecture 11: CRUD Mini-Project, Part 1 — Architecture, Entity & the First Endpoint

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #11 · 1h37m · Code Army · Client + Spring Boot server + MySQL; Controller–Service–Repository

Why a CRUD project matters

This mini-project connects a Spring Boot app to a database and performs CRUD: Create, Read, Update, Delete. It sounds simple, but CRUD is the backbone of every backend:

  • Instagram or YouTube create content (create).
  • Scrolling reels is a read.
  • Editing or removing a post is an update or a delete.

Once CRUD in Spring Boot is easy for you, any business logic on top becomes manageable. For the first time, client, server and database work together.

Some things, like how Spring Data JPA writes SQL for you, will feel magical. That's intentional. This lecture gives the overview, and later lectures open up JDBC, Hibernate and Spring MVC internals. Hold on to your curiosity until then.

The finished app (preview)

Postman plays the client. The MySQL database student_crud_db has a student table, initially empty. Part 1 (this lecture) builds only the create endpoint, with a stubbed repository. The rest, including the real database, comes in the next lecture.

RequestEffect
POST localhost:8080/api/students + JSON body (name, email, rollNumber, age, subject)Inserts a row, responds with the saved student
GET /api/students/1Returns student 1
GET /api/studentsReturns a list of all students
PUT /api/students/1 + full JSON bodyUpdates student 1 (e.g. age 28 → 29, subject Spring Boot → Spring Framework)
DELETE /api/students/1Deletes the row permanently: "Student deleted permanently"
PATCH /api/students/2/soft-deleteSoft delete: sets is_deleted = 1. The row stays but is hidden from reads

The IntelliJ console shows the SQL that ran for each request (insert, select, update…). We never write that SQL ourselves; Spring Data JPA generates it.

The big picture: client, server, database

HTTP methods vs CRUD operations
CRUD operationHTTP methodMeaning
CreatePOSTCreate a new resource
ReadGETRetrieve data (no body)
UpdatePUTUpdate an existing resource
DeleteDELETERemove a resource
(Partial update)PATCHChange part of a resource. Used here for soft delete
  • The client could be a React or vanilla-JS frontend, a browser or a mobile app. There's no frontend in this project, so Postman sends requests. It's used throughout the series and supports GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS…
  • Host: localhost:8080, since both Postman and the server run on your machine (Lectures 1–2). Deployed, this would be a real domain such as codearmy.in.
  • Endpoint: the part after the host, e.g. /api/students. A full URL maps to a method in a class, so /api/teachers would hit a different method (a 404 here, since none exists).
  • Request parts: method (POST), host, endpoint, headers, and a JSON body.
  • Headers here: Accept: application/json (the response format the client accepts) and Content-Type: application/json (the format of the body sent). Postman adds sensible defaults.

Requirements

  • Postman, from its website (Windows / Mac).
  • A MySQL server. It's a relational (SQL) database; PostgreSQL or Oracle would work equally for simple CRUD, and later projects use Postgres and H2. Install and set a password; the steps are in the lecturer's notes.
  • A GUI client to view tables, instead of the terminal or command prompt:
    • DBeaver, used here: free, open source, cross-platform.
    • MySQL Workbench, the official one but more complex.
    • Sequel Ace, Mac only.

Project setup: three dependencies

On start.spring.io:

  • Java, Maven, Boot 4.1.0.
  • Group in.strikes, artifact crud-spring-boot-demo.
  • Jar, Properties, Java 21.
Initializr dependencyStarter in pomWhy
Spring Webspring-boot-starter-webmvcWeb app: controllers and embedded Tomcat
Spring Data JPAspring-boot-starter-data-jpaTalk to the DB without writing SQL. JPA = Jakarta Persistence API (formerly Java Persistence API), with Hibernate underneath
MySQL Drivermysql-connector-j (runtime scope)The JDBC driver that connects to MySQL

The pom also contains data-jpa-test and webmvc-test, which are unused here.

First run fails: "Failed to configure a DataSource"

APPLICATION FAILED TO START
Failed to configure a DataSource: 'url' attribute is not specified
and no embedded datasource could be configured.
  • Just adding the dependencies broke startup. That's auto-configuration (Lecture 9): JPA and a MySQL driver on the classpath make Boot assume you want a database, so it tries to create a DataSource bean.
  • A DataSource needs a URL, username and password, normally in application.properties. None are there yet.

Temporary workaround (the real fix comes next lecture) is to exclude that auto-configuration:

@SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)
public class CrudSpringBootDemoApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(CrudSpringBootDemoApplication.class, args);
    }
}

Now the app starts, and the logs show "Tomcat started on port 8080". localhost:8080 in a browser shows the Whitelabel Error Page, because no endpoint is mapped yet.

Worth knowing (added):
The proper fix is to set spring.datasource.url, spring.datasource.username and spring.datasource.password, which the next part does. The package of DataSourceAutoConfiguration is version-dependent: Boot 4 reorganized auto-configurations into per-technology modules, so let the IDE auto-import it rather than copying an old import line.

Why not put everything in one StudentService?

A single class could do it all:

  1. Listen to the endpoint.
  2. Convert the incoming JSON.
  3. Apply business logic.
  4. Talk to the database to store the data.
  5. Send the response back to the client.

That's too many jobs. Spring's architecture says one class, one responsibility (SRP), and a class delegates other work to injected dependencies, exactly the Spring Core material from earlier lectures. So the responsibilities are split into layers.

Controller – Service – Repository architecture

LayerClassSingle responsibility
ControllerStudentControllerHandle HTTP: map an endpoint to a method, receive parameters and the body (JSON to object), return the response
ServiceStudentServiceBusiness logic and validation (e.g. subject must be a CS subject, roll number within a range). Coordinates between controller and repository
RepositoryStudentRepositoryTalk to the database only
EntityStudentThe data itself: a class that maps to a DB table
  • This is the pattern for every Spring Boot app in the series.
  • The controller isn't really the first thing to see a request. Spring MVC does work before it, covered in a later lecture. For now, treat it as the entry point.
  • Later a DTO (data transfer object) will sit between the JSON and the entity. It's skipped here to keep things simple.
Anticipated question: "The service just passes the request on. Why have it?"
In simple CRUD it does little. But validation and business rules belong there, not in the controller (HTTP concerns) or the repository (DB concerns). As the app grows, the service is where the logic lives, and it can combine several repositories or call other services.

Package structure

in.strikes.crudspringbootdemo
├── CrudSpringBootDemoApplication.java     (main class stays at the top)
├── controller/   StudentController
├── service/      StudentService
├── repository/   StudentRepository
└── entity/       Student                  (sometimes called "model")

Dumping every class into the root package isn't good practice. Real apps have many entities (students, teachers…), so group classes by layer. All sub-packages sit under the main class's package, so component scanning finds them (Lecture 9).

The entity: Student

What does a student need to store? From the JSON body: name, email, age (a number, not a string), rollNumber and subject. The incoming JSON must map onto a Java class with the same fields.

{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Aditya",
  "email": "aditya@gmail.com",
  "age": 28,
  "rollNumber": 1001,
  "subject": "Spring Framework"
}
package in.strikes.crudspringbootdemo.entity;

import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;

@Entity                                 // "map this class to a database table"
public class Student {

    @Id                                 // primary key
    private Long id;                    // Long: ids can grow large

    private String name;
    private String email;
    private Integer age;
    private int rollNumber;
    private String subject;

    // getters and setters for all fields (Generate → Getter and Setter)
}
  • @Entity says this Java class should be stored in, or mapped to, the database.
  • Adding @Entity alone gives an error: "Persistent entity 'Student' should have a primary key". A DB table needs a unique primary key.
  • Could an existing field be the key? name, age and subject repeat. email is unique, and so might rollNumber be within one college. Good practice is a separate id, so private Long id is added and marked @Id.
An entity is not a Spring bean:
Open @Entity: it has no @Component meta-annotation. So the Spring IoC container does not manage Student objects. You create them with new, or JPA creates them when loading rows. JPA (its persistence context) manages entities, not the IoC container.

What JPA saves you from: SQL by hand

In DBeaver, the lecture created the database student_crud_db and wrote the SQL manually:

CREATE TABLE student (
    id          INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name        VARCHAR(255),
    age         INT,
    email       VARCHAR(255),
    roll_number INT,
    subject     VARCHAR(255)
);

INSERT INTO student VALUES (1, 'Aditya', 28, 'aditya@gmail.com', 1001, 'Spring Framework');

Refresh, and the row appears. The same fields exist three times: in the JSON, in Student.java and in the table. So something has to turn a Student object into that INSERT, and it would naturally be the repository. Must we write these queries in the repository? No. Spring Data's idea is that a developer can work with the DB without writing SQL. You call methods, and the SQL is generated and run for you, even the CREATE TABLE, derived from the entity. SQL knowledge is still very important; it just isn't required for this.

Definition: ORM (Object-Relational Mapping):
One Student object corresponds to one row. s1 = new Student() with name Aditya, age 28… is one row, and s2 with Rohit, 29… is another. Class maps to table, field to column, object to row. Hibernate (a JPA implementation) does this conversion using JDBC underneath, as later lectures show.
Correction: the lecture expands ORM as "Object Relation Model". The standard term is Object-Relational Mapping.

Designing the REST endpoints

All endpoints share the prefix /api/students. What makes each one unique is the method + path combination:

OperationMethodEndpointBody?
CreatePOST/api/studentsYes: student JSON
Read oneGET/api/students/{id}No
Read allGET/api/studentsNo
UpdatePUT/api/students/{id}Yes: full student JSON, so any field(s) can change with one endpoint
DeleteDELETE/api/students/{id}No
  • POST /api/students and GET /api/students share a path, but their methods differ, so there's no clash. Two methods with the same method and same path would confuse Spring: it wouldn't know which Java method to call.
  • For update, the lecture prefers one endpoint taking the full body over separate updateName, updateEmail… endpoints, which would need a new endpoint for every new field.
  • An alternative style, used temporarily in this lecture, puts actions in the path: /api/students/create, /get/{id}, /getAll, /update, /delete/{id}. The lecturer prefers the method + path style shown in the table, and returns to it later.
Worth knowing: REST naming convention (added):
REST treats URLs as nouns (resources), and the HTTP method is the verb. So POST /api/students, not POST /api/students/create. Verbs in paths are widely considered an anti-pattern, because they duplicate what the method already says. Plural resource names (/students) and ids as path segments (/students/1) are the norm.

The controller: the first endpoint

package in.strikes.crudspringbootdemo.controller;

@RestController                          // controller whose return values become the HTTP body
@RequestMapping("/api/students")         // common prefix for every method in this class
public class StudentController {

    private final StudentService studentService;

    public StudentController(StudentService studentService) {   // constructor injection
        this.studentService = studentService;
    }

    @PostMapping("/create")              // POST /api/students/create  (temporary style)
    public ResponseEntity<Student> createStudent(@RequestBody Student student) {
        System.out.println("Inside student controller");
        Student createdStudent = studentService.createStudent(student);
        System.out.println("Exiting student controller");
        return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.CREATED)          // 201
                .body(createdStudent);
    }

    // readStudent, updateStudent, deleteStudent: next lecture
}
  • @RestController marks this as a REST controller: it takes REST calls and returns JSON (or another format). It's meta-annotated with @Controller, which is meta-annotated with @Component, so it's a bean in the IoC container. @Component alone is too generic, and Spring offers these specialized annotations. Plain @Controller comes later.
  • @RequestMapping("/api/students") at class level means every endpoint in this class starts with /api/students.
  • @PostMapping("/create") means: call this method for HTTP POST on prefix + /create. That combination is unique, so Spring routes to it. How the mapping works inside comes in a later lecture.
  • @RequestBody Student student: the incoming JSON is converted to a Student automatically. Spring uses the Jackson library, matching JSON keys to fields. There's no manual mapping of each field.

Proof of the mapping: with a void method that prints student.getName() and student.getEmail(), sending the POST prints Aditya and aditya@gmail.com in the console. Postman gets no body, since nothing is returned.

Worth knowing: what Jackson needs (added):
Jackson creates the object with the no-arg constructor, then fills it through setters (or fields), matching JSON keys by name. So rollNumber in the JSON must match the field name exactly. Unknown JSON keys are ignored by Spring Boot's default settings. JPA also requires entities to have a no-arg constructor.
