The service and the (stub) repository

@Service                                  // specialized @Component: "business logic lives here"
public class StudentService {

    private final StudentRepository studentRepository;

    public StudentService(StudentRepository studentRepository) {
        this.studentRepository = studentRepository;
    }

    public Student createStudent(Student studentRequest) {
        System.out.println("Inside student service");
        // business logic / validation would go here
        Student studentResponse = studentRepository.saveStudent(studentRequest);
        System.out.println("Exiting student service");
        return studentResponse;
    }
}

@Component                                // for now; real JPA repository next lecture
public class StudentRepository {

    public Student saveStudent(Student studentRequest) {
        System.out.println("Inside student repository");
        // no DB yet: return a dummy student
        Student s1 = new Student();       // plain 'new': entities aren't beans
        s1.setName("Aditya");
        s1.setAge(28);
        s1.setEmail("aditya@gmail.com");
        s1.setRollNumber(1001);
        s1.setSubject("Spring Framework");
        System.out.println("Exiting student repository");
        return s1;
    }
}
  • @Service is meta-annotated with @Component. It also tells readers (and teammates) that this class holds business logic called from a controller. @Component would work too.
  • Without @Component on StudentRepository, the service showed "Could not autowire. No beans of 'StudentRepository' type found" (Lecture 5).
  • Every layer is wired by constructor injection, with no @Autowired needed for a single constructor. That's the Spring Core material in practice.

Console after one POST, showing the call path down and back up:

Inside student controller
Inside student service
Inside student repository
Exiting student repository
Exiting student service
Exiting student controller

The response: JSON body and status code

  • With the return type String ("Student created"), Postman shows plain text. Its JSON view can't render it, so it appears raw.
  • With the return type Student, Postman gets JSON with id: null (never set) and the other fields. Jackson converts the returned object to JSON, the reverse of @RequestBody.
  • A response has three parts: body, status code and headers. So far the status is always 200 OK, because the controller defaults to it.

To choose the status, return ResponseEntity<Student>. It's a generic wrapper extending HttpEntity that carries a status, headers and a body.

return ResponseEntity.ok(createdStudent);                        // 200 OK

return ResponseEntity.status(201).body(createdStudent);          // by number
return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(createdStudent);   // by enum → 201 Created
  • Creating a resource should return 201 Created, not 200.
  • HttpStatus is an enum: OK (200), CREATED (201), ACCEPTED (202), UNAUTHORIZED (401), NOT_FOUND (404)… Valid codes range from 100 to 999 in its valueOf check.
  • After the change, Postman shows 201 Created with the JSON body.
Transcript slips / corrections:
  • The lecture says "2001" for created. The status is 201 Created.
  • ResponseEntity.created(…) exists, but it takes a URI, which becomes the Location header pointing to the new resource, e.g. /api/students/1. That's why passing a Student failed. ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/api/students/" + id)).body(created) is the most REST-correct form.
  • An invalid code number throws at runtime. Standard HTTP codes are 3 digits (100–599).

Where things stand

Done: the architecture, packages, the Student entity, and a working create endpoint through all three layers returning 201. Not yet done:

  • Real database access: the repository returns a dummy, and the DataSource is excluded.
  • The read, update and delete endpoints.

Both come next lecture, split out to avoid overwhelming beginners. The lecturer's note on theory: building projects matters, but in interviews you're asked how your project works inside. The internals make you strong, and anyone can generate a project with ChatGPT.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody. That's why return values are written into the response body as JSON instead of being treated as view (HTML template) names.
  • Prefer @Repository for repository classes. It's another specialized @Component, and it also enables Spring's translation of DB exceptions into DataAccessException. With Spring Data JPA, you'll usually write an interface extending JpaRepository instead of a class.
  • Generated ids. With a DB AUTO_INCREMENT key, annotate @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) next to @Id. Then the client shouldn't send id in a create request; the DB assigns it.
  • Soft vs hard delete. A hard delete removes the row. A soft delete flips a flag (is_deleted), so data can be restored, audited or referenced. The cost: every read query must filter out deleted rows.
  • Returning entities directly is fine for learning. In real APIs it leaks internal fields and couples your API to your table design, which is why DTOs are introduced later.

Lecture 12: CRUD Mini-Project, Part 2 — JpaRepository, Connecting MySQL & Read / Update / Delete

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #12 · 59m · Code Army · continues the crud-spring-boot-demo project from Lecture 11

Where we left off

Lecture 11 built the structure: StudentController (mapped to /api/students), StudentService, a stub StudentRepository and the Student entity. The /create endpoint ran through all three layers but stored nothing. This lecture:

  1. Replaces the stub repository with a Spring Data JPA repository.
  2. Connects the app to MySQL.
  3. Lets JPA create the table.
  4. Adds the read-one, read-all, update and delete endpoints.

The first cleanup removes the "Inside / Exiting" prints from every layer and the dummy student from the repository.

The idea: call methods, not SQL

The repository is the layer that stores and retrieves data. Instead of writing SQL inside it, we call ready-made methods that Spring Data JPA provides. Each one runs the matching SQL internally.

OperationMethodSQL it roughly runs
Createsave(entity)INSERT INTO student …
Read allfindAll()SELECT * FROM student
Read onefindById(id)SELECT * FROM student WHERE id = ?
Updatesave(entity) again, no separate methodUPDATE student SET … WHERE id = ?
DeletedeleteById(id)DELETE FROM student WHERE id = ?
Exists?existsById(id) returns booleanSELECT COUNT(*) … WHERE id = ?
  • JPA = Jakarta Persistence API. Older Spring Boot code (Boot 2.x) imports javax.persistence.*. From Boot 3 the package is jakarta.persistence.*.
  • There's also saveAll, a bulk save of many records, plus saveAndFlush and saveAllAndFlush, which come later.
  • How does save know whether to insert or update? The lecture's rough answer is that it decides from the primary key. The details come with Hibernate internals, and the demo run below shows it.

The repository becomes an interface extending JpaRepository

package in.strikes.crudspringbootdemo.repository;

import in.strikes.crudspringbootdemo.entity.Student;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;

public interface StudentRepository extends JpaRepository<Student, Long> {
    // empty — all CRUD methods are inherited
}
  • The two generic arguments are the entity it manages (Student) and the type of that entity's primary key (Long, matching @Id private Long id).
  • The service now calls the inherited method: 
    public Student createStudent(Student studentRequest) {
    return studentRepository.save(studentRequest);   // returns the saved entity
}

Why an interface, not a class?

As a class, the repository would need its own implementation of saveStudent, and somewhere inside it a hand-written INSERT INTO student …, the very query run manually in DBeaver in Lecture 11. Extending JpaRepository inherits the methods instead. An interface that extends another interface inherits all its methods.

Where does save come from?

Ctrl-clicking save shows it's declared in CrudRepository, the root of the CRUD methods. The chain is StudentRepository → JpaRepository → ListCrudRepository → CrudRepository → Repository.

Anticipated question: "Who implements all these abstract methods?"

An interface's methods must normally be implemented. We'd write something like class StudentRepoImpl implements StudentRepository and @Override every method (save, flush, findAll…). Here we implement nothing, and it still works.

The answer: Spring Data JPA provides the implementation at runtime:
We only say which entity and which id type. Spring Data generates the implementation, creates the bean, stores it in the IoC container and injects it into StudentService. "This is the magic of Spring Data JPA": an empty interface, no SQL, no implementation, and the record is saved.

Do we need @Repository?

  • Spring offers @Repository, a specialised @Component like @Service and @Controller. It tells Spring and other developers that this is a repository class.
  • On a Spring Data interface, no annotation is needed at all. The lecture's reasoning is that the container can't create an object of an interface, only of an implementation, and Spring Data supplies that implementation.
  • @Repository earns its place later, when you write your own repository class. That's needed for complex queries such as joins with no ready-made method. Even then, you can often just declare new methods in the interface without writing SQL, as a later lecture shows.

Setting up the database

Checking MySQL from the terminal

mysql --version              # is MySQL installed?
mysql -u root -p             # connect as root; -p = prompt for the password
mysql> SHOW DATABASES;
mysql> USE student_crud_db;
mysql> SHOW TABLES;          # Empty set (the old table was dropped)
mysql> exit

The terminal works, but DBeaver makes it easier to see and visualise tables.

Connecting DBeaver

  1. Click New Database Connection, choose MySQL, then Next.
  2. Connect by Host localhost. Leave Database empty, since we create it ourselves. Enter username root, created by the MySQL install, and the password set during installation.
  3. The URL view shows jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/; copy it for later. MySQL listens on port 3306 by default, just as Spring Boot's Tomcat uses 8080 (ports: Lecture 2).
  4. Click Test Connection, which should say "Connected", then Finish.

In a SQL editor, run CREATE DATABASE student_crud_db; and refresh. The database appears with no tables. That's the only SQL we write. JPA creates the table and performs every CRUD operation through method calls.

The lecturer's password is 123456. That's acceptable only on localhost; a production deployment would never use a password that simple.

Connecting the app: application.properties

First, remove the Lecture 11 workaround. We now want the DataSource auto-configured:

@SpringBootApplication                     // exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class removed
public class CrudSpringBootDemoApplication { … }

Then tell Boot how to reach the database:

# where the database is: jdbc:mysql://host:port/database
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/student_crud_db
spring.datasource.username=root
spring.datasource.password=123456

# let Hibernate create/alter tables from the @Entity classes
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update

# print the SQL Hibernate runs, nicely formatted
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true
  • spring.datasource.url is the JDBC URL:
    • jdbc:mysql:// is the protocol signature.
    • Then the host: localhost now, or the server's address if MySQL were deployed elsewhere.
    • Then the port 3306 and the database name.
    The DataSource auto-configuration (excluded in Lecture 11) needs this URL.
  • username / password give the same credentials DBeaver used. With URL, username and password, Spring Boot can establish the connection just as we did manually.
  • spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update means: "Hibernate, you take responsibility for the tables." From the Student entity it creates a student table: the class name becomes the table name, and the fields become columns (id, name, age, email, roll_number, subject). update also alters the table when the entity's structure changes. DDL = Data Definition Language.
  • show-sql defaults to false. format_sql pretty-prints the SQL.

"Do you need to memorise these keys? Not at all. I don't either." Know that they exist, and copy the exact names when you need them.

JPA vs Hibernate (corrected wording):
The lecture says "JPA internally implements Hibernate". It's the other way round. JPA is a specification: interfaces and annotations like @Entity and EntityManager. Hibernate is an implementation of it, and the default in Spring Boot. Spring Data JPA sits on top and provides repositories that call JPA, which Hibernate executes over JDBC.
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto values (the lecture defers these; added)
ValueWhat Hibernate does at startupUse for
noneNothingProduction. This is Boot's default for a real (non-embedded) database
validateChecks the tables match the entities, fails if notProduction, alongside migrations
updateCreates missing tables and columns. Never dropsLocal development
createDrops and recreates the schema. Data lostTests, demos
create-dropLike create, and drops the schema on shutdownTests. Default for embedded DBs like H2

Demo run: the table creates itself

  1. Start the app. The logs show the JDBC URL, the MySQL driver and the Hibernate dialect, then "Tomcat started on port 8080".
  2. Refresh DBeaver: a student table exists with id, age, email, name, roll_number and subject, and no CREATE TABLE was written.
  3. After adding show-sql=true and restarting, no CREATE TABLE appears in the logs, because the table already existed. update only creates what's missing. The lecturer drops the table, restarts, and the statement is printed:
Hibernate:
    create table student (
        id bigint not null,
        age integer,
        email varchar(255),
        name varchar(255),
        roll_number integer not null,
        subject varchar(255),
        primary key (id)
    )

Everything is derived from Student.java:

  • @Id becomes primary key (id).
  • Long becomes bigint and String becomes varchar(255).
  • rollNumber becomes the column roll_number: camelCase to snake_case is Spring Boot's default naming strategy.
  • It's not null because int is a primitive and can't be null. The Integer age column is nullable.

Demo run: create through the real database

  1. Postman: POST /api/students/create with Aditya's JSON (including "id": 1). The response is 201 Created with the saved object.
  2. The logs show two statements: a select … where id=? first, then insert into student (…) values (?,?,?,?,?,?). The ? are bind parameters, filled with the values from the Student object that Jackson built.
  3. Refresh DBeaver: the row is there.
  4. POST again with id 2, Rohit, age 29, roll 102, subject "MERN". A second row is inserted, again as select then insert.

The lecturer explains the extra SELECT: save handles both insert and update, so it first checks whether a row with that id exists. If none exists it inserts, otherwise it updates. We learned this "by reading the logs".

Precision note: when save selects first (verified on Boot 4.1.0 / Hibernate 7, H2):
  • Spring Data's save asks: is this entity new? For a wrapper id like Long, "new" means id == null.
  • New: em.persist(), a plain INSERT with no select.
  • Id present: em.merge(). It SELECTs by id, then INSERTs if nothing was found or UPDATEs if the row exists. That's the select-then-insert in the demo, because the JSON carried "id": 1.
  • This entity has no @GeneratedValue. Posting without an id fails with JpaSystemException: Identifier of entity 'Student' must be manually assigned before calling 'persist()'. The client is forced to invent ids, which is fragile.
  • The usual fix is @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) with MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT. Then a POST without an id does a single insert … values (?, default).
  • A POST that sends an id which doesn't exist throws ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException in Hibernate 7, because merge treats it as a deleted row. So with generated ids, the create endpoint should ignore or reject a client-supplied id.

Read one: GET /api/students/get/{id}

Sending the id: path variable vs query parameter

Writing @GetMapping("/get/1") would hard-code the id. The id must come from the request instead. There are two ways to send a value in a GET:

Path variableQuery parameter
URL/api/students/get/1/api/students/get?id=1&name=Aditya
Annotation@PathVariable@RequestParam (covered later)
Typical useIdentifying which resourceFiltering, sorting, paging, optional values
PostmanPart of the pathAuto-filled in the Params tab

This lecture uses a path variable.

Controller

@GetMapping("/get/{id}")                               // {id} = placeholder in the URL
public ResponseEntity<Student> getStudent(@PathVariable Long id) {
    Student studentResponse = studentService.getStudent(id);
    if (studentResponse == null) {
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();      // 404, empty body
    }
    return ResponseEntity.ok(studentResponse);         // 200 + JSON
}
  • @GetMapping is the GET counterpart of @PostMapping.
  • @PathVariable Long id reads the {id} segment from the URL and converts it to Long. This is the path version of what @RequestBody does for the JSON body.
  • ResponseEntity.ok(x) is short for ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.OK).body(x).

Service: findById returns an Optional

public Student getStudent(Long id) {
    Optional<Student> studentResponse = studentRepository.findById(id);
    if (studentResponse.isPresent()) {
        return studentResponse.get();      // unwrap the Student
    }
    return null;
}
  • Student s = studentRepository.findById(id); doesn't compile, because findById returns Optional<Student>.
  • The record may or may not exist. Only ids 1 and 2 exist, so id 3 finds nothing. Rather than returning null and risking a NullPointerException, the method returns an Optional: a box that may or may not contain a value.
  • isPresent() checks for a value, and get() takes it out.

Demo run and the bugs found

  1. The first attempt gave 404 Not Found, even for id 1. The mapping was @GetMapping("/get"), without {id}. The URL /get/1 matched no endpoint, since only /get existed. Adding {id} to the mapping tells Spring where the path variable is.
  2. With /get/{id}, id 1 returns Aditya's JSON and the log shows select … where id=?. Id 2 returns Rohit.
  3. Id 3 returned 200 OK with an empty body. That's wrong: the client should learn that the record wasn't found. The controller's null check was added, first as ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND).body(null), then simplified to ResponseEntity.notFound().build(). Now id 3 gives 404.

A GET sends no body, only the URL, the method and the headers. Anything left in Postman's Body tab is ignored.

Read all: GET /api/students/getAll

// controller
@GetMapping("/getAll")
public ResponseEntity<List<Student>> getAllStudents() {
    List<Student> studentList = studentService.getAllStudents();
    if (studentList.isEmpty()) {
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();      // see correction below
    }
    return ResponseEntity.ok(studentList);
}

// service
public List<Student> getAllStudents() {
    return studentRepository.findAll();                // SELECT all rows
}
  • There's no path variable and no body. The return type is List<Student>, which Jackson serialises as a JSON array.
  • The service just returns the list, and the controller decides the status. The Postman result is an array with Aditya and Rohit.

Update: PUT /api/students/update/{id}

An update needs two inputs: which student (the id as a path variable) and the new data (a JSON body, since PUT carries a body). Example: Rohit (id 2), age 29 → 28 and roll number 102 → 105.

// controller
@PutMapping("/update/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<Student> updateStudent(@PathVariable Long id,
                                             @RequestBody Student studentRequest) {
    Student studentResponse = studentService.updateStudent(id, studentRequest);
    if (studentResponse == null) {
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
    }
    return ResponseEntity.ok(studentResponse);
}

// service
public Student updateStudent(Long id, Student studentRequest) {
    Optional<Student> existingStudent = studentRepository.findById(id);
    if (existingStudent.isEmpty()) {
        return null;                                    // controller turns this into 404
    }
    Student studentToSave = existingStudent.get();
    studentToSave.setName(studentRequest.getName());
    studentToSave.setEmail(studentRequest.getEmail());
    studentToSave.setAge(studentRequest.getAge());
    studentToSave.setRollNumber(studentRequest.getRollNumber());
    studentToSave.setSubject(studentRequest.getSubject());
    // id deliberately NOT copied from the request
    return studentRepository.save(studentToSave);       // id exists → UPDATE
}

Step by step:

  1. Load the existing row with findById. If it's missing (isEmpty(), the opposite of isPresent()), return null, which becomes 404.
  2. Copy the five fields from the request onto the loaded entity. The id isn't copied: whatever id the client puts in the body, the record keeps its original id. The lecturer calls this good practice.
  3. Call save. Because the entity has an existing id, it runs an UPDATE, visible in the logs.

Demo: the first try returned 404 because "update" was misspelled in the mapping. After the fix, PUT /update/2 works, and DBeaver shows age 28 and roll number 105.

Why the loaded entity rather than the request object:
Saving studentRequest directly would trust whatever id the client sent, and could update the wrong row or create a new one. Loading by the path id and copying fields makes the URL decide which row changes.

The lecture also mentions a cleaner alternative: return the Optional itself from the service and let the controller check it, so no layer passes null around. It's kept simple for now, and will be improved later.

Delete: DELETE /api/students/delete/{id}

// controller
@DeleteMapping("/delete/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<String> deleteStudent(@PathVariable Long id) {
    boolean isDeleted = studentService.deleteStudent(id);
    if (!isDeleted) {
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();       // 404
    }
    return ResponseEntity.ok("Record deleted");         // 200 + message
}

// service
public boolean deleteStudent(Long id) {
    boolean isStudent = studentRepository.existsById(id);
    if (!isStudent) {
        return false;
    }
    studentRepository.deleteById(id);                   // returns void
    return true;
}
  • First check existence with existsById. deleteById returns void, so the service returns true itself afterwards.
  • The controller first returned ResponseEntity<Boolean> with true. It was changed to a String, "Record deleted", which is more readable for the client.

Demo:

  • DELETE /delete/3 (doesn't exist) returns 404 with an empty body.
  • DELETE /delete/2 returns 200 "Record deleted", and DBeaver shows Rohit's row gone.

Full request flow

The finished endpoints (lecture's action-in-path style)
OperationMappingInputRepository callSuccess / failure
Create@PostMapping("/create")@RequestBodysave201
Read one@GetMapping("/get/{id}")@PathVariablefindById200 / 404
Read all@GetMapping("/getAll")—findAll200 / 404 on empty
Update@PutMapping("/update/{id}")@PathVariable + @RequestBodyfindById + save200 / 404
Delete@DeleteMapping("/delete/{id}")@PathVariableexistsById + deleteById200 / 404

The lecturer's summary: without a single line of SQL, just save, findById, findAll, existsById and deleteById, all the basic CRUD operations work. A delete-all or update-all would be just as easy.

Next: soft delete

  • So far, delete removes the row permanently. Most applications prefer a soft delete: an is_deleted column flipped from 0 to 1. The row stays in the database but is treated as non-existent: it can't be fetched or updated.
  • Why keep it?
    • Recovering a user's data later.
    • Logs and analytics, such as counting active users.
  • It changes every query: reads and updates must skip deleted rows. So the standard methods (findById…) are no longer enough, and the next lecture shows how to write those queries.

Gaps worth raising in an interview

  • Check-then-act race. existsById then deleteById, or findById then save, are two round trips. Another request can change the row in between. Wrap the service method in @Transactional; for concurrent updates, add optimistic locking with a @Version column.
  • Extra queries. The delete runs count(*), then a select and a delete, because deleteById loads the entity first (verified). Calling findById(id).map(s -> { repo.delete(s); return true; }).orElse(false) saves one query.
  • No validation. A negative age, a blank name or a duplicate email is saved as-is. This is the service-layer validation Lecture 11 promised; Bean Validation (@Valid, @NotBlank) comes later.
  • null as a "not found" signal. It spreads null checks through every layer. Common alternatives:
    • Return Optional to the controller: return service.find(id).map(ResponseEntity::ok).orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    • Throw a custom StudentNotFoundException, handled centrally by @RestControllerAdvice.
  • No pagination. findAll() on a large table loads every row. JpaRepository also has findAll(Pageable).
  • Entity used as the API contract. The same Student class is the request, the response and the table. DTOs separate them.
  • Credentials in application.properties. Use spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD} and supply it from the environment; never commit real passwords.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • The runtime repository is a JDK dynamic proxy. The injected bean's class prints as jdk.proxy2.$Proxy98 (verified, Boot 4.1.0). It implements StudentRepository and delegates the CRUD methods to Spring Data's SimpleJpaRepository. Boot's auto-configuration turns on repository scanning (the equivalent of @EnableJpaRepositories), which finds every interface extending Repository under the main class's package. That's why no annotation is needed on the interface.
  • findAll() returns List only through ListCrudRepository. Since Spring Data 3 (Boot 3), JpaRepository extends ListCrudRepository, so findAll() is a List (an ArrayList, verified). Plain CrudRepository.findAll() returns Iterable.
  • deleteById on a missing id is silent in Spring Data 3+ (verified: it selects, finds nothing, no exception). Older versions threw EmptyResultDataAccessException. So an explicit existence check is how you produce a 404.
  • An empty collection is usually 200 OK with [], not 404. The collection /students exists even when it has no members. Returning 404 for an empty list, as the lecture does, makes clients treat "no students yet" as an error. 404 fits a single resource that doesn't exist.
  • Delete responses: 200 with a message works. Many APIs return 204 No Content (ResponseEntity.noContent().build()) for a successful delete.
  • PUT vs PATCH. The update copies all fields, so a field omitted from the body becomes null. That is correct PUT semantics, since PUT replaces the whole resource. For changing just one field without sending the rest, use PATCH and copy only non-null fields.
  • @PathVariable name matching relies on the compiler keeping parameter names (-parameters). spring-boot-starter-parent enables this. Without it (Spring 6.1+), write @PathVariable("id") explicitly, the same issue seen with XML constructor-arg name in Lecture 8.
  • Inside a @Transactional method, save after modifying a loaded entity is optional. Hibernate's dirty checking writes the changes at commit. Calling save is still harmless and clearer for beginners.
  • The dialect is auto-detected. The logs show MySQLDialect. Modern Hibernate (6+) detects it from the JDBC connection, so spring.jpa.database-platform is no longer needed.
  • REST style: /create, /get/{id}, /getAll, /update/{id} and /delete/{id} put verbs in the path. The resource style from Lecture 11 is POST /api/students, GET /api/students/{id}, GET /api/students, PUT /api/students/{id} and DELETE /api/students/{id}.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"2001 Created" → 201 Created.
"spring.datasource.datasource" → spring.datasource.url.
"Tomcat on port 880" → 8080.
"spring jpa show query" → spring.jpa.show-sql.
"findBy" as a method name → findById.
ResponseEntity<Student> was once typed as "struct".
"public Student get updateStudent" → public Student updateStudent.
In the update, studentRequest.setRollNumber(…) was fixed on screen to studentRequest.getRollNumber().
"an interface's methods must all be overridden" applies to a class implementing it; an interface extending an interface overrides nothing.

Lecture 13: Soft Delete vs Hard Delete, Derived Query Methods, Auto-Increment IDs & @RequestParam

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #13 · 46m · Code Army · continues the CRUD project from Lectures 11–12

The problem: delete erases history

Say the database holds id 1, Aditya, 1001. Calling deleteById(1) makes JPA run a DELETE, and the row is gone from the database. That's a hard delete. In enterprise applications it's risky:

  • You can no longer pull records of all users, including those who left the platform.
  • Logs, audits and analytics lose data.
  • An old account can't be recovered.

The lecturer notes that many people don't talk about this, yet it's a widely used industry practice.

The idea: soft delete

Don't remove the row, mark it. Add a column deleted, default 0 (active). Deleting flips it to 1.

idnameroll_numberdeletedMeaning
1Aditya10010Active
2Rohit1021Deleted, as far as the app is concerned

A soft-deleted row takes part in no CRUD operation. It still exists physically, but the app treats it as non-existent:

  • GET id 2 returns 404 Not Found, even though the row exists.
  • Update id 2 returns "record doesn't exist".
  • Get all leaves Rohit out.
  • Soft-delete again: it's already deleted.
Hard delete vs soft delete
Hard deleteSoft delete
What happensRemoved directly from the DB (DELETE)Data marked as deleted (UPDATE … SET deleted = 1)
Recoverable?NoYes, flip the flag back
History / audit / analyticsLostKept
CostNoneEvery query must filter deleted = false. The table keeps growing
WhenData you'll never need, or must eraseThe default in most real applications
Why storage isn't the argument:
In an enterprise application, "space is not that big a factor; data is". Even marked-deleted rows are useful for logs, recovery and business reports. So soft delete is usually preferred, and hard delete is kept for rare, deliberate cases.

Adding the flag to the entity

@Entity
public class Student {
    …
    private boolean deleted;          // false = active, true = soft-deleted

    public boolean isDeleted() { return deleted; }            // IDE-generated getter for boolean
    public void setDeleted(boolean deleted) { this.deleted = deleted; }
}
  • With ddl-auto=update, restarting the app adds the column. The lecturer dropped the table first to see it clearly.
  • MySQL creates it as deleted bit not null. bit is how MySQL stores a Java boolean, and it's not null because the type is primitive.
  • A row inserted by hand in DBeaver gets deleted = 0, which is exactly what it should be.

Why the flag changes every query

Before the flag, findById(1) meant SELECT * FROM student WHERE id = 1. Now it must mean:

SELECT * FROM student WHERE id = 1 AND deleted = false;   -- read one
SELECT * FROM student WHERE deleted = false;              -- read all

The old standard methods (findById, findAll, existsById) don't know about deleted, so they would still return Rohit. There's no built-in method for "find by id and not deleted". save is the exception: it just saves, so it needs no change.

Derived query methods: SQL from a method name

Do we now have to implement the repository and hand-write these queries? No. Spring Data JPA can build the query from the method's name. You only declare the method, and Spring Data parses the name and provides the implementation at runtime, like it does for findById. How the parsing works comes later.

public interface StudentRepository extends JpaRepository<Student, Long> {

    Optional<Student> findByIdAndDeletedIsFalse(Long id);   // WHERE id = ? AND deleted = false

    List<Student> findByDeletedIsFalse();                   // WHERE deleted = false
}
  • Only declared, never defined. "Defining it is JPA's responsibility."
  • The return type is chosen by you: Optional<Student> for "maybe one", List<Student> for many.
  • IntelliJ autocompletes these names from the entity's fields. After findByIdAnd… it offers Deleted, Age, Subject, Email…, and after a property it offers conditions like IsFalse, IsAfter, IsBefore, Between, Containing, Empty. None of these methods exist beforehand; Spring Data generates them from the name.

SQL Hibernate generated for these methods (verified on Boot 4.1.0):

findByIdAndDeletedIsFalse(2)  →  select … from student s1_0 where s1_0.id=? and s1_0.deleted=false
findByDeletedIsFalse()        →  select … from student s1_0 where s1_0.deleted=false

The naming rule, and the startup error that taught it

The first attempt at "read all" was named findAllAndDeletedIsFalse(). The application failed to start:

Error creating bean with name 'studentRepository' …
Cannot create query for method [StudentRepository.findAllAndDeletedIsFalse()];
No property 'findAll' found for type 'Student'

A derived query must contain By, which separates the action from the criteria. Without it, Spring Data tried to read findAll as a field of Student. Because names are checked when the repository bean is created, a bad name is a startup failure, not a runtime surprise.

  • The pattern is findBy + field name + optional condition, with further fields joined by And / Or.
  • With only one criterion, no And is needed: findByDeletedIsFalse.
  • Field names must match the entity's Java field names (deleted, rollNumber), not the column names (roll_number).
Worth knowing (added, verified):
  • findAllByDeletedFalse() is valid. Any text between find and By is ignored, so findAll…By… works. What failed was the missing By, not the word All.
  • DeletedFalse and DeletedIsFalse are equivalent; Is is optional filler.
  • Other prefixes work the same way: existsBy…, countBy…, deleteBy…. For example existsByIdAndDeletedFalse(id) generates select id … where id=? and deleted=false fetch first ? rows only.
  • Very long names become unreadable. Complex queries are usually written with @Query (JPQL) instead, which a later lecture covers.

Updating each operation for soft delete

All the changes live in StudentService, since business logic belongs in the service.

OperationBeforeAfter
Createsave(request)request.setDeleted(false), then save
Read onefindByIdfindByIdAndDeletedIsFalse
Read allfindAllfindByDeletedIsFalse
UpdatefindById + copy + savefindByIdAndDeletedIsFalse + copy + setDeleted(false) + save
Hard deleteexistsById + deleteByIdUnchanged, by choice (see below)
Soft delete—New: findByIdAndDeletedIsFalse + setDeleted(true) + save

Create: never trust the client with the flag

public Student createStudent(Student studentRequest) {
    studentRequest.setDeleted(false);          // ignore whatever the client sent
    return studentRepository.save(studentRequest);
}

Because Student doubles as the request body, a client could POST "deleted": true and create a record that's deleted from birth. "I shouldn't give the client that much power." Whether a record is deleted is an internal decision, made only when someone calls the soft-delete API. Demo: POSTing Aditya with "deleted": true still saved deleted = false, and the response showed false.

Read one and read all

public Student getStudent(Long id) {
    Optional<Student> studentResponse = studentRepository.findByIdAndDeletedIsFalse(id);
    return studentResponse.isPresent() ? studentResponse.get() : null;   // null → 404 in controller
}

public List<Student> getAllStudents() {
    return studentRepository.findByDeletedIsFalse();
}

Update

Load with findByIdAndDeletedIsFalse, so a soft-deleted student counts as not found, and setDeleted(false) before saving, "so nobody sends deleted true in an update either".

Hard delete: a design choice

Should hard delete work on an already soft-deleted record? That depends on your business logic:

  • Option A, the lecture's choice: hard delete can remove any record, soft-deleted or not. It's rare and deliberate: "when I perform it, I know what I'm doing." So existsById, which ignores the flag, stays.
  • Option B: soft-deleted rows are invisible to hard delete too. Use existsByIdAndDeletedIsFalse instead.

The soft-delete endpoint: PATCH

Which HTTP method fits?

  • It's "a kind of delete", so DELETE would work.
  • But nothing is actually deleted. One field changes, deleted goes 0 → 1, and that is exactly what PATCH is for: modifying part of a record (only the roll number, only the name…).
// controller
@PatchMapping("/delete-soft/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<String> deleteStudentSoftly(@PathVariable Long id) {
    boolean isDeleted = studentService.deleteStudentSoftly(id);
    if (!isDeleted) {
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
    }
    return ResponseEntity.ok("Record deleted");
}

// service
public boolean deleteStudentSoftly(Long id) {
    Optional<Student> existingStudent = studentRepository.findByIdAndDeletedIsFalse(id);
    if (existingStudent.isEmpty()) {
        return false;                          // missing OR already soft-deleted
    }
    Student studentToSave = existingStudent.get();
    studentToSave.setDeleted(true);
    studentRepository.save(studentToSave);     // UPDATE … SET deleted = 1
    return true;
}

Three steps:

  1. Get the record, only if it isn't already deleted.
  2. Set deleted = true.
  3. Save. The id exists, so save issues an UPDATE.

Demo run: soft delete end to end

  1. POST Aditya (id 1) and Rohit (id 2). Both have deleted = 0.
  2. PATCH /delete-soft/2 returns 200 "Record deleted". The logs show the derived select … where id=? and deleted=false, then the update. DBeaver shows Rohit's deleted = 1.
  3. GET /get/2 returns 404 (the derived select found nothing). GET /get/1 returns Aditya.
  4. GET /getAll returns only Aditya.
  5. POST Rahul (id 3, "Django"). A first try gave 405 Method Not Allowed because the URL was still a GET-only endpoint; fixed to /create. Then PATCH /delete-soft/3 sets deleted = 1.
  6. DELETE /delete/3 returns "Record deleted", and the row is physically gone. Hard delete works on a soft-deleted record, as designed.

The client-supplied id bug, and @GeneratedValue

So far every POST body carried an id, and the client chose the primary key. The lecturer then POSTed a new student Rohan with "id": 2, an id that already belonged to Rohit. The response was 201 Created, but DBeaver showed Rohit's row overwritten with Rohan's data.

Why a create became an update:
save handles both insert and update (Lecture 12). With an id present, it first SELECTs by id. The logs show the select found Rohit, then ran an UPDATE. The create API silently modified existing data. The fix is to stop clients from sending ids and let the database generate them. 
@Id
@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)    // DB auto-increment
private Long id;
  • IDENTITY means the database assigns the id through MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT, the basic SQL way to generate primary keys.
  • The catch: the existing table doesn't change. Its id is still bigint not null without auto_increment, and changing a column is DDL. The lecturer dropped the table and restarted, and Hibernate printed create table student (id bigint not null auto_increment, …).
  • Now POST bodies have no id. Rohit gets id 1 and Aditya id 2, automatically. An accidental overwrite through create can't happen, "unless I do it myself".
Precision note (added, verified on Boot 4.1.0 / Hibernate 7):
  • ddl-auto=update never modifies existing columns. It only adds missing tables and columns. So adding @GeneratedValue later needs a manual ALTER TABLE or a recreate, which is why the lecturer dropped the table.
  • @GeneratedValue alone doesn't stop a client from sending an id. Hibernate 7 still takes the merge path:
    • If the id exists, the row is updated, the same overwrite bug.
    • If it doesn't exist, the request fails with ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException, a 500.
    The robust fix is to also call studentRequest.setId(null) in createStudent, as with setDeleted(false), or to accept a DTO that has no id field at all.

Path variables vs request (query) parameters

So far ids travelled in the path: /get/1. The alternative is a request parameter: /get?id=1, and several can be chained with &, as in /get?id=1&name=Aditya. Postman fills these into its Params tab automatically. They travel in the URL of the HTTP request.

When to prefer request parameters:
With several fields, path segments get ambiguous. In /get/1/Aditya, which segment is the id and which is the name? Named parameters (?id=1&name=Aditya) say what each value is. 
@GetMapping("/get")                                    // no {id} in the path any more
public ResponseEntity<Student> getStudent(@RequestParam Long id) { … }

@PutMapping("/update")
public ResponseEntity<Student> updateStudent(@RequestParam Long id,
                                             @RequestBody Student studentRequest) { … }

@DeleteMapping("/delete")
public ResponseEntity<String> deleteStudent(@RequestParam Long id) { … }

@PatchMapping("/delete-soft")
public ResponseEntity<String> deleteStudentSoftly(@RequestParam Long id) { … }
  • @RequestParam Long id means: look in the request parameters for a field named id and put its value in this variable. The parameter name in the URL and the variable name must match, or you name it explicitly with @RequestParam("id").
  • Demo: GET /get?id=1 returns Aditya, and ?id=2 returns the second record. GET /get/1 now returns 404, because no mapping matches that path any more.
@PathVariable vs @RequestParam
@PathVariable@RequestParam
URL/students/1/students?id=1
MappingNeeds {id} in the pathPlain path
Missing valueURL doesn't match, so 404400 Bad Request (required by default)
Optional valuesAwkwardrequired = false or defaultValue = "…"
Typical use (added)Identify one resource: GET /students/1Filter / sort / page a collection: GET /students?subject=MERN&page=0

Homework / suggested extensions

  • Add more endpoints and methods, such as update-all and delete-all.
  • Make the service layer do real work: validations like "roll number must be between 1001 and 9999".
  • Practise derived query methods: combine several fields and see which SQL gets generated, without writing any SQL.

Next lecture: the internals of everything so far, starting from Servlets (briefly, since nobody writes raw servlets today), then Spring MVC, which makes Spring Boot's web layer clear.

Gaps worth raising in an interview

  • Forgetting the filter. Every new query must remember deleted = false, and one missed method leaks deleted data. Hibernate can apply it centrally:
    • @SQLRestriction("deleted = false") on the entity (Hibernate 6.3+, replacing the deprecated @Where), with @SQLDelete(sql = "UPDATE student SET deleted = true WHERE id = ?") so that deleteById becomes a soft delete.
    • Or Hibernate 6.4+'s @SoftDelete, which does both.
    • The trade-off: you then need a native query to see deleted rows.
  • Unique constraints. If email is unique, a soft-deleted user's email blocks a new sign-up with the same address. Options: include deleted in the unique key, or rewrite the email on deletion.
  • Who and when. A boolean loses the time of deletion. Many systems use deleted_at TIMESTAMP NULL (null means active), often with deleted_by. That supports "restore within 30 days" and purge jobs.
  • Legal erasure. Privacy laws such as GDPR's right to erasure may require real deletion or anonymisation. Soft delete is not a universal answer.
  • Index the flag. Nearly every query filters on it. In a large table, an index on (deleted, …) or a partial index (PostgreSQL) keeps reads fast.
  • Restore endpoint. Soft delete's main benefit is undo, and there's no PATCH /restore yet.
  • Race conditions. Find-then-save soft delete is two statements. A single @Modifying @Query("update Student s set s.deleted = true where s.id = :id and s.deleted = false") returning the row count is atomic, and a count of 0 means 404.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • The client doesn't need to know it's a soft delete. The lecture picks PATCH because internally one field changes. Many APIs keep DELETE /students/{id} as the public contract and soft-delete behind it: from the client's view, the resource is gone, since a later GET returns 404. PATCH fits better when the client explicitly edits a status field ({"status": "ARCHIVED"}). Both are defensible; be ready to justify your choice.
  • The flag must be ignored on input, and that applies to id too. The lecture's setDeleted(false) in create is the right instinct. In update it's redundant, because fields are copied one by one onto an entity already loaded with deleted = false. The general fix is request DTOs that simply don't contain server-owned fields.
  • Derived queries are validated at startup. A typo in a property name (findByRollNo when the field is rollNumber) stops the app with PropertyReferenceException. That's a feature: errors surface early.
  • boolean vs Boolean. A primitive gives a NOT NULL column defaulting to false in Java, which is right for a flag. A wrapper would allow null, a meaningless third state. The IDE's getter for a primitive is isDeleted(), and Jackson still maps it to the JSON property "deleted".
  • Column type by database: MySQL bit (from the lecture's log), H2 boolean (verified), PostgreSQL boolean. Hibernate picks it from the dialect.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"200 Created" → the create endpoint returns 201 Created.
"404 Method Not Allowed" → 405 Method Not Allowed.
"saves the student into memory" → into the database.
"GeneratedType.IDENTITY" → GenerationType.IDENTITY.
"the column is created as bigin" → bigint.
The endpoint is written both as "delete-soft" and "delete-softly"; the final one is /delete-soft.

Lecture 14: Java Servlets & Tomcat — The Foundation Under Spring MVC (with a Servlet CRUD App)

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #14 · 1h46m · Code Army · Servlets, servlet container, external vs embedded Tomcat, WAR deployment, servlet lifecycle

Why learn servlets in the Spring Boot era?

Nobody writes raw servlets for new projects. But Spring MVC, and therefore every Spring Boot web app, is built on the Servlet API. Servlets were Java's first technology for web applications, so to understand what Spring does internally, you need to know:

  • What a servlet is.
  • What Tomcat is.
  • The difference between external and embedded Tomcat.

Instead of pure theory, the lecture builds a small CRUD app with plain servlets, deployed to a standalone Tomcat, with Postman as the client.

Recap: client–server

  • The client sends an HTTP request. It can be a frontend app, a mobile app or Postman.
  • The server, where the backend code is deployed, returns an HTTP response. Today the server is Tomcat running our servlets; normally it would be a Spring Boot / Spring MVC app.

The problem: building a web app with core Java alone

Can plain Java build a web application? Yes and no. The java.net package has ServerSocket and Socket, which can listen on a port (say localhost:8080) and accept connections. But a socket gives you only a stream of bytes. It doesn't understand HTTP.

An incoming request like GET localhost:8080/hello carries several parts:

Part of an HTTP requestExample
MethodGET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE
Host and portlocalhost:8080, or codearmy.in when deployed
Endpoint (path)/hello, /login, /courses
HeadersContent-Type: application/json
Query parameters / path variables?id=1
BodyJSON, for POST and PUT. None for GET

What we want is simple: map each endpoint to a Java method. /hello calls hello(), /login calls login(), and the method's result goes back to the client. But that mapping needs the method, path and so on, which a raw socket doesn't give you. You would parse the text yourself:

// what "routing" looks like when you parse raw HTTP yourself
if (endpoint.equals("/hello") && method.equals("GET")) {
    callHelloMethod();
}

Everything you'd hand-build with java.net

  1. Read the raw HTTP text from the socket.
  2. Parse the URL and path.
  3. Parse the headers.
  4. Parse the query parameters.
  5. Read and parse the body.
  6. Identify the HTTP method.
  7. Map the request to the right Java method.
  8. Pass the request data into that method.
  9. Build the response text.
  10. Add the status code manually.
  11. Add the response headers.
  12. Send the response back to the browser.
  13. Manage threads for concurrent users, or everyone waits behind one request, and keep the server running and listening.
The real failure mode:
None of these 13 steps is business logic. They're server plumbing, repeated in every app. A developer should focus on the hello() method, not on parsing bytes. Spring Boot lets you write only the mapped method, and this lecture shows the layer that made that possible.

The fix: a servlet container

Imagine moving all the plumbing (listening, parsing, building responses, threading) into a separate container. Our code shrinks to only the business methods. That container is a servlet container, and the most famous one is Apache Tomcat. It's often just called "the server", since it does all the server work.

Tomcat and servlets, defined

  • Tomcat is a Java web server that runs Java web applications. From the OS's point of view it's a long-running process that stays up and listens on a port, 8080 by default. When a request arrives, it parses it, works out which Java class and method should handle it, and calls that method.
  • A servlet is a special Java class we write. Tomcat creates and manages its objects and calls its methods. A container holds many servlets, each mapped to its own URL. For example, /hello goes to Servlet A and /login to Servlet B. Tomcat knows the mapping from an XML file or from annotations.
Where Spring's ideas came from
SpringServlet world
ContainerIoC container (ApplicationContext)Tomcat (servlet container)
Managed objectsBeansServlets
Who creates themThe container, not youThe container, not you
Lifecycle hooks@PostConstruct / @PreDestroyinit() / destroy()
Dependency injectionYesNo. You wire dependencies with new

Both are just Java classes managed by a container. The lecture's point is that "the idea of an IoC container managing beans came from servlets."

The request and response objects

Java code understands objects, not HTTP text. So for each request Tomcat:

  1. Parses the request into an HttpServletRequest object. It has getters such as getParameter(), getHeader(), getMethod(), getRequestURI() and getReader() for the body.
  2. Creates an empty HttpServletResponse with setters such as setStatus(), setContentType(), setHeader() and getWriter() for the body.
  3. Passes both to the servlet's method.
  4. The servlet reads from the request and fills in the response. It returns nothing, so every handler is void.
  5. Tomcat turns the filled response object into an HTTP response.
Why the handlers are void:
Tomcat passes the servlet a reference to the response object. Whatever the servlet sets through that reference changes the same object Tomcat holds, so there's nothing to return. (Java passes references by value, so both point to one object.)

External Tomcat vs embedded Tomcat, and WAR files

  • Today (Spring Boot): spring-boot-starter-web (spring-boot-starter-webmvc in Boot 4) brings an embedded Tomcat. Tomcat is a library inside your app. You run main() and it starts, packaged as a JAR.
  • Earlier: you downloaded Tomcat separately (external Tomcat), packaged your app as a WAR and deployed it into Tomcat, which then ran it.
  • A WAR (Web Application Archive) is like a JAR. It contains compiled classes, config files, servlet classes, and static HTML/CSS/JS, under a standard WEB-INF/ layout.

Setting up an external Tomcat

  1. Search "Tomcat download" and open the Apache Tomcat site. Under Core, download the zip (Windows) or tar.gz (Mac/Linux) and extract it. The lecture uses Tomcat 10.1.x, and asks you to use Tomcat 10 as well.
  2. The folder contains bin/, conf/, lib/, logs/, temp/, webapps/… In conf/server.xml, search for Connector to find <Connector port="8080" …>. That's why Tomcat listens on 8080.
  3. Before starting, localhost:8080 in a browser gives "This site can't be reached".
  4. On Mac/Linux, give the scripts execute permission (chmod +x bin/*.sh), then run bin/catalina.sh run. On Windows, use bin\catalina.bat run or bin\startup.bat.
  5. The log shows "Server startup in [292] milliseconds", and localhost:8080 now shows the Tomcat welcome page.

Project setup: a WAR with the Servlet API

<packaging>war</packaging>                 <!-- default is jar (Maven lecture) -->

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>jakarta.servlet</groupId>
        <artifactId>jakarta.servlet-api</artifactId>
        <version>6.0.0</version>               <!-- matches Tomcat 10.1; see note -->
        <scope>provided</scope>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

<build>
    <finalName>crud-app</finalName>         <!-- WAR name = URL context path -->
</build>
  • A plain Maven project, servlet-crud-demo, with no Spring at all. Only the servlet API is added (from mvnrepository.com, "jakarta servlet").
  • finalName sets the WAR name to crud-app.war instead of artifactId-version.war. The reason becomes clear at deployment: the name ends up in the URL.
Worth flagging: match the Servlet API to the Tomcat version (version-dependent):
  • The lecture adds jakarta.servlet-api 6.1.0 but runs Tomcat 10.1.
  • Tomcat 10.1 implements Servlet 6.0, and Tomcat 11 implements Servlet 6.1. Compiling against a newer API than the container provides works only while you don't call anything new.
  • So pair them: Tomcat 10.1 with 6.0.0, Tomcat 11 with 6.1.0.
  • Tomcat 9 and older use the old javax.servlet package, while Tomcat 10+ uses jakarta.servlet. The code isn't interchangeable.

The User model and the in-memory "database"

To keep the focus on servlets, there's no real database; JDBC would add boilerplate that isn't covered yet. Users live in a HashMap. The package layout mirrors Spring Boot's layers, minus the repository:

in.strikes
├── model/     User          (id, name, email, mobile + getters/setters + all-args constructor)
├── servlet/   UserServlet   (like a controller)
└── service/   UserService   (map-backed storage)

User is a plain POJO with Integer id, String name, String email and String mobile. There are no annotations, and nothing manages it.

Writing the servlet

@WebServlet("/users")                          // Tomcat: send /users requests here
public class UserServlet extends HttpServlet {

    private UserService userService = new UserService();   // no DI → manual, tightly coupled

    @Override protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response) …
    @Override protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response) …
    @Override protected void doPut(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response) …
    @Override protected void doDelete(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response) …
}
  • Mapping: tell Tomcat which URL this servlet handles. The old way is web.xml, listing each servlet and its URL. The annotation @WebServlet("/users") does the same and is preferred, like Spring's annotations.
  • extends HttpServlet makes it an HTTP servlet. HttpServlet is an abstract class offering init, doGet, doHead, doPost, doPut, doDelete, getLastModified… You override the ones you need. doPatch appears in the lecture's IDE only because it compiled against Servlet 6.1; it was added in 6.1 (Tomcat 11). Under Tomcat 10.1 (Servlet 6.0), HttpServlet doesn't dispatch PATCH.
One endpoint per servlet class, one method per HTTP verb:
In Spring each method gets its own path (@GetMapping("/get/{id}")). A servlet's URL belongs to the class. So POST, GET (one or all), PUT and DELETE all hit /users, and the HTTP method decides which doXxx runs. Read-one and read-all both land in the single doGet, which checks whether an id parameter is present.
OperationRequestHandler
CreatePOST /users?id=1&name=Aditya&email=…&mobile=…doPost
Read oneGET /users?id=1doGet (id present)
Read allGET /usersdoGet (no id)
UpdatePUT /users?id=…doPut (homework)
DeleteDELETE /users?id=…doDelete (homework)

Why the create request uses query parameters instead of a JSON body

  • In Spring Boot, Jackson converts a JSON body into a User automatically (@RequestBody).
  • A plain servlet has no JSON conversion. You'd read the body yourself through request.getReader() (a BufferedReader) and call a JSON library.
  • To keep the demo simple, the lecture sends every field as a query parameter: POST /users?id=1&name=Aditya&email=aditya@gmail.com&mobile=9876543210. Parameters are easy to read.

doPost: read parameters, validate, store, respond

@Override
protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response) throws IOException {
    String idParam = request.getParameter("id");        // parameters always arrive as String
    String name    = request.getParameter("name");
    String email   = request.getParameter("email");
    String mobile  = request.getParameter("mobile");

    if (idParam == null || name == null || email == null || mobile == null) {
        response.setStatus(400);
        response.setContentType("application/json");
        response.getWriter().write("{\"message\": \"Some fields are missing\"}");
        return;
    }
    User user = new User(Integer.parseInt(idParam), name, email, mobile);   // String → Integer by hand
    User createdUser = userService.createUser(user);

    response.setStatus(201);                                 // Created
    response.setContentType("application/json");
    response.getWriter().write("{\"message\": \"User added successfully\"}");
}
  • request.getParameter("id") is what Tomcat saves us from: no hunting for ? and & in a raw string.
  • Parameters are always String, so the id goes through Integer.parseInt.
  • The response is built field by field: status, content type, then the body through getWriter().write(…). The JSON is a hand-written string with escaped quotes (\").
  • getWriter() can throw IOException, so the handler declares throws IOException.
Transcript slips / bugs fixed in the code above:
  • The lecture's check is id == null && email == null && name == null && mobile == null, which rejects only when all fields are missing. It should use ||, "if any is null", as the lecturer intended.
  • It also parses the id before checking. Integer.parseInt(null) throws NumberFormatException, which gives a 500 instead of the intended 400. Check the raw string first.
  • The lecture says "2001" and then "200" for created. The correct status is 201.
  • The lecturer first wrote "User added successfully" into the 400 branch, then swapped it to "Some fields are missing".

doGet: one handler for read-one and read-all

@Override
protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response) throws IOException {
    String idParam = request.getParameter("id");

    if (idParam == null) {                                         // GET /users → all users
        List<User> users = userService.getAllUsers();
        response.setStatus(200);
        response.setContentType("application/json");
        response.getWriter().write(usersToJson(users));
        return;                                                    // forgotten at first → 500
    }
    User userResp = userService.getUserById(Integer.parseInt(idParam));
    if (userResp == null) {
        response.setStatus(404);                                   // no body needed
        return;
    }
    response.setStatus(200);
    response.setContentType("application/json");
    response.getWriter().write(userToJson(userResp));
}

Converting objects to JSON by hand needs two helpers:

private String userToJson(User user) {
    return "{\"id\": " + user.getId()
         + ", \"name\": \"" + user.getName() + "\""
         + ", \"email\": \"" + user.getEmail() + "\""
         + ", \"mobile\": \"" + user.getMobile() + "\"}";
}

private String usersToJson(List<User> users) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("[");
    for (int i = 0; i < users.size(); i++) {           // index loop, so we know the last element
        sb.append(userToJson(users.get(i)));
        if (i < users.size() - 1) sb.append(",");       // no trailing comma, or the JSON is invalid
    }
    return sb.append("]").toString();
}
  • A JSON array is [ {…}, {…} ]. The loop reuses userToJson and adds commas between items, but not after the last, since a trailing comma is invalid JSON.
  • A for-each loop can't tell which item is last, so it was replaced with an index loop.
  • In Spring Boot, all of this is return user; and Jackson does the rest.

UserService

public class UserService {
    private Map<Integer, User> userDb;

    public UserService() {
        userDb = new HashMap<>();                 // initialise fields in the constructor
    }

    public User createUser(User userRequest) {
        userDb.put(userRequest.getId(), userRequest);
        return userRequest;
    }

    public User getUserById(Integer id) {
        return userDb.getOrDefault(id, null);
    }

    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        List<User> usersResponse = new ArrayList<>();
        for (User user : userDb.values()) {
            usersResponse.add(user);
        }
        return usersResponse;                      // or: new ArrayList<>(userDb.values())
    }
}
  • The lecture first wrote return (List<User>) userDb.values(); and got a ClassCastException. values() returns a Collection view, which isn't a List, so it can't be cast. It must be copied into a list.
  • UserServlet creates its UserService with new. There's no @Autowired here; the class is tightly coupled to its dependency. "This is exactly why we moved to the Spring Framework."

Deploying and testing

  1. Maven → Lifecycle → package creates target/crud-app.war.
  2. Copy it into Tomcat's webapps/ folder. Tomcat unpacks it into webapps/crud-app/, containing META-INF/ and WEB-INF/classes/in/strikes/… with the compiled model, service and servlet classes.
  3. Restart Tomcat (bin/catalina.sh run). Unlike in Spring Boot, you can't just run main() in the IDE, because there's no embedded server.
  4. Postman: POST http://localhost:8080/users?… returns 404. The correct URL includes the WAR name: http://localhost:8080/crud-app/users?…, which returns "User added successfully". Rohit (id 2) is added the same way.
  5. GET /crud-app/users?id=1 returns Aditya's JSON (200), and ?id=2 returns Rohit.
  6. GET /crud-app/users first gave a ClassCastException, fixed as described above. Each fix meant repackaging, replacing the WAR and restarting Tomcat. Because the map is in memory, every restart wiped the users, so they had to be POSTed again.
  7. Then the list came back, but with 500 Internal Server Error: the read-all branch had no return. Execution fell through to Integer.parseInt(null). After adding return and redeploying, the result was 200 with the full list.

Verified (added): I ran the corrected code in an embedded Tomcat 10.1:

  • POST with all fields: 201.
  • POST with missing fields: 400.
  • GET ?id=1: 200. GET ?id=5: 404.
  • GET /crud-app/users: 200 with a JSON array.
  • PUT with no doPut override: 405 Method Not Allowed.
  • /users without the context path: 404.

Why the URL needs /crud-app: one Tomcat, many applications

  • An external Tomcat can host many applications: every WAR in webapps/ becomes one. Each app gets a context path, its own URL prefix, taken from the WAR file name. That's why finalName was set to a short, clean crud-app.
  • Each application has many servlets, each with its own path. Each servlet has many doXxx methods but one endpoint.
  • Tomcat resolves /crud-app/users as: application crud-app, then UserServlet, then the handler for the HTTP method.

Why scope is provided

  • The jakarta.servlet-api JAR supplies HttpServlet, HttpServletRequest, HttpServletResponse… We need it to compile, and Maven's package phase runs compile first.
  • But Tomcat already ships these classes. It has to, because it creates and calls servlets. So the WAR shouldn't bundle them.
  • provided means "on the compile classpath, but left out of the package, because the runtime provides it." Bundling a second copy invites class-loading conflicts, where Tomcat can't decide whether to use its own copy or yours.

Servlet lifecycle

Tomcat manages a servlet's creation and destruction, like the IoC container does for beans, but without dependency injection. There are three callbacks:

MethodWhenSpring analogueUse for
init()Once, right after the constructor@PostConstructLoading expensive resources, warming caches
service(req, res)On every request—Dispatching to doGet/doPost…
destroy()Once, on shutdown or undeploy@PreDestroyClosing resources, flushing caches
  • Lazy by default: the servlet object is created when its URL is first requested, not at startup. This is configurable (see below).
  • service() is normally not overridden. HttpServlet.service() looks at the HTTP method and calls doGet, doPost, doPut, doDelete, doOptions…, plus doPatch from Servlet 6.1. Our override of doGet wins through ordinary polymorphism.

Demo run: HelloServlet

@WebServlet("/hello")
public class HelloServlet extends HttpServlet {
    public HelloServlet()    { System.out.println("HelloServlet constructor called"); }
    @Override public void init()    { System.out.println("init method called"); }
    @Override protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response) throws IOException {
        response.setStatus(200);
        response.setContentType("text/plain");        // plain text, not JSON
        response.getWriter().write("Hello");
    }
    @Override public void destroy() { System.out.println("destroy method called"); }
}
  1. Repackage, replace the WAR and restart Tomcat.
  2. The prints appear in Tomcat's terminal, not IntelliJ, because the code runs inside Tomcat.
  3. The first GET /crud-app/hello returns 200 "Hello", and the log shows "HelloServlet constructor called" then "init method called".
  4. In a second terminal, run bin/shutdown.sh (Windows: bin\shutdown.bat). The log prints "destroy method called" before Tomcat stops.

Verified (added): in Tomcat 10.1, two consecutive GET /hello calls ran on different threads (http-nio-exec-1, exec-2) but on the same servlet instance. The constructor and init ran once, before the first request.

From many servlets to one front controller: the road to Spring MVC

As an app grows, each servlet repeats the same chores: reading input, writing responses, validation, logging, routing. The idea is to put one central servlet in front:

  1. Tomcat sends every request to the central servlet.
  2. It does the common work: logging, validation, reading the request, writing the response.
  3. It forwards the request to the right lightweight handler.
The key link:
Spring MVC didn't discard servlets; it uses them. Its central servlet is the DispatcherServlet. The small per-feature servlets become controllers (beans). Spring Boot doesn't build the web layer itself; it boots Spring MVC with auto-configuration and an embedded Tomcat. The next lecture covers DispatcherServlet in depth.

Homework / suggested extensions

  • Implement doPut (update the map entry from query parameters) and doDelete (remove it) to complete the servlet CRUD app.
  • Extract the repeated status / content-type / writer code into a helper method.

Gaps worth raising in an interview

  • Servlets are singletons shared across threads. Tomcat creates one instance per servlet and calls it from many request threads at once, from a thread pool (default maxThreads 200). The lecture's HashMap in a field is therefore not thread-safe: concurrent POSTs can corrupt it. Use ConcurrentHashMap and keep request data in local variables, not fields. Spring's singleton controllers have exactly the same rule.
  • Hand-built JSON is unsafe. A name containing " or \ produces invalid JSON, and nothing is escaped. Use Jackson's ObjectMapper both ways: mapper.readValue(request.getReader(), User.class) and mapper.writeValue(response.getWriter(), user).
  • Create data belongs in the body. Query parameters end up in server logs, browser history and proxies, and have length limits. Parameters are fine for the demo only.
  • Character encoding. Call response.setCharacterEncoding("UTF-8") before getWriter(), or non-ASCII names may be garbled.
  • Unchecked parse. ?id=abc makes Integer.parseInt throw, which is a 500. Catch NumberFormatException and return 400.
  • Slow redeploy cycle. Package, copy and restart on every change. Tomcat's autoDeploy (on by default) hot-deploys a WAR dropped into webapps/ without a restart, and IDE Tomcat integrations automate the rest. Embedded servers avoid it entirely.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Core Java does have an HTTP server. The JDK has shipped com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer since Java 6. It parses HTTP and gives you method, headers and body, and JDK 18 added the jwebserver tool. They're fine for tiny tools but have no servlet model, routing framework or production features. The lecture's point about raw java.net sockets stands.
  • HttpServletRequest / HttpServletResponse are interfaces. Tomcat supplies the implementation classes. The lecture's getHostName/getEndpoint names were illustrative; the real ones include getServerName(), getRequestURI(), getHeader(), getParameter() and getReader().
  • HttpServlet is abstract but has no abstract methods. You aren't forced to override anything. Every doXxx you skip answers 405 Method Not Allowed (verified with PUT).
  • @WebServlet("/users") is an exact match. /crud-app/users/1 returns 404 (verified). To accept path segments, map "/users/*" and read request.getPathInfo(). That's why the lecture used query parameters for ids.
  • Eager servlet loading: @WebServlet(urlPatterns = "/users", loadOnStartup = 1), or <load-on-startup> in web.xml, makes Tomcat create the servlet and call init at deploy time, avoiding a slow first request.
  • Lifecycle signatures: the container actually calls init(ServletConfig), which stores the config and then calls the no-arg init() the lecture overrode. The real dispatcher is service(HttpServletRequest, HttpServletResponse), reached from the generic service(ServletRequest, ServletResponse).
  • Filters are the servlet API's answer to repeated per-request chores. A jakarta.servlet.Filter wraps servlets for logging, auth, CORS and encoding. Spring Security is built as a chain of filters in front of DispatcherServlet.
  • Tomcat is a servlet container, not a full application server. Internally it's Catalina (the servlet container), Coyote (the HTTP connector) and Jasper (the JSP engine). Full Jakarta EE servers such as WildFly and GlassFish add EJB, JMS and more. Jetty and Undertow are alternative servlet containers, and Spring Boot can embed any of them.
  • A 404 is a client error (4xx), meaning the resource wasn't found. The lecture's "it's not an error, it's not-found" means it isn't a server fault.
  • ROOT.war deploys at the empty context path, so URLs have no /crud-app prefix. Spring Boot's embedded Tomcat also uses the root context by default (server.servlet.context-path changes it).
Transcript slips to ignore:
"port 880" → 8080.
"We extend HttpServlet so its methods must be overridden" → it's optional.
"init is like pre-construct / destroy is like pre-construct" → init ≈ @PostConstruct, destroy ≈ @PreDestroy.
"HTTP request class" → HttpServletRequest (an interface).
"user service" said for "user servlet" in places.
"BS catalina.run" → bin/catalina.sh run.
"web.jar" → the webapps folder.

Lecture 15: Spring MVC Internals — DispatcherServlet, HandlerMapping, a Boot-less MVC App & JSP Views

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #15 · 1h15m · Code Army · the last "internals" lecture before the series moves fully to Spring Boot

Why this lecture closes the internals

Spring Boot web apps sit on Spring MVC, and Spring MVC sits on servlets and Tomcat (Lecture 14). Once Spring MVC's architecture is clear, "Spring Boot's entire internal architecture is done". Boot is an auto-configuration layer on top of Spring MVC.

What Spring MVC is, and what Boot adds

  • Spring MVC is Spring's actual web framework. The module is Spring Web MVC (artifact spring-webmvc), usually just called Spring MVC. It builds two kinds of apps:
    • REST APIs returning JSON, the focus of this series.
    • Server-rendered web apps returning HTML/JSP pages (views), shown at the end of the lecture.
  • The web annotations belong to Spring MVC, not Spring Boot: @Controller, @RestController, @RequestMapping, @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @RequestBody…
  • Spring Boot makes Spring MVC easy. In the Lecture 11–13 CRUD app we wrote only business logic (controller → service → repository) and configured nothing. With plain Spring MVC you'd start Tomcat, declare the DispatcherServlet and pick dependencies yourself. This lecture does exactly that, to show what Boot hides.

The problem: who connects Tomcat to my controller?

We know the right half of the picture: controller → service → repository → DB, where @GetMapping("/hello") on HelloController.hello() handles GET /hello. But:

  • A controller doesn't listen on port 8080; Tomcat does.
  • Tomcat talks only to servlets, and HelloController isn't a servlet.
  • So who maps GET /hello to HelloController.hello()? That is the unanswered question.

Step 1: the plain-servlet world, and its repetition

Recap from Lecture 14:

  1. Tomcat maps URLs to many servlets, such as UserServlet, OrderServlet and PaymentServlet.
  2. For /users it parses the request into HttpServletRequest, creates an empty HttpServletResponse and passes both to UserServlet.
  3. The servlet fills in the response, and Tomcat sends it back.

Every servlet repeats the same non-business chores:

  • Checking request parameters.
  • Converting JSON to Java objects, and Java objects back to JSON.
  • Building the response: status, headers, body.
  • Exception handling.

Step 2: Spring's idea, one front servlet

Tomcat stays, since it's the container that listens for requests. But instead of many servlets, Tomcat hands everything to a single servlet, the DispatcherServlet. It does the common chores once, then routes to plain controller beans: UserController, OrderController, PaymentController. We no longer write servlets; we write controllers.

Why @RequestBody "just works":
When Postman sends {"id": 1, "name": "Aditya"} and the controller declares @RequestBody User user, the object arrives already filled. It isn't magic: the JSON-to-Java conversion happened before your method was called, in the dispatcher's machinery.

Inside the dispatcher: HandlerMapping

DispatcherServlet is only the entry point; it delegates to internal components. The first one to know is HandlerMapping, which builds a mapping table from request to controller method:

What HandlerMapping conceptually holds
HTTP method + pathHandler (controller method)
GET /studentsStudentController.getAllStudents()
POST /studentsStudentController.createStudent()

How the table is built

  1. The IoC container creates all beans at startup: controllers (@Controller/@RestController are meta-annotated with @Component), services and repositories.
  2. HandlerMapping scans the controller beans for @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, @RequestMapping…
  3. From them it builds the table.
  4. On each request, DispatcherServlet looks up the table and invokes the right method.

Who does what: the IoC container creates the controller objects, and the dispatcher calls them. The lecture adds that the actual invocation goes through a HandlerAdapter, but the two names to remember are DispatcherServlet and HandlerMapping.

Where each piece of client data gets bound

A client can send data three ways:

DataExampleLecture's explanationMore precisely (added)
Request body (JSON){"id":1,"name":"Aditya"}DispatcherServlet uses Jackson to map JSON keys onto the class fieldsAn HttpMessageConverter (the Jackson converter) invoked by the argument resolver for @RequestBody. The same converters write return values as JSON
Path variable/users/1HandlerMapping matches /users/{id}, via a "handler method argument resolver"The mapping extracts the URI template variables; a HandlerMethodArgumentResolver (PathVariableMethodArgumentResolver) binds id and converts it to Long
Query parameter/users?id=1Tomcat already parses these into HttpServletRequestTomcat parses; RequestParamMethodArgumentResolver reads getParameter() and converts types for @RequestParam

The way back mirrors this: the repository returns to the service, the service to the controller, and the controller to the dispatcher. The dispatcher converts the returned object to JSON into the HttpServletResponse, and Tomcat sends it. The servlet methods are void, so the response is filled in rather than returned (Lecture 14).

The complete request flow

Worth adding: the full cast, for interviews:
  • HandlerMapping (RequestMappingHandlerMapping) finds the handler and returns a HandlerExecutionChain: the handler plus any HandlerInterceptors.
  • HandlerAdapter (RequestMappingHandlerAdapter) invokes it, using HandlerMethodArgumentResolvers for parameters and HandlerMethodReturnValueHandlers for results.
  • HttpMessageConverters turn the body into objects and back (JSON through Jackson).
  • HandlerExceptionResolver turns exceptions into responses. This is how @ExceptionHandler and @ControllerAdvice work.
  • ViewResolver turns a view name into a template, for non-REST pages (below).

Building a Spring MVC app without Spring Boot

This time Tomcat is embedded, not external: a library inside the app, started from main(). Same flow, no WAR deployment. The project is a plain Maven project, spring-mvc-demo, and it needs three dependencies that Boot's single starter would have given us:

DependencyWhyVersion used
org.springframework:spring-webmvcSpring MVC: DispatcherServlet, the web annotations7.0.7
org.apache.tomcat.embed:tomcat-embed-coreEmbedded Tomcat (not tomcat-embed-jasper, which is for JSP)11.0.22
com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databindJSON ↔ Java conversion2.x (the lecturer picked one with fewer listed vulnerabilities)
Worth flagging: version pairing (version-dependent):
  • Spring Framework 7 targets Jakarta EE 11 / Servlet 6.1, hence Tomcat 11. Spring 6 pairs with Tomcat 10.1.
  • Spring 7's primary JSON support is Jackson 3 (tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind). Jackson 2 (com.fasterxml…) is still supported but deprecated. I verified that Jackson 2.22 still works with spring-webmvc 7.0.5.
  • With Boot, the starter chooses all of these compatible versions for you.

Application layers: the same as in Spring Boot
