  • entity/Student: a POJO with Long id, String name, String email, getters and setters. It's called "entity" but has no @Entity; there's no JPA here.
  • repository/StudentRepository (@Repository): a HashMap<Long, Student> named studentDb, created in the constructor. Its methods borrow JPA's names for practice: save, findById (studentDb.get(id), null if absent) and findAll (new ArrayList<>(studentDb.values())).
  • service/StudentService (@Service): constructor-injects the repository, with createStudent, getStudent and getAllStudents delegating to it.
  • controller/StudentController:
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/students")
public class StudentController {
    private final StudentService studentService;

    public StudentController(StudentService studentService) { this.studentService = studentService; }

    @PostMapping                                             // POST /students
    public ResponseEntity<Student> createStudent(@RequestBody Student studentRequest) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(studentService.createStudent(studentRequest));
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")                                     // GET /students/1
    public ResponseEntity<Student> getStudent(@PathVariable("id") Long id) {
        Student studentResponse = studentService.getStudent(id);
        if (studentResponse == null) return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
        return ResponseEntity.ok(studentResponse);
    }

    @GetMapping                                              // GET /students
    public ResponseEntity<List<Student>> getAllStudents() {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(studentService.getAllStudents());   // empty list is fine: 200 []
    }
}

Up to here it's identical to a Boot app. In Boot we'd now run main(), but Spring MVC needs two more pieces.

Missing piece 1: a configuration class

@Configuration
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "in.strikes")     // default would scan only in.strikes.config
@EnableWebMvc
public class WebConfig {
}
  • @Configuration and @ComponentScan are Spring Core (Lecture 5). Without basePackages, scanning starts from this class's package, in.strikes.config, and would miss the controllers.
  • @EnableWebMvc switches on the MVC machinery. The lecture puts it as: without it, @RequestBody, @PostMapping and the rest aren't active.
Precision note (added):
@EnableWebMvc imports DelegatingWebMvcConfiguration, which registers the infrastructure beans: RequestMappingHandlerMapping, RequestMappingHandlerAdapter, message converters (Jackson when it's on the classpath), validators and so on. Don't add @EnableWebMvc in a Spring Boot app. It tells Boot you're taking full control, and Boot's MVC auto-configuration backs off (static resources, converters customisation…). To customise MVC in Boot, implement WebMvcConfigurer instead.

Missing piece 2: the bootstrap code in main()

public static void main(String[] args) throws LifecycleException {
    // 1. embedded Tomcat on port 8080
    Tomcat tomcat = new Tomcat();
    tomcat.setPort(8080);
    tomcat.getConnector();                               // creates the connector that listens on the port

    // 2. a web application ("context") inside Tomcat
    String contextPath = "";                             // root: no /crud-app prefix
    String baseDoc = new File("src/main/webapp").getAbsolutePath();   // folder must exist
    Context context = tomcat.addContext(contextPath, baseDoc);

    // 3. the Spring IoC container: a *web* application context
    AnnotationConfigWebApplicationContext springContext = new AnnotationConfigWebApplicationContext();
    springContext.register(WebConfig.class);

    // 4. the front controller, given the container so it can find controller beans
    DispatcherServlet dispatcherServlet = new DispatcherServlet(springContext);
    Tomcat.addServlet(context, "dispatcherServlet", dispatcherServlet);   // static method
    context.addServletMappingDecoded("/", "dispatcherServlet");            // every request → dispatcher

    // 5. start and keep running
    tomcat.start();
    System.out.println("Tomcat started on port 8080");
    tomcat.getServer().await();                           // block main thread, keep server up
}

What each step means:

  • Connector: getConnector() initialises the component that actually listens on 8080.
  • Context = one web application. An external Tomcat holds many apps in webapps/, each with a context path (/crud-app, Lecture 14). Embedded or external, Tomcat needs:
    • A context path: empty here, so there's no URL prefix.
    • A physical base folder. The lecturer creates an empty src/main/webapp and passes its absolute path.
  • Web application context: the first attempt used AnnotationConfigApplicationContext, and new DispatcherServlet(…) refused it because it needs a WebApplicationContext. The web flavour is AnnotationConfigWebApplicationContext. It has no config-class constructor, so the config is added with register(WebConfig.class). "The IoC container is the same; only the implementation class differs": annotation, XML or web variants.
  • Why the dispatcher needs the container: HandlerMapping has to scan the controller beans for mapping annotations, so the dispatcher is given the container.
  • Register and map the servlet: Tomcat.addServlet(context, name, servlet) registers it, and mapping "/" sends every request to it.
  • Start and wait: start() throws LifecycleException. getServer().await() keeps the process alive. The "Tomcat started" line is printed by hand; Boot logs it for you.

Demo run and the bugs hit

  1. The first run failed at the base-document line. The lecturer had tried to build the path through System.getProperty(…); using new File("src/main/webapp").getAbsolutePath() directly fixed it. Then the log showed "Tomcat started on port 8080".
  2. POST localhost:8080/students with Aditya's JSON returned 200. The URL has no /api and no app prefix, because the context path is empty. Rohit was added too.
  3. GET /students/1 failed. The fix was to name the variable explicitly: @PathVariable("id") Long id. After restarting and re-posting (the map is in memory), GET /students/1 and /2 worked, and GET /students returned both.
Correction: why @PathVariable Long id failed (verified on Spring 7.0.5):
  • The lecture's explanation, that Spring can't match 1 to Long because longs are written 1L, is wrong. The real error is:
    IllegalArgumentException: Name for argument of type [java.lang.Long] not specified, and parameter name information not available via reflection. Ensure that the compiler uses the '-parameters' flag.
  • A plain Maven project doesn't compile with -parameters, so Spring can't learn that the parameter is called id. Since Spring 6.1 it no longer falls back to reading debug info.
  • spring-boot-starter-parent turns -parameters on, which is why the bare form worked in the Boot CRUD app. It's the same issue as XML constructor-arg name in Lecture 8.
  • Fixes: name it (@PathVariable("id")), or set <maven.compiler.parameters>true</maven.compiler.parameters>.

The whole bootstrap is replaced in Boot by spring-boot-starter-web (-webmvc in Boot 4) plus @SpringBootApplication. Tomcat starts itself on 8080, and there's no WebConfig with base packages and no main() wiring.

@Controller + @ResponseBody = @RestController

Switching StudentController to plain @Controller and adding @ResponseBody on each handler works exactly as before. @RestController is meta-annotated with both @Controller and @ResponseBody, so it applies @ResponseBody to every method.

Why @ResponseBody exists: Spring MVC predates the REST-API era. By default, a @Controller method's String return value is a view name: a page to render. @ResponseBody says "write the return value into the HTTP body (as JSON) instead".

Precision note (added, verified):
  • A @Controller method that returns ResponseEntity needs no @ResponseBody. ResponseEntity is handled as a body by its own return-value handler (HttpEntityMethodProcessor). With @Controller, ResponseEntity and no @ResponseBody, the result was 200 with JSON.
  • A plain object returned from @Controller without @ResponseBody is treated as a view lookup. It came back 404, since no matching view exists.
  • So the lecture's extra annotations were harmless but, for ResponseEntity methods, unnecessary.

MVC = Model, View, Controller

LetterMeaningIn Spring MVC
ModelData carried from the controller to the viewA Model object: model.addAttribute("message", …)
ViewThe page shown to the userAn HTML/JSP (or Thymeleaf) template
ControllerHandles HTTP requests@Controller classes with mapping methods

Today the view layer is usually a separate frontend (React, Vue, plain JavaScript), and Spring MVC mostly serves REST APIs. The name "MVC" stayed. JSP appears mainly in legacy code, but it's good to know.

Worked example: a JSP page with Spring MVC

This is a separate project, jsp-demo. Dependencies:

  • spring-webmvc and tomcat-embed-core, as before.
  • No Jackson, since there's no JSON.
  • tomcat-embed-jasper (11.0.22), the JSP engine for Tomcat.

The controller returns view names

@Controller                                       // NOT @RestController: we return views
public class HelloController {

    @GetMapping("/")                              // home page
    public String showHomePage(Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("message", "Enter your name");
        return "home";                            // a VIEW NAME, not text: resolves to home.jsp
    }

    @PostMapping("/greet")                        // the form posts here
    public String greetUser(@RequestParam String name, Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("message", "Hello " + name);
        return "home";                            // same page, new message
    }
}

The view: src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/views/home.jsp

  • webapp/ holds static content and views, mirroring an external Tomcat app, which had META-INF and WEB-INF. The lecturer first named the file hello.jsp and renamed it to home.jsp to match the returned view name.
  • The page is HTML plus Java expression language: <p>${message}</p> prints the model attribute.
  • It has a <form action="/greet" method="post"> with <input type="text" name="name"> and a submit button.
  • Styles live in webapp/assets/style.css.

Extra configuration for views

@Configuration
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "in.strikes")
@EnableWebMvc
public class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {

    @Override
    public void addResourceHandlers(ResourceHandlerRegistry registry) {      // serve CSS
        registry.addResourceHandler("/assets/**").addResourceLocations("/assets/");
    }

    @Bean
    public ViewResolver viewResolver() {
        InternalResourceViewResolver resolver = new InternalResourceViewResolver();
        resolver.setPrefix("/WEB-INF/views/");      // where views live
        resolver.setSuffix(".jsp");                 // "home" → /WEB-INF/views/home.jsp
        return resolver;
    }
}
  • ViewResolver maps a returned name to a file: prefix + name + suffix. Without Boot it isn't auto-configured, so it's declared as a bean.
  • Resource handler: without it the CSS doesn't load. With the DispatcherServlet mapped to "/", a request for /assets/style.css goes to Spring. Spring needs to be told that the path is a static file.

The main() changes from the REST demo:

  • tomcat.addWebapp(…) instead of addContext. addWebapp applies Tomcat's default web setup, including its JSP servlet.
  • context.addServletContainerInitializer(new JasperInitializer(), null) initialises the JSP engine.
  • One more line, from the lecture's notes. Because the dispatcher on "/" would otherwise grab everything, it makes .jsp requests get handled separately by the JSP servlet.

Demo run

  1. Open localhost:8080/. GET / runs showHomePage, and the view resolver turns "home" into home.jsp. The page shows "Enter your name" and a form.
  2. Type "Aditya" and submit. The browser POSTs /greet with name=Aditya, @RequestParam String name receives it, and the page shows "Hello Aditya". "Rohit" gives "Hello Rohit".

Series milestone

With Spring Core, servlets and Spring MVC internals covered, "congratulations": the foundation under Boot is understood. From here on, every application is built in Spring Boot, because nobody wants to write this boilerplate each time. The goal now is writing business logic fast, with Boot's features.

Spring MVC vs Spring Boot

Plain Spring MVCSpring Boot (web)
What it isThe web framework itselfAuto-configuration + starters + embedded server on top of Spring MVC
DependenciesPick spring-webmvc, Tomcat, Jackson and compatible versions yourselfOne starter, managed versions
ServerStart Tomcat in code, or deploy a WAR externallyEmbedded Tomcat starts automatically
DispatcherServletCreate, register and map it by handAuto-configured and mapped to /
IoC containerCreate an AnnotationConfigWebApplicationContext, register configSpringApplication.run creates it
Component scan@ComponentScan(basePackages = …)Implied by @SpringBootApplication
View resolver / static files / JSONConfigure manuallySensible defaults (/static, Jackson, Thymeleaf if present)
-parametersOff unless configuredOn through the starter parent

Corrections & worth knowing

  • JSP stands for JavaServer Pages, not "Java Servlet Pages" as the lecture says. JSPs are compiled into servlets by Jasper, which is probably the source of the mix-up. In Spring Boot, JSP has limitations with executable JARs; Thymeleaf is the usual server-side template engine today.
  • Form fields are not query parameters. A method="post" form sends name=Aditya in the request body as application/x-www-form-urlencoded. @RequestParam still reads it because the Servlet API's getParameter() merges query-string and form-body parameters.
  • Views live under WEB-INF for a reason. The container never serves files inside WEB-INF directly, so users can't open home.jsp without going through the controller.
  • Conversion isn't done by DispatcherServlet itself. JSON conversion, argument binding and exception handling are delegated to HttpMessageConverters, HandlerMethodArgumentResolvers and HandlerExceptionResolvers, orchestrated through the HandlerAdapter. The dispatcher coordinates; it doesn't do the work. Knowing these names answers "how does @RequestBody work?" precisely.
  • Interceptors vs filters. A servlet Filter runs in Tomcat, before the DispatcherServlet. A Spring HandlerInterceptor runs inside it, around the controller, with access to the chosen handler. Auth and logging can live in either; Spring Security uses filters.
  • Where Boot does it: DispatcherServletAutoConfiguration creates and registers the dispatcher. ServletWebServerFactoryAutoConfiguration starts the embedded Tomcat, and WebMvcAutoConfiguration supplies what WebConfig did here: static resources from classpath:/static, message converters and view resolvers. Package names moved in Boot 4's modularisation.
  • Context hierarchy (legacy setups): classic web.xml apps often had a root WebApplicationContext (services, repositories) plus a child context per DispatcherServlet (controllers). Boot and this demo use a single context.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"port 880" → 8080.
"Handler Mapping Resolver" / "Handler Method Resolver" → HandlerMethodArgumentResolver.
"@SpringBootApplication uses @EnableAutoConfiguration" is correct; "@SpringBoot annotation" → @SpringBootApplication.
"WebMvcConfigurer" is an interface you implement, as the lecture does.
The JSP file is referred to both as hello.jsp and as home.jsp; the final name is home.jsp.

Lecture 16: DTOs (Data Transfer Objects) & Request Validation

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #16 · 1h04m · Code Army · request/response DTOs, entity↔DTO mapping, Bean Validation with @Valid

Recap: the entity does everything

The flow so far:

  1. The client sends JSON, e.g. POST /api/students with {"id": 1, "name": "Aditya", …}.
  2. The controller maps it (Jackson, through the DispatcherServlet machinery of Lecture 15) straight into the Student entity.
  3. The entity travels to the service, then the repository, and is saved as a row. The class becomes the table, and its fields become columns.
  4. The saved entity travels back and is serialised to JSON for the response.

So one class has four jobs:

  • Request model.
  • Object passed between layers.
  • Database mapping.
  • Response model.

Its only real job should be database mapping. The fix is DTOs, Data Transfer Objects.

Setup

A fresh Initializr project (crud-dto-demo: Boot 4.1.0, Java 21, Spring Web, Spring Data JPA, MySQL Driver) is used to rebuild the layers once:

  • controller, service, repository and entity packages.
  • A Student entity with @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY).
  • StudentRepository extends JpaRepository<Student, Long>.
  • A create endpoint that takes @RequestBody Student and returns ResponseEntity<Student>.

The real work is then done on the Lecture 13 CRUD project (renamed dto-demo). Its entity has id, name, age, email, rollNumber, subject and deleted, and its endpoints are create, get, getAll, update, delete and soft-delete. Posting a student returns 201 with the entity.

The problem: why using the entity everywhere breaks

ProblemWhat happens
Client can set internal fieldsThe request is mapped onto the whole entity, so a client can send "deleted": true, or createdAt/updatedAt metadata. Every such field needs a manual override in the service (setDeleted(false)…). Forget one and the client writes it into the DB.
Internal fields leak outThe response is the whole entity, so the client sees deleted. Why should a React frontend know how soft delete works? Tomorrow it could be a password hash or other sensitive data.
DB schema = API contractSplitting name into firstName/lastName in the table changes the JSON too, so every client breaks and must be told the API contract changed.
Validation piles into the serviceAll the defensive checks land in business code.
The key idea: two worlds:
Clients calling your API over the internet are the external world. Once a request reaches the controller, you're in the internal world. The entity belongs to the internal world: it describes what's stored. The external world should talk to separate classes, so the two can change independently.

The fix: DTOs

  • A DTO is a plain Java class (POJO) with fields and getters/setters, like the entity. It contains only the fields the client should send, or should receive.
  • It's essentially a subset (sometimes a superset) of the entity, shaped for one conversation.
  • Requests and responses can differ. For example, the response adds a message the request never had. So there are separate request DTOs and response DTOs.

Worked example: create with DTOs

1. Request DTO: what the client may send

package in.strikes.demo.dto;

public class CreateStudentRequestDto {       // no id (DB generates it), no deleted, no timestamps
    private String name;
    private Integer age;
    private String email;
    private Integer rollNumber;
    private String subject;
    // getters and setters
}

The controller now accepts it: createStudent(@RequestBody CreateStudentRequestDto studentRequestDto). A client can't set deleted any more; the field doesn't exist. The API contract is now exactly these five keys.

2. Who converts DTO ↔ entity?

The options are the controller, the service or the repository.

  • The lecture puts it in the service, the home of business logic, as private helper methods.
  • As a project grows, move the conversion into dedicated mapper classes (a mapper package) that the service calls.

3. Response DTO: what the client gets back

public class CreateStudentResponseDto {
    private Long id;                // so a frontend can fetch the record later
    private String name;
    private Integer age;
    private String email;
    private Integer rollNumber;
    private String subject;
    private String message;         // extra field the entity doesn't have
    private LocalDateTime createdAt;
    private LocalDateTime updatedAt;
    // getters and setters
}

The message field is just a demonstration that responses can carry extra data. A proper response envelope comes with exception handling in a later lecture.

4. Service: map in, save, map out

public CreateStudentResponseDto createStudent(CreateStudentRequestDto studentRequestDto) {
    Student student = mapToEntity(studentRequestDto);
    student.setCreatedAt(LocalDateTime.now());
    student.setUpdatedAt(LocalDateTime.now());
    Student studentResponse = studentRepository.save(student);
    return mapToDto(studentResponse);
}

private Student mapToEntity(CreateStudentRequestDto dto) {
    Student student = new Student();
    student.setName(dto.getName());
    student.setAge(dto.getAge());
    student.setEmail(dto.getEmail());
    student.setRollNumber(dto.getRollNumber());
    student.setSubject(dto.getSubject());
    student.setDeleted(false);                 // server-owned field set here, not by the client
    return student;
}

private CreateStudentResponseDto mapToDto(Student student) {
    CreateStudentResponseDto responseDto = new CreateStudentResponseDto();
    responseDto.setId(student.getId());
    responseDto.setName(student.getName());
    responseDto.setAge(student.getAge());
    responseDto.setEmail(student.getEmail());
    responseDto.setRollNumber(student.getRollNumber());
    responseDto.setSubject(student.getSubject());
    responseDto.setCreatedAt(student.getCreatedAt());
    responseDto.setUpdatedAt(student.getUpdatedAt());
    responseDto.setMessage("Student saved successfully");
    return responseDto;                         // no "deleted" → never leaks
}
  • The controller returns ResponseEntity<CreateStudentResponseDto>.
  • Setting fields one by one risks forgetting one. The lecture says the Builder pattern will replace this later (see Builder in the LLD notebook, Lecture 28).

Demo: POST Saurav (27, roll 108, React) returns exactly the chosen fields: id, name, age, email, rollNumber, subject and message, with no deleted. "Now I'm in control of what the client sends and receives."

5. Adding createdAt / updatedAt: the decoupling pays off

  • Two fields are added to the entity: private LocalDateTime createdAt and updatedAt, as a Java date-time type rather than a string of epoch values.
  • The service sets both to LocalDateTime.now() on create. Update will refresh only updatedAt.
  • The response DTO exposes them, but the request DTO doesn't accept them.
  • The client's request didn't change at all. The entity (and the table) changed, but the external contract didn't: the worlds are decoupled.

After recreating the table, the log shows created_at and updated_at as datetime columns. The POST response now includes both timestamps, and the row in DBeaver matches.

One DTO per operation: update

First the classes are renamed per operation: CreateStudentRequestDto and CreateStudentResponseDto. IntelliJ's Refactor → Rename updated every usage. The lecturer also fixed class names that were accidentally in camelCase; class names use PascalCase.

Business rule for the example: email can't be changed after creation, which is common in real apps. So the update DTO simply has no email field:

public class UpdateStudentRequestDto {     // name, age, rollNumber, subject; no email, no id
    private String name;
    private Integer age;
    private Integer rollNumber;
    private String subject;
    // getters and setters
}

public class UpdateStudentResponseDto {    // like the create response, but only updatedAt
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private Integer age;
    private String email;
    private Integer rollNumber;
    private String subject;
    private String message;
    private LocalDateTime updatedAt;
    // getters and setters
}

In updateStudent:

  1. Load with findByIdAndDeletedIsFalse, returning null (404) if missing.
  2. Copy name, age, rollNumber and subject. The old setEmail(…) line no longer compiles, because getEmail() doesn't exist on the DTO. The type system enforces the rule.
  3. Set updatedAt = LocalDateTime.now(), save, then mapToUpdateDto(savedStudent) (message "Student updated successfully").
Why separate create/update response DTOs even when they look alike:
The lecturer could have used one StudentResponseDto. Keeping them apart means that if the update response later needs more or fewer fields, nothing else changes. The lecture's rule: what each endpoint returns is a business decision. The update response omits createdAt purely to show that freedom.

Demo: PUT /api/students/update?id=1 (id as a request parameter, Lecture 13) with name "Saurabh" and subject "MERN" returns the update DTO with a fresh updatedAt, and the DB row changes.

Read endpoints reuse a response DTO

  • getStudent returns mapToDto(student), a CreateStudentResponseDto, instead of the entity.
  • getAllStudents maps the list with streams:
return studentList.stream()
        .map(this::mapToDto)
        .toList();                     // Java 16+; a for-loop works too

Delete and soft delete neither take nor return an entity, so they stay unchanged. GET /api/students/get?id=1 returns the DTO.

Validation: stop bad input at the door

DTOs limit which fields arrive, but not what's in them. A client can send:

  • A blank name, or one that's only spaces.
  • An email without @ or a domain.
  • Age 4: "how is a four-year-old using our app?"
  • A missing roll number.

Checks could be written in the service, or in a validator class it calls. But these are malformed requests, not business rules. The service is "special" and reserved for business logic, so bad input should be rejected at the controller, before it ever reaches the service.

Dependency: spring-boot-starter-validation

  • On Initializr it's the "Validation" dependency. For an existing project, add it to the pom (the lecture copied it from mvnrepository).
  • Omit the <version>. spring-boot-starter-parent manages compatible versions for all starters (Lecture 9), so there's no risk of mixing, say, a 4.0.6 starter with a 4.1.0 project.
  • Do you need to memorise starter names? No. Initializr adds them, and the pom shows the real names (spring-boot-starter-data-jpa, spring-boot-starter-webmvc…).

Annotate the request DTO

public class CreateStudentRequestDto {

    @NotBlank(message = "Name cannot be null, empty or blank")
    @Size(min = 2, max = 50, message = "Student name must be within 2 to 50 characters long")
    private String name;

    @NotNull(message = "Age is required")
    @Min(value = 18, message = "Student must be at least 18 years old")
    private Integer age;                       // Integer, not int: see below

    @NotBlank(message = "Student email cannot be blank")
    @Email(message = "Student email must be valid")
    private String email;

    @NotNull(message = "Roll number is required")
    private Integer rollNumber;

    @NotBlank(message = "Subject is required")
    private String subject;
    // getters and setters
}

Trigger it with @Valid

@PostMapping("/create")
public ResponseEntity<CreateStudentResponseDto> createStudent(
        @Valid @RequestBody CreateStudentRequestDto studentRequestDto) { … }

Without @Valid the annotations do nothing. It's what tells Spring to run the constraints on this argument.

Common constraints (package jakarta.validation.constraints)
AnnotationRejectsTypical use
@NotNullnull onlyAny type: Integer, objects
@NotEmptynull, "" (and empty collections)Strings, lists. " " still passes
@NotBlanknull, "", whitespace-onlyThe usual choice for strings
@Size(min, max)Length or size outside the rangeName length, list size
@Min / @MaxNumbers below or above a valueAge ≥ 18
@EmailMalformed emailEmail fields
@PositiveZero and negativesAmounts, counts
@Past / @FutureDates on the wrong side of nowBirth date, expiry date
@Pattern(regexp) (added)Strings not matching a regexPhone numbers, codes
Why Integer, not int, for validated numbers:
A primitive int can never be null. A missing field silently becomes 0, so @NotNull is meaningless on it. With Integer, a missing value is null, and @NotNull catches it. Also note that @Min, @Email, @Size and most others treat null as valid. That's why each is paired with @NotNull/@NotBlank.

Demo run: validation fires, but the messages don't show

  1. POST /create with a blank name and blank email returns 400 Bad Request, with Spring Boot's default body: timestamp, status, error: "Bad Request" and path. The service was never called.
  2. Even after adding custom messages and restarting, the same generic body appears. The client learns that something is wrong, but not what.
  3. With valid data (name "Aditya", age 19, a proper email), the request succeeds.

Boot's default error response doesn't include the validation messages. Showing them requires custom exception handling, the next lecture's topic.

Entity vs DTO

EntityDTO
PurposeMaps to a DB tableCarries data across the API boundary
Annotations@Entity, @Id, JPA mappingsValidation (@NotBlank…), JSON (@JsonProperty…)
ShapeEvery column, including internal onesOnly what one operation needs
Lives inService, repository (internal world)Controller boundary (external contract)
Changes whenThe schema changesThe API contract changes (versioned, communicated)
Managed byJPA persistence contextNobody: a plain object

Gaps worth raising in an interview

  • Validate the update DTO too. The lecture validated only create. UpdateStudentRequestDto needs its own constraints and @Valid on the update endpoint.
  • Unknown fields are silently ignored. A client sending "email" or "deleted" to update gets no error: Boot's Jackson setup has FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES off. That's safe, since the field is discarded, but surprising. Turn it on (spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties=true) for strict contracts.
  • Hand-written mapping doesn't scale. Dozens of setters per DTO are error-prone. Options: a builder (Lombok @Builder), a static factory (StudentResponseDto.from(student)), or a mapping library such as MapStruct (compile-time generated, fast) or ModelMapper (reflection).
  • Timestamps by hand can be forgotten. Let the framework set them: JPA @PrePersist/@PreUpdate callbacks, Hibernate @CreationTimestamp/@UpdateTimestamp, or Spring Data auditing (@CreatedDate/@LastModifiedDate with @EnableJpaAuditing). Prefer Instant or OffsetDateTime over LocalDateTime when servers and clients span time zones.
  • Structural vs business validation. Annotations cover shape (blank, range, format). Rules that need the DB, such as "email must be unique" or "roll number not taken", still belong in the service. Only the database's unique constraint makes them race-safe.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • The attack has a name: mass assignment (over-posting). Binding a request straight to an entity lets clients set fields they shouldn't, such as deleted, role or balance. It's a well-known API security flaw (OWASP API Security Top 10 lists it). DTOs are the standard defence.
  • Returning entities has JPA-specific pitfalls too. Serialising an entity with relationships can trigger LazyInitializationException, extra queries (N+1) or infinite recursion on bidirectional links. Response DTOs avoid all of these. This matters once relationships appear.
  • Java records make great DTOs (Java 16+): public record CreateStudentRequest(@NotBlank String name, @NotNull @Min(18) Integer age) {}. They're immutable, have no boilerplate getters, and Jackson and Bean Validation support them.
  • What @Valid really does. It comes from Jakarta Bean Validation (the jakarta.validation API), implemented by Hibernate Validator, which the starter brings in. On failure, Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException, which is mapped to 400. For nested objects, put @Valid on the nested field too. To validate @RequestParam/@PathVariable values or use validation groups, Spring's @Validated is involved.
  • Seeing the messages without custom handling: Boot hides binding errors in the default error body. spring.web.error.include-binding-errors=always (and include-message) exposes them, which is handy while developing. In Boot 4 these moved from server.error.* to spring.web.error.*; the old server.error.include-message no longer has any effect (verified on Boot 4.1.0). A @RestControllerAdvice handler (next lecture) is the proper solution.
  • @Email is lenient. Hibernate Validator's @Email accepts addresses like a@b (no top-level domain). Add @Pattern if you need a stricter format, and remember that only a confirmation email proves an address is real.
  • ddl-auto=update would have added the new columns. The lecture says the new timestamp fields "won't be added by default" and drops the table. In fact update adds missing columns (as nullable). What it never does is change existing ones, such as adding auto-increment (Lecture 13). Dropping was only needed to start clean.
  • Dates in JSON: Boot's Jackson configuration serialises LocalDateTime as an ISO-8601 string ("2026-09-28T01:23:45.123"), not as a timestamp array. MySQL stores it as datetime(6).
Transcript slips to ignore:
"2001 Created" → 201.
"student.setSubject(studentRepository.getSubject())" → studentRequestDto.getSubject().
"epochs value" → an epoch timestamp (seconds or milliseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC).

Lecture 17: Exception Handling in Spring Boot — Status Codes, @RestControllerAdvice, Custom Exceptions & Error DTOs

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #17 · 1h27m · Code Army · continues the DTO/validation CRUD project of Lecture 16

Why exception handling matters in an API

Java exception handling is familiar. In a backend it has one more job: when something goes wrong, the client must get a proper response that says what went wrong. The lecturer calls it important both for interviews and for building your own apps.

Every API response has three parts:

PartWhat it carries
Status codeThe meaning of the response: success or failure, whose fault, what kind. The most important part
HeadersKey–value metadata about the response
BodyThe data, as JSON
The lecture's point: professional vs beginner APIs:
The difference shows in how carefully those three are chosen. A beginner API returns 200 for everything, even 200 with {"message": "No data found"}. The body says failure while the status says success. A professional API picks the status that matches the situation, and returns error bodies in one consistent format.

One request, many outcomes

Take GET localhost:8080/api/students/1. It can end many ways, and each deserves its own response:

CaseWhose faultStatusExample body
1. Student exists—200 OK{"id": 1, "name": "Aditya", "email": "ad@gmail.com"}
2. Student doesn't existClient asked for a missing resource404 Not Found{"message": "Student with id 1 not found"}
3. Invalid request (id not a number, path vs param mix-up, bad body)Client400 Bad Request{"message": "Student id must be a number"}
4. DB down, server down, a bug nobody can classifyServer500 Internal Server Error{"message": "Something went wrong"}

The lecturer first wrote 400 for "not found" and then corrected it to 404. 400 is Bad Request. 500 is the generic "we couldn't pin it down" code, and it's the one you see most often in the wild.

Step 1: clean up the endpoints (REST convention)

The Lecture 13 project used verbs in paths: /create, /get, /getAll, /update, /delete. Method + path is already unique, so the extra segments go:

BeforeAfter
POST /api/students/create@PostMapping → POST /api/students
GET /api/students/get?id=1@GetMapping("/{id}") + @PathVariable → GET /api/students/1
GET /api/students/getAll@GetMapping → GET /api/students
PUT /api/students/update?id=1@PutMapping → PUT /api/students/{id}
DELETE /api/students/delete?id=1@DeleteMapping → DELETE /api/students/{id}
PATCH /api/students/delete-softKept as-is. PATCH means "change part of a resource" in general, not only soft delete

Demo: POST /api/students with Rohit (29, roll 103, rohit@gmail.com, Node.js) returns 201 and a new row.

The problem: the controller is full of if/else

Status codes were already right in some places, but look at the controller:

  • getStudent: if (response == null) return notFound(); else return ok(…).
  • getAllStudents checks isEmpty(), which it shouldn't even do. An empty list is still a success.
  • updateStudent repeats the null check, and delete/softDelete check a boolean.

Meanwhile the service returns null or false to signal problems. GET /api/students/100 returns a bare 404 with an empty body.

Why this is wrong:
The controller's job is fixed: take the request, hand it to the service, and return the service's result. Deciding what to answer for every edge case is exception handling. Scattering it as if/else in every method makes controllers bulky and ugly, and makes error bodies inconsistent. The fix is to split the code into a happy flow (controller) and an exception flow (a dedicated handler class).

Step 2: what Spring Boot does if you handle nothing

As an experiment, the service stops checking and calls Optional.get() directly:

return mapToDto(studentRepository.findById(id).get());   // throws NoSuchElementException if absent

The exception isn't caught in the service, so it propagates to the controller, where it isn't caught either. GET /api/students/100 now returns:

HTTP 500 Internal Server Error
{
  "timestamp": "…",
  "status": 500,
  "error": "Internal Server Error",
  "path": "/api/students/100"
}
  • The client didn't receive a raw exception. Spring Boot's default error handling built a proper response: status, headers and a body with timestamp, status, error and path.
  • The real cause, NoSuchElementException: No value present, shows up only in the IntelliJ console. It's hidden from the client for security, because it reveals internal classes and logic.

To see the message in the response while debugging (local only, never in production):

spring.web.error.include-message=always

With this setting the body gains "message": "No value present".

Version note (verified on Boot 4.1.0):
In Boot 4 the property is spring.web.error.include-message, as the lecture uses. In Boot 2.x/3.x it was server.error.include-message, which no longer has any effect in Boot 4: I tested both. Most tutorials online still show the old name.

How the default works: the /error endpoint

  • An unhandled exception is re-routed to a special endpoint, /error. That's why the body shows the original path separately.
  • The /error handler serves the right format for the client: JSON for Postman, and the Whitelabel Error Page (HTML) for a browser. Opening the same URL in a browser showed "This application has no explicit mapping for /error, so you are seeing this as a fallback", with the type, status 500, timestamp and message.

Anticipated question: "If Boot already handles exceptions, why write our own?"

Because the default is generic: nearly always 500, and always the same four fields.

  • It can't say "student with id 100 does not exist".
  • It can't list which validation rule failed. Lecture 16's custom messages ("Name cannot be null, empty or blank") still arrive only as a generic 400.

HTTP status code families

FamilyMeaningCodes to know
1xxInformational100 Continue, 101 Switching Protocols (added)
2xxSuccess200 OK; 201 Created (a new resource, the usual POST result); 204 No Content
3xxRedirection301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified (added)
4xxClient-side error400 Bad Request; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict (e.g. email already registered); 401/403 (added, below)
5xxServer-side error500 Internal Server Error; 503 Service Unavailable (added)
204 vs 404: don't mix them up:
204 No Content is a success: "done, and there's nothing to return". It's the professional reply to a successful DELETE. 404 Not Found is a client failure: "the thing you wanted to act on doesn't exist, so nothing happened".

ResponseEntity is what gives you control. Without it Spring would always reply 200. With it you can return:

  • Status + body: ResponseEntity.ok(x), which is short for ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.OK).body(x).
  • Status + headers + body.
  • Status only: ResponseEntity.notFound().build(), noContent().build().

Step 3: the exception flow

@RestControllerAdvice: a helper for all controllers

package in.strikes.cruddemo.exception;

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {
    // one method per exception type
}
  • @ControllerAdvice marks a class as a helper for every controller. Behaviour common to all controllers is written here once. Exception handling is the main use; model attributes and data-binding setup are others. The lecture adds that this connects to AOP (aspect-oriented programming), covered later.
  • @RestControllerAdvice = @ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody, just as @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody (Lecture 15). Use it for REST APIs returning JSON. Use @ControllerAdvice for view-returning apps, or add @ResponseBody per method.

@ExceptionHandler: like a catch block for the whole app

@ExceptionHandler(RuntimeException.class)
public ResponseEntity<String> handleRuntimeException(RuntimeException ex) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)   // enum; value 500
                         .body(ex.getMessage());
}

@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)                  // safety net: last fallback
public ResponseEntity<String> handleGenericException(Exception ex) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)
                         .body("Something went wrong, please try again later");
}
  • A thrown RuntimeException no longer bubbles up to the controller. It lands here, and GET /api/students/100 returns 500 with body "No value present". Our handler has replaced Boot's default.
  • Handlers form a hierarchy, like catch (ArithmeticException) → catch (RuntimeException) → catch (Exception). The handler for Exception is the safety net for anything the specific handlers miss.
  • Order doesn't matter, unlike catch blocks. Spring picks the handler whose exception type is closest to the thrown exception's class, wherever it's written.

Replacing Optional juggling with orElseThrow

An intermediate attempt, findById(id).orElse(null) followed by mapToDto(student), threw a NullPointerException. It was caught by the RuntimeException handler, giving 500 with "Cannot invoke …Student.getId() because student is null". That message leaks the package and class names. It "works", but it's neither meaningful nor safe.

The clean version throws a business exception that says exactly what happened:

public CreateStudentResponseDto getStudentById(Long id) {
    Student studentResponse = studentRepository.findById(id)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException("Student with id " + id + " not found"));
    return mapToDto(studentResponse);             // reaching this line means it exists
}

Step 4: custom exceptions

public class ResourceNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public ResourceNotFoundException(String message) {
        super(message);                         // parent stores the message
    }
}

public class DuplicateResourceException extends RuntimeException {
    public DuplicateResourceException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }
}
  • Neither exists in Java; they're ours. Extending RuntimeException makes them unchecked, so there's no throws clause everywhere.
  • A custom exception is mostly a marker. Its type carries the meaning, and the message is passed to the parent.
  • Now the service speaks in business terms ("resource not found", "duplicate resource") instead of generic runtime errors.

Demo: without a dedicated handler, ResourceNotFoundException is still caught by the RuntimeException handler, giving 500 with "Student with id 100 not found". Right message, wrong status. Adding a dedicated handler fixes it:

@ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
public ResponseEntity<…> handleResourceNotFoundException(ResourceNotFoundException ex, HttpServletRequest request) {
    … HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND …                  // 404
}

@ExceptionHandler(DuplicateResourceException.class)
public ResponseEntity<…> handleDuplicateResourceException(DuplicateResourceException ex, HttpServletRequest request) {
    … HttpStatus.CONFLICT …                   // 409
}

Now GET /api/students/100 returns 404 "Student with id 100 not found". "A new handler per exception, because each needs its own status code."

Duplicate email → 409 Conflict

// service, inside createStudent
Student student = mapToEntity(createStudentRequestDto);      // also sets createdAt/updatedAt now
if (emailExists(student)) {
    throw new DuplicateResourceException("Student with email " + student.getEmail() + " already exists");
}

private boolean emailExists(Student student) {
    return studentRepository.existsByEmail(student.getEmail());   // derived query (Lecture 13)
}

// repository
boolean existsByEmail(String email);

Demo: posting "Mahesh" with saurav@gmail.com, already taken, returns 409 Conflict "Student with email saurav@gmail.com already exists".

The lecturer's performance aside:
email isn't the primary key and isn't indexed. existsByEmail therefore scans the table, which is fine for a demo but slow with millions of rows. A real app would index the column, and would often keep frequently read data in a cache layer.

Step 5: controllers become one-liners

@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<CreateStudentResponseDto> getStudent(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(studentService.getStudentById(id));      // if we got here, it exists
}

@GetMapping
public ResponseEntity<List<CreateStudentResponseDto>> getAllStudents() {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(studentService.getAllStudents());       // empty list is still 200
}

@DeleteMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<Void> deleteStudent(@PathVariable Long id) {
    studentService.deleteStudent(id);
    return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();                        // 204, no body
}

The same pattern is applied across the service:

  • update: findByIdAndDeletedIsFalse(id).orElseThrow(…ResourceNotFoundException…). Copy the fields onto that existingStudent (one variable now instead of two), save, map. The controller returns ok(…).
  • hard delete: findById(id).orElseThrow(…), then studentRepository.delete(studentToBeDeleted). The method becomes void: a boolean "was it deleted?" is pointless, because failure is now an exception.
  • soft delete: findByIdAndDeletedIsFalse(id).orElseThrow(…), then setDeleted(true), save, and void. The controller also returns 204. To the client, soft and hard delete look the same.
The payoff:
No if/else in any controller. Each controller method calls the service and returns its result. The service either returns data or throws a named exception. The layers now have clean single responsibilities: the controller never sees entities, the repository never sees DTOs, and only the service knows both.

Step 6: one consistent error body

Returning a plain String isn't professional; it isn't structured. Every error should share one shape, modelled on Boot's default fields:

public class ExceptionResponseDto {
    private LocalDateTime timestamp;   // when
    private int statusCode;            // 404
    private String error;              // "Not Found"
    private String message;            // meaningful, safe message we chose
    private String path;               // which endpoint
    // all-args constructor + getters/setters
}

@ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
public ResponseEntity<ExceptionResponseDto> handleResourceNotFoundException(
        ResourceNotFoundException ex, HttpServletRequest request) {
    ExceptionResponseDto exceptionResponse = new ExceptionResponseDto(
            LocalDateTime.now(),
            HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND.value(),            // 404
            HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND.getReasonPhrase(),  // "Not Found"
            ex.getMessage(),
            request.getRequestURI());                // path, from the servlet request (Lecture 14)
    return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND).body(exceptionResponse);
}
  • The class was first named ExceptionDto and renamed ExceptionResponseDto for clarity.
  • The path comes from the HttpServletRequest that the dispatcher already holds. Adding it as a handler parameter is enough to receive it.
  • The same builder is used in the duplicate (CONFLICT), runtime and generic (INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR) handlers. Only the status changes.

Step 7: surfacing validation errors

When @Valid fails (Lecture 16), Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException. It's a built-in exception, not a custom one, but without a handler for it the generic safety net answered. The error DTO also needs a map of field → message, since several fields can fail at once:

public class ValidationExceptionResponseDto {
    private LocalDateTime timestamp;
    private int statusCode;
    private String error;
    private String message;
    private String path;
    private Map<String, String> fieldErrors;    // "age" → "Student must be at least 18 years old"
    // all-args constructor + getters/setters
}

@ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
public ResponseEntity<ValidationExceptionResponseDto> handleMethodArgumentNotValidException(
        MethodArgumentNotValidException ex, HttpServletRequest request) {
    Map<String, String> fieldErrors = new HashMap<>();
    ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors()
      .forEach(error -> fieldErrors.put(error.getField(), error.getDefaultMessage()));

    ValidationExceptionResponseDto response = new ValidationExceptionResponseDto(
            LocalDateTime.now(),
            HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST.value(),           // 400 (the first draft said CONFLICT)
            HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST.getReasonPhrase(),
            "Validation failed",                      // our own message, not ex.getMessage()
            request.getRequestURI(),
            fieldErrors);
    return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST).body(response);
}
  • getBindingResult().getFieldErrors() gives a list of FieldError, each with a getField() and a getDefaultMessage() (the message = "…" from the annotation).
  • ex.getMessage() was replaced with "Validation failed" because Spring's message is huge and full of internal detail.

Demo:

  • Too long a name, age 17 and saurav.gmail.com return 400 with fieldErrors: name "Name cannot be null, empty or blank", email "Student email must be valid", age "Student must be at least 18 years old".
  • A valid Aliya (27, roll 114) returns 201.
  • Reusing saurav@gmail.com returns 409 with the structured body and path.

Gaps worth raising in an interview

  • A catch-all Exception handler turns client errors into 500s (verified on Boot 4.1.0). With only @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class), Spring's own exceptions are swallowed:
    RequestWithout the catch-allWith the catch-all
    Unknown path404 (NoResourceFoundException)500
    Wrong HTTP method405 (HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException)500
    /students/abc400 (MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException)500
    Malformed JSON400 (HttpMessageNotReadableException)500
    Fix it by handling those explicitly, or by extending ResponseEntityExceptionHandler, which already maps Spring MVC's exceptions to correct statuses. You then override its handleMethodArgumentNotValid instead of declaring your own @ExceptionHandler for it, since declaring both is ambiguous.
  • The field-error map loses errors (verified). A blank name violates both @NotBlank and @Size(min = 2). Spring reported 2 errors, but map.put kept only one. Use Map<String, List<String>> (computeIfAbsent(…).add(…)) or merge the messages.
  • Log what you hide. The generic handlers return "Something went wrong" but log nothing, so the stack trace is lost. Log the exception (log.error("…", ex)) and ideally include a correlation or trace id in both the log and the response.
  • Check-then-insert is racy. Two concurrent sign-ups can both pass existsByEmail. Put a unique constraint on email (@Column(unique = true) or a migration) and translate DataIntegrityViolationException to 409. The unique index also fixes the full-scan concern.
  • Missing codes. Authentication and authorisation failures need 401 Unauthorized (not authenticated) vs 403 Forbidden (authenticated but not allowed), covered with Spring Security. Semantic validation failures are sometimes returned as 422 Unprocessable Content.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • There's a standard error format: Problem Details (RFC 9457, formerly RFC 7807). Spring 6+ has ProblemDetail. Return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "…") (with type, title, status, detail, instance and custom properties), throw ErrorResponseException, or enable spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true. It's worth mentioning as the "industry standard" alternative to a home-grown ExceptionResponseDto.
  • @ResponseStatus on the exception class is a lighter option for simple cases: @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND) class ResourceNotFoundException …. It sets the status without a handler, but you lose control of the body.
  • How @ExceptionHandler is picked: within an advice, Spring sorts candidate handlers by how close the declared type is to the thrown exception (ExceptionDepthComparator), so declaration order doesn't matter. Between several advice classes, order them with @Order. An @ExceptionHandler inside a controller applies only to that controller and takes priority over the global advice.
  • Where /error comes from: Boot registers an error page with the servlet container that forwards to BasicErrorController at /error. It picks JSON or the Whitelabel HTML page based on the request's Accept header. Exceptions handled by your advice never reach it.
  • What the defaults show (verified, with include-message on): unknown path gives 404 "No static resource nope."; wrong method gives 405; /abc for a Long gives 400; bad JSON gives 400 "JSON parse error…"; and validation gives 400 "Validation failed for object='req'. Error count: 2". Boot's default is sensible for framework errors. Your advice should keep those statuses, not flatten them.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"400 Not Found" → 404 Not Found (corrected in the lecture).
"2001 Created" → 201; "3001" → 301.
"field not found exception is a runtime exception" → the exception from Optional.get() is NoSuchElementException.
"@ExceptionHandler takes the reflection of the class" → the class literal (RuntimeException.class).
The validation handler's first draft used CONFLICT; the correct status is BAD_REQUEST.

Lecture 18: Configuration & Profiles — .properties vs YAML, Profile-Specific Files, External Config & @Profile

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #18 · 51m · Code Army · builds on Lecture 10 (application.properties, @Value)

The problem: same code, different environments

A Spring Boot app has two parts:

CodeConfiguration
WhatControllers, services, repositories: the main logicDB URL, username, password, server port, custom settings
Across environmentsDoesn't change. The same build runs everywhere (features are still added over time)Does change per environment

The same code runs in several environments:

  • Local: your machine, localhost:8080, not reachable from outside.
  • Dev: a shared environment where developers test.
  • QA / staging / pre-prod (names vary by company): a production-like environment where the QA team and developers look for bugs before going live.
  • Production: live, used by real users.

A local DB may use a simple password like 123; production has a different URL and a strong password. Configuration must vary; code must not. That's the problem profiles solve.

Setup

On Initializr: profile-demo, Boot 4.1.0, Java 21, only Spring Web. A small controller:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/demo")
public class DemoController {

    @Value("${app.welcome.message}")      // read from configuration, not hard-coded
    private String message;

    @Value("${app.welcome.code}")
    private Integer code;

    @GetMapping
    public ResponseEntity<String> greet() {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(message + " : " + code);
    }
}
# application.properties
app.welcome.message=Hello, welcome to my application
app.welcome.code=200
# predefined Boot key; Tomcat default is 8080
server.port=9090

(In .properties, # starts a comment only at the beginning of a line. A trailing # … would become part of the value.)

GET /api/demo returns the message. After setting server.port=9090, the log says "Tomcat started on port 9090" and 8080 no longer answers.

Why not just hard-code values?

  1. Every change means a code change, then commit, push and redeploy, even to tweak a message.
  2. Per-environment values force commenting tricks, such as localDbUrl vs prodDbUrl with one commented out before each deploy. That's fragile and error-prone.
  3. Security: code goes to Git (GitHub or similar). Hard-coded DB URLs, usernames and passwords leak with it.
  4. Tight coupling: the code becomes hard to change.
Precision note from the lecture:
application.properties is still internal configuration. It's inside src/main/resources, so it's packaged into the JAR. Moving values there fixes points 1 and 4, but not the per-environment and secrets problems. External configuration means values supplied from outside the JAR.

.properties vs YAML

Initializr offers either format. Both serve the same purpose, and @Value reads both the same way. Only the syntax differs:

application.propertiesapplication.yml
StructureFlat key–value pairs joined with dotsTree: hierarchy by indentation (like Python), with no dots or brackets
RepetitionPrefix repeated on every lineCommon parent written once
ListsComma-separated, or indexed key[0]=…Comma string, or a YAML sequence (- item)
PitfallLong repetitive keysIndentation errors; tabs not allowed
 
# application.properties                       # application.yml
spring.application.name=profile-demo            spring:
server.port=9090                                  application:
app.welcome.message=Hello, welcome to my app        name: profile-demo
app.welcome.code=200                            server:
app.welcome.users=Aditya, Rohit, Rohan, Sohan     port: 9090
                                                app:
                                                  welcome:
                                                    message: Hello, welcome to my app
                                                    code: 200             # sibling of message
                                                    users: Aditya, Rohit, Rohan, Sohan
  • In the tree, app → welcome → {message, code} produces the keys app.welcome.message and app.welcome.code. Keys at the same indentation are siblings.
  • Quotes around YAML strings are optional.
  • A comma-separated value binds to a list: @Value("${app.welcome.users}") List<String> names printed [Aditya, Rohit, Rohan, Sohan].
  • For complex, nested structures, @ConfigurationProperties is the better tool (Lecture 10).
  • Internally Spring flattens YAML into the same dotted keys. Which format to use is personal preference.
Correction: both files are loaded; .properties wins only on conflicts (verified on Boot 4.1.0):
  • The lecture says Boot "reads the properties file" if both exist, and deletes the .properties file to make YAML take effect.
  • In fact both are loaded and merged. For a key defined in both, the .properties value takes precedence. A key only in the .yml still resolves.
  • In the test, message came from properties, while a yml-only key was read fine. Keeping both is legal but confusing, so pick one.
Worth flagging: YAML sequences and @Value (verified):
A real YAML list: 
users:
  - Aditya
  - Rohit
It is flattened to app.welcome.users[0], [1]…, so ${app.welcome.users} doesn't exist (null in the test). @Value on it fails. Use the comma-separated form with @Value, as the lecture did, or bind sequences with @ConfigurationProperties.

Profiles: one file per environment

Spring Boot's feature for varying configuration per environment is profiles. Name files application-{profile}.properties (or .yml):

src/main/resources/
├── application.properties            # COMMON to all environments (+ local defaults)
├── application-dev.properties        # dev only
├── application-staging.properties    # staging only
└── application-prod.properties       # prod only
Fileserver.portapp.welcome.message
application.properties(none, so 8080)Local: Hello, welcome…
application-dev.properties9090Dev: Hello, welcome…
application-staging.properties8080Staging: Hello, welcome…
application-prod.properties8191Prod: Hello, welcome…

The common file keeps values shared by all environments: spring.application.name, app.welcome.code=200 and the users list. The lecturer first misnamed the staging file application.staging.properties and renamed it to use a hyphen, since the hyphen is required.

Activating a profile

# in application.properties
spring.profiles.active=dev
  • Boot then loads application.properties + application-dev.properties. The profile file is added on top, and its values override the common ones.
  • With dev: "Tomcat started on port 9090", and GET returns "Dev: Hello, welcome to my application : 200". The 200 and the users list come from the common file.
  • Switching to staging gives port 8080 and "Staging: …". Calling 9090 now fails.

Anticipated question: "Didn't we just move the problem?"

Yes. spring.profiles.active sits inside application.properties, inside the JAR. Deploying to dev means editing it to dev and pushing; staging means editing it again. That's the same "change code for every environment" problem as hard-coding. The value must come from outside the JAR.

External configuration: supplying config from outside

Two common sources:

  • Command-line arguments.
  • Environment variables: key–value pairs from the OS (set in a terminal), a CI/CD pipeline, Kubernetes, or the host server. Covered properly with deployment later.

Command-line demo, with spring.profiles.active removed from the file:

mvn spring-boot:run                                     # no profile → "No active profile set, falling back to default"
                                                        #   → port 8080, "Local: …"

mvn spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=prod     # → "The following profiles are active: prod"
                                                        #   → port 8191, "Prod: Hello, welcome…"

Now the same JAR/code picks its configuration at launch. Nothing in the source changes per environment. The same approach applies to DB URL, username and password per environment.

Worth knowing: all the ways to set the profile (added):
  • Maven plugin: mvn spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=prod (the lecture's form).
  • Packaged JAR: java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod, or java -Dspring.profiles.active=prod -jar app.jar.
  • Environment variable: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod. This is the usual choice in Docker and Kubernetes.
Relaxed binding maps env vars to keys: APP_WELCOME_MESSAGE overrides app.welcome.message, and SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD overrides spring.datasource.password. I verified both overrides (command-line --app.welcome.message=… and env var APP_WELCOME_MESSAGE=…) on Boot 4.1.0.

@Profile: choosing beans per environment

New scenario: a NotificationController (POST /api/notification) calls a NotificationService that sends real email or SMS.

  • In production that's right.
  • In dev, testing a new notification feature would send real messages. That costs money (SMS more than email) and spams real people.

We need a different implementation per environment, not just different values. The first test returned 404 because the method had no mapping; adding @PostMapping fixed it.

public interface NotificationService {               // no @Service: it's only a contract
    String send();
}

@Service
@Profile("prod")                                     // bean exists ONLY when prod is active
public class NotificationServiceImpl implements NotificationService {
    @Override
    public String send() {
        // real email / SMS sent here
        return "Here is a notification";
    }
}

@Service
@Profile({"dev", "default", "staging"})              // any of these profiles
public class DummyNotificationServiceImpl implements NotificationService {
    @Override
    public String send() {
        // no real notification is sent
        return "Here is a dummy notification";
    }
}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/notification")
public class NotificationController {
    private final NotificationService notificationService;   // interface, injected by constructor

    public NotificationController(NotificationService notificationService) {
        this.notificationService = notificationService;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<String> sendNotification() {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(notificationService.send());
    }
}
  • With one implementation, Spring injects it automatically.
  • With two and no @Profile, startup fails: two candidate beans for one injection point.
  • @Primary/@Qualifier (Lecture 5) choose between beans within one environment. Here the choice must depend on the environment, which is what @Profile does.

Demo run

  1. Initially only @Profile("dev") and @Profile("prod"). With -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=dev (port 9090), the response is "Here is a dummy notification".
  2. With prod (port 8191): "Here is a notification".
  3. With no profile, startup fails: "Consider defining a bean of type NotificationService in your configuration". No implementation exists for the default profile.
  4. Changing the dummy to @Profile({"dev", "default", "staging"}) makes a plain run (8080) return the dummy notification.

Profile-specific files vs @Profile

Profile-specific config files@Profile annotation
VariesValues: ports, URLs, credentials, messagesBeans / behaviour: which implementation exists
Howapplication-{profile}.properties / .yml, layered over application.propertiesOn @Component/@Service classes, @Configuration classes or @Bean methods
ExampleProd DB URL vs local DB URLReal vs dummy notification sender
Selected byThe same active profile(s): spring.profiles.active, a command-line argument or an env var

Gaps worth raising in an interview

  • Profile files don't keep secrets out of Git. application-prod.properties in src/main/resources is committed with the code. Put only placeholders there, spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}, and inject real values through env vars or a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Kubernetes Secrets).
  • Don't commit spring.profiles.active. Set it at deploy time. Use spring.profiles.default if you want a fallback other than default.
  • Failing safe. Here, forgetting the profile in production would silently use the dummy sender, because default maps to it. For critical beans, consider making the real one the default and the dummy explicit (@Profile("!prod") for "everything except prod"), or fail fast when no profile is set.
  • Feature flags vs profiles. Toggling one feature in one environment is often cleaner with @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "notifications.enabled", havingValue = "true") than with a new profile.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Configuration precedence (simplified, highest first):
    1. Command-line arguments.
    2. Java system properties (-D).
    3. OS environment variables.
    4. Profile-specific files outside the JAR.
    5. Profile-specific files inside the JAR.
    6. application.properties outside the JAR (e.g. ./config/ next to it).
    7. application.properties inside the JAR.
    8. @PropertySource, then defaults.
    Knowing that "command line beats env vars, which beat packaged files" answers most interview questions on this.
  • External files: a config/application.properties placed next to the JAR is picked up automatically, and --spring.config.location or spring.config.import can point elsewhere. That's another way to change config without rebuilding.
  • One YAML file can hold all profiles: separate documents with ---, each with spring.config.activate.on-profile: dev. It's compact, but large files get hard to read.
  • Several profiles can be active at once (spring.profiles.active=prod,metrics). Later ones win on conflicting keys. Profile groups (spring.profiles.group.prod=proddb,prodmq) bundle them.
  • @Value defaults: @Value("${app.welcome.message:Hello}") supplies a fallback when the key is missing. Without it, a missing key fails startup.
  • The default profile is active only when no other profile is set. That's why the dummy bean needed "default" for a plain local run.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"real payment" (said a few times) → real notification.
"profiling" → the Spring feature is profiles. "Profiling" usually means performance profiling.

Lecture 19: Filters — Cross-Cutting Work Before the DispatcherServlet

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #19 · 1h06m · Code Army · logging, authentication, request IDs, timing and error responses with servlet filters

The problem: work that every request needs

The flow so far is: client → DispatcherServlet → controller → service → repository, and back. Now a new requirement arrives, for example for GET localhost:8080/api/students:

  • Before the business logic:
    • Log the request.
    • Authenticate the user: no logged-in user or token, no access.
    • Generate a unique request ID (1001, 1002, …).
  • After the response is built:
    • Add the request ID to the response, and possibly other headers.
  • This applies to every API, not just one.

Naive approach: do it in the controller

The first instinct is the controller, since requests land there. With 50 or more endpoints, it breaks down:

AttemptWhy it breaks
Write the logging/auth/ID code in every controller methodThe same code is repeated in 50+ places
Move it to a helper class that every controller callsEvery controller still has to remember to call it, and controllers stay tightly coupled to infrastructure code
Why the controller is the wrong place:
Logging, authentication and request IDs are infrastructure / security concerns, not controller concerns. By the Single Responsibility Principle (the S of SOLID), a controller receives an API request and passes it to the service; that's all. The series has kept moving responsibilities out of it: business logic to services, and error handling to @RestControllerAdvice (Lecture 17). Cross-cutting request work needs its own place too. That's filters, and later interceptors.

Where a filter sits

  • A filter runs before the DispatcherServlet, on the way in, and after it, on the way out.
  • It sees the raw request. The dispatcher hasn't yet used HandlerMapping (Lecture 15), so a filter doesn't know which controller will handle the request. That suits generic work common to every request.
  • Interceptors (next topic) sit after the dispatcher but before the controller, so they do know the handler.
  • Because it's in front of the dispatcher, a filter also sees requests that never reach a controller: static resources (/static/logo.png), /error and /favicon.ico.

What filters are used for

UseExample
LoggingLog request method/URI, the response status, possibly bodies. Mask sensitive data like card numbers
Security / authenticationCheck an auth header or token; block the request if it's missing
Modify the responseAdd headers such as a request ID, so a client or third party can quote it when asking for logs
Modify the requestPossible, but discouraged: it changes the original request. Use DTOs for shaping data
EncodingForce UTF-8 character encoding
TimingMeasure total request duration (turnaround time) end to end
Early error responsesReject with a status and JSON body without ever touching the dispatcher

A filter can inspect headers, cookies and auth information, add response headers, wrap the request or response, block or allow a request, log it, and measure its duration.

Setup

  • Initializr: filter-demo, with only Spring Web.
  • StudentController (@RequestMapping("/api/students")) has a @PostMapping createStudent that calls StudentService.createStudent(), which just prints "Student created". The controller returns ResponseEntity.ok("Done").
  • Later, a Student DTO (Long id, name, email) is taken with @RequestBody, and the service prints its name and email.

The Filter interface

package jakarta.servlet;                       // Servlet API, NOT Spring

public interface Filter {
    default void init(FilterConfig filterConfig) throws ServletException {}
    void doFilter(ServletRequest request, ServletResponse response, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException;          // the only abstract method
    default void destroy() {}
}
  • Filters come from the Servlet API, not Spring. The package is jakarta.servlet. Spring Boot 3+ uses jakarta.*; Boot 1/2 used javax.*, so check imports in old code. Use a current Boot.
  • Lifecycle (like servlets, Lecture 14):
    • init on creation.
    • doFilter per request, where the work happens.
    • destroy on shutdown.
    init/destroy have default bodies and are rarely used. Only doFilter must be implemented.
  • Why ServletRequest, not HttpServletRequest? The Servlet API was designed to be protocol-generic, not HTTP-only. HttpServletRequest and HttpServletResponse are the HTTP-specific subtypes. Since about 90% of real work is HTTP, you cast. Spring offers a base class that avoids the casting (see "Worth knowing").

The filter chain

There can be many filters, which form a chain:

  • chain.doFilter(request, response) means "I'm done, next one's turn". The FilterChain knows who's next. After the last filter, it invokes the servlet: the DispatcherServlet, whose doPost handles our POST.
  • Code after chain.doFilter(…) runs when the response comes back, like the unwinding of a recursive call.
  • Returning without calling chain.doFilter stops the request, and whatever the filter wrote to the response goes back to the client.
  • FilterChain is itself an interface. Tomcat's ApplicationFilterChain is one implementation, alongside mock and pass-through ones.

Worked example 1: a logging filter

@Component                       // make it a bean → Spring Boot registers it for all requests
@Order(2)
public class LoggingFilter implements Filter {

    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest servletRequest, ServletResponse servletResponse,
                         FilterChain filterChain) throws IOException, ServletException {

        HttpServletRequest httpRequest = (HttpServletRequest) servletRequest;     // cast to HTTP
        HttpServletResponse httpResponse = (HttpServletResponse) servletResponse;

        long startTime = System.currentTimeMillis();
        String requestId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        httpResponse.setHeader("X-Request-ID", requestId);          // BEFORE the chain (see below)

        System.out.println("Incoming request: " + httpRequest.getMethod()
                           + " " + httpRequest.getRequestURI());    // e.g. POST /api/students
        try {
            filterChain.doFilter(servletRequest, servletResponse);  // pass the ORIGINAL objects on
        } finally {                                                 // runs even if an exception escapes
            long duration = System.currentTimeMillis() - startTime;
            System.out.println("Response status: " + httpResponse.getStatus());
            System.out.println("API response time: " + duration + " ms");
        }
    }
}

Built up in steps:

  1. Enter/exit prints. "Request entered in LoggingFilter", then chain.doFilter, then "Request exiting LoggingFilter". The console showed: entered → "Student created" → exiting.
  2. Real logging. getMethod(), getRequestURI() and, afterwards, getStatus() gave "Incoming request: POST /api/students … Response status: 200". In a real app this goes to a log file, through a logging library covered later.
  3. Request ID. UUID.randomUUID().toString(), unique per request, put in the X-Request-ID response header. Postman showed a new ID on every send. A client can quote it to get the logs for that exact call.
  4. Timing. First run: "API response time: 43 ms". With Thread.sleep(2000) in the service to mimic a slow DB or Redis call, it's about 2 seconds.
  5. try/finally: if a later layer throws, the post-processing still runs.
Why the request-ID header is set before chain.doFilter (verified on Boot 4.1.0):
By the time control comes back to the filter, the controller has usually written the body, so the response is committed: headers have already been sent. A header set afterwards is silently dropped. In the test, X-Before reached the client, while X-After (set after the chain, with isCommitted() = true) did not. Set response headers on the way in.

Worked example 2: an authentication filter

A simplified rule: every request must carry a header token: 12345. Real apps use JWTs or other bearer tokens and Spring Security, covered later. A second rule, added at the end, requires a header X-API-Key: secret123, answering with a JSON error body if it's missing.

@Component
@Order(1)                                        // runs first
public class AuthenticationFilter implements Filter {

    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest servletRequest, ServletResponse servletResponse,
                         FilterChain filterChain) throws IOException, ServletException {

        HttpServletRequest httpRequest = (HttpServletRequest) servletRequest;
        HttpServletResponse httpResponse = (HttpServletResponse) servletResponse;

        String token = httpRequest.getHeader("token");
        if (!"12345".equals(token)) {                              // null-safe
            httpResponse.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_UNAUTHORIZED);   // 401
            return;                                                // chain NOT called → blocked
        }

        String apiKey = httpRequest.getHeader("X-API-Key");        // header names are case-insensitive
        if (!"secret123".equals(apiKey)) {
            httpResponse.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_UNAUTHORIZED);
            httpResponse.setContentType("application/json");
            httpResponse.getWriter().write("{\"message\": \"Invalid or missing API key\"}");
            return;
        }

        filterChain.doFilter(servletRequest, servletResponse);     // authenticated → continue
    }
}
  • HttpServletResponse has named constants for common codes, such as SC_UNAUTHORIZED = 401. They read better than bare numbers.
  • The first test still returned 200 with a wrong token, because the class had no @Component. It wasn't a bean, so it wasn't registered. With the annotation, 12345 gives 200 "Done", and 1234 gives 401 Unauthorized.
  • API-key demo: a missing key gives 401 with the JSON message. A wrong comparison (equals where !equals was meant) was fixed. Then secret123 is accepted.
Correction: write the checks null-safe:
The lecture's check reads "token == null and token not equal to 12345". Combined with &&, a null token passes the check, and a present-but-wrong token doesn't get rejected. The intent is "missing or wrong", i.e. token == null || !token.equals("12345"). Simplest of all is !"12345".equals(token), since a literal's equals(null) is just false.

Ordering filters with @Order

With both filters active, authentication should run first, and logging only for authenticated requests:

@Component @Order(1) public class AuthenticationFilter implements Filter { … }
@Component @Order(2) public class LoggingFilter        implements Filter { … }
