  • A lower number runs earlier on the way in (and later on the way out).
  • Correct token and key give 200 "Done", with the logging filter's timing printed. A wrong key or token gives 401, and the logging filter never runs.
  • Without @Order a chain still forms, but Spring chooses the order, and it isn't guaranteed to stay the same across machines or runs. Set it whenever order matters.
  • One responsibility per filter. A logging filter logs, an auth filter authenticates. Don't build a "master filter"; the chain exists so work can be separated.

Verified (Boot 4.1.0): with @Order(1) auth and @Order(2) logging, the console showed auth IN → logging IN → controller → logging OUT → auth OUT.

Filter vs interceptor vs @RestControllerAdvice

Servlet FilterHandlerInterceptor (next)@RestControllerAdvice
Belongs toServlet API (Tomcat)Spring MVCSpring MVC
RunsBefore and after the DispatcherServletInside the dispatcher, around the controllerWhen a controller-layer exception is thrown
Knows the handler?NoYes (which controller method)Yes
Sees non-controller requestsYes: everything reaching the servlet containerOnly those routed through the dispatcher: static resources (ResourceHttpRequestHandler) and the /error forward (BasicErrorController) do reach interceptors (verified in Lecture 21)No
Typical useAuth, logging, CORS, encoding, request IDsPer-handler checks, model tweaks, timing per endpointError responses

Gaps worth raising in an interview

  • Log before you reject. With auth at @Order(1), rejected requests are never logged and get no request ID, which is exactly the traffic you often want to see (attacks, broken clients). Commonly the request-ID/logging filter is outermost and auth comes next.
  • Put the request ID in every log line. Store it in SLF4J's MDC (MDC.put("requestId", id), cleared in finally). Then every log statement for that request carries it automatically. Also reuse an incoming X-Request-ID if an upstream gateway already set one.
  • Reading the body in a filter consumes it. The request input stream can be read once. A filter that logs the body leaves the controller with nothing. Use ContentCachingRequestWrapper/ContentCachingResponseWrapper, and never log passwords or card data.
  • Hard-coded secrets and naive comparison. Keep keys in config or env (Lecture 18), compare them in constant time (MessageDigest.isEqual), and for real authentication use Spring Security, which is itself a chain of servlet filters.
  • Status in finally can lie (verified). When an exception escapes the controller with no @RestControllerAdvice, the filter's finally still sees status 200. The 500 is only set afterwards by Boot's error handling, and the client got 500. Also, a filter without try/finally skipped its post-processing entirely in that case.

Worth knowing

  • OncePerRequestFilter is the Spring base class the lecture alluded to. Extend it and implement doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest, HttpServletResponse, FilterChain): no casting, and it guarantees a single execution per request even across forwards and async dispatches. It's the usual choice in Spring apps.
  • Registering filters. A @Component filter is registered by Boot for all URLs (/*). To limit it (e.g. only /api/*), or to set order and name without annotations, declare a FilterRegistrationBean: 
    @Bean
FilterRegistrationBean<LoggingFilter> loggingFilter() {
    var reg = new FilterRegistrationBean<>(new LoggingFilter());
    reg.addUrlPatterns("/api/*");
    reg.setOrder(2);
    return reg;
}
    Don't also annotate that class with @Component, or it's registered twice. Plain servlet-style @WebFilter works with @ServletComponentScan.
  • Dispatcher types (verified). Boot registers bean filters for normal REQUEST dispatches. When the failing request was forwarded to /error, our filters did not run a second time.
  • Built-in filters you'll meet: CharacterEncodingFilter (Boot adds it for UTF-8), CorsFilter, ForwardedHeaderFilter, and Spring Security's SecurityFilterChain.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"Spring MVC gave a special servlet to avoid casting" → a special filter base class, OncePerRequestFilter.
The 2-second sleep's reading was said as "255 ms" → it's about 2000+ ms.

Lecture 20: Filters, Part 2 — Altering Requests & Responses, Wrappers, FilterRegistrationBean & OncePerRequestFilter

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #20 · 1h13m · Code Army · continues Lecture 19; what filters can change, what they shouldn't, and the "body disappeared" trap

Recap and goal

  • The chain from Lecture 19: client → filter 1 → filter 2 → filter 3 → DispatcherServlet → controller → service → repository, then back out through filters 3, 2, 1.
  • Filters come from the Servlet API, not Spring. Interceptors (between the dispatcher and the controller) are the next topic.
  • The project from Lecture 19 is kept but all filters are removed. It has a Student DTO (id, name, email) and POST /api/students, whose service just prints.

This lecture's question: a filter can observe requests and responses; can it also alter them? What can be changed, and what should be?

Altering the response

A response has three parts: status code, headers and body.

1. Headers: easy, if set before the chain

@Component
public class ResponseHeaderFilter implements Filter {
    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest servletRequest, ServletResponse servletResponse,
                         FilterChain filterChain) throws IOException, ServletException {
        HttpServletResponse httpServletResponse = (HttpServletResponse) servletResponse;
        String requestId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        httpServletResponse.setHeader("X-Request-ID", requestId);   // key-value, BEFORE doFilter
        filterChain.doFilter(servletRequest, servletResponse);
    }
}
  • Only the response needs casting here; the request isn't used.
  • Postman showed X-Request-ID with a new random value on every call.
  • Moving the setHeader after doFilter made the header disappear.
Why "after" doesn't work:
The controller only returns ResponseEntity.ok(…). The dispatcher then writes the body into the HttpServletResponse through its writer, which is an output stream. Once written, the response is committed and can't be changed. When control returns to the filter, it's too late (verified in Lecture 19). Strictly, the HttpServletRequest/HttpServletResponse objects are created by Tomcat and passed to the dispatcher. The lecture's diagrams simplify this as "the dispatcher builds them".

2. Status code and body, when answering from the filter itself

A filter can end the request early with its own status and body. This is the auth filter from Lecture 19:

@Component
public class AuthenticationFilter implements Filter {
    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest servletRequest, ServletResponse servletResponse,
                         FilterChain filterChain) throws IOException, ServletException {
        HttpServletRequest httpServletRequest = (HttpServletRequest) servletRequest;
        HttpServletResponse httpServletResponse = (HttpServletResponse) servletResponse;

        String token = httpServletRequest.getHeader("token");
        if (!"12345".equals(token)) {                                     // missing or wrong
            httpServletResponse.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_UNAUTHORIZED);   // 401
            httpServletResponse.setContentType("application/json");
            httpServletResponse.getWriter().write("{\"message\": \"Authentication is required\"}");
            return;                                                       // never reaches the dispatcher
        }
        filterChain.doFilter(servletRequest, servletResponse);
    }
}

With token 12345 the result is 200 "Done". With 123 it's 401 with {"message": "Authentication is required"}.

Worth knowing:
This time the lecture phrases the check correctly as "token is null or not 12345" (token == null || !token.equals("12345")). !"12345".equals(token) is the same check in one null-safe call.

3. Body: modifying what the controller produced, via a wrapper

Goal: the controller returns {"name": "Aditya", "message": "Student is saved successfully"}, and a filter should add "appName": "Student Management System". Doing it after doFilter fails for the same reason as headers: the body is already committed.

The trick: hand the chain a fake response:
Pass a wrapper around the real response down the chain. The dispatcher and controller think it's the normal HttpServletResponse, but everything they "write" is buffered in the wrapper instead of being sent. Back in the filter, you read the buffer, change it, and copy the final version into the real response. The lecture compares this to the Decorator pattern (LLD notebook): a wrapper that behaves like the object it wraps. 
@Component
public class ResponseBodyFilter implements Filter {
    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest servletRequest, ServletResponse servletResponse,
                         FilterChain filterChain) throws IOException, ServletException {
        HttpServletResponse httpServletResponse = (HttpServletResponse) servletResponse;
        ContentCachingResponseWrapper wrappedResponse =
                new ContentCachingResponseWrapper(httpServletResponse);

        filterChain.doFilter(servletRequest, wrappedResponse);      // downstream writes into the wrapper

        byte[] originalBodyBytes = wrappedResponse.getContentAsByteArray();   // body = stream of bytes
        String originalBody = new String(originalBodyBytes, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);

        String modifiedBody = """
                {"originalResponse": %s, "appName": "Student Management System"}"""
                .formatted(originalBody);

        wrappedResponse.resetBuffer();                              // drop the original body first!
        wrappedResponse.getWriter().write(modifiedBody);
        wrappedResponse.copyBodyToResponse();                       // push buffer into the real response
    }
}

The controller now returns a StudentResponseDto (name, message) built in the service, with the message "Student is saved successfully".

  • Why nest the original instead of adding a field? The original JSON ends with }, so you can't simply append , "appName": … to the string. Wrapping it as "originalResponse": {…} avoids editing JSON text. (Parsing it with Jackson and adding a field is the robust way.)
  • Text blocks ("""…""", standard since Java 15) with %s placeholders and .formatted(…) (also Java 15) avoid lots of \" escapes and + concatenation.
  • The bug hit in the demo: the first run returned both JSONs back-to-back. The wrapper still held the controller's body, and the modified body was appended after it. resetBuffer() clears the buffer before writing.

Verified (Boot 4.1.0): the client received {"originalResponse": {"name":"Aditya","message":"Student is saved successfully"}, "appName": "Student Management System"}, with a correct Content-Length, which copyBodyToResponse sets.

Possible ≠ advisable:
Changing headers from a filter is fine. Rewriting a response body produced by the controller is bad practice:
  • The client expects the controller's contract, but gets something else.
  • Disabling or changing the filter silently changes the API.
  • Response shape belongs in the controller/service layer, not in infrastructure code.
Returning your own body when rejecting a request (the 401 above) is fine.

Altering the request

A request carries a method, an endpoint (URI), headers, request parameters and a body.

PartRead in a filterChange in a filter?
HTTP methodgetMethod()No setter
EndpointgetRequestURI()No setter
HeadersgetHeader("token") (null if absent)No setHeader: read-only
Request parametersgetParameter(…), getParameterMap()No setter: read-only
BodygetInputStream() / getReader(). There's no getBody()Only through a wrapper, and reading it consumes it
  • HttpServletRequest offers only setAttribute and setCharacterEncoding. Everything the client sent is read-only, and that makes sense. The client's method, path, headers and parameters are the contract; a filter adding or changing them is the wrong layer.
  • The hacky way exists: extend HttpServletRequestWrapper and override getHeader/getHeaders/getHeaderNames or getParameter/getParameterMap/getParameterNames/getParameterValues to add values, then pass the wrapper down the chain. It works, but don't.

The trap: logging the request body makes it disappear

Suppose you don't want to change the body, only log it. The lecturer learned the next part "the hard way" at work.

@Component
public class RequestFilter implements Filter {
    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest servletRequest, ServletResponse servletResponse,
                         FilterChain filterChain) throws IOException, ServletException {
        HttpServletRequest httpServletRequest = (HttpServletRequest) servletRequest;

        BufferedReader reader = httpServletRequest.getReader();
        StringBuilder body = new StringBuilder();
        String line = reader.readLine();
        while (line != null) {                   // read line by line until null
            body.append(line);
            line = reader.readLine();
        }
        System.out.println(body);                // logged fine…

        filterChain.doFilter(servletRequest, servletResponse);   // …but downstream gets nothing
    }
}

Demo result: the body printed correctly, then 500 Internal Server Error:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: getReader() has already been called for this request

The dispatcher (Jackson, for @RequestBody) needs to read the same body to build the Student object, and can't.

Why the body is a stream, and why it can be read only once

  • Behind the dispatcher sits Tomcat (Lecture 14). Tomcat parses the method, URI, host, headers and parameters into the HttpServletRequest, so those are easy getters.
  • The body could be anything: JSON, HTML, plain text, a PDF, audio, video, a 2 GB file. Tomcat can't know or buffer it all, so it exposes the body as a stream of bytes. Everything is bytes in the end.
  • Java reads a stream with getInputStream() (bytes) or getReader() (a BufferedReader of characters).
  • A stream is not stored; the data flows past. Reading moves a pointer forward ({, ", i, d…) until the end, and there's no rewind. Whoever reads first consumes it. Normally that's Jackson, which stores what it reads into your object.

Fixes

  1. Re-supply the body: after reading, store the bytes, and pass a request wrapper (HttpServletRequestWrapper) whose getInputStream()/getReader() serve those stored bytes again. Downstream reads from the copy.
  2. Spring's ready-made version: ContentCachingRequestWrapper. It caches bytes as they are read. See the precision note below.

The same wrapper technique could also modify the body before passing it on. Again: possible, but never do it.

Precision note: ContentCachingRequestWrapper caches lazily (verified on Boot 4.1.0):
It doesn't pre-read the body. It records bytes as downstream code (Jackson) consumes them. Wrapping the request and reading getContentAsByteArray() before chain.doFilter returned an empty string. Reading it after the chain returned {"name":"Aditya"}, while the controller still received the body normally. So log the request body after the chain. Spring 6.1+ also requires/offers a cache size limit: new ContentCachingRequestWrapper(request, limit).

Registering a filter with FilterRegistrationBean

Instead of @Component on the filter, you can declare it as a bean in a configuration class, which unlocks extra settings:

public class DummyFilter implements Filter {            // NO @Component
    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest servletRequest, ServletResponse servletResponse,
                         FilterChain filterChain) throws IOException, ServletException {
        System.out.println("Dummy filter called");
        filterChain.doFilter(servletRequest, servletResponse);
    }
}

@Configuration
public class FilterConfig {

    @Bean
    public FilterRegistrationBean<DummyFilter> getDummyFilterBean() {
        FilterRegistrationBean<DummyFilter> registrationBean = new FilterRegistrationBean<>();
        registrationBean.setFilter(new DummyFilter());
        registrationBean.setOrder(1);                            // same role as @Order
        registrationBean.addUrlPatterns("/api/*", "/admin/*");   // ONLY these paths
        registrationBean.setName("dummyFilter");                 // useful in logs
        return registrationBean;
    }
}
  • addUrlPatterns is the key extra. The filter is not even invoked for other paths. With /api/*, /api/students and /api/teachers match; anything else skips it.
  • The @Component alternative: check the path inside doFilter. If getRequestURI() doesn't start with /api/, call chain.doFilter immediately and return. It works, but the filter still runs for every request. URL patterns are the cleaner way.
  • Demo: POST /api/students printed "Dummy filter called".
Worth flagging (added):
Don't combine @Component on the filter class with a FilterRegistrationBean for it, or Boot registers it twice. Also note that servlet URL patterns are simple: /api/* matches everything under /api/. The Ant-style /api/** used in Spring MVC and Security isn't a servlet pattern.

Spring's own base class: OncePerRequestFilter

@Component
public class SpringDemoFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {    // extends a class, not implements

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request,      // already HTTP-typed
                                    HttpServletResponse response,
                                    FilterChain filterChain) throws ServletException, IOException {
        // pre-work
        filterChain.doFilter(request, response);
        // post-work
    }

    @Override
    protected boolean shouldNotFilter(HttpServletRequest request) {  // default: false (filter everything)
        String uri = request.getRequestURI();
        return !uri.startsWith("/api/");                             // true → skip this filter
    }
}
  • It comes from Spring MVC (org.springframework.web.filter), built on the Servlet Filter.
  • You implement doFilterInternal, which receives HttpServletRequest/HttpServletResponse directly, so there's no casting.
  • shouldNotFilter puts the skip condition in its own method instead of an if inside the logic. Return true to skip.
  • As the name says, it guarantees one execution per request, even across internal forwards/includes and async dispatches, where a plain filter could run again.
  • It's the usual base class for custom filters in Spring apps. Spring Security's filters extend it too.

What a filter may change: summary

TargetPossible?Should you?
Response headersYes, set before doFilterYes: request IDs, security headers, CORS
Response status + body when rejectingYes, then returnYes: 401/403/429 with an error message
Response body produced by the controllerVia ContentCachingResponseWrapperNo: it breaks the API contract
Request method / URINo settersNo
Request headers / parametersOnly by overriding getters in HttpServletRequestWrapperNo: it's a hack
Request body: logVia a caching wrapper; read after the chainCarefully: size limits, mask secrets
Request body: modifyVia a custom wrapperNo

Gaps worth raising in an interview

  • Memory cost of caching wrappers. ContentCachingResponseWrapper buffers the whole response in memory, which breaks streaming and hurts with large downloads. Skip it for file or streaming endpoints (shouldNotFilter), and set a cache limit on request wrappers.
  • Always copyBodyToResponse(). If a response wrapper is used and this call is skipped, for example because an exception jumped past it, the client gets an empty body. Put it in finally.
  • Charset. Decode and encode bodies with an explicit charset (StandardCharsets.UTF_8, or the response's own encoding). The platform default may garble non-ASCII text.
  • Sensitive data in logs. Request bodies contain passwords, tokens and card numbers. Mask or exclude them before logging, and keep logs out of reach.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"Java has a wrapper called ContentCachingResponseWrapper" → it's Spring's (org.springframework.web.util). HttpServletRequestWrapper is from the Servlet API.
"text blocks came in Java 15 or 16" → standard in Java 15 (previewed in 13/14).

Lecture 21: Interceptors — HandlerInterceptor, preHandle/postHandle/afterCompletion & Filters vs Interceptors

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #21 · 1h13m · Code Army · builds on Lectures 19–20 (filters) and 15 (DispatcherServlet internals)

The problem: filters are blind to the controller

  • From Lecture 19: client → Tomcat → filter chain → DispatcherServlet → controller → service → repository, and back.
  • Filters handle infrastructure work every controller needs:
    • Logging requests.
    • Authenticating users.
    • Measuring API response time.
    • Adding response headers.
  • So why a second concept? Filters are a Servlet technology, not a Spring one. They sit between Tomcat and the dispatcher and receive the raw request.
  • Only the DispatcherServlet, through HandlerMapping, decides which controller method will run (Lecture 15). A filter can't know it.

The idea: hook in after the dispatcher, before the controller

  • Interceptors are a Spring MVC concept. They chain like filters, but run inside the dispatcher, after the mapping is resolved.
  • They can do everything a filter does (log, check auth, time requests), plus anything that needs the handler:
    • Log which controller and method were called.
    • Authorisation per endpoint.
    • Apply logic only to specific controllers or paths.
  • Timing in an interceptor measures just the controller/service part. A filter's timing also includes the dispatcher.

The HandlerInterceptor interface

public interface HandlerInterceptor {                 // org.springframework.web.servlet
    default boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                              Object handler) throws Exception { return true; }
    default void postHandle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                            Object handler, @Nullable ModelAndView modelAndView) throws Exception {}
    default void afterCompletion(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                                 Object handler, @Nullable Exception ex) throws Exception {}
}
  • All three are default methods, so you override only what you need. A filter had one method (doFilter), with code before and after chain.doFilter. An interceptor splits those moments into separate methods.
  • The request and response are already HTTP-typed, so there's no casting as in a plain Filter.
MethodWhenExtra parameterTypical use (REST APIs)
preHandleBefore the controller methodObject handlerLog request and handler, checks, start a timer. Return true to continue, false to stop
postHandleAfter the controller returns, before the view is rendered. Only if no exceptionModelAndView (null for REST)Server-rendered views: add model data. Rarely useful for REST
afterCompletionAfter the whole request completes, including view rendering, even on exceptionException ex (null if none or already handled)Log the response status, stop the timer, log unhandled exceptions, clean up

What is a "handler"?

Spring uses the generic word handler because the thing serving a request isn't always a controller method. It can be a static resource, a view and so on. For REST controllers, the handler is a HandlerMethod, which wraps the controller bean and the java.lang.reflect.Method. Interceptors wrap the handler in layers, which the lecture calls the "onion-peel model".

Worked example: a logging interceptor

@Component
public class LoggingInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {

    @Override
    public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                             Object handler) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("Incoming request");
        System.out.println("HTTP method: " + request.getMethod());               // POST
        System.out.println("Request URI: " + request.getRequestURI());           // /api/students
        System.out.println("Request parameters: " + request.getQueryString());   // name=Aditya&age=28 (or null)
        System.out.println("Client IP: " + request.getRemoteAddr());
        System.out.println("Token header: " + request.getHeader("token"));

        if (handler instanceof HandlerMethod handlerMethod) {                    // safe cast (pattern matching)
            System.out.println("Controller called: " + handlerMethod.getBeanType().getName());
            System.out.println("Controller method: " + handlerMethod.getMethod().getName());
        }
        return true;                               // continue to next interceptor / controller
    }

    @Override
    public void afterCompletion(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                                Object handler, Exception ex) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("Response status: " + response.getStatus());
        if (ex != null) {
            System.out.println("Exception: " + ex.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
  • Casting safely: the lecture first cast (HandlerMethod) handler directly, then switched to an instanceof check. A direct cast throws for non-controller handlers, such as static resources.
  • Output:
    • method POST, URI /api/students, parameters null (or name=Aditya&age=28 when sent).
    • The client IP is loopback, and the token header is 123.
    • in.strikes…StudentController / createStudent, then "Controller called", then "Response status: 200".
  • ex in afterCompletion is non-null only for exceptions that escaped. If a @RestControllerAdvice (Lecture 17) already handled it, ex is null.
  • postHandle is simply not overridden, as is usual for REST APIs.

Registering it: @Component isn't enough

With only @Component, the first run printed "Controller called" and nothing from the interceptor. Unlike filters, which Boot auto-registers, interceptors must be added to the interceptor registry through a WebMvcConfigurer:

@Configuration
public class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {

    private final LoggingInterceptor loggingInterceptor;
    private final AuthenticationInterceptor authenticationInterceptor;
    private final AuthorizationInterceptor authorizationInterceptor;

    public WebConfig(LoggingInterceptor loggingInterceptor,                 // constructor injection
                     AuthenticationInterceptor authenticationInterceptor,
                     AuthorizationInterceptor authorizationInterceptor) {
        this.loggingInterceptor = loggingInterceptor;
        this.authenticationInterceptor = authenticationInterceptor;
        this.authorizationInterceptor = authorizationInterceptor;
    }

    @Override
    public void addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry registry) {       // note: addInterceptorS
        registry.addInterceptor(authenticationInterceptor)
                .addPathPatterns("/api/**")
                .excludePathPatterns("/api/auth/login", "/api/public/**")
                .order(1);
        registry.addInterceptor(authorizationInterceptor)
                .addPathPatterns("/api/**")
                .order(2);
        registry.addInterceptor(loggingInterceptor)
                .order(3);
    }
}
  • The first attempt overrode a misspelled addInterceptor, so @Override flagged it. The method is addInterceptors.
  • After registration: preHandle → "Controller called" → postHandle → afterCompletion.

Path patterns (Spring MVC, not servlet)

PatternMatchesExample
/apiExactly that path/api only
/api/*Exactly one more segment/api/students, /api/teachers, but not /api/students/1
/api/**Any depth below/api/students, /api/students/1/courses
  • Servlet filter patterns (Lecture 20) are cruder: /api/* there means "everything under /api".
  • excludePathPatterns carves out exceptions, such as a login endpoint or public pages that anyone can view without logging in (the lecture's X/Twitter example). Without it, authentication would block the login request itself.

More interceptors: authentication and authorisation (homework, sketched)

@Component
public class AuthenticationInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {
    @Override
    public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                             Object handler) throws Exception {
        String apiKey = request.getHeader("x-api-key");            // header names are case-insensitive
        if (!"secret123".equals(apiKey)) {
            response.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_UNAUTHORIZED);  // 401: who are you?
            return false;                                          // stop here
        }
        return true;
    }
}

@Component
public class AuthorizationInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {
    @Override
    public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                             Object handler) throws Exception {
        String userRole = request.getHeader("x-user-role");
        if (!"ADMIN".equals(userRole)) {
            response.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_FORBIDDEN);  // 403: known, but not allowed
            response.setContentType("application/json");
            response.getWriter().write("{\"message\": \"You are not authorized to perform this action\"}");
            return false;
        }
        return true;
    }
}
401 vs 403:
  • Authentication is "have you logged in / who are you?". Failure gives 401 Unauthorized, a misleading name for "unauthenticated".
  • Authorisation is "are you allowed to do this?", e.g. only admins may delete. Failure gives 403 Forbidden.

Demo:

  • With x-api-key: secret123 and x-user-role: ADMIN: 200 and full logs.
  • With the role user: 403 with the JSON message. It showed as plain text until setContentType("application/json") was added.
  • With a wrong key: an empty response (only return false, no status set in the demo) and no logging. Logging is order 3, so it never ran.

Further homework: a timing interceptor that starts in preHandle and stops in afterCompletion, porting the filter examples from Lecture 19, and adding admin-only delete/soft-delete to the CRUD app.

How it really executes: the dispatcher drives each phase

The simple onion picture hides that the three methods run at different moments, each called by the DispatcherServlet:

Correction: the "after" methods run in reverse order (verified on Boot 4.1.0):
The lecture's diagram shows postHandle 1 → 2 and afterCompletion 1 → 2. With interceptors A (order 1) and B (order 2), the real sequence was:
A.preHandle → B.preHandle → controller → B.postHandle → A.postHandle → B.afterCompletion → A.afterCompletion
It's a true onion: the first in is the last out, just like filters.
More verified behaviour worth knowing:
  • preHandle returns false: the controller and later interceptors are skipped, and postHandle never runs. afterCompletion still runs for the interceptors whose preHandle already returned true. When B denied, only A.afterCompletion ran.
  • postHandle can't change a REST response. For @ResponseBody/ResponseEntity the body is written inside the handler call, so in postHandle the response was already committed (isCommitted() = true, modelAndView = null), and a header set there never reached the client. Set headers in preHandle (or use a ResponseBodyAdvice).
  • Exceptions: when the controller threw, postHandle was skipped and afterCompletion received the exception.
  • Interceptors also see non-controller requests that go through the dispatcher. A static file ran with handler = ResourceHttpRequestHandler. After an exception, the /error forward ran every interceptor again with BasicErrorController. That's why the instanceof HandlerMethod check matters, and why error dispatches can be double-logged.

Filters vs interceptors

FilterInterceptor
Belongs toServlet API (jakarta.servlet.Filter)Spring MVC (HandlerInterceptor)
PositionAround the DispatcherServletInside it, around the handler
Knows controller/method?NoYes (HandlerMethod)
HooksOne doFilter (before/after chain.doFilter)preHandle, postHandle, afterCompletion
Stop a requestDon't call chain.doFilterReturn false from preHandle
Registration@Component (auto) or FilterRegistrationBeanWebMvcConfigurer.addInterceptors (required)
Path matchingServlet patterns (/api/*)Spring patterns (/api/* vs /api/**), plus excludes
Wrap/replace request or response objectsYes (wrappers, Lecture 20)No, it can only use the objects it's given
Best forGlobal concerns: request IDs, encoding, CORS, security, global loggingHandler-aware concerns: per-endpoint logging/metrics, per-controller rules, custom annotations
The lecture's guidance:
  • Generic, global logic goes in filters. Controller-specific logic goes in interceptors. Real apps use both.
  • Don't do authentication or authorisation in interceptors. It's the worst place: the request has already passed the dispatcher. Reject bad users in the filter layer, and in practice use Spring Security, which is itself a chain of filters, covered later. The auth interceptors above are exercises.
  • As with filters, changing request/response bodies is possible (e.g. in preHandle) but not good practice.
  • Interceptors combine well with custom annotations, e.g. check handlerMethod.hasMethodAnnotation(AdminOnly.class). This comes up in a later project.

Worth knowing

  • Order: .order(n) on the registration; lower runs first. Without it, the order is the registration order in addInterceptors. That's more deterministic than unordered filters, but explicit is clearer.
  • Client IP behind proxies: getRemoteAddr() returns the proxy or load balancer address in production. Read X-Forwarded-For, or better, enable Boot's forwarded-header support (server.forward-headers-strategy=framework). Locally it shows IPv6 loopback, 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1.
  • getBeanType().getName() gives the fully qualified class name. Use getSimpleName() for StudentController.
  • Async requests: for async handlers, postHandle/afterCompletion aren't called on the first dispatch. AsyncHandlerInterceptor.afterConcurrentHandlingStarted runs instead.
  • Don't add @EnableWebMvc to the WebMvcConfigurer in a Boot app (Lecture 15). Implementing the interface is enough.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"AuthorizationInterceptor implements HandlerMapping" → HandlerInterceptor.
"addInterceptor" override → addInterceptors (fixed in the lecture).
"client IP 0.0.0.1" → the loopback address.

Lecture 22: Introduction to AOP — Cross-Cutting Concerns, Scattering & Tangling, and the Decorator Road to Aspects

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #22 · 49m · Code Army · the motivation for Aspect-Oriented Programming; the mechanics come next lecture

From filters and interceptors to "any method"

MechanismWhat it wrapsLecture
FilterThe raw incoming request, before the DispatcherServlet19–20
InterceptorA controller (handler)21
AOPAny method of any Spring bean: services, repositories, utilities…22+

Services, repositories and helper classes also need logic run before, after or around their methods. Aspect-Oriented Programming is a separate module of the Spring Framework for exactly that. People often find it hard at first; the lecture builds up to it from the problem.

Setup

A small project (aop-introduction-demo, Spring Web only) with:

  • A Student DTO: name, age, rollNumber, subject.
  • A StudentController with POST /api/students → studentService.createStudent(student), returning "Done".
  • A StudentService whose createStudent prints "Student is saved successfully". In a real app it would call studentRepository.save(student) and return a response DTO.

The problem: production code buries the business logic

The business logic of createStudent is one line: save the student. Ask the method "how is a student created?" and that line is the answer. A production version, though, needs much more around it:

public StudentResponseDto createStudent(Student student) {
    securityService.checkPermission("CREATE_STUDENT");          // permission check
    log.info("StudentService : createStudent called");          // logging
    long start = System.currentTimeMillis();                    // execution time
    try {
        studentRepository.save(student);                        // ← the ONLY business logic
        auditService.record("CREATE_STUDENT", student);         // auditing
        StudentResponseDto result = mapToDto(student);
        cache.put(student.getRollNumber(), result);             // caching
        return result;
    } catch (Exception ex) {
        log.error("createStudent failed", ex);                  // error logging
        throw ex;
    } finally {
        long duration = System.currentTimeMillis() - start;     // execution time
        log.info("createStudent took {} ms", duration);
    }
}
  • Permission checks can't rely only on filters or interceptors. Not every call starts at an API. One service can call another internally (e.g. a PrincipalService calling createStudent), bypassing the web layer entirely.
  • Multiply this by 50 methods per class and hundreds or thousands of classes, and "you spend half your time reading infrastructure code before you find the business logic".

Two kinds of logic, two kinds of concern

Business logicInfrastructure / supporting logic
ExamplesCreate a student, place an order, verify a paymentLogging, security, execution timing, auditing, caching, exception handling
Varies byDomain: each app is differentHardly varies: it's the same boilerplate in every app, just different keys and values
Shape of the concernVertical: all student logic lives in StudentService, all payment logic in PaymentServiceHorizontal: logging is needed in every class
NameCore / business concernsCross-cutting concerns
Definition: concern and cross-cutting concern:
A concern is an area of interest of the application: student management, payment management, order management. A cross-cutting concern is one that cuts across many classes and modules instead of living in one, like logging, security or timing. Spring AOP's stated purpose is to handle cross-cutting concerns, so the term is worth knowing precisely.

The two symptoms

SymptomMeaningSeen in
ScatteringOne concern's code is spread across many classesLogging calls in StudentService, OrderService, PaymentService, TeacherService…
TanglingOne method mixes many concerns togethercreateStudent interleaving security, logging, timing, auditing and caching with one save

Attempt 1: helper / utility classes

public class LoggingServiceUtil {                    // no @Component: static helpers
    public static void logStart(String className, String methodName) {
        System.out.println("Executing " + className + " : " + methodName);
    }
    public static void logEnd(String className, String methodName) {
        System.out.println("Finishing " + className + " : " + methodName);
    }
}

// in StudentService.createStudent:
LoggingServiceUtil.logStart("StudentService", "createStudent");
studentRepository.save(student);
LoggingServiceUtil.logEnd("StudentService", "createStudent");

Why it fails:

  • The logic is reusable now, but the calls are still in every method: still scattered and tangled.
  • A developer can forget to call it, and audit logs silently go missing.
  • Success and failure paths need a try/catch with separate logs, so the method keeps growing.

Attempt 2: inheritance

Make every service extend a base LoggingService with the helper methods. Same failure: each method must still call logStart()/logEnd() itself. On top of that, Java has single inheritance, so one base class can't supply logging, security and timing all together.

Attempt 3: wrappers, the Decorator pattern

Keep the business class clean and wrap it in another object that implements the same interface, adds behaviour, and then delegates. That's the Decorator pattern (LLD notebook); wrappers came up in Lecture 20 too.

public interface StudentService {
    void createStudent(Student student);
}

@Service
public class StudentServiceImpl implements StudentService {        // business logic ONLY
    @Override
    public void createStudent(Student student) {
        studentRepository.save(student);
        System.out.println("Student saved");
    }
}

@Component
public class LoggingDecorator implements StudentService {           // is-a StudentService
    private final StudentServiceImpl studentServiceImpl;            // has-a StudentService

    public LoggingDecorator(StudentServiceImpl studentServiceImpl) {
        this.studentServiceImpl = studentServiceImpl;
    }

    @Override
    public void createStudent(Student student) {
        LoggingServiceUtil.logStart("StudentServiceImpl", "createStudent");   // before
        studentServiceImpl.createStudent(student);                           // delegate
        LoggingServiceUtil.logEnd("StudentServiceImpl", "createStudent");     // after
    }
}

@Component
@Primary                                     // controller gets the OUTERMOST wrapper
public class ExecutionTimeService implements StudentService {
    private final LoggingDecorator loggingDecorator;

    public ExecutionTimeService(LoggingDecorator loggingDecorator) {
        this.loggingDecorator = loggingDecorator;
    }

    @Override
    public void createStudent(Student student) {
        long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
        loggingDecorator.createStudent(student);
        long duration = System.currentTimeMillis() - start;
        System.out.println("Duration: " + duration);
    }
}

// StudentController now depends on the interface:
private final StudentService studentService;     // Spring injects the @Primary one
  • The injection conflict: with two, then three, StudentService beans, the controller's injection is ambiguous ("more than one bean of StudentService"). @Primary on the outermost wrapper resolves it (Lecture 5). @Qualifier would work too.
  • Demo:
    • "Executing …" → "Student saved" → "Finishing …".
    • The duration showed 0 ms until a Thread.sleep(2000) was added to the business method, to simulate slow work. Then it showed about 2000 ms.
  • StudentServiceImpl contains only business logic. Decorators can be stacked indefinitely (decorator 3 = authentication…).

Verified (Boot 4.1.0): the injected bean was ExecutionTimeDecorator. The output was "Executing …" → "Student saved: Aditya" → "Finishing …" → "Duration: 204 ms", with a 200 ms sleep.

Why decorators still aren't the answer:
  • Every service needs its own wrapper class for every concern: classes × concerns wrappers. A 20-method service needs every method re-implemented in every decorator.
  • Wiring the chain by hand is error-prone. Give decorator 3 decorator 1 by mistake, and decorator 2 silently never runs. Forget a wrapper, and a concern is missing.
The idea is right; writing it by hand is the problem. AOP generates these wrappers for you.

AOP: declare what, where and when once

AOP answers three questions, declaratively and in one place:

QuestionExampleAOP term (added)
What should happen?LogAdvice: the code to run
Where?All methods of all service classesPointcut: an expression selecting join points (method executions)
When?At method start and at method endAdvice type: @Before, @After, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, @Around
  • An aspect is a class that bundles advice and pointcuts for one concern.
  • Spring then wraps the matching beans automatically, "somewhere in the background, where we don't see the code". Just as IoC freed us from managing objects, AOP frees us from spreading infrastructure code: it lifts it into its own module.
OOP vs AOP (the lecture's comparison)
OOPAOP
Unit of modularityClass (models a real entity: Student, StudentService)Aspect (models a concern: logging, security)
OrganisesBusiness logic, verticallyCross-cutting concerns, horizontally
RelationshipComplementary: AOP works on top of OOP code without changing it
One-liner from the lecture:
"Just as Spring gave us beans so we don't manage objects, it gave us AOP so we don't manage infrastructure logic in every class." How an aspect is written and how it works internally comes next lecture.

Worth knowing (preview, added)

  • Under the hood, Spring AOP creates proxies: automatically generated wrappers around your beans, the decorators from Attempt 3 written for you.
    • A JDK dynamic proxy is used when proxying through an interface.
    • A CGLIB subclass is used otherwise, and is Spring Boot's default.
    Strictly this is the Proxy pattern (same interface, control access) rather than Decorator, but the structure is identical.
  • You already use AOP: @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @PreAuthorize and @Retryable are all implemented as aspects or proxies.
  • Known limitations of Spring AOP, which follow from proxies:
    • It works only on Spring beans, and only on method execution.
    • Self-invocation (this.otherMethod() inside the same class) bypasses the proxy, so its advice doesn't run.
    • private/final methods can't be intercepted.
    AspectJ (compile- or load-time weaving) lifts these limits.
  • Design note on the demo: the decorators depend on concrete classes (StudentServiceImpl, LoggingDecorator). Depending on the StudentService interface, selected with @Qualifier, makes decorators reorderable and reusable. That's the Decorator pattern as usually taught.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"What, how and when" → the lecturer corrects it to what, where and when.
"the monolith / microservices both have concerns" was said as "agolith" → monolith.

Lecture 23: Writing Your First Aspect — @Aspect, Pointcuts and the Five Advice Types

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #23 · 1h28m · Code Army · continues Lecture 22; pointcut syntax and JoinPoint methods come next lecture

Recap: the decorator chain, and "is it Proxy or Decorator?"

Lecture 22 ended with the conceptual picture: the controller never talks to the service directly. It talks to the outermost wrapper, each wrapper does its work and hands on to the next, and the return value travels back the same way.

Spring internally calls these wrappers proxies. That raises a classic interview question: does Spring AOP use the Proxy pattern or the Decorator pattern?

The lecture's answer:
  • Structurally the two are the same: draw both UML diagrams and they look almost identical (Decorator usually adds an abstract decorator layer so decorators can stack).
  • They differ in intent. A Decorator enhances an object: it adds features (logging, authentication…) layer by layer. A Proxy controls access to an object: you cannot reach the real object except through it (remote proxy, virtual proxy, protection proxy…).
  • So both answers are defensible. Spring's own name is "proxy"; if you are adding behaviour to a service you can call it a decorator. Explain the shared structure and the different intent, and the interviewer is satisfied.
Worth adding:
One Spring proxy object holds a chain of advice (an interceptor chain) rather than one proxy per aspect, so the "stack of decorators" is really one proxy running a list of interceptors in order. The Proxy and Decorator patterns are covered in the LLD notebook.

Setup: the AOP dependency (renamed in Boot 4)

The demo project aop-demo starts with only spring-boot-starter-webmvc (plus its test starter). Searching Maven Central for "aop" shows spring-aop and spring-boot-starter-aop, but the old starter does not work with Boot 4. It has been renamed:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-aspectj</artifactId>
</dependency>
  • Boot 3.x: spring-boot-starter-aop. Boot 4.x: spring-boot-starter-aspectj (verified on Boot 4.1.0).
  • Drop the <version> and <scope> copied from Maven Central; the Boot parent manages the version.
  • AspectJ is a separate, full AOP library; Spring AOP borrows its annotations and pointcut language (more below).
Worth knowing:
In Spring Boot you do not need @EnableAspectJAutoProxy; the starter's auto-configuration turns proxying on. In plain Spring you add it to a @Configuration class. (Added.)

The target: a tiny controller and service

Packages controller and service (no repository or DTO yet, to keep the focus on AOP):

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/students")
public class StudentController {
    private final StudentService studentService;

    public StudentController(StudentService studentService) {
        this.studentService = studentService;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<String> createStudent() {
        String s = studentService.createStudent();
        return ResponseEntity.ok(s);
    }
}

@Service
public class StudentService {
    public String createStudent() {
        System.out.println("Student saved");
        return "Student saved";
    }
}

A POST /api/students from Postman returns Student saved. The goal: print "A student is going to be saved" before the service method runs, without writing that line inside createStudent(), because that would mix infrastructure logic into business logic again (Lecture 22).

AOP can intercept any Spring-bean method (controller, repository…). Services are the usual target because controllers already have interceptors and filters, and the business logic lives in services.

Writing the aspect: @Component + @Aspect

AOP classes go in their own package, conventionally aspect, because an AOP class is called an aspect. The first one is LoggingAspect:

package in.strikes.demo.aspect;

import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Aspect;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Before;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Aspect
@Component
public class LoggingAspect {

    @Before("execution(String in.strikes.demo.service.StudentService.createStudent())")
    public void logBeforeMethod() {
        System.out.println("A student is going to be saved");
    }
}
  • @Component — the aspect must be a bean; the IoC container manages aspects just as it manages services. Without it the aspect is ignored.
  • @Aspect — tells Spring this bean is special: its methods intercept other methods. @Aspect alone is not a stereotype, so you need both.
  • Each method in the aspect is a piece of interception logic; the class name says what kind (logging).

Annotating the class is not enough. The aspect still has to answer the three questions from Lecture 22:

QuestionFor this exampleAnswered byAOP term
What to do?Print the logging lineThe body of logBeforeMethod()Advice (method + timing annotation)
When?Before createStudent runs@Before
Where?StudentService.createStudent()The expression inside @Before(...)Pointcut expression

The pointcut used here, read left to right:

  • execution(...) — intercept the execution of a method.
  • String — its return type.
  • in.strikes.demo.service.StudentService.createStudent — the fully qualified class and method name (copy the package path).
  • () — its parameter list, empty here.

Run it and hit the endpoint. The console shows:

A student is going to be saved
Student saved

The service was intercepted without touching its code. Pointcut syntax (wildcards, whole packages, all 20 methods of a service) is next lecture; this lecture keeps the pointcut fixed and focuses on advice.

The vocabulary

  • Aspect — the class (LoggingAspect): a module for one cross-cutting concern.
  • Advice — the method plus its timing annotation (@Before + logBeforeMethod()): what to do and when.
  • Pointcut — the expression that selects where (execution(...)).
  • Target — the real object whose method is intercepted (the StudentService bean).
  • Proxy — the wrapper through which the target is reached.
Precision note (added):
The lecture calls the aspect method itself "the proxy". Strictly, the proxy is the object Spring generates at startup (a CGLIB subclass named like StudentService$$SpringCGLIB$$0, verified); your aspect method is the advice the proxy calls. Also missing from the lecture's list: a join point is one point in execution where advice can run; in Spring AOP that is always a method execution. A pointcut is a predicate that selects join points. Weaving is linking aspects to targets; Spring does it at runtime by creating proxies.

What happens inside: the proxy sits between controller and service

Without AOP, StudentController depends directly on StudentService, and its createStudent() calls the service's createStudent(). With the aspect present, when Spring injects the dependency it notices an aspect is ready to intercept StudentService, so it does not hand over the real object. Conceptually it builds a StudentProxy:

  • StudentProxy is-a StudentService (a subclass, or both implement a common interface as in Lecture 22), so the controller cannot tell the difference.
  • It overrides createStudent(): first call LoggingAspect.logBeforeMethod(), then call the real StudentService.createStudent() through a reference it holds.
You never touch the proxy yourself:
Internally there are two objects, the target and the proxy, but for you only one bean exists: StudentService. The proxy is Spring's own; you interact only with the service type and Spring swaps in the proxy.

The five advice types: one try/catch/finally explains them all

All five annotations answer the same question, when: @Before, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, @After, @Around. Instead of memorising each one, the lecturer maps them onto a single Java try/catch/finally block (recall: try runs; catch only on an exception; finally always):

// what the proxy conceptually does around the target method
beforeLogic();                          // @Before
try {
    Object result = targetMethod();     // the intercepted method
    afterReturningLogic(result);        // @AfterReturning  (success only)
    return result;
} catch (Exception ex) {
    afterThrowingLogic(ex);             // @AfterThrowing   (failure only)
    throw ex;                           // rethrown to the caller (controller)
} finally {
    afterLogic();                       // @After           (always)
}
// @Around = you write this whole block yourself
AdviceRunsPosition in the blockTypical uses
@BeforeBefore the targetAbove the tryLogging entry, auth checks, precondition validation
@AfterReturningOnly if the target returned normallyAfter the call, inside tryLog/audit the result
@AfterThrowingOnly if the target threwcatchLog/monitor/audit failures
@AfterAlways, success or failurefinallyRelease locks, free resources, clear caches
@AroundWraps the whole callThe entire blockTiming, retries, changing args/result, swallowing exceptions
The common confusion, settled:
If the target never throws, @After and @AfterReturning look identical. They differ as soon as an exception appears: @AfterReturning is skipped, @AfterThrowing runs, and @After runs in both cases, "just like a finally block".

@Before: runs first, can block only by throwing

Good for logging that must print at the start, authentication, or any precondition check. (For real authentication/authorisation use Spring Security; a @Before auth check is fine for small apps, as with the filters and interceptors in Lectures 19–21.)

Can @Before stop the target method from running?

  • Not by returning. A return; in the advice just ends the advice; the target still runs. The demo prints both lines (verified).
  • Yes, indirectly, by throwing. If the advice throws, the proxy never reaches the target:
@Before("execution(String in.strikes.demo.service.StudentService.createStudent())")
public void logBeforeMethod() {
    System.out.println("A student is going to be saved");
    boolean allowed = false;               // stand-in for a real auth check
    if (!allowed) {
        throw new RuntimeException("Method execution not allowed");
    }
}

Result: Postman gets a 500; the console shows "A student is going to be saved" then the exception. "Student saved" never prints: the service never ran.

Reading the target's arguments with JoinPoint

Any advice method may take a JoinPoint parameter. It carries information about the intercepted call (the target method, its arguments…; the full API is next lecture):

@Before("execution(String in.strikes.demo.service.StudentService.createStudent())")
public void logBeforeMethod(JoinPoint joinPoint) {
    Object[] arr = joinPoint.getArgs();   // arguments, as an Object array
    System.out.println("A student is going to be saved");
}

The lecture's rule: in @Before (and the other non-around advice) you can read the arguments but not modify them. Changing arguments, or the return value, is @Around's job.

Precision note (verified on Boot 4.1.0):
getArgs() returns a copy of the argument array, so args[0] = somethingElse has no effect on the target (verified: the target still saw the original Student). But the elements are the same object references, so mutating a mutable argument (((Student) args[0]).setName(...)) does reach the target (verified). That is the same hack the lecture later shows for @AfterReturning, and just as bad practice.

@AfterReturning: success only, and it cannot change the result

@AfterReturning("execution(String in.strikes.demo.service.StudentService.createStudent())")
public void logAfterReturningMethod() {
    System.out.println("logAfterReturningMethod called");
}

Output: "Student saved" then "logAfterReturningMethod called". (The lecturer comments out the @Before advice from here on so only one advice runs at a time.)

When the target throws

  • Service prints "Student saved", then throw new RuntimeException("Some error occurred"). The exception goes to the proxy; with no catch there it propagates to the controller. @AfterReturning does not run. Postman gets a 500.
  • Service throws and catches its own exception (try { throw … } catch (RuntimeException e) {}), then returns normally. The proxy never learns an exception happened, so @AfterReturning runs as usual.
  • Could the advice catch the target's exception itself? No: there is no way to call the target from inside @AfterReturning, so there is nothing to wrap in a try. That needs @Around.

Capturing the return value: returning = "..."

@AfterReturning(
    value = "execution(String in.strikes.demo.service.StudentService.createStudent())",
    returning = "result")
public void logAfterReturningMethod(String result) {
    System.out.println("Target method returned: " + result);
}
  • returning = "result" must match the parameter name result exactly.
  • The parameter type is the type you expect back (String here; Object if unknown).
  • Once you add a second attribute, the pointcut must be named (value = …, or pointcut = …); the IDE flags a bare string.

Output: "Student saved", "Target method returned: Student saved".

Experiment: return a modified string from the advice

The lecturer changes the advice to return String and returns result + .... Postman still gets the original Student saved (verified). Whatever an @AfterReturning method returns is ignored; the caller always gets what the target returned. So declare these advice methods void.

Experiment: mutate a returned object (possible, but don't)

The lecturer adds a DTO Student (private String name; private int age; with getters/setters). The controller takes @RequestBody Student student, passes it to studentService.createStudent(student), which prints "Student saved" and returns the same object. Postman sends {"name": "Aditya", "age": 28} and gets it back.

  1. Change the advice parameter to Student result and call result.setName("Rohit"); result.setAge(21);.
  2. First run: nothing happens, not even the advice's print. Why: the pointcut still says String …createStudent(), but the method now returns Student and takes a Student, so the pointcut no longer matches. (Before that, an advice parameter typed String also silently never fires for a Student return: the returning type narrows matching.)
  3. Fix the pointcut with fully qualified names: return type in.strikes.demo.dto.Student and parameter (in.strikes.demo.dto.Student). Types in pointcuts must be fully qualified (except java.lang types like String).
  4. Run: Postman receives {"name": "Rohit", "age": 21} (verified). It works because the advice mutated the same object the controller then returns.
  5. Shortcut, explained next lecture: execution(* in.strikes.demo.service.StudentService.createStudent(..)) — * for any return type, (..) for any parameters.
The lecture's verdict:
"Possible, but a very wrong practice." It only works for mutable objects; it cannot replace the result or change a String (strings are immutable). If you need to modify or replace a return value, use @Around.

@AfterThrowing: failure only, observe but not handle

@AfterThrowing(
    value = "execution(* in.strikes.demo.service.StudentService.createStudent(..))",
    throwing = "exception")
public void logAfterThrowingMethod(Throwable exception) {
    System.out.println("Exception type: " + exception.getClass().getName());
    System.out.println("Exception message: " + exception.getMessage());
}
  • With a service that does not throw, the advice never prints; only "Student saved" appears.
  • Service throws new RuntimeException("Some error happened"). Console: "Student saved", then the advice's lines (java.lang.RuntimeException, "Some error happened"), then the exception continues to the controller and Postman gets a 500. Exactly the catch { log; throw ex; } of the model.
  • throwing = "exception" must match the parameter name, like returning.

The parameter type filters which exceptions trigger it

  • Throwable (parent of everything) matches any exception.
  • RuntimeException matches the demo's exception.
  • NullPointerException does not: the advice silently doesn't run for a plain RuntimeException (verified), because NPE is a subclass of RuntimeException, not a parent.

What it cannot do

  • Catch/consume the exception. A catch without a try won't compile, and you can't write the try because you can't invoke the target yourself here.
  • Replace the outcome. Returning "done" from the advice changes nothing: the exception still reaches the controller (verified). Keep it void.

Use it for monitoring: logging exceptions, auditing, alerting.

@After: always runs, like finally

@After("execution(* in.strikes.demo.service.StudentService.createStudent(..))")
public void logAfterMethod() {
    System.out.println("logAfterMethod executed");
}
  • Service throws: "Student saved", "logAfterMethod executed", then the exception propagates.
  • Service returns normally: "Student saved", "logAfterMethod executed", then the normal result.

In both cases the caller receives exactly what the service produced; @After can neither change the return value nor consume the exception. Use it for anything you'd put in finally: releasing a lock, freeing a resource, clearing a cache.

Summary from the lecture:
@AfterReturning = success case. @AfterThrowing = failure case. @After = both, "whatever happens", like a finally block. None of these three can modify the result or handle the exception; they can only monitor.

@Around: the most powerful advice

@Around runs before and after the target, and you decide if and when the target runs. It can change arguments, change the return value, consume exceptions, and even call the target several times.

First attempt: two prints, "Before target method" and "After target method". But how does Spring know the target should run between them? It needs to be told, via ProceedingJoinPoint, a child of JoinPoint that holds everything about the call and can execute the target:

@Around("execution(* in.strikes.demo.service.StudentService.createStudent(..))")
public void logAroundMethod(ProceedingJoinPoint joinPoint) throws Throwable {
    System.out.println("Before target method");
    joinPoint.proceed();                    // run the target now
    System.out.println("After target method");
}
  • proceed() declares throws Throwable (the target might throw and the exception must be able to pass through), so the advice declares it too, or wraps it in try/catch.
  • Console prints all three lines in order, but Postman gets an empty body. The advice is void and ignores proceed()'s result, so the proxy returns null: the controller then returns ResponseEntity.ok(null), a 200 with no body.
Worth knowing (verified):
If the intercepted method returns a primitive (e.g. int) and a void @Around swallows the result, the call fails with AopInvocationException: Null return value from advice does not match primitive return type. An around advice should almost always return Object and return what proceed() gave it.

Fixed version: capture and return the result. proceed() returns Object (it can't know the target's type), so cast if you need the concrete type:

@Around("execution(* in.strikes.demo.service.StudentService.createStudent(..))")
public Student logAroundMethod(ProceedingJoinPoint joinPoint) throws Throwable {
    System.out.println("Before target method");
    Student student = (Student) joinPoint.proceed();
    student.setAge(31);          // around may legitimately change the result
    student.setName("Rohit");
    System.out.println("After target method");
    return student;
}

Postman now shows the modified student. Unlike @AfterReturning, here the advice's return value is what the caller gets, so it could even return a completely different object, or a changed String.

Not calling proceed() at all

Remove the proceed() call (and make the method void, since there's nothing to return): the console shows only "Before target method" and "After target method"; "Student saved" never prints and Postman gets an empty body. The advice fully controls whether the target runs. Timing a method is the obvious use: start a timer before proceed(), stop it after (as done with filters and interceptors earlier).

Exceptions inside @Around

Around behaves "just like a Java method calling another method". If the target throws and the advice doesn't catch, the line after proceed() is skipped and the exception goes to the controller: the console shows "Before target method", "Student saved", and nothing more.

Worked example: a generic around advice that is all four others

@Around("execution(* in.strikes.demo.service.StudentService.createStudent(..))")
public Object logAroundMethod(ProceedingJoinPoint joinPoint) throws Throwable {
    System.out.println("Starting " + joinPoint.getSignature().getName()); // like @Before
    try {
        Object result = joinPoint.proceed();
        System.out.println("Execution successful");                     // like @AfterReturning
        return result;
    } catch (Exception e) {
        System.out.println("Execution failed: " + e.getMessage());      // like @AfterThrowing
        throw e;                                                        // rethrow to the controller
    } finally {
        System.out.println("Execution completed");                      // like @After
    }
}
  • joinPoint.getSignature().getName() gives the method name (createStudent).
  • Returns Object and names the variable result, so it works for any target without casting.

Demo run

CaseConsole outputPostman
Service throws "Some error happened"Starting createStudent → Student saved → Execution failed: Some error happened → Execution completed500
Service returns normallyStarting createStudent → Student saved → Execution successful → Execution completedThe student JSON

Replace throw e; with return null; and the exception is consumed: the controller never learns there was one.

Don't use @Around for everything:
Around is so powerful it is tempting to use it everywhere; the lecture calls that the wrong approach. Use the most specific advice: @Before if you only need work beforehand; @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing or @After for work afterwards, depending on whether you care about success, failure, or both. (Added reason, from the Spring docs: a narrower advice can't accidentally forget to call proceed(), drop the return value, or swallow an exception.)
Worth flagging (added):
The lecture's generic advice catches Exception, so an Error (e.g. OutOfMemoryError) or a sneaky-thrown checked Throwable would skip the "failed" log. Catch Throwable if the log must cover everything (it is rethrown anyway).

Around's full power: changing arguments and the return value, calling the target twice

A new endpoint and service method just for experiments:

// StudentController
@GetMapping
public ResponseEntity<String> dummyMethod() {
    String s = "Aditya";
    return ResponseEntity.ok(studentService.dummyMethod(s));
}

// StudentService
public String dummyMethod(String s) {
    System.out.println("dummy method called");
    return s;
}

Without an aspect, GET /api/students returns Aditya. The aspect targets execution(* in.strikes.demo.service.StudentService.dummyMethod(..)). Plain proceed() needs no arguments: the controller's argument is passed through automatically.

Changing the arguments: proceed(Object[] args)

@Around("execution(* in.strikes.demo.service.StudentService.dummyMethod(..))")
public Object logAroundMethod(ProceedingJoinPoint joinPoint) throws Throwable {
    Object[] arr = joinPoint.getArgs();
    String originalString = (String) arr[0];               // one String parameter
    String modifiedString = originalString.toUpperCase();
    Object[] modifiedArr = { modifiedString };
    String returnType = (String) joinPoint.proceed(modifiedArr); // target gets "ADITYA"
    returnType = returnType + " intercepted";                    // change the result too
    return returnType;
}
  • The target receives ADITYA; Postman shows ADITYA intercepted. Comment out the modification and it shows Aditya again.
  • proceed takes arguments only as an Object[] (that's how the proxy receives them), so wrap the new value in a fresh array.
  • (The lecture names the result variable returnType; it holds the returned value, not a type.)
Worth knowing (verified):
The array must have the same number of arguments as the method: passing two for a one-arg method throws IllegalArgumentException: Expecting 1 arguments to proceed, but was passed 2 arguments. The values must also be type-compatible with the parameters. And proceed(newArgs) replaces the join point's arguments: a later plain proceed() in the same advice reuses the modified ones (verified: the second call also saw "ADITYA").

Calling the target more than once

Object return1 = joinPoint.proceed();
System.out.println("Intercepted request, calling again");
Object return2 = joinPoint.proceed();
return return2;

Console: "dummy method called", "Intercepted request, calling again", "dummy method called". The target ran twice; loops (e.g. retries) are possible too.

Why this is dangerous:
Only do this for idempotent operations. If the target charges a payment or sends an email, calling proceed() twice charges twice or sends two emails. This is exactly the concern with retry aspects.

Advice types compared

Capability@Before@AfterReturning@AfterThrowing@After@Around
Parameter typeJoinPointJoinPoint + resultJoinPoint + exceptionJoinPointProceedingJoinPoint (required)
Read argumentsYesYesYesYesYes
Replace argumentsNoNoNoNoYes, proceed(args)
See return valueNoYes (returning)NoNoYes
Replace return valueNoNo (return ignored)NoNoYes
See exception—NoYes (throwing)NoYes
Swallow exception—NoNoNoYes
Prevent target from runningOnly by throwingNo (already ran)NoNoYes, skip proceed()
Run target several timesNoNoNoNoYes

Anticipated question: "If one aspect has all five advices on one method, what order do they run in?"

(Not covered in the lecture; commonly asked.) Since Spring 5.2.7, advice in the same aspect on the same join point runs with precedence @Around, @Before, @After, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, and the "after" advices behave like AspectJ, with @After as the outer finally. Observed on Boot 4.1.0:

SuccessFailure
@Around (before part) → @Before → target → @AfterReturning → @After → @Around (after part)@Around (before part) → @Before → target → @AfterThrowing → @After → @Around (finally part) → exception to caller

This matches the lecture's try/catch/finally model exactly, with @Around wrapping everything. Two advices of the same type in one aspect have undefined order; across different aspects use @Order (or Ordered) on the aspect class, where a lower value is the outer wrapper.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • @Aspect comes from AspectJ in Boot 3 too. The lecture says that under Boot 3 the import would be from an "aop.lang.annotation" package. Spring has never had its own @Aspect: in both Boot 3 (spring-boot-starter-aop) and Boot 4 (spring-boot-starter-aspectj) it is org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Aspect, from the aspectjweaver jar. Only the starter's name changed.
  • JoinPoint and ProceedingJoinPoint are interfaces (from org.aspectj.lang), not classes; Spring passes in its own implementation. ProceedingJoinPoint extends JoinPoint and adds proceed() / proceed(Object[]). It is only allowed in @Around advice.
  • The aspect method is the advice, not the proxy. The proxy is generated by Spring (CGLIB subclass by default in Boot); see the precision note above.
  • Spring AOP uses AspectJ's annotations and pointcut language, not AspectJ's weaver. Spring AOP is proxy-based and runtime-only: it can intercept only public (and, with CGLIB, protected/package-visible non-final) methods of Spring beans, called from outside the bean. Full AspectJ weaves bytecode at compile or load time and can also intercept constructors, field access, private methods and self-calls (Lecture 22's limits).
  • Silent non-matching is the most common AOP bug. Seen three times in this lecture: a pointcut whose signature no longer matches after a refactor, a returning parameter of the wrong type, and an @AfterThrowing parameter that is a subclass of the thrown exception. None produce an error; the advice just never runs. Keep pointcuts broad enough (*, (..)) or target custom annotations (next lecture's pointcut designators).
  • Advice "return values" from non-around advice are ignored (verified). This applies to @Before, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing and @After: make them void.
  • Real uses of each type: @Transactional and @Cacheable are around advice (begin/commit/rollback; return the cached value without proceeding). Spring Retry's @Retryable is around advice that calls proceed() in a loop, hence the idempotency warning. Micrometer's @Timed is around advice timing proceed().
Transcript slips to ignore:
"prog-ji" / "prog-gee" = proxy.
"login aspect" / "login logic" = logging aspect / logic.
"in.stries.dm" = the package in.strikes.demo (spelled variously in the auto-captions).
"LED video" = the LLD video series.
"String is non-immutable" → strings are immutable; that's exactly why @AfterReturning couldn't change the returned String.
"when and what together we call an advice" and, a minute later, "it answers what and when" — both mean the same: advice = what + when.

Lecture 24: Pointcut Expressions — Wildcards, Designators, Named Pointcuts and this vs target

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #24 · 1h19m · Code Army · answers AOP's "where?" question (Lecture 23 answered "what" and "when")

Setup: the same demo, slightly extended

  • StudentController — POST /api/students → createStudent(@RequestBody Student); GET /api/students → getStudent().
  • StudentService — createStudent(Student) prints "Student saved" and returns the student; getStudent(...) prints and returns "All student data".
  • Student DTO — name, age.
  • LoggingAspect — emptied; every experiment below is a @Before advice printing "Method intercepted".

Anatomy of an execution pointcut

The first word of a pointcut is the designator (execution, within, bean…). Inside execution(...) come, in order:

execution( [access-modifier]  return-type  [declaring-type.]method-name(params)  [throws exception] )
execution( public             String       in.strikes.aopdemo.service.StudentService.getStudent(String) )
PartRequired?Example
Access modifierOptional (omitted = any)public, protected
Return typeRequiredString, *
Declaring class + method nameMethod name required; class is optional (see Corrections)in.strikes.aopdemo.service.StudentService.getStudent
ParametersRequired (even if empty ())(String), (), (..)
ExceptionOptionalthrows java.io.IOException
  • The access modifier is usually left out: intercepted service methods are public anyway. Write protected if you want protected ones (proxy-based AOP can only reach public/protected/package methods).
  • First demo: @Before("execution(String in.strikes.aopdemo.service.StudentService.getStudent())") → GET prints "Method intercepted" then "All student data".
  • The lecturer then makes getStudent(String s) take its string from the controller; the pointcut must change to getStudent(String) or it stops matching.

Intercepting createStudent(Student) exactly needs fully qualified types everywhere (only java.lang types like String can be short):

@Before("execution(in.strikes.aopdemo.dto.Student " +
        "in.strikes.aopdemo.service.StudentService.createStudent(" +
        "in.strikes.aopdemo.dto.Student))")
public void logBeforeMethod2() { System.out.println("Method intercepted"); }

Why exact pointcuts defeat the point of AOP

Three lines to target one method. With 20 service methods you'd write 20 pointcuts (or 20 aspects), which is the scattering AOP was meant to remove (Lecture 22). The fix is wildcards: describe a pattern of methods instead of naming each one.

Wildcard 1: * — exactly one "anything"

PointcutMatches
execution(* …StudentService.getStudent(String))getStudent(String) with any return type (String, Integer, Long, void, an object…)
execution(* …StudentService.getStudent(*))…taking exactly one parameter of any type
execution(* …StudentService.getStudent(*, *))exactly two parameters, any types
execution(* …StudentService.getStudent(*, int))two parameters, the second an int
execution(* …StudentService.*(*))any method of StudentService with one parameter: now both createStudent and getStudent are covered by one advice
execution(* …StudentService.get*(*))methods whose name starts with get
execution(* …StudentService.*Student(*))names ending with Student
execution(* in.strikes.aopdemo.service.*.*(*))any method of any class directly in the service package (first * = class, second = method)
execution(* *(*))any one-arg method anywhere (too broad; see below)

Verified: execution(* in.strikes.aopdemo.service.*.*(*)) intercepted createStudent and getStudent but not the zero-arg dummyMethod(). A * in the package position stands for one segment only, so a class in service.subservice is not matched; that needs .. (next).

Wildcard 2: .. — "zero or more"

A new zero-argument method public int dummyMethod() { return 0; } escapes (*). Writing (..) matches any number of parameters, zero included. Similarly in the package position .. means this package and all sub-packages.

Where*..
Return typeAny typeNot allowed (a method has exactly one return type)
PackageExactly one segmentAny depth of sub-packages
Class / method nameAny name, or part of one (get*)Not meaningful: you match one method at a time
ParametersExactly one, any typeZero or more, any types
  • execution(* in.strikes.aopdemo.service.StudentService.*(..)) — every method of StudentService.
  • execution(* in.strikes.aopdemo.service..*(..)) — every method of every class in service or any sub-package (verified: also hit service.sub.Dummy.hello()). The Spring docs write the same thing as service..*.*(..); both behaved identically.

The "match everything" pointcut crashes startup
