The lecturer tries execution(* *(..)): any method, anywhere. The app fails to start:

Error creating bean with name '…TomcatServletWebServerAutoConfiguration':
Could not generate CGLIB subclass of class …TomcatServletWebServerAutoConfiguration
Caused by: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Cannot subclass final class …

Why: the pointcut also matches Spring's own beans, so Spring tries to proxy all of them, and some can't be proxied. (Verified on Boot 4.1.0, the exact cause is that the Tomcat auto-configuration class is final, and CGLIB proxies are subclasses.)

The fix is to limit to your base package:

@Before("execution(* in.strikes.aopdemo..*(..))")

Now a POST prints "Method intercepted" twice, then "Student saved": once for StudentController.createStudent, once for StudentService.createStudent.

Worth knowing (verified):
A base-package pointcut also catches @Bean factory methods of your @Configuration classes (in the test it intercepted the main class's CommandLineRunner bean method at startup). Base-package-wide advice is rarely what you want; prefer layer-level pointcuts (within(…service..*)).

Designator 2: within — match whole classes

execution works at method level (full signature); within works at class level: every method of the matching type(s), no return type or parameters to spell out.

@Before("within(in.strikes.aopdemo.service.StudentService)")  // all methods of one class
@Before("within(in.strikes.aopdemo.service.*)")               // classes directly in service
@Before("within(in.strikes.aopdemo.service..*)")              // whole service layer, sub-packages too

Anything expressible with within could be written with execution, but within reads far better for "this whole class / layer".

Designator 3: @annotation — match methods carrying an annotation

Put an annotation on a method and target it. The demo borrows an existing one, jdk.jfr.Timestamp, placed on createStudent:

@Before("@annotation(jdk.jfr.Timestamp)")
public void logBeforeMethod() { System.out.println("Method intercepted"); }

Only createStudent is intercepted (verified). The annotation needs its fully qualified name, and it must have RUNTIME retention.

Why this is the most useful designator

With your own annotations (creating them comes in a later lecture), the method just declares what it needs and the logic lives in an aspect:

  • @Authenticate → an AuthenticationAspect checks a token/key first (for real apps use Spring Security).
  • @Audit → an audit aspect logs/records metrics.
  • @EvaluateTime → an around advice times the call.
  • Stack them: @Audit @EvaluateTime on one method runs both aspects.
@Around("@annotation(in.strikes.aopdemo.annotation.EvaluateTime)")
public Object evaluateTimeMethod(ProceedingJoinPoint joinPoint) throws Throwable {
    long startTime = System.currentTimeMillis();
    Object result = joinPoint.proceed();
    long endTime = System.currentTimeMillis();
    System.out.println("Took " + (endTime - startTime) + " ms");
    return result;       // the lecture's sketch omits this; see Lecture 23
}

This is exactly how Spring's own @Transactional, @Cacheable and @Async work: an annotation-based pointcut plus an aspect.

Designator 4: bean — match by bean name

@Before("bean(studentService)")
  • Intercepts every method of the bean named studentService (the default name is the class name with a lower-case first letter, from the Spring Core lectures).
  • Also works for beans created by @Bean methods, using that bean's name.
  • bean(...) is Spring-only; it does not exist in AspectJ. Wildcards work: bean(*Service). (Added.)
The four you'll use 95% of the time:
execution, within, @annotation, bean. The rest (below) are for edge cases.

Combining pointcuts: &&, ||, !

// every method of StudentService OR StudentController
@Before("bean(studentService) || bean(studentController)")

// every PUBLIC method in the service layer
@Before("within(in.strikes.aopdemo.service..*) && execution(public * *(..))")

bean(studentService) && bean(studentController) would match nothing: no method belongs to both. In XML config the operators are spelled and, or, not (added).

Named pointcuts: @Pointcut

Using the same long expression in @Before, @After and @Around means copy-pasting it. Instead, name it once: an empty void method annotated with @Pointcut. The method's name becomes the pointcut's name:

@Pointcut("within(in.strikes.aopdemo.service..*) && execution(public * *(..))")
public void logPublicServiceMethod() {
    // empty body: this method only carries the pointcut
}

@Before("logPublicServiceMethod()")
public void logBefore() { … }

@Around("logPublicServiceMethod()")
public Object logAround(ProceedingJoinPoint jp) throws Throwable { return jp.proceed(); }

Name the method for what it matches, so reading the name tells you the scope. The method is never actually called at runtime.

Industry practice: one ApplicationPointcuts class

Keep all reusable pointcuts in one class in the aspect package; every aspect (LoggingAspect, an AuthenticationAspect, an evaluation aspect…) refers to them by fully qualified name. Build broad ones first, then combine them into narrower ones:

public class ApplicationPointcuts {

    @Pointcut("within(in.strikes.aopdemo.controller..*)")
    public void controllerLayer() {}

    @Pointcut("within(in.strikes.aopdemo.service..*)")
    public void serviceLayer() {}

    @Pointcut("execution(public * *(..))")
    public void publicMethod() {}

    @Pointcut("serviceLayer() && publicMethod()")
    public void publicServiceMethod() {}

    @Pointcut("execution(* get*(..)) && publicMethod()")
    public void getterMethod() {}
}

// in LoggingAspect
@Before("in.strikes.aopdemo.aspect.ApplicationPointcuts.publicServiceMethod()")
public void logBeforeMethod() { System.out.println("Method intercepted"); }
  • Add a repository layer, public controller methods, setters… the same way.
  • Write a pointcut inline only when it's very narrow and used once.
  • Verified: the pointcut-holder class needs no annotations (not a bean, no @Aspect) for references to it to work.
Worth flagging:
getterMethod() as written matches every public get* method on every bean, including Spring's. Combine it with a layer pointcut (serviceLayer() && getterMethod()), or it risks the same startup crash as execution(* *(..)). And naming conventions are fragile: anyone naming a method getX silently opts into the advice.

Rarer designators: @within and @target

Both take an annotation and work at class level: intercept every method of any class carrying that annotation.

@Before("@within(org.springframework.stereotype.Service)")   // all methods of @Service classes
@Before("@target(org.springframework.stereotype.Service)")

Compare: within takes a class name; @within/@target take a class-level annotation; @annotation takes a method-level annotation.

The difference shows up with inheritance

  • @within looks at the class that declares the method. saveStudent is declared in BaseService, which has no @Service → not intercepted.
  • @target looks at the runtime object the method is called on. It's a StudentService, which has @Service → intercepted.
  • Without inheritance, both behave the same. Verified on Boot 4.1.0 exactly as described.
Worth knowing (verified):
@target(...) on its own crashes startup with the same "Cannot subclass final class" error: because it's decided at runtime, Spring has to proxy every bean that might match. Always pair it with a scope, e.g. @target(…Service) && within(in.strikes.aopdemo..*). Plain within(StudentService) also skips the inherited saveStudent, just like @within.

Rarer designators: args and @args

Both work at method level, based on the runtime arguments.

  • args(in.strikes.aopdemo.dto.Student) — any method called with a single Student argument.
  • @args(jdk.jfr.Timestamp) — any method called with a single argument whose class carries @Timestamp (the lecturer puts @Timestamp on the Student class).

Alone, args(Student) crashes startup the same way. The lecturer's explanation: "only one method takes a Student" isn't what Spring sees; countless framework methods take an Object parameter that could receive a Student at runtime, so they all become candidates. Scope it:

@Before("args(in.strikes.aopdemo.dto.Student) && within(in.strikes.aopdemo.service..*)")
@Before("@args(jdk.jfr.Timestamp) && within(in.strikes.aopdemo.service..*)")

Both now intercept only createStudent (verified). The lecturer finds @args confusing and rarely used: "interesting, not very useful".

Pattern in the @ designators:
  • @annotation — annotation on the method.
  • @within / @target — annotation on the class (declaring / runtime).
  • @args — annotation on the argument's class.
Worth adding:
args is mostly used to bind arguments to advice parameters rather than to filter: @Before("serviceLayer() && args(student)") public void log(Student student) gives the advice a typed argument instead of casting joinPoint.getArgs()[0]. The same binding works with @annotation(evaluateTime) to read the annotation's attributes.

Background for this/target: CGLIB vs JDK dynamic proxies

With AOP, StudentController holds a proxy that holds the StudentService. In AOP terms the real object is the target, and the proxy is this. Spring can build that proxy two ways:

JDK dynamic proxyCGLIB proxy
HowProxy implements the same interface as the service (like Lecture 22's decorators)Proxy extends the concrete class, overrides its methods, runs advice, then calls super.method()
NeedsAn interface the service implementsA non-final class, non-final methods
Proxy instanceof StudentService?No, only the interface (verified: jdk.proxy2.$Proxy63)Yes (verified: StudentService$$SpringCGLIB$$0)
DefaultPlain Spring (@EnableAspectJAutoProxy) when an interface existsSpring Boot (since 2.0), even when there's an interface

Switching Boot to JDK proxies needs two things

  1. An interface: the lecturer adds StudentServiceInterface (declaring createStudent, getStudent), and StudentService implements it with @Overrides. (Normally you'd name them StudentService and StudentServiceImpl.)
  2. In application.properties: spring.aop.proxy-target-class=false (default true).
  • Only the property, no interface → Spring still uses CGLIB (it can't invent an interface).
  • Only the interface, no property → Boot still uses CGLIB.
  • After switching, startup failed with "expected a bean of type …StudentService": the controller still injected the concrete class, and a JDK proxy isn't one. Fix: inject StudentServiceInterface. That's the point of an interface anyway (loose coupling, multiple implementations like service V1/V2/V3).

Rarer designators: this vs target

Both take a type (class-level, like within):

  • target(in.strikes.aopdemo.service.StudentService) — is the real object a StudentService?
  • this(in.strikes.aopdemo.service.StudentService) — is the proxy a StudentService?
Proxy typetarget(StudentService)this(StudentService)
CGLIB (Boot default)Matches (target is a StudentService)Matches (proxy extends StudentService)
JDK dynamic proxyMatchesNo match: proxy only implements the interface

Lecture demo, verified on Boot 4.1.0: with CGLIB both intercept POST and GET; after switching to JDK proxies, target still does, this intercepts nothing.

The lecturer's point:
Many tutorials say this and target "work the same". They only look the same because Boot uses CGLIB by default, where this, target and within all behave alike. The difference appears with JDK proxies, which you may well want for interface-based, loosely coupled code.
Worth flagging (verified):
Even with CGLIB they are not identical. In the test, this(StudentService) did not fire for the inherited BaseService.saveStudent(), while target(StudentService) did. For "any call on this kind of object" prefer target.

Designator cheat sheet

DesignatorLevelTakesMatchesUse
executionMethodSignature patternMethods matching the patternVery common
withinClassType / package patternAll methods declared in those typesVery common
@annotationMethodAnnotationMethods carrying itVery common
beanBeanBean name (wildcards OK)All methods of that beanCommon (Spring-only)
@withinClassAnnotationMethods declared in annotated classesRare
@targetClassAnnotationCalls on objects whose runtime class is annotatedRare; scope it
argsMethodTypesCalls whose runtime args are those typesMostly for binding; scope it
@argsMethodAnnotationCalls whose argument's class is annotatedRare; scope it
thisClassTypeProxy is that typeRare
targetClassTypeTarget object is that typeRare

Corrections & worth knowing

  • The declaring type in execution is optional. The lecture says class name + method name are mandatory. Only the method name (pattern) is: execution(* dummyMethod(..)) is valid and matches dummyMethod in any class (verified). The formal grammar is execution(modifiers? ret-type declaring-type? name(params) throws?).
  • Named pointcuts are resolved when the context starts, not by the Java compiler. The lecture says Java resolves the mapping "at compile time". javac treats the string as an ordinary annotation value; Spring (using AspectJ's parser) resolves logPublicServiceMethod() when it builds the proxies at startup. A typo in a pointcut therefore fails at startup, not compilation. (Full AspectJ's ajc compiler would check it at compile time.)
  • "Too broad" crashes are about proxying beans that can't be proxied. Designators Spring can decide from the class alone (execution, within, @annotation, bean, @within) only proxy matching beans. The runtime-evaluated ones (args, @args, @target, this, target) force Spring to proxy every bean that might match. So always combine them with within(your.base.package..*). Even when startup succeeds, broad pointcuts slow every call.
  • Plain Spring's default is "JDK proxy if there's an interface, else CGLIB". The lecture says plain Spring uses JDK proxies by default. That holds only when the bean implements an interface; otherwise even plain Spring falls back to CGLIB. Boot sets spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true (CGLIB always) because injecting the concrete class then keeps working.
  • Why the startup error mentions CGLIB even for "JDK" setups: classes without interfaces always get CGLIB proxies, and CGLIB can't subclass final classes or override final/private methods. Kotlin classes are final by default, hence the kotlin-spring (all-open) compiler plugin.
  • Precedence in combined expressions: ! binds tighter than &&, which binds tighter than ||. Use parentheses when mixing them.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"the first star represents the class name and the second star represents the package name" → in service.*.*(..) the first * is the class, the second the method.
".. means zero or one argument" → the lecturer immediately corrects it: zero or more.
"wild guards" = wildcards; "prog-ji" = proxy; "SGLIB" / "CG LIB" = CGLIB.
"login aspect" = logging aspect; "Postman" is sometimes captioned "post run" / "post one".
"log bifore service method" in the @Around example = the named pointcut logPublicServiceMethod() defined just above.
"StudentService overrides the interface" → implements it.

Lecture 25: Custom Annotations with AOP — @TrackExecutionTime, Meta-Annotations, and Where Proxies Are Born

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #25 · 43m · Code Army · the last AOP lecture: building your own annotations and how BeanPostProcessor creates proxies

Starting point: @annotation with a borrowed annotation

Same aop-demo project: StudentController (POST/GET /api/students), StudentService (createStudent(Student) returns the student; getStudent(String) prints and returns "All student data"), a Student DTO and an empty SimpleAspect.

  1. @Before("execution(String in.strikes.aopdemo.service.StudentService.getStudent(String))") prints "Method intercepted": works, as in Lecture 24.
  2. Switch to @Before("@annotation(jdk.jfr.Timestamp)") and put @Timestamp on getStudent: still works.

The real power comes when the annotation is your own: @PerformLog, @Authenticate… Put it on exactly the methods that need the behaviour; the logic lives in an aspect.

Why custom annotations are a "superpower":
They are declarative. The method only states "authenticate me first" or "time me"; the infrastructure logic that does it sits in an aspect, cleanly separated from business logic (Lecture 22's goal).

Creating an annotation: @interface

New package annotation, new type TrackExecutionTime (first named EvaluateTime): it will measure how long any annotated method takes, as done earlier with filters and interceptors.

package in.strikes.aopdemo.annotation;

public @interface TrackExecutionTime {
}
  • An annotation type is declared with @interface, not class or plain interface.
  • This is already a complete, usable annotation. With no elements it's a marker annotation: it only marks methods, and the aspect decides what that means.

The aspect: time any method marked @TrackExecutionTime

Timing needs code before and after the call, so @Around with a ProceedingJoinPoint (Lecture 23):

@Around("@annotation(in.strikes.aopdemo.annotation.TrackExecutionTime)")
public Object measureExecutionTime(ProceedingJoinPoint joinPoint) throws Throwable {
    long startTime = System.currentTimeMillis();
    try {
        return joinPoint.proceed();
    } finally {
        long endTime = System.currentTimeMillis();
        long duration = endTime - startTime;
        String methodName = joinPoint.getSignature().getName();
        System.out.println("Time taken by " + methodName + ": " + duration + " ms");
    }
}

Each design choice, as the lecturer explains it:

  • Returns Object and returns proceed()'s result. Targets return String, Student, long…; a void around advice would swallow the value and the client would get null.
  • try without catch. If the target throws, measuring time isn't this aspect's job to handle: single responsibility. Let the exception propagate to a global exception handler (Lecture 17) or another aspect.
  • finally. The end time is recorded even when the target throws.
  • throws Throwable. proceed() can throw anything and we don't handle it.

Demo run

  1. @TrackExecutionTime on getStudent → "Time taken by getStudent: 0 ms": the method does almost nothing.
  2. Simulate slowness in getStudent: try { Thread.sleep(2000); } catch (InterruptedException e) {}. Postman waits ~2 s; the log shows about 2000 ms (verified: 2002 ms).
  3. Add it to createStudent as well → "Student saved", "Time taken by createStudent: 0 ms". One annotation, and any method is timed.
Worth adding:
Swallowing InterruptedException in an empty catch is fine for a demo, but in real code restore the flag: Thread.currentThread().interrupt();. For measuring durations prefer System.nanoTime(), which is monotonic; currentTimeMillis() can jump if the wall clock is adjusted.

Meta-annotations: telling Java where and how long

When creating an annotation you can answer two questions, using meta-annotations (annotations placed on annotations):

  1. Where can it be applied? → @Target
  2. How long is it kept? → @Retention

@Target(ElementType...): where

@Target(ElementType.METHOD)                        // methods only
@Target({ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.TYPE})    // several: methods and classes
ElementTypeAllowed on
TYPEClasses, interfaces (incl. annotation interfaces), enums, records
METHODMethods
FIELD, PARAMETER, CONSTRUCTOR, LOCAL_VARIABLEWhat the names say
ANNOTATION_TYPEOther annotations; this is what makes a meta-annotation (@Target itself uses it)
PACKAGE, TYPE_PARAMETER, TYPE_USE, MODULE, RECORD_COMPONENTRarer targets
  • With @Target(ElementType.TYPE), putting it on a method is a compile error: "'@TrackExecutionTime' not applicable to method".
  • Without @Target, it can go on (almost) any declaration. Restrict it anyway: timing a whole class makes no sense, so METHOD only.

@Retention(RetentionPolicy...): how long

PolicyKept inTypical use
SOURCESource only; discarded by the compiler@Override, Lombok, compile-time checks
CLASSThe .class bytecode, but not visible via reflection at runtimeBytecode tools
RUNTIMEBytecode and visible via reflection at runtimeAnything a framework reads while running: Spring, JPA, validation, AOP

AOP matching happens at runtime (when the context starts and beans are created), so use RUNTIME.

@Documented

Only affects Javadoc: the annotation shows up in the generated docs of annotated elements. Harmless either way.

@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Documented
public @interface TrackExecutionTime {
}

Now the annotations you've been using make sense: open @RestController or @Service and you'll find @Target(ElementType.TYPE), @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME), @Documented (plus @Controller and @ResponseBody for @RestController, Lecture 11).

Worth knowing (added):
Two more meta-annotations: @Inherited (a class-level annotation is inherited by subclasses; no effect on methods or interfaces) and @Repeatable (the same annotation can appear several times). Spring also treats annotations as composable: @RestController is @Controller + @ResponseBody, and you can build your own composed annotations the same way.

Two ways to reference the annotation in the pointcut

FormPointcutAdvice signature
Type-matching@annotation(in.strikes.aopdemo.annotation.TrackExecutionTime)(ProceedingJoinPoint joinPoint)
Binding@annotation(trackExecutionTime)(ProceedingJoinPoint joinPoint, TrackExecutionTime trackExecutionTime)

In the binding form, the name inside @annotation(...) must match the parameter name; the parameter's type tells Spring which annotation to look for, so no fully qualified name is needed. Bonus: the advice receives the annotation instance itself, which is essential for the next step.

Configured annotations: adding elements

A marker only says "time this". To carry extra information, declare elements: method-like declarations in the @interface, optionally with default values. The lecture adds a slow-method threshold and a readable operation name:

@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Documented
public @interface TrackExecutionTime {
    long warnAfter() default 2000;   // ms; warn if the method is slower
    String operation() default "";   // human-readable label
}
  • With defaults, existing @TrackExecutionTime uses keep compiling and running unchanged.
  • An element without a default becomes mandatory at every use site.
  • Why a threshold: an audit trail of slow methods tells developers what to optimise. (Even 1 s is slow; 2 s very slow.)
@TrackExecutionTime(warnAfter = 1500, operation = "Get student data")
public String getStudent(String s) { … }       // sleeps 2 s, so it should warn

@TrackExecutionTime(warnAfter = 2000, operation = "Creating new student")
public Student createStudent(Student student) { … }

Worked example: the aspect reads the annotation's values

@Around("@annotation(trackExecutionTime)")
public Object measureExecutionTime(ProceedingJoinPoint joinPoint,
                                   TrackExecutionTime trackExecutionTime) throws Throwable {
    long startTime = System.currentTimeMillis();
    try {
        return joinPoint.proceed();
    } finally {
        long duration = System.currentTimeMillis() - startTime;

        String operation = trackExecutionTime.operation();
        if (operation.isBlank()) {
            operation = joinPoint.getSignature().getName();   // fall back to the method name
        }
        long warningThreshold = trackExecutionTime.warnAfter();

        if (duration >= warningThreshold) {
            System.out.println("SLOW OPERATION ALERT: Time taken by " + operation + ": " + duration + " ms");
        } else {
            System.out.println("Time taken by " + operation + ": " + duration + " ms");
        }
    }
}

Demo run

  • GET → "All student data", "SLOW OPERATION ALERT: Time taken by Get student data: 2002 ms" (verified).
  • POST → "Student saved", "Time taken by Creating new student: 0 ms".
  • A method with a bare @TrackExecutionTime logs its method name instead (verified: "Time taken by dummyMethod: 0 ms").
Worth adding:
In a real app use a logger (log.warn(...) for slow calls, log.info/debug otherwise) rather than System.out, or record a metric. Micrometer's @Timed is a production-grade version of exactly this annotation-plus-aspect idea.

Where proxies are created: BeanPostProcessor in the bean lifecycle

Revisiting the bean lifecycle, there are two steps that were skipped earlier because they only matter now: the BeanPostProcessor callbacks around initialization.

  1. Read bean definitions.
  2. Instantiate the bean.
  3. Inject dependencies.
  4. *Aware callbacks.
  5. BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization
  6. Initialization callbacks (@PostConstruct, afterPropertiesSet, init-method).
  7. BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization ← proxies are created here
  8. Bean ready for use … destruction callbacks at shutdown.
public interface BeanPostProcessor {
    default Object postProcessBeforeInitialization(Object bean, String beanName) throws BeansException { return bean; }
    default Object postProcessAfterInitialization(Object bean, String beanName)  throws BeansException { return bean; }
}

Both receive the bean and its name and return a bean: either the same object or a replacement. Whatever is returned is what the container stores and injects.

  • Before initialization — light preparation: initial configuration, validation, getting the bean ready.
  • After initialization — the bean is fully ready. Spring checks whether any aspect's pointcut applies to it. StudentService has @TrackExecutionTime methods, so SimpleAspect applies → a proxy is returned. Wherever StudentController asks for a StudentService, it gets that proxy. With no applicable aspect, the plain target object is returned.

Verified on Boot 4.1.0 with a logging BeanPostProcessor:

BPP before-init: StudentService
@PostConstruct on StudentService
BPP after-init (ours): StudentService$$SpringCGLIB$$0

The proxy exists only after @PostConstruct. Consequence: calls made inside @PostConstruct run on the raw object, so aspects don't apply there.

Anticipated question: "Does Spring scan every aspect for every bean and every call?"

No. The lecture's answer: at application startup, Spring collects all aspects and pointcuts once and keeps them in an efficient structure, so it doesn't re-read every aspect's annotations for each bean or each method call.

Precision note (added):
  • Once at startup: the @Aspect beans are parsed into advisors (advice + pointcut) and cached.
  • Once per bean, at creation: the auto-proxy creator (AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator, itself a BeanPostProcessor) checks each advisor's pointcut against the bean's class and methods, and decides proxy-or-not.
  • Per method, on first call: the proxy computes that method's interceptor chain and caches it, so later calls just run the cached chain.
  • Only the runtime designators (args, this, target, @target, @args, Lecture 24) need a check on every call. That's another reason to prefer the static ones.

AOP wrap-up (Lectures 22–25)

LectureQuestion answeredKey ideas
22Why AOP?Cross-cutting concerns, scattering/tangling, decorator road, what/where/when
23What & when@Aspect, the five advice types, JoinPoint/ProceedingJoinPoint
24WhereWildcards, designators, named pointcuts, CGLIB vs JDK proxies, this vs target
25Real-world usage & internalsCustom annotations, meta-annotations, binding form, BeanPostProcessor creates proxies

Corrections & worth knowing

  • The default retention is CLASS, not RUNTIME. The lecture says RUNTIME is the default, "which is why it worked before we added @Retention". Per the JLS, with no @Retention the policy is CLASS (verified with javap: the annotation is stored as RuntimeInvisibleAnnotations). It still "worked" because Spring's AspectJ matcher can read the annotation from bytecode. Verified on Boot 4.1.0: with a test annotation @NoRet (no @Retention), the type-matching form @annotation(…NoRet) still fired, but the binding form @annotation(n) silently stopped matching, and plain reflection (method.getAnnotation(...)) returns null. Always declare @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME).
  • Annotation "methods" are called elements. Their types are limited to primitives, String, Class, enums, other annotations, and 1-D arrays of those, and default values must be compile-time constants (no null, hence operation() default ""). An element named value can be set without its name: @MyAnno("x").
  • The binding form relies on parameter names. @annotation(trackExecutionTime) matches the advice parameter by name, which needs the -parameters compiler flag (the Boot parent POM enables it; see the Lecture 15 note on @PathVariable). Otherwise use argNames or the type-matching form.
  • @PostConstruct itself is run by a BeanPostProcessor. CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor calls it from its postProcessBeforeInitialization, and several *Aware callbacks (e.g. ApplicationContextAware) are also delivered by a before-init post-processor. The neat "Aware → BPP-before → init → BPP-after" list is a simplification of the same mechanism.
  • Proxies can also be created earlier, for circular references. If another bean needs StudentService while it's still being created (a circular dependency), the auto-proxy creator hands out an early proxy through getEarlyBeanReference instead of waiting for after-init.
  • The same mechanism powers Spring's own annotations. @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @Validated and @PreAuthorize are all "annotation + advisor + proxy created by a BeanPostProcessor". So the Lecture 22 limits apply to all of them: no self-invocation, no private/final methods, only Spring beans.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"Time taken by getStudent is 255 milliseconds" after a 2-second sleep → the captions garbled it; it's about 2005 ms.
"System.getCurrentTimeMillis" → System.currentTimeMillis().
"inspection logic" → interception logic; "cash block" → catch block.
"Student aspect is applying" → the lecturer corrects it to SimpleAspect.
"BeanPostProcessor is a special class" → it's an interface (as the lecturer then shows).
"@PostConstruct" is captioned variously; "IntelliJ" as "intelligent"; "Postman" as "post run".

Lecture 26: JDBC from Scratch — Drivers, Connection, Statement, PreparedStatement, ResultSet and Transactions

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #26 · 1h32m · Code Army · plain Java + MySQL, no Spring; the foundation for Spring JDBC, Hibernate and JPA in later lectures

The problem: a Java app talking to a database on another server

The lecture deliberately steps away from Spring Boot, so it also works for viewers who only know Java. Picture:

  • A Java application (say Demo.java) running on a JVM on Server A.
  • A relational database (MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server, H2, PostgreSQL…) running on Server B: maybe the same machine, maybe across a network.

The app wants to run CRUD queries like SELECT * FROM student. In Java that query is just a String. To run it you must:

  1. Open a connection to the database server, following some protocol, as in client–server architecture.
  2. Send the query over the network.
  3. The database evaluates it and sends back a response.
  4. Translate that response. Java works with objects; a database works with rows and columns.

Why the app can't just "talk to the database" directly

Every database comes from a different vendor with its own rules for:

  • establishing a connection and authenticating a user;
  • packaging an SQL query to send;
  • representing SQL data types (e.g. VARCHAR in MySQL vs other names elsewhere);
  • returning query results and communicating errors;
  • managing transactions.

If Java itself had to support each database, it would need separate classes and methods for MySQL, for PostgreSQL, for Oracle…, and your code would change with every database.

The idea: JDBC = standard interfaces + vendor drivers

JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) is Java's standard API for talking to any relational database, just as the Collections Framework and Reflection are standard APIs. It lives in java.sql.

The analogy: the Collections Framework

  • Collection is an interface declaring common methods: add, remove…
  • ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet each override them in their own way (append at the end; traverse to the last node; hash into a bucket).
  • A client holding a Collection just calls add. It doesn't know or care which concrete class is behind it. That's polymorphism: one method, many forms.

JDBC works the same way:

  • JDBC defines the interfaces: Connection, Statement, PreparedStatement, ResultSet…
  • A JDBC driver for each database implements those interfaces and knows that database's protocol.
  • Your code calls only the JDBC interfaces; swapping MySQL for PostgreSQL means swapping the driver (and the URL), not your code.
DatabaseDriver (Maven artifact)URL prefix
MySQLMySQL Connector/J (com.mysql:mysql-connector-j)jdbc:mysql://
PostgreSQLPostgreSQL JDBC Driver (org.postgresql:postgresql)jdbc:postgresql://
OracleOracle JDBC driver (com.oracle.database.jdbc:ojdbc11)jdbc:oracle:thin:@
H2com.h2database:h2jdbc:h2:

(The table's artifact names and URL prefixes are added for reference.)

Setup: MySQL server, a client, and a Maven project

  • MySQL server installed locally (default port 3306), with a username/password set during install.
  • A GUI client: the lecture uses DBeaver (open source, same UI on Windows and Mac). MySQL Workbench (the official one), SQLyog etc. work too.
  • An IntelliJ project jdbc-demo with Maven as the build system (dependencies go in pom.xml; see the Maven lecture). The main class lives under src/main/java/in/strikes/….

JDBC itself ships with the JDK, but the driver is an external library, so it's added as a dependency (the lecture picks 9.6.0 from mvnrepository.com):

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
        <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
        <version>9.6.0</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

After reloading Maven, External Libraries shows mysql-connector-j plus protobuf-java, a transitive dependency the connector uses internally.

Database and table (in DBeaver)

New connection → MySQL, host localhost, port 3306, user/password → Test Connection → Finish. Create database student_db, then:

USE student_db;

CREATE TABLE students (
    id    BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    name  VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    age   INT
);

The table starts empty; rows will be inserted from Java.

The model class

A model package with a POJO mirroring the table:

public class Student {
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private String email;
    private int age;

    public Student() {}                                    // needed by mapRow
    public Student(String name, String email, int age) {  // id is auto-generated
        this.name = name; this.email = email; this.age = age;
    }
    // getters, setters, toString()
}

Opening a connection: URL, username, password + DriverManager

Connecting needs the same three things DBeaver asked for:

String url      = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/student_db";
String username = "root";
String password = "123456";
  • jdbc:mysql: — the JDBC sub-protocol, which tells DriverManager which driver handles the URL.
  • localhost:3306 — host and port of the MySQL server (a remote IP if it runs elsewhere).
  • /student_db — the database to use.

Connection is an interface (java.sql.Connection), so you can't new it; the driver supplies the implementation. You get one from the utility class DriverManager:

try {
    Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(url, username, password);
    System.out.println("Database connected successfully");
    connection.close();
} catch (SQLException e) {
    System.out.println("Database connection failed");
    e.printStackTrace();
}
Step by step, what getConnection does:
  1. DriverManager (which manages the registered drivers) hands the URL to the MySQL driver.
  2. The driver checks the URL is one it understands (jdbc:mysql:), reads host, port and database.
  3. It opens a network connection to MySQL and authenticates with the username/password.
  4. On success it returns its own Connection implementation; on failure an SQLException (a checked exception, hence the try/catch).
  • A connection is an expensive resource: always close() it.
  • Verified (added): with no MySQL running, Connector/J 9.6.0 throws com.mysql.cj.jdbc.exceptions.CommunicationsException (SQLState 08S01, "communications link failure").

Sending queries: Statement and its three execute methods

With a connection open, a query travels inside a Statement, a wrapper around your SQL string, created from (and tied to) a connection:

Statement statement = connection.createStatement();
MethodUse forReturns
executeUpdate(sql)INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE (despite the name, not just updates)int: rows affected
executeQuery(sql)SELECT (reading)ResultSet
execute(sql)General purpose: any of the aboveboolean (see below)

The lecture moves the DB code into a repository package: StudentRepository holds the URL/credentials and one method per operation, and Main just does new StudentRepository().createUser() etc. (A repository layer is the class that talks to the database, the same role as in the Spring lectures.)

Worked example: CRUD with a plain Statement (hard-coded values)

Create

public void createUser() {
    try {
        Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(url, username, password);
        Statement statement = connection.createStatement();
        String sql = "INSERT INTO students (name, email, age) " +
                     "VALUES ('Aditya', 'ad@gmail.com', 28)";
        int result = statement.executeUpdate(sql);
        if (result == 1) System.out.println("Create operation successful");
        else             System.out.println("Creation failed");
        connection.close();
    } catch (SQLException e) {
        System.out.println("Database connection failed");
        e.printStackTrace();
    }
}
  • Inside the double-quoted Java string, SQL string literals use single quotes.
  • result is rows affected: 1 new row → 1.
  • First run failed: "Table 'student_db.student' doesn't exist". The table is students. Fixed, re-run: "Create operation successful", and DBeaver (after refresh) shows the row.

Update and delete

Same skeleton, different SQL (the lecture copies the method and changes the query and messages):

String sql = "UPDATE students SET age = 30 WHERE id = 1";   // updateUser(): age 28 → 30
String sql = "DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 1";           // deleteUser()

Both print "… successful" when exactly one row is affected; DBeaver confirms age 30, then the row gone. Main comments out the earlier calls so each run performs one operation, simulating one API call at a time.

Reading: executeQuery and the ResultSet cursor

A SELECT returns a ResultSet: the database's row-by-row answer. Each row is logically one Student, and all rows together are logically a List<Student>, but JDBC won't convert them for you. You read each row and build the object yourself.

A ResultSet for SELECT id, name, email, age FROM students
(cursor)idnameemailage
→ starts before row 1
after 1st next()1Adityaa@gmail.com28
after 2nd next()2………
after 3rd next()3………
4th next() → falseno more rows: exit the loop
  • The ResultSet keeps a cursor that starts before the first row (as the JDBC docs state). You must call next() once before reading anything. Verified: reading first fails with "No data is available".
  • next() moves to the next row and returns true, or false when rows run out, so reading many rows is a while (rs.next()) loop.
  • Read columns by label (rs.getLong("id"), rs.getString("name"), rs.getInt("age")) or by index (rs.getLong(1), rs.getString(2)…).
  • Column indexes are 1-based, unlike Java arrays.
Tip from the lecture: don't write SELECT *:
* says "everything" but not what everything is. Name the columns (SELECT id, name, email, age FROM students) so a reader knows exactly what's fetched without opening the database, and so you fetch only what you need. (Added: it also stops code from silently breaking or over-fetching when someone adds a column.)

Mapping a row to an object

private Student mapRow(ResultSet resultSet) throws SQLException {
    Student student = new Student();
    student.setId(resultSet.getLong("id"));
    student.setName(resultSet.getString("name"));
    student.setEmail(resultSet.getString("email"));
    student.setAge(resultSet.getInt("age"));
    return student;
}

// getUserById()
ResultSet resultSet = statement.executeQuery(
        "SELECT id, name, email, age FROM students WHERE id = 7");
resultSet.next();                        // move the cursor onto the first row
Student student = mapRow(resultSet);
System.out.println(student);             // println calls toString()

A toString() is generated on Student so it prints as Student{id=7, name='Aditya', email='…', age=28}. The id is 7 because earlier inserts consumed ids 1–6: auto-increment never reuses values.

execute(): one method, a boolean telling you what came back

executeUpdate returns an int and executeQuery a ResultSet; execute accepts any statement, so it can't return both. It returns a flag instead:

boolean result = statement.execute(sql);
if (result) {                                          // true  → the result is a ResultSet
    ResultSet resultSet = statement.getResultSet();
    // read rows as before
} else {                                               // false → it was an update count
    int rowsAffected = statement.getUpdateCount();
}
  • It is not "succeeded or failed". Failure throws SQLException.
  • Verified: execute("SELECT …") → true (update count -1); execute("DELETE …") → false, update count 0.
  • Useful when the SQL is only known at runtime; normally prefer the two specific methods.

Removing hard-coded values: why string formatting is the wrong fix

Real methods take input: createStudent(Student student). First idea: build the SQL with a text block and formatted():

String sql = """
        INSERT INTO students (name, email, age)
        VALUES ('%s', '%s', %d)
        """.formatted(student.getName(), student.getEmail(), student.getAge());

It works (inserting Rohit). But the lecture lists the problems:

  • No proper handling of NULL.
  • Binary data and SQL date syntax can't be expressed cleanly.
  • Poor readability.
  • The developer must know each format type (%s for strings, %d for ints).
The real failure mode (added): SQL injection:
The lecture never names the biggest problem. Pasting input into SQL lets the input become SQL. Verified on H2 with the email x' OR '1'='1: the formatted query … WHERE email = 'x' OR '1'='1' returned every row, while the PreparedStatement version returned 0. Even an innocent name like O'Brien breaks the formatted INSERT with a syntax error. Never build SQL by concatenating or formatting user input.

The fix: PreparedStatement with ? placeholders

Write the SQL once with ? where values go (no types, no quotes), then bind values by 1-based index with typed setters:

public void createStudent(Student student) {
    String sql = """
            INSERT INTO students (name, email, age)
            VALUES (?, ?, ?)
            """;
    try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(url, username, password);
         PreparedStatement preparedStatement = connection.prepareStatement(sql)) {

        preparedStatement.setString(1, student.getName());
        preparedStatement.setString(2, student.getEmail());
        preparedStatement.setInt(3, student.getAge());

        int rowsAffected = preparedStatement.executeUpdate();   // NO sql argument here
        if (rowsAffected == 1) System.out.println("Create student successful");
        else                   System.out.println("Create student failed");
    } catch (SQLException e) {
        e.printStackTrace();
    }
}
  • The SQL goes to connection.prepareStatement(sql) at creation; nothing runs until you execute.
  • Setters for every type: setInt, setString, setLong, setBoolean, setBigDecimal, setDate/setObject, setArray, setBinaryStream… and setNull.
  • Demo: new Student("Rohan", "rohan@gmail.com", 21) → "Create student successful", visible in DBeaver.
Why PreparedStatement wins:
  • Values are sent separately from the SQL text, so input can never change the query's structure: no SQL injection.
  • The driver handles quoting, escaping, NULL, dates and binary data per database.
  • Readable SQL; no %s/%d bookkeeping.
  • The database (or driver) can reuse the parsed statement/plan when it runs repeatedly with different values (added).
The bug hit in the lecture:
The update, get-by-id and get-all methods first failed with "You have an error in your SQL syntax" because the code called preparedStatement.executeUpdate(sql) / executeQuery(sql), passing the SQL again. Those inherited Statement overloads run the raw text (with literal ?s) and ignore the bound values. The JDBC spec says they must throw on a PreparedStatement: H2 refuses outright ("This method is not allowed for a prepared statement", verified), while MySQL surfaced it as a syntax error. Always call the no-argument executeUpdate() / executeQuery().

Closing resources properly: finally, then try-with-resources

Closing the connection as the last line of try is risky: if executeUpdate throws, control jumps to catch and close() never runs, leaking the connection. The lecture's steps:

  1. Move close() into finally, which always runs. That forces declaring Connection connection = null; (and the PreparedStatement) outside the try. And close() itself throws SQLException, so it needs its own nested try/catch. Close the PreparedStatement first, then the Connection it came from. The finally keeps growing.
  2. Clean-code fix: try-with-resources (see the Java exception-handling lecture). Declare the resources in try ( … ) and they are closed automatically, in reverse order, even on exceptions. No finally, no manual close(). The SQL string is built outside the try since it can't throw.

A ResultSet must be closed too, before its statement. Since the statement needs its parameters set before executeQuery(), the lecture nests a second try-with-resources:

public void getStudentById(long id) {
    String sql = """
            SELECT id, name, email, age
            FROM students
            WHERE id = ?
            """;
    try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(url, username, password);
         PreparedStatement preparedStatement = connection.prepareStatement(sql)) {

        preparedStatement.setLong(1, id);
        try (ResultSet resultSet = preparedStatement.executeQuery()) {
            if (resultSet.next()) {                 // the id might not exist
                Student student = mapRow(resultSet);
                System.out.println(student);
            }
        }
    } catch (SQLException e) {
        e.printStackTrace();
    }
}

The rest of the refactored CRUD

  • updateStudent(Student student, long id) — one query updates several columns: UPDATE students SET name = ?, email = ?, age = ? WHERE id = ?, binding indexes 1–3 from the student and setLong(4, id). Demo: id 8L (the literal needs L for long), "Rohit" → "Rohit Negi", age 27 → 26.
  • deleteStudent(long id) — DELETE FROM students WHERE id = ?; demo deletes id 9.
  • getStudents() — SELECT id, name, email, age FROM students; while (resultSet.next()) maps each row and adds it to a List<Student> (new ArrayList<>()). Initially failed with "Column 'id' not found": the SELECT listed name, email, age but mapRow reads id. Fixed by selecting id too.
  • Methods were renamed from createUser etc. to createStudent, updateStudent, deleteStudent, getStudentById.
Anticipated question: "Shouldn't update first SELECT the row to check it exists?"
The lecture's answer: no, that's two round trips. Just run the UPDATE. If no row has that id, rowsAffected is 0 and you print "failed". (Verified: UPDATE … WHERE id = 10 on a missing id returns 0.) Added caveat: the check-then-act version is also a race condition, since the row can vanish between the two queries.

Transactions: all-or-nothing with setAutoCommit(false)

A transfer of ₹1000 from A to B is two queries: debit A, credit B. They must both happen or neither. Money must never leave A without reaching B. A set of queries executed as one all-or-nothing unit is a transaction.

By default JDBC is in auto-commit mode: each statement is committed (saved) as soon as it runs. For a transaction, turn that off and commit or roll back yourself:

try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(url, username, password)) {
    connection.setAutoCommit(false);                 // don't save after each statement
    try (PreparedStatement debit  = connection.prepareStatement(
                 "UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ?");
         PreparedStatement credit = connection.prepareStatement(
                 "UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE id = ?")) {

        debit.setInt(1, 1000);  debit.setLong(2, aId);  debit.executeUpdate();
        credit.setInt(1, 1000); credit.setLong(2, bId); credit.executeUpdate();

        connection.commit();                         // both succeeded: make them permanent
    } catch (SQLException e) {
        connection.rollback();                       // anything failed: undo everything since the last commit
        throw e;
    }
}

Verified on H2 with balances of 1000 each: a transfer of 300 committed (700 / 1300); a second transfer that threw right after the debit was rolled back, and the balances stayed 700 / 1300, with no half-transfer. (The lecture sketches this with comments; the code above is a complete version.)

Where this is heading:
In Spring you get the same with @Transactional on a method: an around advice (the AOP lectures 22–25) that sets auto-commit off, commits on success and rolls back on a runtime exception. Transactions get their own deep-dive later.

The pain points that motivate Spring JDBC / JPA

  • Open a connection, create a statement, bind every parameter by hand, and close everything, in every method.
  • Map each ResultSet row to an object manually (mapRow).
  • Checked SQLException everywhere; vendor-specific error codes.
  • Manual transaction plumbing: setAutoCommit / commit / rollback.

Upcoming lectures show what Spring JDBC (JdbcTemplate), Hibernate and JPA take off your hands.

Statement vs PreparedStatement

StatementPreparedStatement
Created withconnection.createStatement()connection.prepareStatement(sql)
SQL passedAt execution: executeQuery(sql)At creation; execute with no argument
ParametersConcatenated/formatted into the string? + typed setters (1-based)
SQL injectionVulnerable with user inputSafe
NULLs, dates, binaryManual, error-pronesetNull, setObject, setBinaryStream…
Repeated executionRe-parsed each timeCan reuse the prepared plan
Use whenStatic SQL, DDL, scriptsAlmost always (the lecture's preference)

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Drivers come from the database vendors, not from JDBC. The lecture says "JDBC has given different drivers". JDBC only defines the interfaces; Oracle, the PostgreSQL project, MySQL etc. publish the drivers (that's why you add them as Maven dependencies).
  • No Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver") needed since JDBC 4.0 (Java 6). Drivers self-register through META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver (ServiceLoader). Verified: DriverManager.drivers() listed com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver just from the jar being on the classpath. Old tutorials still show the Class.forName line.
  • executeUpdate returns the number of rows affected, not a 0/1 success flag. result == 1 is right for a by-id change, but an UPDATE without WHERE returns every row it touched (verified: 2 rows → 2), and DDL like CREATE TABLE returns 0 even when it succeeds. Real failures come as SQLException.
  • getInt turns SQL NULL into 0. Verified: getInt("age") on a NULL age returned 0. Check rs.wasNull(), or read rs.getObject("age", Integer.class) into an Integer field (returned null). The model's int age can't represent "unknown".
  • Text blocks are standard since Java 15 (preview in 13–14), as is String.formatted(). The lecture says "Java 15 or 16".
  • Opening a new connection per operation is slow. Each getConnection is a TCP handshake plus authentication. Real apps use a connection pool behind a DataSource; Spring Boot's default is HikariCP, and close() on a pooled connection returns it to the pool.
  • Don't hard-code credentials in source. Read them from configuration or environment variables (Lecture 18's external config).
  • Restore auto-commit when reusing connections. With a pool, a connection left in autoCommit(false) leaks that state to the next user. Frameworks reset it for you; hand-written code should call setAutoCommit(true) in finally.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"executeUpdate is used for create, insert, delete" → the lecturer corrects it to create/insert, update, delete.
"result = statement.executeQuery" in the refactored update method → it's executeUpdate().
"getRoll number" in mapRow → the lecturer corrects it to age.
"MySQL connector J" / "Mys sequel" / "SQL" captions = MySQL; "DBVer" / "DB" = DBeaver; "IntelliJ" as "intelligent"; "pom.xml" as "pm.xml".
"CRED" / "curd" operations = CRUD; "cash exception" = catch; "percentile s / percentile d" = the format specifiers %s, %d.

Lecture 27: Spring JDBC — Template Method Pattern, DataSource, HikariCP, JdbcTemplate, RowMapper and Exception Translation

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #27 · 1h05m · Code Army · rewrites Lecture 26's raw-JDBC repository with Spring JDBC

Starting point: Lecture 26's raw-JDBC code inside a Spring Boot app

The project spring-jdbc-demo wraps last lecture's repository in the usual layers:

  • StudentController (/api/students):
    • POST create, returning "done".
    • GET all students, and GET /{id}.
    • PUT update and DELETE.
  • StudentService — constructor-injects StudentRepository and delegates each call.
  • StudentRepository — unchanged raw JDBC:
    • Hard-coded URL, username and password.
    • PreparedStatements in try-with-resources.
    • executeUpdate / executeQuery, and the private mapRow.
  • Student model — id, name, email, age.

It works from Postman: add "Sohan", get /10, get all. Nothing new yet.

The problem: every method repeats the same boilerplate

Look at createStudent, updateStudent, deleteStudent… Each one repeats the same code:

Same in every method (boilerplate)Different in every method
Open a connection (DriverManager.getConnection)The SQL query
Create a (prepared) statementThe parameter values
Close the statement and connectionThe result mapping (row → Student, Teacher, Order…)
Catch SQLException (it's checked: catch or declare throws)

Spring's idea: it handles the part that never changes, and you supply only the part that does. That is Spring JDBC. It is not a replacement for raw JDBC but an enhancement on top of it. Internally it still uses Connection, PreparedStatement and SQLException; you just stop touching them and call Spring JDBC methods instead.

Also a design smell (the lecture's point):
The raw repository breaks the Single Responsibility Principle. Its job is querying student data, yet it also manages connections, creates and closes statements and wraps queries: infrastructure, not business logic.

The pattern behind it: Template Method

Suppose a job must always run m1() → m2() → m3() → m4(), in that order. The steps may pass results to one another; either way the order must never change.

  1. Naive: a class Demo defines m1…m4, and the client must remember to call them in order. The client is tightly coupled to the sequence; if an m5 is later inserted between m2 and m3, every client breaks.
  2. Template method: add one method, template(), that calls m1–m4 in order. Clients call only template(); the order lives in one place.
  3. Variable steps: say m1 and m3 never change but m2 and m4 do. Make Demo abstract: define m1, m3 and template(), and only declare m2, m4. Concrete subclasses (DemoConcrete1, DemoConcrete2) supply their own m2/m4 and inherit the rest. A new variation is just a new subclass.
Standard definition (GoF):
"Define the skeleton of an algorithm in an operation, deferring some steps to subclasses. Template Method lets subclasses redefine certain steps of an algorithm without changing the algorithm's structure." (Covered in depth in the LLD notebook.)

JdbcTemplate: the template for database access

Map the pattern onto JDBC:

StepWho does it
Get a connectionJdbcTemplate
Create the PreparedStatementJdbcTemplate
The SQL + parameter valuesYou (the "m2/m4")
Execute, iterate the ResultSetJdbcTemplate
Turn one row into an objectYou (a RowMapper)
Close statement, then connection (reverse order)JdbcTemplate
Catch SQLException and translate itJdbcTemplate
Precision note (added):
JdbcTemplate doesn't make you subclass it. The varying steps are passed in as callback objects (RowMapper, PreparedStatementSetter, ResultSetExtractor, often lambdas). So it's the Template Method idea implemented via callbacks, a mix of Template Method and Strategy. Spring's RestTemplate, JmsTemplate and TransactionTemplate use the same style.

DataSource: where connections come from

javax.sql.DataSource is an interface with one main job: hand out a Connection.

// raw JDBC (Lecture 26)
Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(url, username, password);

// with a DataSource
Connection c = dataSource.getConnection();

The URL and credentials are configured once, in application.properties, rather than passed on every call.

Why a new connection per call doesn't scale: connection pooling

So far each method opened a connection and closed it at the end. A real connection is expensive:

  1. A network connection to the database server, usually on another machine or IP.
  2. The driver sends username and password, and the database authenticates them.
  3. A session is created; only now can data flow.

That's fine for a four-method demo. But with 10,000 requests per second you can't open 10,000 connections: it's slow, and the database has limited throughput.

The connection pool

Like a thread pool: keep a container of already-open connections (say 5) and lend them out.

  • Borrow: createUser takes an idle connection from the pool.
  • "Close": connection.close() (manual or via try-with-resources) doesn't close the physical connection; it returns it to the pool for reuse.
  • Exhaustion: if concurrent calls (create, get, update, delete…) hold all 5, the next request waits until one is returned, or times out after a configurable time.
  • Side benefit: the pool size caps how many simultaneous queries hit the database.

HikariCP: Spring Boot's default pool

  • A production-grade pool, pulled in automatically by spring-boot-starter-jdbc. You can swap in another pool by adding its dependency.
  • Configured under spring.datasource.hikari.*: maximum-pool-size, connection-timeout, idle-timeout, connection-test-query…
  • Bigger is not automatically better, since every connection is load on the database. Size it from load testing.
  • Verified on Boot 4.1.0: the default is 10 (maximumPoolSize=10).
Worth knowing:
A DataSource need not pool. Spring's DriverManagerDataSource opens a fresh physical connection on every getConnection(), the same as raw DriverManager. It's fine for tests and tiny apps, but by default Boot gives you Hikari.

Setup: the dependency and the properties

From Spring Initializr you'd tick "JDBC API". In an existing project, add from mvnrepository.com (no version or scope needed; the Boot parent manages them):

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jdbc</artifactId>
</dependency>

Alongside the existing spring-boot-starter-webmvc and mysql-connector-j. Choose spring-boot-starter-jdbc, not the plain spring-jdbc library. Then move the credentials out of the repository:

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/student_db
spring.datasource.username=root
spring.datasource.password=123456
# optional pool tuning, e.g.
# spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10

(No quotes around values in .properties.)

How Boot builds the DataSource and JdbcTemplate beans

  1. Detects Spring JDBC on the classpath (from the starter).
  2. Detects a JDBC driver (MySQL Connector/J).
  3. Reads the spring.datasource.* properties.
  4. Looks for a pool implementation and prefers HikariCP.
  5. Creates a DataSource and registers it as a Spring bean in the IoC container.
  6. Creates a JdbcTemplate bean wired to that DataSource (added: this is JdbcTemplateAutoConfiguration).

Proof from the lecture: inject DataSource into the repository's constructor and print it in a @PostConstruct method:

@PostConstruct
public void init() {
    System.out.println(dataSource.getClass());
}
// class com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource

Verified on Boot 4.1.0 too: the bean is com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource, and the auto-configured JdbcTemplate uses that same instance. You normally don't touch the DataSource yourself: you talk to JdbcTemplate; JdbcTemplate talks to the DataSource.

The three JdbcTemplate methods you'll use most

JdbcTemplateRaw JDBC equivalentUse forReturns
update(sql, args...)executeUpdateINSERT, UPDATE, DELETEint rows affected
query(sql, rowMapper, args...)executeQuery + loopSELECT, many rows (0 is fine)List<T>; empty if no rows
queryForObject(sql, rowMapper, args...)executeQuery + one next()SELECT expecting exactly one rowT; throws if 0 or >1 rows

Worked example: rewriting the repository

@Repository
public class StudentRepository {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;

    public StudentRepository(JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate) {
        this.jdbcTemplate = jdbcTemplate;
    }

Create, update, delete: update(...)

public void createStudent(Student student) {
    String sql = """
            INSERT INTO students (name, email, age)
            VALUES (?, ?, ?)
            """;
    int rowsAffected = jdbcTemplate.update(sql,
            student.getName(),
            student.getEmail(),
            student.getAge());
    if (rowsAffected == 1) System.out.println("Create student successful");
    else                   System.out.println("Create student failed");
}

public void updateStudent(Student student, long id) {
    String sql = """
            UPDATE students SET name = ?, email = ?, age = ?
            WHERE id = ?
            """;
    int rowsAffected = jdbcTemplate.update(sql,
            student.getName(), student.getEmail(), student.getAge(), id);
    // print success / failure as before
}

public void deleteStudent(long id) {
    int rowsAffected = jdbcTemplate.update("DELETE FROM students WHERE id = ?", id);
    // print success / failure as before
}
  • No connection, no PreparedStatement, no try/catch, no close(). The ? values are passed as varargs in placeholder order.
  • Demo: POST "Raman", age 19 → "done" → the row appears in DBeaver.

Reading: tell Spring how to map one row: RowMapper<T>

Spring will do everything the raw version did (execute, loop with next(), collect a list). What it can't know is how a row becomes a Student. That's not JPA/Hibernate ORM (later lectures), so you supply it. RowMapper<T> is a functional interface with one method:

T mapRow(ResultSet rs, int rowNum) throws SQLException;

The same logic as Lecture 26's private mapRow, now in a class Spring calls for you:

public class StudentRowMapper implements RowMapper<Student> {
    @Override
    public Student mapRow(ResultSet rs, int rowNum) throws SQLException {
        Student student = new Student();
        student.setId(rs.getLong("id"));
        student.setName(rs.getString("name"));
        student.setEmail(rs.getString("email"));
        student.setAge(rs.getInt("age"));
        return student;
    }
}
private final StudentRowMapper studentRowMapper = new StudentRowMapper(); // stateless: create once

public List<Student> getStudents() {
    String sql = "SELECT id, name, email, age FROM students";
    return jdbcTemplate.query(sql, studentRowMapper);
}

public Student getStudentById(long id) {
    String sql = "SELECT id, name, email, age FROM students WHERE id = ?";
    return jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(sql, studentRowMapper, id);   // mapper BEFORE the args
}
What query(...) does internally:
Exactly the loop you wrote by hand in Lecture 26: 
ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery();
List<T> list = new ArrayList<>();
int rowNum = 0;
while (rs.next()) {
    list.add(rowMapper.mapRow(rs, rowNum++));
}
return list;

Demo: GET /api/students/12 → Sohan; /13 → Raman; GET /api/students → all rows; DELETE id 13 → gone.

Anticipated question: "Why queryForObject instead of query + take the first?"

  • query for a missing id quietly returns an empty list.
  • queryForObject enforces exactly one row:
    • 0 rows throws EmptyResultDataAccessException.
    • More than 1 row throws IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException.
    You can map those to a 404 in a global exception handler (Lecture 17).
  • Verified on Boot 4.1.0: missing id 99 gives [] with query and EmptyResultDataAccessException with queryForObject; a query returning two rows gives IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException.

Skipping the mapper class: BeanPropertyRowMapper

When column names match the model's property names (id, name, email, age here), Spring can map by name:

private final RowMapper<Student> rowMapper = new BeanPropertyRowMapper<>(Student.class);
  • A ready-made RowMapper implementation, like your own StudentRowMapper. It uses the no-arg constructor and setters, matching columns to properties by name.
  • It also maps snake_case to camelCase: column full_name → property fullName (verified).
  • After switching, StudentRowMapper can be deleted; GET /10 still works.
  • Write your own mapper when names differ substantially or you need custom conversion (more control).
Worth adding:
Since RowMapper is a functional interface, a lambda often replaces the class: (rs, rowNum) -> new Student(rs.getLong("id"), rs.getString("name"), …). BeanPropertyRowMapper uses reflection, so it's slower than a hand-written mapper; that matters only for large result sets. (Spring 5.3+ also has DataClassRowMapper, which maps via constructor, e.g. for records.)

Exception translation: from SQLException to DataAccessException

The rewritten repository has no catch at all. Where did the checked SQLException go?

The problem with SQLException

  • It's generic: database unreachable, bad grammar, constraint violation, no connection → all the same exception type.
  • The only way to tell them apart is getSQLState(), getErrorCode(), getMessage(), and those codes differ by vendor (MySQL vs PostgreSQL…). Branching on them couples your app to one database.
  • It's checked, so it forces try/catch or throws everywhere.

What Spring does

JdbcTemplate catches the SQLException internally and rethrows a specific, unchecked subclass of DataAccessException, chosen from the vendor's error codes. You catch it only if you want to.

ExceptionWhen
DuplicateKeyExceptionUnique/primary-key violation, e.g. inserting an existing email (unique column)
DataIntegrityViolationExceptionOther integrity violations: NOT NULL, foreign key…
BadSqlGrammarExceptionSQL syntax errors, unknown table/column
EmptyResultDataAccessExceptionqueryForObject found 0 rows
IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessExceptionqueryForObject found more than 1 row
CannotGetJdbcConnectionExceptionCouldn't obtain a connection (DB down, wrong credentials)

Verified on Boot 4.1.0 (H2 in MySQL mode; unreachable MySQL via Connector/J), with the real class hierarchy:

(DataAccessException actually extends NestedRuntimeException, and CannotGetJdbcConnectionException has one more level, NonTransientDataAccessResourceException; both omitted above.)

Where to handle them

Don't handle exceptions in the repository: its job is querying. Let them propagate to the service or a @RestControllerAdvice (Lecture 17). Or translate to a domain exception where it makes sense:

try {
    jdbcTemplate.update(sql, student.getName(), student.getEmail(), student.getAge());
} catch (DuplicateKeyException e) {
    throw new EmailAlreadyExistsException("Email exists");   // your own exception, mapped to 409 by the advice
}

When to use Spring JDBC vs JPA/Hibernate

  • You still write SQL by hand. For simple CRUD, a developer who doesn't want to write SQL goes one level up to JPA / Hibernate: method names become queries, as in the CRUD lectures 11–13 (covered next).
  • Spring JDBC stays very much in use for data-intensive apps with complex queries (heavy joins, reporting, tuned SQL), where ORM mappings get complicated. You write the exact SQL and JdbcTemplate removes the boilerplate.
  • Raw JDBC is rarely used directly now: Spring JDBC is the standard wrapper over it.

Raw JDBC vs Spring JDBC

Raw JDBC (Lecture 26)Spring JDBC
ConnectionsDriverManager.getConnection per callFrom a pooled DataSource (HikariCP)
ConfigurationURL/credentials in codespring.datasource.* properties
Statements and closingYou, in try-with-resourcesJdbcTemplate
ParameterssetString(1, …)…Varargs to update/query
Row mapping loopYou write while (rs.next())You supply a RowMapper; Spring loops
ErrorsChecked, generic SQLExceptionUnchecked, specific DataAccessException subclasses
TransactionsManual setAutoCommit/commit/rollback@Transactional (uses the same pooled connection)

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Spring's exceptions form a hierarchy, not a flat list. The lecture draws them all as direct children of DataAccessException. In fact DuplicateKeyException extends DataIntegrityViolationException, and EmptyResultDataAccessException extends IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException (verified). So catch order matters: a handler for the parent also catches the child; put the specific handler first, or let @ExceptionHandler's closest-match rule pick.
  • HikariCP is Spring Boot's default, not "Java's". The lecture says "Java uses HikariCP internally". The JDK has no pool; Spring Boot picks HikariCP when it's on the classpath, which the JDBC and JPA starters ensure.
  • JdbcTemplate is thread-safe; share one instance. Constructor-inject the auto-configured bean rather than new JdbcTemplate(dataSource) per repository. The same goes for stateless RowMappers: create once, as the lecture does.
  • Named parameters and the fluent JdbcClient. NamedParameterJdbcTemplate lets you write WHERE id = :id instead of counting ?s. Spring Framework 6.1+ (Boot 3.2+) adds JdbcClient: jdbcClient.sql("SELECT … WHERE id = :id").param("id", id).query(Student.class).optional(). It returns an Optional instead of throwing EmptyResultDataAccessException. Boot auto-configures both.
  • Getting the generated id. update() returns only rows affected. To learn the new AUTO_INCREMENT id, use update(PreparedStatementCreator, KeyHolder) or SimpleJdbcInsert.
  • Transactions with Spring JDBC: @Transactional on a service method makes all JdbcTemplate calls in it share one connection and commit or roll back together. That replaces Lecture 26's manual setAutoCommit(false)/commit/rollback. Boot auto-configures the DataSourceTransactionManager.
  • Pool sizing rule of thumb: HikariCP's own guidance is that a small pool (roughly cores × 2 + disks) usually beats a large one. Too many connections make the database thrash. It supports the lecture's "bigger is not better".
Transcript slips to ignore:
"JdbcTemplate follows the JDBC design pattern" → the Template design pattern.
"SQL result has to be caught" → the lecturer corrects it to catching SQLException.
"Hari CP" / "hikari CB" = HikariCP; "Spring Initt" = Spring Initializr; "JDVC" = JDBC.
"curd" = CRUD; "IntelliJ" as "intelligent"/"intelligence".

Lecture 28: Hibernate & JPA Basics — ORM, EntityManager CRUD and Entity Mapping (@Column, Enums, Converters, @Embedded, @ElementCollection)

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #28 · 1h12m · Code Army · no more hand-written SQL; internals (why update needs no method) come next lecture

Setup: same layers, empty repository

Project hibernate-demo:

  • StudentController (/api/students) — create, get-by-id, update, delete.
  • StudentService — delegates to StudentRepository (stubs returning null for now).
  • Student model — id, name, email, age.
  • StudentRepository — empty, to be filled with Hibernate.

Compare with the Spring JDBC version (Lecture 27): every method had a hand-written SQL string, manual parameter passing (jdbcTemplate.update(sql, name, email, age)) and a StudentRowMapper converting each ResultSet row into a Student.

The problem: the object–relational impedance mismatch

Java sideDatabase side
Class Student (a blueprint)Table students
Fields id, name, email, ageColumns id, name, email, age
One objectOne row
Understands classes, inheritance, polymorphism, object referencesUnderstands tables, rows, columns, primary/foreign keys

Both describe the same student, but in completely different ways. That gap is the object–relational impedance mismatch. It's why JDBC code is full of manual work: writing queries, binding parameters, mapping rows to objects and back. It forces every Java developer to write SQL and couples the code tightly to the database.

The idea: ORM (Object–Relational Mapping)

If the class and the table describe the same thing, map them once:

  • class name → table name;
  • fields → columns;
  • each object you save → a new row.

Then the framework can use that mapping for every CRUD operation.

Responsibilities of an ORM framework

  • Metadata mapping — class ↔ table, property ↔ column.
  • SQL generation — SQL syntax is fixed (INSERT INTO … VALUES, UPDATE … SET … WHERE); only the table, column names and values vary, and the mapping supplies all three.
  • Parameter binding — object field values become the query's parameters.
  • Result-set mapping — rows come back as objects, no RowMapper.
  • Relationship management — e.g. a Student holding an Address (later lectures).
  • Caching — avoid a database round trip for data it already has.
  • Transaction integration — all-or-nothing units of work.

JPA vs Hibernate vs JDBC: who does what

  • JPA = Jakarta Persistence API (formerly Java Persistence API). It's only a specification: interfaces, annotations and rules. It doesn't store anything itself; a common misconception is that it does.
  • Hibernate = an ORM framework and the default implementation of JPA in Spring. It can be swapped for another provider (e.g. EclipseLink).
  • JDBC is still underneath. Hibernate only generates the SQL; JDBC connections, prepared statements and the driver actually carry it to the database.
  • In practice you use the JPA API (EntityManager, @Entity…) and Hibernate runs behind it. You could use native Hibernate APIs directly, but it's rarely done.

spring-boot-starter-data-jpa (the only data dependency in pom.xml, plus webmvc) brings JPA and Hibernate. Verified: Boot 4.1.0 ships Hibernate 7.4.1. The MySQL driver (mysql-connector-j) must be added too: the "driver class not found" error in application.properties disappears once it's in the POM.

Configuration: data source + Hibernate properties

The old students table is dropped first (DROP TABLE students;) so Hibernate can create its own.

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/student_db
spring.datasource.username=root
spring.datasource.password=123456

spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true

ddl-auto: who manages the schema (DDL: create/alter/drop table)

ValueAt startup
createDrop and recreate the tables from the entities: all data lost on every restart
create-dropLike create, and also drops them at shutdown (Boot's default for embedded DBs like H2)
updateCompare entities with the schema and add missing tables/columns (the lecture's choice: data survives restarts)
validateOnly check the schema matches the entities; fail at startup if not
noneDo nothing: you create tables yourself (Boot's default for MySQL etc.)
Production rule from the lecture:
Don't let ddl-auto manage production schemas. It's for learning and staging. In production use migration tools like Flyway or Liquibase (versioned SQL scripts).
  • show-sql=true prints every SQL statement Hibernate generates.
  • format_sql=true pretty-prints them over several lines instead of one unreadable line.

Making Student an entity

@Entity
public class Student {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private String email;
    private int age;

    public Student() {}                              // JPA needs a no-arg constructor
    public Student(String name, String email, int age) { … }
    // getters and setters
}
  • @Entity — "map this class to a table".
  • @Id — the primary key. Without it the IDE errors: "Persistent entity 'Student' should have primary key".
  • @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) — the database auto-increments it (1, 2, 3…), as in the CRUD lectures 11–13.

Worked example: CRUD with EntityManager

@Repository
public class StudentRepository {

    @PersistenceContext
    private EntityManager entityManager;

    public void save(Student student) {
        entityManager.persist(student);                 // INSERT
    }

    public Student findById(Long id) {
        return entityManager.find(Student.class, id);   // SELECT by primary key; null if absent
    }

    public void remove(Student student) {
        entityManager.remove(student);                  // DELETE
    }
    // no update() method at all
}
  • EntityManager is the JPA interface you do everything through. @PersistenceContext injects it (both explained next lecture).
  • Compare: one line per operation vs Lecture 27's SQL string + update(...) + row mapper.
  • find takes the entity class (Student.class, so it knows what to build) and the id.
  • remove takes the entity object, not an id. The lecture first wrote remove(id), got a type error, and fixed it: the service finds the student, then removes it.
@Service
public class StudentService {
    private final StudentRepository studentRepository;
    // constructor injection

    @Transactional
    public Student createStudent(Student student) {
        studentRepository.save(student);
        return student;
    }

    @Transactional
    public Student getStudentById(Long id) {
        return studentRepository.findById(id);
    }

    @Transactional
    public void updateStudent(Long id, Student studentRequest) {
        Student student1 = studentRepository.findById(id);
        if (student1 == null) throw new RuntimeException("Student not found");
        student1.setName(studentRequest.getName());
        student1.setAge(studentRequest.getAge());
        student1.setEmail(studentRequest.getEmail());
        // no save / update call!
    }

    @Transactional
    public void deleteStudent(Long id) {
        Student student = studentRepository.findById(id);
        if (student == null) throw new RuntimeException("Student not found");
        studentRepository.remove(student);
    }
}
  • @Transactional wraps the method in a transaction: all or nothing (details later).
  • The update method takes the id as @PathVariable: @PutMapping("/{id}").
  • The "not found" RuntimeException would normally be mapped by the global exception handler (Lecture 17).

Demo run
