  1. Startup — the log shows Hibernate's own DDL: create table student (id …, age …, email …, name …, primary key (id)), generated purely from the entity. DBeaver shows a new, empty student table.
  2. POST Raman (19) and Aditya (29) → "done"; rows with ids 1 and 2 appear.
  3. GET /1 → Raman; /2 → Aditya.
  4. PUT /2 age 29 → 28 first returned 405 Method Not Allowed: the mapping was @PutMapping without "/{id}". Fixed.
  5. PUT again → "done", but the age is still 29. The log shows only a SELECT, no UPDATE. Cause: updateStudent had no @Transactional. Added it (and to delete).
  6. Restart — with ddl-auto=update no create table runs and the data survives. PUT age 25 → log shows SELECT then UPDATE; DBeaver shows 25.
  7. DELETE /2 → row gone.
Why the update needs no method (preview, verified):
Inside a transaction, an entity loaded by find is managed. Hibernate keeps a snapshot of it and, at commit, compares the current field values with the snapshot. If anything changed, it issues the UPDATE itself. This is dirty checking. Without a transaction the entity is detached immediately after find, so changes go nowhere. Verified on Boot 4.1.0: setting the name in a non-transactional method left it unchanged; the same code with @Transactional produced select then update with no save call. The next lecture covers this in depth (persistence context, entity states).

Entity mapping in depth

@Table: naming the table

@Entity
@Table(name = "students")
public class Student { … }
  • @Entity (required) says the class is persistent. @Table (optional) says which table.
  • Without @Table, the table is named after the class in lower snake case (Student → student); after adding it, students is created on restart.

@Column: per-column settings

@Column(name = "student_name", nullable = false, length = 100)
private String name;

@Column(unique = true, nullable = false, length = 150)
private String email;
AttributeMeaningDefault
nameColumn name in the DB (field stays name in Java; SQL convention is snake_case)derived from the field
nullablefalse → NOT NULLtrue
lengthMax length → varchar(100)255
uniqueNo two rows may share the value (email, not name)false
insertable / updatableWhether the column is included in generated INSERT / UPDATE statementstrue
precision / scaleTotal digits / digits after the decimal point (for BigDecimal)—

On restart the generated DDL shows student_name varchar(100) not null, email varchar(150) not null with a unique key. DBeaver's properties confirm the lengths and uniqueness.

More types: BigDecimal, dates, enums, large objects, transient fields

@Column(precision = 5, scale = 2)
private BigDecimal percentage;          // DECIMAL(5,2): up to 999.99; 100.00 fits

private LocalDate dateOfBirth;          // DATE
private LocalDateTime createdAt;        // DATETIME(6) on MySQL
// private LocalTime someTime;          // TIME

@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
private StudentStatus status;           // enum StudentStatus { ACTIVE, INACTIVE, SUSPENDED }

@Lob
private String profileDescription;      // LONGTEXT on MySQL

@Transient
private String displayName;             // NOT a column; Java-only field
  • BigDecimal for exact decimals like percentages; precision = 5, scale = 2 allows 5 digits in total, 2 after the point.
  • @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) stores the constant's name. EnumType.ORDINAL stores its position, which is unreadable in the DB. MySQL shows the column as enum('ACTIVE','INACTIVE','SUSPENDED').
  • @Lob (large object) tells the DB to prepare a large-text/binary column. The lecture warns: don't store big blobs (images, files) in the database. Put them in object storage (an S3-style bucket) and store only the URL.
  • @Transient keeps a field purely in Java: no column is created (verified: no display_name).

On restart with update, the log shows alter table student add column created_at …, date_of_birth, percentage, profile_description, status enum(…). The new fields then need getters/setters and an updated all-args constructor.

AttributeConverter: store true/false as "yes"/"no"

A boolean isMonitor would be stored as a bit (0/1), which is easy to misread. To keep boolean in Java but store yes/no in the DB, write a converter:

public class BooleanToStringConverter implements AttributeConverter<Boolean, String> {

    @Override
    public String convertToDatabaseColumn(Boolean aBoolean) {   // Java → DB
        if (aBoolean == null) return null;
        return aBoolean ? "yes" : "no";
    }

    @Override
    public Boolean convertToEntityAttribute(String s) {         // DB → Java
        if (s == null) return null;
        return "yes".equals(s);
    }
}

// in Student
@Convert(converter = BooleanToStringConverter.class)
private boolean isMonitor;

Demo: POST with "isMonitor": true → the INSERT runs → DBeaver shows yes. Hibernate even added check (is_monitor in ('no','yes')) (verified). displayName is still not stored.

Fix applied (added):
The lecture's simplified return s.equals("yes"); throws NullPointerException for a NULL column. Write "yes".equals(s), or keep the null check first. (Hibernate also ships ready-made converters: org.hibernate.type.YesNoConverter stores 'Y'/'N' and TrueFalseConverter stores 'T'/'F'.)

Value objects: @Embeddable + @Embedded

An Address (houseNumber, street, city, state, pinCode) can't exist on its own: it only makes sense inside a Student. In LLD terms that's composition. So it shouldn't be an @Entity with its own table; its fields should be embedded as columns of the student table.

@Embeddable
public class Address {
    private String houseNumber;
    private String street;
    private String city;
    private String state;
    private String pinCode;
    public Address() {}
    // all-args constructor, getters, setters
}

// in Student
@Embedded
private Address address;

On restart: alter table student add column city …, house_number, pin_code, state, street. But the old columns (percentage etc., since commented out) were not removed: update only adds. The lecture drops the table in DBeaver so it's recreated cleanly with id, age, email, student_name, city, house_number, pin_code, state, street.

Embed vs separate entity:
A Department can exist independently: deleting a student must not delete the department. It gets its own table, linked by a foreign key (relationship mappings in upcoming lectures). Embed only what lives and dies with the owner.

Two addresses of the same type: @AttributeOverrides

currentAddress and permanentAddress would both produce columns house_number, city…, which collide. Rename one set of columns per field:

@Embedded
@AttributeOverrides({
    @AttributeOverride(name = "houseNumber", column = @Column(name = "current_house_number")),
    @AttributeOverride(name = "street",      column = @Column(name = "current_street")),
    @AttributeOverride(name = "city",        column = @Column(name = "current_city")),
    @AttributeOverride(name = "state",       column = @Column(name = "current_state")),
    @AttributeOverride(name = "pinCode",     column = @Column(name = "current_pin_code"))
})
private Address currentAddress;

// same block with "permanent_..." names on permanentAddress

name is the Java property inside Address; @Column(name) is the new DB column. Result (after dropping and recreating the table): current_city, current_house_number, current_pin_code, current_state, current_street, permanent_city, ….

Collections: @ElementCollection + @CollectionTable

A Set<String> skills can't fit in one column: no SQL type holds a Java collection. It needs its own table with the student's id as a foreign key, one row per skill:

student_skills (one student → many rows)
student_id (FK)skills
1Spring Boot
1Java
1Python
 
@ElementCollection
@CollectionTable(name = "student_skills",
                 joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "student_id"))
private Set<String> skills;
  • @ElementCollection — this field is a collection of basic values or embeddables, stored in a separate table.
  • @CollectionTable(name) — that table's name.
  • @JoinColumn(name = "student_id") — the foreign-key column pointing back to students.id.

Startup now runs two create table statements: students (id, age, email, student_name, with no skills column) and student_skills (student_id, skills). The collection table has no id of its own, since it's dependent on the student. To give rows their own primary key you'd make it a separate @Entity.

A collection of embeddables

@ElementCollection
@CollectionTable(name = "student_address",
                 joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "student_id"))
private Set<Address> addresses;

Creates student_address(student_id, city, house_number, pin_code, state, street), one row per address. Any collection type works (List, Set…), of primitives/wrappers, strings or embeddables.

Mapping cheat sheet

JavaAnnotationDatabase result
Class@Entity (+ @Table)Table
Primary key@Id + @GeneratedValue(IDENTITY)bigint auto_increment primary key
Field(none) or @Column(…)Column
BigDecimal@Column(precision, scale)decimal(p,s)
LocalDate / LocalTime / LocalDateTime(none)date / time / datetime(6)
Enum@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)Name text (MySQL enum(…))
Big text/binary@Loblongtext / longblob
Java-only field@TransientNo column
Custom conversion@Convert(converter = …)Whatever the converter returns
Value object@Embeddable / @Embedded (+ @AttributeOverrides)Columns inside the owner's table
Collection of values@ElementCollection + @CollectionTableSeparate table with FK to the owner

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Enum ordinals start at 0, not 1. The lecture says ordinal stores "1, 2, 3". Verified: INACTIVE (the second constant) stored as 1, with check (ordinal_status between 0 and 2). The real danger of ORDINAL (the default if you write @Enumerated alone) is that reordering or inserting a constant silently remaps existing rows. Always use STRING.
  • LocalDateTime maps to datetime(6) on MySQL, as DBeaver showed, not timestamp as the lecture first says. (Instant/OffsetDateTime are the zone-aware choices.)
  • Prefer Spring's @Transactional. The lecture imports jakarta.transaction.Transactional. Spring honours it, but org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional offers readOnly, propagation, isolation, rollbackFor, timeout. It's an AOP proxy (Lectures 22–25), so self-invocation and private methods are not transactional.
  • ddl-auto=update never drops or alters existing columns (seen in the lecture: old columns lingered). It also can't handle renames, since it adds a new column. That's another reason for Flyway/Liquibase.
  • Deleting an owner also deletes its element-collection rows. Verified: remove(student) issued delete from student_skills where student_id=? before deleting the student. Element collections live and die with their owner.
  • @ElementCollection is lazily loaded and costly to modify. Changing one element of a List element collection can make Hibernate delete and re-insert all rows. For large or frequently changed collections, use a real @OneToMany entity (upcoming). (Verified: with a Set<String>, Hibernate 7 added a unique constraint on (student_id, skills).)
  • The injected EntityManager is a thread-safe proxy. A real EntityManager is not thread-safe. @PersistenceContext (or constructor injection) gives a shared proxy that routes to the current transaction's EntityManager, which is why a singleton repository can hold it safely.
  • Logging SQL properly: show-sql writes to System.out. In real apps prefer logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=debug (and org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=trace to see bound values).
  • Where this is going: with Spring Data JPA you don't even write persist/find. Extending JpaRepository<Student, Long> (Lectures 11–13) generates the repository, and it uses this same EntityManager underneath.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"Hibernation logic" / "hibernet" = Hibernate; "hybrid demo" = hibernate-demo.
"jakarta.transactional" → jakarta.transaction.Transactional.
"ElementCollection makes a column" → the lecturer corrects it: a new table, not a column.
"Y or N" when explaining the converter → the code actually stores "yes"/"no".
"I've set insertable false" → both were left at the default true.
"Spring Unit" = Spring Initializr; "DBVer" = DBeaver; "IntelliJ" as "intelligent"/"intelligence".

Lecture 29: Hibernate Internals — Persistence Context, EntityManager(Factory), Transactions, Dirty Checking, Entity States and Flush

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #29 · 1h13m · Code Army · explains why Lecture 28's update worked with no update method

Why study the internals

Spring Data JPA is built on JPA, and JPA's implementation is Hibernate. Understand Hibernate's internals and you understand what happens behind every repository call. That's useful in interviews, and for debugging "why didn't my query run?" in your own projects.

The demo (hibernate-internals-demo) is Lecture 28's app:

  • StudentController with POST/GET/PUT/DELETE.
  • StudentService, @Transactional on every method: create, get, update-by-setters, delete-after-find.
  • StudentRepository, with an @PersistenceContext EntityManager and save (persist), findById (find) and remove.
  • A Student entity (id, name, email, age).
  • ddl-auto=update, and SQL logging on.

Posting Aditya (29) creates row 1. Four objects explain everything:

  1. the persistence context
  2. the EntityManager
  3. the EntityManagerFactory
  4. database transactions

1. The persistence context: a tracked cache of entities

Whenever you find or persist, Hibernate puts the entity into a workspace, a container: the persistence context. Two things happen:

  • The entity is cached, keyed by type and id (Student#1, Student#2…).
  • The entity is tracked: if its fields change, Hibernate notices and writes the change to the database itself.

Proof from the lecture: two finds, one SELECT

public Student findById(Long id) {
    Student s1 = entityManager.find(Student.class, id);
    Student s2 = entityManager.find(Student.class, id);   // same transaction
    return s2;
}

GET /api/students/1 → the log shows one select … from student … where id=?. Verified on Boot 4.1.0, and s1 == s2 is true: the same instance. The same two finds in separate transactions ran two SELECTs: each transaction gets a fresh context.

The name for it:
The persistence context acts as the first-level cache (L1), scoped to one context. A second-level cache, shared across contexts, comes in a later lecture.

2. EntityManager: the API to the persistence context

You never touch the persistence context directly. You go through the EntityManager, and its methods talk to the persistence context, not straight to the database:

MethodWhat it does to the context
persist(e)Makes a new entity managed; INSERT is scheduled
find(Class, id)Returns from the context, or SELECTs and adds to it
remove(e)Marks a managed entity for deletion; DELETE is scheduled
flush()Sends pending SQL to the database now
clear()Detaches all entities (empties the context)
detach(e) / merge(e) / refresh(e) / contains(e)Covered below

3. EntityManagerFactory: makes EntityManagers

  • A factory (Factory design pattern): each new unit of work asks it for an EntityManager.
  • Lifetime: the factory lives as long as the application. EntityManagers are created and destroyed many times within that lifetime.
  • Every new EntityManager comes with its own new persistence context. When it ends, the context ends too.

JPA interfaces vs Hibernate's own types

Hibernate is an independent framework and predates JPA. JPA later standardised its concepts as interfaces, and Hibernate adapted by extending them:

JPA (what you use)Hibernate interfaceHibernate implementation class
EntityManagerSession (extends EntityManager)SessionImpl
EntityManagerFactorySessionFactory (extends EntityManagerFactory)SessionFactoryImpl

So "session" in Hibernate docs means an EntityManager. The lecture swaps EntityManager for Session in the repository and everything still works: persist, find, remove are the same calls. Stick to the JPA layer anyway.

@PersistenceContext: why not plain constructor injection of a singleton?

  • StudentRepository is a singleton bean (Spring Core lectures).
  • A real EntityManager is not thread-safe. A single shared one would break when concurrent requests run persist/find/remove at once.
  • @PersistenceContext injects a proxy instead (like the AOP proxies of Lectures 22–25). On each call, the proxy routes to the EntityManager bound to the current transaction, creating one via the factory when a new transaction starts.
Don't confuse the two "persistence contexts":
@PersistenceContext (the annotation) only arranges that you get the right EntityManager; the factory creates it. The persistence context (the concept) is the entity container that EntityManager manages.

The chain for one service call:

  1. @Transactional method starts.
  2. A new transaction begins.
  3. The factory creates a new EntityManager, and with it a new persistence context.
  4. Repository calls go through the proxy to that EntityManager.
  5. The method ends: commit, and the EntityManager and context are closed.

4. Transactions: all or nothing

Transferring ₹1000 from person A (id 1) to person B (id 2) takes two statements:

UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1000 WHERE id = 2;

If the first succeeds and the database fails before the second, A loses the money and B never gets it. A transaction makes the pair succeed together or fail together:

BEGIN;
  UPDATE ... A;          -- if anything fails here or below:
  UPDATE ... B;          --   ROLLBACK (A's debit is undone)
COMMIT;                  -- otherwise make both permanent

Everything between BEGIN and COMMIT/ROLLBACK is one unit of work: 0 or 1, never in between.

Raw Hibernate vs Spring

// raw Hibernate
Session session = sessionFactory.openSession();
Transaction tx = session.beginTransaction();       // BEGIN
try {
    session.persist(student);
    tx.commit();                                   // COMMIT
} catch (Exception e) {
    tx.rollback();                                 // ROLLBACK
}

// Spring
@Transactional
public void createStudent(Student student) {
    studentRepository.save(student);
}

@Transactional is exactly the AOP pattern from Lecture 25. A pointcut matches the annotation, and an around advice does the rest:

  • Before the method runs: begin the transaction.
  • Then proceed() into your method.
  • After it returns: commit. If it throws: roll back.

You write one annotation instead of the try/commit/catch/rollback block.

Where to put @Transactional (the lecture's advice):
On the service layer. It works on repository methods too, but that's too narrow (a transaction should span a whole business operation, e.g. both halves of a transfer), and it mixes responsibilities. AOP advice belongs on services. It can be skipped for pure reads, but "adding it does no harm". (Added: use @Transactional(readOnly = true) for reads; see Corrections.)

Why update needs no method: dirty checking + flush

Walk through updateStudent(1, {name: "Rohit", email: "rohit@gmail.com", age: 25}):

  1. @Transactional → new transaction, EntityManager and persistence context.
  2. findById(1) → entityManager.find asks the context: empty. It generates SELECT … WHERE id = 1 and runs it via the DataSource/JDBC (Lecture 27). The row becomes a Student object on the heap, and the context tracks it, keeping a snapshot of its original state.
  3. setName, setAge, setEmail change only the heap object; no SQL runs.
  4. The method ends, so the transaction is about to commit. Before closing, the context compares each tracked entity with its snapshot: name, email and age differ, so the entity is dirty.
  5. Hibernate flushes: it generates and runs UPDATE student SET name = 'Rohit', email = …, age = 25 WHERE id = 1. Then it commits, and the EntityManager, context and transaction end.

Demo: PUT /api/students/1 → log shows select then update; DBeaver shows Rohit / 25. That's also why Lecture 28's first PUT failed without @Transactional: no transaction, so no managed entity and no flush at commit.

Why the persistence context exists:
  • Fewer queries. A repeat find in the same context is served from memory.
  • Automatic updates. Change the object; Hibernate writes the SQL.
  • Batched writes (write-behind). Changes are collected and sent together at flush, not one round trip per setter.

The four entity states (lifecycle)

StateMeaningHow you get there
TransientA plain object on the heap; no context knows itnew Student(…)
ManagedIn a persistence context and tracked; changes are flushed automatically (the important one)persist, find (or merge)
DetachedWas managed, no longer tracked; changes are ignoredThe method/transaction ends, or detach(e) / clear()
RemovedScheduled for deletion; DELETE runs at flushremove(e) on a managed entity

Demos

  • Detach: findById then entityManager.detach(s1); PUT Aditya → Rohan / 21 → "done", but the database is unchanged and the log shows only the SELECT. Verified: contains(s) is false after detach and no UPDATE runs.
  • clear() detaches every entity in the context at once (vs detach for one).
  • Merge: the lecture adds detach(Student) and attachAgain(Student) (calling entityManager.merge) to the repository. In the service, detach then student1 = studentRepository.attachAgain(student1) → PUT "Mohit" → name changes (select + update). Without the merge, "Arun" isn't saved.
  • Remove: deleteStudent finds (managed), then remove (removed). The DELETE runs when the transaction flushes, not necessarily at the remove line.
  • contains(e) returns whether the context currently manages the entity (rarely needed).
Worth knowing (verified on Boot 4.1.0):
  • merge does not re-attach the object you pass. It copies its state onto a managed instance (loading one with a SELECT if needed) and returns that copy. Verified: merge(s) == s was false; contains(original) was false and contains(returned) was true; a second SELECT ran before the UPDATE. That's why the lecture must reassign student1 = …attachAgain(student1). Keep using the returned object.
  • Removed comes only from Managed. remove on a detached entity threw IllegalArgumentException ("Given entity is not associated with the persistence context"). Hence find-then-remove.

Flush: write-behind, and flushing manually

Flush synchronises the persistence context with the database. Hibernate is write-behind: it doesn't flush after every change, only when the transaction ends. Three setters therefore produce one UPDATE, not three round trips.

You can force it: add flush() to the repository and call it after each setter. The log then shows select + three updates (Smita, age 25, new email). Pointless here, since it takes away write-behind.

Where manual flush is useful: batch processing

Persisting a million students in one loop would keep a million managed objects in the context (memory, and dirty-checking cost), and nothing reaches the DB until the end. Flush and clear every N instead:

@Transactional
public void saveAll(List<Student> students) {
    int count = 0;
    for (Student student : students) {
        entityManager.persist(student);
        count++;
        if (count % 100 == 0) {       // every 100 entities
            entityManager.flush();    // send the pending INSERTs
            entityManager.clear();    // free the context
        }
    }
}   // the remainder is flushed at commit

This keeps both the context and the database working in manageable batches of 100.

Fix applied:
The lecture checks counter % 100 == 0 before persisting and incrementing. On the very first iteration (0) it flushes an empty context, and each batch boundary is off by one. Increment first, then test, as above.

refresh: when the database changed behind Hibernate's back

If someone edits the row directly (e.g. renames Smita to Arun in DBeaver), the context doesn't know. It tracks the heap object, not the table. entityManager.refresh(student) re-reads the row and overwrites the entity's state. Verified: a local unsaved change was discarded by refresh, which issued a fresh SELECT. In real apps nobody edits JPA-managed tables by hand, so it's rarely needed.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • It's "dirty checking", not "dirty read". The lecture calls detecting changed entities a dirty read. A dirty read is a different concept: a transaction-isolation anomaly where you read another transaction's uncommitted data. What Hibernate does is dirty checking; the changed entity is a "dirty entity" (that part the lecture gets right).
  • Flush ≠ commit. The lecture describes flush as "store it in the database". Flush only sends SQL inside the still-open transaction; it can still roll back. Verified: persist + explicit flush() (the INSERT ran) followed by an exception left 0 rows. Only commit makes changes permanent.
  • Flush also happens before queries, not only at the end. With the default FlushMode.AUTO, Hibernate flushes pending changes before a JPQL/HQL query that could see them. Verified: modify a name, run a select count(…) JPQL query, and the UPDATE ran before the SELECT. So "write-behind until the method ends" is the common case, not a guarantee.
  • Spring Boot keeps the EntityManager open for the whole web request. The lecture says the EntityManager and context die when the @Transactional method ends. In a web request, Boot's default Open Session In View (spring.jpa.open-in-view=true, which logs a startup warning) binds one EntityManager to the entire request. Verified: an entity returned from a @Transactional service was still managed (contains == true) in the controller. With no transaction active there, changes made in the controller are still not flushed. Many teams set open-in-view=false so lazy-loading bugs surface early.
  • Batch inserts with IDENTITY ids are not JDBC-batched. Flush/clear bounds memory, but true JDBC batching also needs spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=100. And Hibernate disables insert batching for GenerationType.IDENTITY, because it must run each INSERT immediately to learn the generated id. For bulk inserts use SEQUENCE (PostgreSQL/Oracle) or plain JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate (Lecture 27).
  • @Transactional(readOnly = true) for reads. It's more than documentation: Spring sets Hibernate's flush mode to manual, skipping dirty checking and snapshots. Verified: a name changed inside a readOnly method was not saved. (Use Spring's org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional; the jakarta one has no readOnly.)
  • Default rollback rule: Spring rolls back on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException, Error) but commits on checked exceptions unless you add rollbackFor = Exception.class. And being AOP-based, @Transactional doesn't apply to self-invocation or private methods (Lecture 22).
  • persist/find/remove are JPA methods. The lecture calls them "Hibernate's methods". They're defined by the JPA EntityManager interface (which Session inherits). Hibernate's older native save/update/saveOrUpdate are deprecated since Hibernate 6.
  • Transactions give ACID: Atomicity (the all-or-nothing described here), Consistency, Isolation (where dirty reads come in), Durability. A standard interview follow-up.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"JPA has its own class SessionFactoryImpl" → SessionImpl / SessionFactoryImpl are Hibernate's classes.
"DataStore object" used for the database connection → the DataSource (Lecture 27).
"sirf 1000 rupees ... +100" in the second UPDATE → both statements move ₹1000.
"atrocity" → inconsistency; "hyper net" / "hibernation" = Hibernate; "S1 dot ID" = the table alias s1_0.id in Hibernate's SQL.
"Postman" as "post run"/"post one"; "IntelliJ" as "intelligent"; "DBVer" = DBeaver.

Lecture 30: JPA Relationships — @ManyToOne/@OneToMany, @OneToOne, @ManyToMany, Owning vs Inverse Side (plus Lombok)

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #30 · 1h23m · Code Army · builds on the Hibernate CRUD lecture (28)

Setup: an empty project, and Lombok to kill boilerplate

jpa-relationship-demo starts with an empty controller, service and repository (the last with an @PersistenceContext EntityManager), and a Student entity with just id and name. Dependencies: spring-boot-starter-data-jpa, webmvc, mysql-connector-j.

Lombok

Instead of generating getters, setters and constructors in the IDE, add Lombok (org.projectlombok:lombok; no version, the Boot parent manages it) and annotate:

@Getter @Setter              // getId/setId, getName/setName, ... (standard naming)
@NoArgsConstructor           // JPA needs it
@AllArgsConstructor
@Entity
public class Student { … }
  • @Data — getters, setters, toString, equals/hashCode in one go (but see the warning below).
  • @Builder — generates a Builder-pattern API.
  • IntelliJ may prompt "Enable annotation processing": accept.
Worth knowing (verified on Boot 4.1.0, JDK 23):
Adding the dependency alone isn't enough on JDK 23+. The JDK stopped running annotation processors implicitly, so mvn compile failed with "cannot find symbol: method setName". Lombok never ran. Declare it as a processor, as Spring Initializr does for Lombok projects: 
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <annotationProcessorPaths>
            <path><groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId><artifactId>lombok</artifactId></path>
        </annotationProcessorPaths>
    </configuration>
</plugin>
Mark the Lombok dependency <optional>true</optional> too; it's compile-time only. (Boot 4.1 manages Lombok 1.18.46.)

The problem: an object inside an object

@Entity
public class Student {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) private Long id;
    private String name;
    private Department department;      // error: "Basic attribute should not be 'Department'"
}

public class Department {
    private Long id;
    private String name;                // more fields later
}

In Java, a field referencing another object is natural. A table column can't hold an object, though. The relational way:

  • a separate department table (id, name);
  • the student table stores only dept_id, a foreign key to department.id.
student
idnamedept_id (FK)
1Aditya1001
2Rohit1002
department
id (PK)name
1001CSC
1002Physics

In Java, getting Aditya's department is student.getDepartment(). In SQL it's a join: … WHERE students.dept_id = departments.id. With raw JDBC you'd store deptId in Student, fetch the student, then run a second query in a DepartmentRepository. The goal of JPA relationships: keep the natural object model, and let Hibernate generate the joins and foreign keys.

Relationship vocabulary

Cardinality

CardinalityExampleReads as
Many-to-one (N:1)Student → DepartmentMany students belong to one department
One-to-many (1:N)Department → StudentOne department has many students (the same relationship seen from the other end)
One-to-one (1:1)User ↔ ProfileOne user has one profile, and vice versa
Many-to-many (N:M)Student ↔ CourseA student takes many courses; a course has many students

Direction

  • Unidirectional — only one side references the other (Student has department; Department knows nothing of students). Drawn as an arrow.
  • Bidirectional — both sides reference each other (Department also has List<Student> students). The "many" end holds a single object; the "one" end holds a collection.

Owning vs inverse side

  • Owning side — the entity whose table holds the foreign key (Student owns dept_id). It carries @JoinColumn.
  • Inverse side — the other end (Department). In a bidirectional mapping it says mappedBy = "…": "the other side manages this".

Many-to-one (unidirectional): Student → Department

@Getter @Setter @NoArgsConstructor @AllArgsConstructor
@Entity
public class Student {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String name;

    @ManyToOne
    @JoinColumn(name = "dept_id")          // FK column in the student table
    private Department department;
}

@Getter @Setter @NoArgsConstructor
@Entity
public class Department {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String name;
}
  • @ManyToOne tells Hibernate the cardinality.
  • @JoinColumn(name = "dept_id") names the FK column. Hibernate knows it references Department's primary key: an FK always points at the other table's PK.
  • Department must itself be an @Entity with an @Id; that's what fixes the "Basic attribute" error.

Startup DDL (with ddl-auto=update): create table department (id, name), create table student (id, name, dept_id), and an alter table student add constraint … foreign key (dept_id) references department. DBeaver's Diagram tab draws the many-to-one link.

Nullable or mandatory?

@ManyToOne(optional = false)                        // Java/JPA side: association required
@JoinColumn(name = "dept_id", nullable = false)     // DDL side: dept_id NOT NULL
private Department department;

By default a student can exist with dept_id = NULL (e.g. Raman with no department). Set both attributes to forbid it: optional is the entity-level rule, nullable goes into the generated schema.

Worked example: saving students with departments

The lecture adds DepartmentController (POST /api/department), DepartmentService (@Transactional) and DepartmentRepository (save = persist, getDepartmentById = find). Posting {"name": "CSC"} first stored null: Department had no Lombok @Setter, so JSON binding couldn't set name. After adding it (and dropping the tables), CSC, Physics and History are created.

Into an existing department

// StudentController: POST /api/student?deptId=1   body {"name": "Aditya"}
@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<String> createStudent(@RequestBody Student student,
                                            @RequestParam Long deptId) { … }

// StudentService
@Transactional
public void createStudent(Student student, Long deptId) {
    Department department = departmentRepository.getDepartmentById(deptId);  // SELECT department
    student.setDepartment(department);
    studentRepository.save(student);                                        // INSERT student
}
  • The service may use several repositories (that's business logic); the repository only saves.
  • First attempt used /{deptId} as a path variable and returned 404 without it. The lecture switches to @RequestParam deptId.
  • Log: select department, then insert student. Aditya and Rohit get dept_id = 1, Sohan 2.

Creating the department on the fly

// POST /api/student/with-department?deptName=Political Science   body {"name": "Monika"}
@Transactional
public void createStudent(Student student, String deptName) {
    Department department = new Department();
    department.setName(deptName);
    departmentRepository.save(department);     // INSERT department
    student.setDepartment(department);
    studentRepository.save(student);           // INSERT student with the new FK
}

The two overloaded @PostMappings first clashed ("ambiguous mapping": same path, differing only in a param), so this one got the path /with-department. Result: a new department (id 4) and Monika pointing at it; the log shows the two inserts.

Worth knowing (verified):
There's no cascading by default. Here the department is explicitly persisted first. Persisting a student that references an unsaved department throws TransientPropertyValueException: … references an unsaved transient instance of 'Department' (persist the transient instance before flushing). Either persist the parent first (as the lecture does), or add cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST to the association.

One-to-many (bidirectional): Department → List<Student>

Could department hold a student_id column instead? No. With two CSC students you'd need two rows with the same department id 1001, violating the primary key. So the FK always lives on the "many" side. One-to-many is the same table layout as many-to-one, just viewed from the other end.

// in Department
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "department")      // = the field name in Student
private List<Student> students = new ArrayList<>();
  • mappedBy = "department" means "I don't own this. Student.department (with its @JoinColumn) does." It names the Java field, not a table or column.
  • After restart the schema is unchanged: department(id, name), student(id, name, dept_id). No new column or table.
  • Gain: navigate both ways, department.getStudents() and student.getDepartment().
  • Initialise the list (= new ArrayList<>()). The lecture hit a 500 "department.getStudents() is null" until it did.

The cost: keep both sides in sync yourself

With a bidirectional mapping, when you set student.setDepartment(dept) you must also do dept.getStudents().add(student). Otherwise Rohan's department says CSC, but CSC's student list doesn't include Rohan: an inconsistent in-memory model. So both service methods now add to both sides:

student.setDepartment(department);
department.getStudents().add(student);
studentRepository.save(student);
// no departmentRepository.save(department) needed: it is managed (Lecture 29)

The reverse endpoint POST /api/department/with-student?studentName=Anamika (body {"name": "Physics"}) creates a student and a department together and links both ways. Anamika gets dept_id = 4. The log shows insert student, insert department, then update student.

Why insert, insert, update (verified):
The code persisted the student before the department. Hibernate inserts the student with dept_id = NULL (the department has no id yet), inserts the department, then issues an UPDATE to fill in the FK. Persist the parent first and you get just two inserts.

Helper methods: centralise the syncing

// in Student (instead of Lombok's setter)
public void addDepartment(Department department) {
    this.department = department;
    department.getStudents().add(this);
}

public void removeDepartment() {
    if (this.department != null) {
        this.department.getStudents().remove(this);   // remove FIRST...
        this.department = null;                        // ...then clear the reference
    }
}
Fix applied:
The lecture's sketch marks the helper private, which is unusable from the service; it must be public. Its remove version sets department = null before calling this.department.getStudents().remove(this), which throws NullPointerException. Reverse the order, as above.

One-to-one: User ↔ Profile

Either table could hold the FK: user.profile_id or profile.user_id. Neither violates a primary key, since each user has at most one profile. The lecture puts it in profile:

@Entity
public class Profile {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) private Long id;
    private String bio;

    @OneToOne
    @JoinColumn(name = "user_id")        // Profile is the owning side
    private User user;
}

@Entity
public class User {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) private Long id;
    private String name;

    @OneToOne(mappedBy = "user")         // optional: makes it bidirectional
    private Profile profile;
}

Two constraints keep it truly one-to-one:

  • FK constraint: profile.user_id references user.id.
  • Unique constraint on profile.user_id. Without it, two profiles could point at user 1 and it would silently become one-to-many.

Verified on Boot 4.1.0: Hibernate adds the unique constraint by itself for @OneToOne (user_id bigint unique). Adding mappedBy on User changes nothing in the schema.

The lecture's advice on direction:
"Don't assume bidirectional is always better." It adds sync work (helper methods) and complexity. If you only ever go profile.getUser(), keep it unidirectional.

Many-to-many: Student ↔ Course, and the join table

Neither table can hold the FK:

  • student.course_id would need two rows "1, Aditya" (Spring and MERN), which duplicates the student PK.
  • course.student_id would need two rows "1001, Spring" (Aditya and Rohit), which duplicates the course PK.

The solution is a third table, the join table, holding pairs of foreign keys:

student_course (join table)
student_id (FK)course_id (FK)
11001
11002
21001
21002
 
@Entity
public class Student2 {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) private Long id;
    private String name;

    @ManyToMany
    @JoinTable(name = "student_course",
               joinColumns        = @JoinColumn(name = "student_id"),   // owning side's FK
               inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "course_id"))    // other side's FK
    private List<Course> courses = new ArrayList<>();
}

@Entity
public class Course {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) private Long id;
    private String name;

    @ManyToMany(mappedBy = "courses")      // optional inverse side
    private List<Student2> students = new ArrayList<>();
}

Startup creates student2(id, name), course(id, name) and student_course(student_id, course_id). Neither entity table gets a new column; links live only in the join table, and both directions query through it.

Summary: where the foreign key goes

MappingFK locationOwning side annotationInverse side
Many-to-one / one-to-manyAlways the many side's table@ManyToOne + @JoinColumn@OneToMany(mappedBy = "…")
One-to-oneEither table (plus a unique constraint)@OneToOne + @JoinColumn@OneToOne(mappedBy = "…")
Many-to-manyNeither: a separate join table@ManyToMany + @JoinTable@ManyToMany(mappedBy = "…")

Homework / suggested extensions

  • Build create/read/update/delete endpoints for the one-to-one (User/Profile) and many-to-many (Student/Course) mappings, as done for Student/Department.
  • Update a student's department and check both tables; add helper methods for the bidirectional sides.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Only the owning side is written to the database. The lecture frames syncing both sides as a data-integrity must. It is for the in-memory model, but Hibernate reads only the owning side (Student.department) when writing the FK. Verified: adding a student only to department.getStudents() saved it with dept_id = NULL; setting student.setDepartment(d) saved dept_id = 1. Likewise "saving the student auto-saves the department because student is the owning side" isn't what happens: the department is saved because it's managed (found or persisted in the transaction), not because of ownership or cascade.
  • A List in @ManyToMany gets no primary key and is slow to modify. The lecture says the two FK columns together form the join table's primary key. Verified on Hibernate 7.4: with List<Course> the join table was created without any primary key; with Set<Course> it got primary key (course_id, student_id). And removing one course from the List made Hibernate delete all of the student's rows and re-insert the rest (a "bag"). Use Set for many-to-many.
  • Don't use Lombok's @Data (or @ToString/@EqualsAndHashCode) on bidirectional entities. The generated toString/hashCode walk both sides forever. Verified: StackOverflowError. The same infinite loop happens when Jackson serialises a bidirectional entity returned from a controller. Use @Getter/@Setter, exclude associations, and return DTOs (Lecture 16) rather than entities.
  • Fetch types and the N+1 problem (announced but not covered). Defaults: @ManyToOne/@OneToOne are EAGER; @OneToMany/@ManyToMany are LAZY. Loading N students and touching each one's lazy association fires 1 + N queries. The usual fixes are @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) plus a JOIN FETCH query or an @EntityGraph where you need the data.
  • Cascade and orphan removal: @OneToMany(mappedBy = "department", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true) makes persisting or removing the parent propagate to its children, and deletes a child removed from the collection. Use them only for genuine parent–child ownership, never on @ManyToMany (removing a student would delete shared courses).
  • Join table with extra data: once the link needs attributes (enrolment date, grade), replace @ManyToMany with an Enrollment entity holding two @ManyToOnes.
  • Avoid reserved table names: an entity named User maps to table user, a reserved word in some databases (H2, PostgreSQL). Use @Table(name = "app_user") or similar.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"between them is a one-to-many relationship" (for Student → Department) → many-to-one from the student side, as the lecturer then draws.
"mern" = MERN; "lombak" / "LMB" = Lombok; "JPI relationship demo" = jpa-relationship-demo.
"the value of mappedBy is the other table" → it's the field name on the owning entity.
"cascade delete" in DBeaver = dropping the tables with dependent constraints, not JPA cascading.
"Postman" as "post one", "IntelliJ" as "intelligent", "DBVer" = DBeaver.

Lecture 31: Cascading, Lazy vs Eager Loading, the N+1 Problem and Entity Graphs

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #31 · 57m · Code Army · the last JPA-relationships lecture; Spring Data JPA starts next

Starting point: Lecture 30's Student ↔ Department mapping

  • Student (id, name) — @ManyToOne @JoinColumn(name = "dept_id") Department department. It's the owning side: the FK column dept_id lives in student.
  • Department (id, name) — @OneToMany(mappedBy = "department") List<Student> students, the inverse side. No column is added for it.
  • Controllers and services for both, repositories with an EntityManager, all with Lombok getters and setters.

Startup creates department(id, name), student(id, name, dept_id) and the FK constraint. POST /api/department {"name": "CSC"} stores a department, and no student appears.

The problem: saving a parent means saving every child by hand

A new department (Physics) arrives with four new students already enrolled. The lecture simulates this in DepartmentService.createDepartment:

@Transactional
public void createDepartment(Department department) {
    Student s1 = new Student(); s1.setName("Aditya");
    Student s2 = new Student(); s2.setName("Rohit");
    Student s3 = new Student(); s3.setName("Rohan");
    Student s4 = new Student(); s4.setName("Sonika");
    for (Student s : List.of(s1, s2, s3, s4)) s.setDepartment(department);  // owning side
    department.getStudents().addAll(List.of(s1, s2, s3, s4));                // inverse side

    departmentRepository.save(department);    // persist department
    studentRepository.save(s1);               // ...and each student, one by one
    studentRepository.save(s2);
    studentRepository.save(s3);
    studentRepository.save(s4);
}

It works: five INSERTs, and all four students get dept_id = 2. But every child needs its own save call. Forget one and it's silently not stored; all of them are new objects, so none is in the persistence context.

Some children only make sense with their parent: a college department without students, an Order without OrderItems. Saving or deleting the parent should do the same to its children.

The idea: cascading operations from parent to children

// in Department
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "department", cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST)
private List<Student> students = new ArrayList<>();

"When I persist a department, also persist every student in its students list." With the four studentRepository.save calls commented out, the demo (after dropping and recreating the tables) still stores Physics and Aditya, Rohit, Rohan and Sonika.

CascadeType.REMOVE: deleting the parent deletes the children

// DepartmentController
@DeleteMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<String> deleteDepartment(@PathVariable Long id) { … }

// DepartmentService
@Transactional
public void removeDepartment(Long deptId) {
    Department department = departmentRepository.findById(deptId);   // em.find
    departmentRepository.removeDepartment(department);               // em.remove(department)
}
  • With REMOVE: DELETE /api/department/1 removes the department and all its students. The log shows the department SELECT, a SELECT of its students, one DELETE per student, then the department DELETE. There's no manual child cleanup and no helper methods.
  • Without any cascade (recreate the data, remove the cascade, delete again): it fails with "Cannot delete or update a parent row: a foreign key constraint fails". The database won't let you delete a department that students still reference.
Anticipated question: "But a student might belong to several departments?"
Not with this model. Student → Department is many-to-one: each student has exactly one department. If students could have many departments, the relationship would be many-to-many, and cascading removal would be wrong. The cascade rule follows from the cardinality.

Cascade types

CascadeTypePropagates
PERSISTpersist(parent) → persist new children
REMOVEremove(parent) → remove children
MERGEmerge(parent) → merge children (added)
REFRESH / DETACHrefresh / detach of the parent → children (added)
ALLEvery one of the above

The lecture's advice: ALL exists, but prefer listing exactly what you mean (e.g. {PERSIST, REMOVE}).

The problem: loading the whole object graph

A real Student may hold many complex associations:

  • Department (many-to-one), which has Teachers;
  • Profile (one-to-one);
  • List<Course> (many-to-many), each with Instructors.

entityManager.find(Student.class, 1001) would, naively, query all of it: department and teachers, profile, courses and instructors. That's many queries for one student. The lecture calls this the reachable object graph.

The idea: lazy vs eager loading

  • Eager: load the association together with the entity (typically a join).
  • Lazy: load only the entity's basic columns (id, name…). For each association, put a proxy in the field, and query the real data only when you first use it.
@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
@JoinColumn(name = "department_id")
private Department department;

@OneToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
@JoinColumn(name = "profile_id")
private Profile profile;

Demo run

The lecture adds a Profile (id, bio) with ProfileRepository. createStudent builds a new department (CSC) and profile ("simple bio"), saves both, sets them on the student and saves it. GET /api/student/{id} returns the student.

  1. First GET: infinite JSON. Department still had its students list, and Jackson loops Student → Department → students → … (the Lecture 30 warning). Fix: remove that back-reference, then drop and recreate the tables.
  2. Without LAZY: the GET returns the full student. The log shows one SELECT with LEFT JOIN department and LEFT JOIN profile, i.e. eager.
  3. With LAZY on both: the JSON shows "hibernateLazyInitializer" inside department and profile, the mark of Hibernate proxies. The log shows three separate SELECTs (student, then department, then profile), triggered when Jackson read the proxies to build JSON.
  4. Proof of laziness in fetchStudentById: 
    Student s1 = studentRepository.findById(id);
System.out.println("lazily fetched student");
Department d1 = s1.getDepartment();
System.out.println("lazily fetched department");
Profile p1 = s1.getProfile();
System.out.println("lazily fetched profile");
return s1;
    All three messages print before any department or profile SELECT. A proxy is loaded only when you touch its data (e.g. d1.getName()), not by merely calling getDepartment().
When to use which (the lecture's advice):
Lazy saves a lot of work when the graph is deep and you often don't need all of it. You may load a student and never look at its department. Use eager only where the data is always needed.

The N+1 problem

List<Student> students = …;                 // SELECT * FROM students   (1 query, e.g. 100 rows)
for (Student s : students) {
    System.out.println(s.getDepartment().getName());   // lazy proxy: 1 query per student
}
  • 1 root query returns N = 100 students.
  • The loop then fires N more queries, one per student's department: 1 + 100 = 101 round trips.
  • It looks harmless (the list is "already in memory") and is a classic mistake by developers who don't know the internals.

How to spot it: the endpoint is slow and the SQL log shows the same SELECT … WHERE id = ? repeated for every row.

The first-level cache softens it

Many students share a department (many-to-one). Once a department is loaded into the persistence context (Lecture 29), later students of that department reuse it with no query. With 100 students in 3 departments, it's really 1 + 3. With 100 distinct departments it's back to 1 + 100. Verified on Boot 4.1.0: 12 students in 3 departments, loop over getDepartment().getName() → 1 student SELECT + 3 department SELECTs.

The lecture's point: lazy loading isn't the villain:
N+1 appears when lazy loading is used without knowing how it works. Lazy loading still solves the bigger problem of loading entire graphs. Know when a code path will touch the association, and fetch it up front there.

The fix: tell JPA to fetch specific associations for specific queries

Keep associations LAZY globally, and for the query that needs them, fetch them in the same SQL. The lecture uses an entity graph:

public interface StudentRepository extends JpaRepository<Student, Long> {

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "department")          // this query fetches department too
    @Query("select s from Student s")
    List<Student> findAllWithDepartment();

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"department", "profile"})
    Optional<Student> findById(Long id);
}
  • The rest of the app still loads department lazily. Only these methods fetch it eagerly, because their callers loop over it.
  • Several paths can be listed: any association you know callers will touch.
  • Verified: the Spring Data method with @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "department") produced one SELECT … LEFT JOIN department instead of 1 + 3.
Correction: @EntityGraph is a Spring Data annotation:
The lecture puts @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "department") on a method of its hand-written @Repository class that uses EntityManager. That annotation (org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.EntityGraph) is only honoured on Spring Data repository interface methods. (jakarta.persistence.EntityGraph is an interface, not an annotation.) Verified: on the EntityManager-based method it was silently ignored, still 1 + 3 queries. With plain EntityManager use one of:
  • JOIN FETCH: em.createQuery("select s from Student s join fetch s.department", Student.class). Verified: 1 query.
  • A JPA entity graph passed as a hint: EntityGraph<Student> g = em.createEntityGraph(Student.class); g.addAttributeNodes("department"); then em.find(Student.class, id, Map.of("jakarta.persistence.fetchgraph", g)), or query.setHint(…). Or declare @NamedEntityGraph on the entity.

N+1 fixes compared

ApproachQueries for 12 students / 3 deptsNotes
LAZY + loop (the problem)1 + 3 (1 + N when departments are distinct)Verified
Make it EAGER1 + 3Does not fix N+1 for queries; see Corrections
JOIN FETCH in JPQL1Works with plain EntityManager (verified)
@EntityGraph on a Spring Data method1The lecture's approach (verified)
Batch fetching: hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=50 or @BatchSize1 + 1 (… WHERE id IN (…))Keeps laziness and loads proxies in batches (added)
DTO projection (select new …(s.name, d.name) from Student s join s.department d)1No entities, no proxies; best for read-only views (added)

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Eager loading does not prevent N+1 for queries. @ManyToOne and @OneToOne are EAGER by default (the lecture's first GET showed the join). But EAGER only guarantees the data is loaded, not how. For find() Hibernate uses a join. For a JPQL query like select s from Student s it runs the query and then a separate SELECT per distinct department. Verified: an EAGER @ManyToOne with a plain JPQL query fired 1 + 3 queries even though the code never touched the department. That's why the usual advice is to make @ManyToOne/@OneToOne LAZY and fetch explicitly per query. (@OneToMany/@ManyToMany are LAZY by default.)
  • Cascade REMOVE is chatty and only covers the mapped association. Verified: removing a department loaded its students, then issued one DELETE per student, then the department DELETE. For large child sets prefer a bulk JPQL DELETE or a database-level ON DELETE CASCADE. And it only follows the annotated collection: another table referencing the department (not mapped with cascade) still made the delete fail with a foreign-key violation.
  • Where cascade belongs: on the parent's @OneToMany (or a one-to-one it truly owns). Never cascade REMOVE from the "many" side (@ManyToOne): deleting one student would delete the whole department. Never cascade it on @ManyToMany: shared courses would vanish.
  • orphanRemoval = true is different from REMOVE. REMOVE deletes children when the parent is removed; orphanRemoval also deletes a child that is merely removed from the collection.
  • Returning entities with lazy proxies as JSON is fragile. The "hibernateLazyInitializer" field in the output is Hibernate internals leaking into the API. It only worked because Open Session In View (Lecture 29) kept the EntityManager open during serialisation. With spring.jpa.open-in-view=false you'd get a LazyInitializationException. Map entities to DTOs (Lecture 16) inside the transaction instead.
  • Hibernate also offers fetch profiles and @Fetch(FetchMode.SUBSELECT) as further tools, but JOIN FETCH, entity graphs, batch size and DTO projections cover almost every case.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"escaping" / "cascade tape" = cascading / CascadeType.
"relationship is one-to-one" (for Student → Department, after removing cascade) → it's many-to-one.
"remove calls refresh" in the repository → it calls entityManager.remove.
"n + 1 is not bad" → the lecturer means lazy loading is not bad.
"lazy initializer" / "hibernate lazy initializer" in the JSON = the proxy's hibernateLazyInitializer field.

Lecture 32: Spring Data JPA Masterclass — Repository Interfaces, Runtime Proxies, Derived Queries, @Query/JPQL, Sorting and Pagination

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #32 · 1h47m · Code Army · ties together JDBC (26), Spring JDBC (27) and Hibernate/JPA (28–31)

The road so far, and the boilerplate that remains

LayerWhat it removedWhat was still manual
Raw JDBC (26)—Connections, statements, SQL, mapping, closing
Spring JDBC (27)Connections, statements, closing (Template pattern)SQL strings, row mappers
Hibernate / JPA (28–31)SQL: just call persist/find/removeThe repository class itself
Spring Data JPAThe repository implementationOnly an interface

Every hand-written JPA repository looks the same:

@Repository
public class StudentRepository {
    @PersistenceContext private EntityManager entityManager;
    public void save(Student student)       { entityManager.persist(student); }
    public Student findById(Long id)        { return entityManager.find(Student.class, id); }
    public void delete(Student student)     { entityManager.remove(student); }
}

A DepartmentRepository or UserRepository is identical except for two things: the entity type and the id type. The logic (persist, find, remove) never changes. Writing it isn't hard, just repetitive.

The idea: declare an interface, Spring supplies the implementation

  1. Spring provides base interfaces (e.g. Repository, JpaRepository) that declare the standard methods.
  2. You write an interface that extends one of them. Extend it, don't implement it, and write no method bodies.
  3. You inject your interface into the service and call its methods.
  4. Spring creates the implementation at runtime.

That's the "magic" already used in the CRUD lectures (11–13). This lecture explains it.

Spring Data vs Spring Data JPA

  • Spring Data is an umbrella project. It defines one repository programming model (the interfaces, method naming, paging and sorting) regardless of the underlying store.
  • Each store has a module implementing that model:
    • Spring Data JPA (relational/SQL, via JPA and Hibernate);
    • Spring Data MongoDB;
    • Spring Data Redis, Cassandra, Neo4j…
  • Benefit (polymorphism again): the method names stay the same (save, findById…). With JPA they become SQL through Hibernate; with MongoDB, document operations.
  • Don't confuse JPA (the spec: EntityManager, @Entity, @Column…) with Spring Data JPA (the repository abstraction on top of it).

Worked example: the minimal Spring Data repository

Project spring-data-jpa-demo:

  • StudentController (/api/student: POST create, GET /{id}).
  • A Student entity (id auto-generated, name, email, age; Lombok getters/setters).
  • An empty service and an empty repository package.
public interface StudentRepository extends JpaRepository<Student, Long> {
    // nothing, not even @Repository
}

@Service
public class StudentService {
    private final StudentRepository studentRepository;
    public StudentService(StudentRepository studentRepository) {
        this.studentRepository = studentRepository;
    }

    public void createStudent(Student student) {
        studentRepository.save(student);
    }

    public Student fetchStudentById(Long id) {
        Optional<Student> studentOptional = studentRepository.findById(id);
        return studentOptional.get();       // happy path only; see Corrections
    }
}
  • JpaRepository<Student, Long> — the two generic parameters are exactly the two things that vary: the entity and the type of its primary key.
  • findById returns Optional<Student>, since the id may not exist.
  • Demo: startup creates the student table. POST {"name": "Aditya", "email": "ad@gmail.com", "age": 29} → "done" and an INSERT. GET /api/student/1 → the student and a SELECT.
  • No implementation was written anywhere.

The repository interface hierarchy

InterfaceWhat you get
Repository<T, ID>Nothing. A marker naming the entity and id type. You declare only the methods you want exposed.
CrudRepositorysave, saveAll, findById, existsById, findAll, findAllById, count, delete, deleteById, deleteAll… Bulk methods return Iterable.
ListCrudRepositorySame, but saveAll/findAll/findAllById return List (no manual conversion)
PagingAndSortingRepositoryfindAll(Sort) (returns Iterable) and findAll(Pageable) (returns Page)
ListPagingAndSortingRepositoryfindAll(Sort) returning List
JpaRepositoryAll of the above plus flush, saveAndFlush, saveAllAndFlush, deleteAllInBatch, deleteAllByIdInBatch…

The marker Repository: declare-only-what-you-need

public interface StudentRepository extends Repository<Student, Long> {
    void save(Student student);
    Optional<Student> findById(Long id);
}

With plain Repository, studentRepository.save(…) first fails to compile, because the interface is empty. Declare the two methods (no bodies) and it works: after dropping the table, POST and GET succeed with INSERT/SELECT in the log. Spring matched the names save and findById to its standard implementations.

The benefit is control: only what you declare is callable. For example, leave out any delete method so services can't delete students.

How it works at runtime: proxy → SimpleJpaRepository or query engine

  1. At startup Spring finds your interface and creates a runtime proxy implementing it; that proxy is what's autowired into StudentService. Verified: the bean is a jdk.proxy2.$Proxy… whose target is org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.support.SimpleJpaRepository.
  2. For a standard method (save, findById…), the proxy delegates to SimpleJpaRepository<T, ID>. It's an ordinary, pre-written class implementing JpaRepository generically with the EntityManager. Nothing is generated; the logic is the same for every entity: 
    // conceptually, inside SimpleJpaRepository<T, ID>
public <S extends T> S save(S entity) {
    if (entityInformation.isNew(entity)) { entityManager.persist(entity); return entity; }
    else                                  { return entityManager.merge(entity); }
}
public Optional<T> findById(ID id) {
    return Optional.ofNullable(entityManager.find(domainClass, id));
}
  3. For a custom method (findByEmail), no standard implementation exists. The proxy hands it to the query-method infrastructure, which parses the method name (or reads its @Query) into a query, again run through the EntityManager.

Because everything still goes through the EntityManager, all of Lecture 29 still applies: the persistence context, dirty checking, flush, entity states.

What the standard methods really do

  • save doesn't write to the database immediately. It calls persist (new entity) or merge (existing/detached entity), which puts the entity into the persistence context. The INSERT/UPDATE happens at flush/commit (or right away with saveAndFlush).
  • saveAll(list) isn't one bulk SQL statement. It loops, calling save for each element. Writes are collected by the persistence context and flushed together (Lecture 29's write-behind).
  • findById is entityManager.find wrapped in an Optional; findAll is all rows.
  • existsById doesn't load the entity, only a count. Verified SQL: select count(*) from student s1_0 where s1_0.id=?.
  • count, delete, deleteById, deleteAll, plus JpaRepository's flush, saveAndFlush (save + flush), saveAllAndFlush, deleteAllInBatch (the older deleteInBatch is deprecated).

Update without an update method

@Transactional                     // required: see below
public void updateStudent(Student studentRequest, Long id) {
    Student student = studentRepository.findById(id).get();   // now managed
    student.setAge(studentRequest.getAge());
    student.setName(studentRequest.getName());
    // no save needed: dirty checking flushes an UPDATE at commit (Lecture 29)
}
Correction: this needs @Transactional on the service method:
The lecture writes this method without @Transactional and says the persistence context will flush the change. Without a surrounding transaction, findById runs in its own short transaction (Spring Data repository methods are transactional by themselves), so the returned entity is already detached when you call the setters. Verified: without @Transactional the age stayed 29 and no UPDATE ran. With it, select + update ran and the age became 77. The alternative is to call studentRepository.save(student) explicitly.

Derived queries: queries from method names

Split a name at By:

  • The part before is the subject: what to do.
  • The part after is the predicate: the conditions, naming entity properties.
Optional<Student> findByEmail(String email);
//      subject: find    predicate: Email
//  → select ... from student where email = ?
Subject keywordsPredicate keywords
find…By, exists…By, count…By, delete…By, findTop3By, findDistinctByAnd, Or, Not, Like, Containing, StartingWith, EndingWith, GreaterThan, LessThan, Between, In, NotIn, IsNull, IsNotNull, True, False, IgnoreCase, OrderBy…Asc/Desc
  • findByEmailAndAge(String email, int age) → … where email = ? and age = ? (parameters in order).
  • findByEmailOrderByNameAsc(String email) → … where email = ? order by name asc.
  • findByEmailLike(String pattern) → … where email like ?.
  • IntelliJ auto-completes valid names from the entity's properties: type findBy and it suggests Email, Age, AgeAfter…
Worth knowing (verified):
  • Like doesn't add wildcards; Containing does. findByEmailLike("a1@gmail") returned []; you must pass "%a1@gmail%" yourself. findByEmailContaining("a1@gmail") found the row (Spring adds the %). Likewise StartingWith/EndingWith.
  • Bad names fail at startup, not at runtime. A typo like findByEmial stopped the app with "No property 'emial' found for type 'Student'". The name is the query, and it's validated when the proxy is built.

When names get out of hand

findTop10ByNameContainingIgnoreCaseAndAgeGreaterThanAndActiveTrueAndDepartmentNameOrderByAdmissionDateDesc(…)

It works (top-10 limit, case-insensitive contains, age >, active = true, department name, ordering), but it's unreadable, easy to get subtly wrong, and DepartmentName is ambiguous: a departmentName field on Student, or Student.department.name? (Added: Spring prefers the longest matching property, and an underscore forces traversal: Department_Name.) For complex logic, write the query yourself.

Custom queries with @Query

Native SQL

@Query(value = """
        SELECT * FROM student WHERE email = :email
        """, nativeQuery = true)
Optional<Student> findByEmail(@Param("email") String email);

// positional alternative
@Query(value = "SELECT * FROM student WHERE email = ?1 AND name = ?2", nativeQuery = true)
Optional<Student> findByEmailAndName(String email, String name);
  • nativeQuery = true means "this is plain SQL; pass it to JDBC/the database unchanged". It uses table and column names.
  • Named parameters: :email in the query, bound via @Param("email"); order doesn't matter. Positional: ?1, ?2 follow the parameter order.
  • With @Query present, the method name no longer matters for the query, so keep it short and meaningful.
  • Best for complex SQL: multiple joins, database-specific features.

JPQL (Jakarta Persistence Query Language)

SQL-like, but written against entities and their properties, not tables and columns. Useful when you think in the entity model or can't rely on the physical schema. Hibernate translates it to SQL (Hibernate's own dialect is called HQL, essentially the same thing).

SQL (native)JPQL
SELECT * FROM student WHERE email = :emailSELECT s FROM Student s WHERE s.email = :email
Table student, column user_emailEntity Student (case-sensitive), property email
JOIN department d ON s.dept_id = d.idJOIN s.department d (navigate the association)

Joins in JPQL: explicit vs implicit

-- explicit join
SELECT s FROM Student s JOIN s.department d WHERE d.active = true

-- implicit join (path navigation, no JOIN keyword)
SELECT s FROM Student s WHERE s.department.active = true

-- both become SQL like:
-- select s.id, s.name, s.dept_id from student s
--   join department d on s.dept_id = d.id where d.active = true

You never mention dept_id: the mapping (Lecture 30) supplies the join condition. LEFT JOIN, inner joins and so on work as in SQL.

Sorting with Sort

Sorting in the database (ORDER BY) beats fetching unsorted rows and sorting in Java. Sort generates the clause:

Sort sort = Sort.by("age").descending();                        // ORDER BY age DESC
Sort sort = Sort.by(Sort.Direction.ASC, "name");                 // ORDER BY name ASC
Sort sort = Sort.by("name").ascending()
                .and(Sort.by("age").descending());               // ORDER BY name ASC, age DESC
List<Student> students = studentRepository.findAll(sort);

Default direction is ascending. Demo: four Adityas (ages 29, 27, 25, 24) returned 24→29 ascending, 29→24 with .descending(). GET /api/student/name/Aditya needed its own path, because /{name} clashed with /{id}: IllegalStateException: Ambiguous handler methods.

Correction: the lecture's endpoint ignores the name:
fetchAll(String name) calls studentRepository.findAll(sort), which sorts all students. name is never used. It looked right only because every row was an Aditya. Verified: with a Rohit added, the "Aditya" endpoint returned Rohit too. Filter and sort with a derived query that takes a Sort: 
List<Student> findByName(String name, Sort sort);   // where name = ? order by age
// verified: returned only the four Adityas, sorted

Pagination with Pageable, Page and Slice

Fetching 2 million rows at once overloads the database, the network and the API. Fetch pages instead: 10,000 rows, then the next 10,000…

Pageable pageable = PageRequest.of(0, 2);          // page number (0-based), page size
Page<Student> page = studentRepository.findAll(pageable);
List<Student> students = page.getContent();
  • Pageable is an interface; PageRequest.of(page, size) (optionally with a Sort) is its implementation.
  • Page numbers are 0-based. PageRequest.of(4, 10) skips pages 0–3 (40 rows) and returns rows 41–50.
  • Demo: page 0 size 2 → ages 29, 27; page 1 → 25, 24.
  • In practice take page and size from query parameters, so the frontend asks for the next page.
Page methodReturns
getContent()The rows of this page
getNumber() / getSize() / getNumberOfElements()Page index / requested size / rows actually on this page
getTotalElements() / getTotalPages()Totals across all pages (need a count query)
hasNext() / hasPrevious() / isFirst() / isLast()Navigation

Page vs Slice

  • Page extends Slice and adds getTotalElements()/getTotalPages(). To know them it runs a second, count query.
  • Verified: findAll(PageRequest.of(0, 2)) ran … offset ? rows fetch first ? rows only plus select count(s1_0.id) from student, giving totalElements = 5, totalPages = 3.
  • Verified: a Slice<Student> findSliceByName(String name, Pageable p) ran only one query, and still knew hasNext() (it fetches size + 1 rows).
  • Use Slice for infinite-scroll / "load more" when you don't need totals; the count over millions of rows is expensive.

Spring Data JPA's five responsibilities (recap)

  1. Common CRUD operations, via SimpleJpaRepository.
  2. Repository implementation at runtime, via the proxy.
  3. Deriving queries from method names, via the query-method infrastructure.
  4. Custom queries: @Query, native SQL or JPQL.
  5. Pagination and sorting: Sort, Pageable, Page/Slice.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • save decides persist vs merge by "is the entity new?", not by "is it detached?". For an entity with a generated id, "new" means id == null (or a @Version of null). An entity whose id you set manually is considered not new, so save calls merge, which first SELECTs to check existence. Verified: saving a Manual entity with id = 5 ran select … where id=? then insert. Implement Persistable<ID> to control isNew() if that extra select matters.
  • Don't call Optional.get() blindly. It throws NoSuchElementException for a missing id. Use orElseThrow(() -> new StudentNotFoundException(id)) and map it to 404 in the @RestControllerAdvice (Lecture 17).
  • Repository methods are already transactional. SimpleJpaRepository is annotated @Transactional(readOnly = true), with read-write transactions on modifying methods. A service method calling several repository methods still needs its own @Transactional to make them one unit (and for dirty-checking updates, as shown above).
  • Always sort when paginating. Without an ORDER BY the database may return rows in any order, so pages can overlap or skip rows between requests. Use PageRequest.of(page, size, Sort.by("id")).
  • Modifying queries need @Modifying. An @Query("update Student s set s.age = :age where s.id = :id") must also carry @Modifying (and run in a transaction). It bypasses the persistence context, so add clearAutomatically = true if managed entities could go stale.
  • Projections: return an interface or record (interface StudentNameOnly { String getName(); }) from a repository method to fetch only some columns, which is often a better fix than loading whole entities.
  • Returning Page from a controller: since Spring Data 3.3, serialising PageImpl directly logs a warning because its JSON shape isn't stable. Return page.getContent() plus your own metadata DTO, or enable @EnableSpringDataWebSupport(pageSerializationMode = VIA_DTO). Controllers can also take a Pageable parameter directly (?page=0&size=20&sort=age,desc).
  • Interface hierarchy change (Spring Data 3.0): PagingAndSortingRepository no longer extends CrudRepository, and the List… variants were added. Older tutorials show the previous chain. getById/getOne are deprecated in favour of getReferenceById.
  • JPQL is "Jakarta" Persistence Query Language now (the lecture corrects itself mid-sentence), and entity names in JPQL are the entity names (@Entity(name = …), default: the simple class name), not table names.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"the @Query clause WHERE email = email" → named parameters need a colon: WHERE email = :email.
"saveAll calls entityManager.save" → it calls the repository's own save (i.e. persist/merge); EntityManager has no save.
"the proxy decides between SimpleJpaRepository or something else" → the "something else" is the query-method (derivation/@Query) infrastructure, as explained.

Lecture 33: Transactions — ACID, Begin/Commit/Rollback and @Transactional

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #33 · 49 min · Code Army · builds on Hibernate's persistence context (29), AOP around advice (23) and Spring Data JPA (32)

The problem: a money transfer that half-happens

Transfer ₹10,000 from account A to account B. In SQL terms that's two statements:

  1. UPDATE account A: balance − 10,000.
  2. UPDATE account B: balance + 10,000.

Suppose query 1 succeeds, then the database crashes (or query 2 fails for any reason) before query 2 runs. When the database comes back, A has lost ₹10,000 and B never received it. The sum of the two balances has dropped by ₹10,000: money was destroyed in transit, breaking the "conservation of money" principle that money can be neither created nor destroyed.

Definition (transaction):
A group of operations executed as one block: either all of them succeed or none of them take effect. "First succeeded, second failed" is impossible. A block can hold 2 operations or 50; they're all part of the same transaction. Use transactions for critical resources (money, inventory, bookings), where a failure halfway through must never leave a partial result.

ACID: what a transaction promises

PropertyMeaningLecture example
AtomicityLike an atom (the indivisible unit): the transaction can't be split. All or nothing.Debit A and credit B both happen, or neither does
ConsistencyA successful transaction moves the database from one valid state to another valid stateA has ₹5,000 and tries to send ₹10,000. Without a balance check A would end at −₹5,000, an invalid state.
IsolationConcurrent transactions must not corrupt each other's reads and writes; each should see correct, updated valuesTwo withdrawals on account C, below
DurabilityOnce committed, the result survives later failures (crash, restart). It isn't lost or accidentally rolled back.The transfer completes, then the DB crashes. After restart B still has the ₹10,000.
Consistency is partly your job:
The lecturer stresses that the database can't know "balance must not go negative" unless you tell it. The application enforces it with validations (the debitAccount checks below). Database constraints (CHECK (balance >= 0), foreign keys, NOT NULL) are a second line of defence (added).

Isolation: the two-withdrawal example

Account C has ₹6,000. T1 withdraws ₹2,000 and T2 withdraws ₹3,000, at the same time:

Interleaving that breaks isolation (a "lost update")
StepT1T2Balance in DB
1reads 6,0006,000
2reads 6,0006,000
3computes 6,000 − 2,000, writes 4,0004,000
4computes 6,000 − 3,000, writes 3,0003,000 — wrong

₹5,000 was withdrawn, so ₹1,000 should remain. T1's update was lost because both read the same starting value. The correct outcome: T1 reads 6,000 and writes 4,000, then T2 reads 4,000 and writes 1,000.

The lecturer's nuance: isolation doesn't necessarily mean "only one transaction runs at a time". Both can run and make progress; the question is what T2 is allowed to read while T1 is running. The answer is always the correct value. (Isolation levels are promised for the next lecture.)

ACID is a property of relational databases. If you use a SQL database, you get these guarantees; transactions are a database concept, not a Spring invention.

Transactions in SQL, and the physical transaction

BEGIN;                                                    -- MySQL: START TRANSACTION also works
UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 10000 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 10000 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;                                                   -- or ROLLBACK; if something went wrong
  • BEGIN starts the transaction's boundary.
  • COMMIT means "all operations done; make them permanent, nothing more to add".
