  • ROLLBACK means "something failed; take every operation back to the state before BEGIN".
  • Rollback example: A goes 15,000 → 5,000 (succeeded), then crediting B throws. Rollback undoes A's update, so A is back at 15,000.
  • A physical transaction is the actual transaction inside the database. Spring Boot just uses the database's transactions. The lecturer mentions Spring can also create "virtual" transactions, explained later. (Spring's term is a logical transaction: several @Transactional methods sharing one physical transaction, which is what propagation, next lecture, is about.)
Rollback isn't a reverse UPDATE that you or Spring issue:
The lecture's point: nobody runs "add the ₹10,000 back". The database tracks the transaction's changes and simply undoes them, and the lecturer compares it to Cmd+Z, or popping a stack. Precision note (added): the database does do internal work. MySQL InnoDB keeps an undo log of before-images and applies it on rollback (so rolling back a huge transaction takes time); PostgreSQL's MVCC just marks the transaction aborted, so its new row versions are never visible. Either way no application-level "compensating" SQL is involved.

The same transfer at each layer of the stack

The stack from the earlier lectures is Spring Data JPA → JPA/Hibernate (Hibernate implements JPA) → JDBC. The higher the layer, the more the transaction handling is abstracted:

LayerHow you demarcate a transaction
JDBC (26)conn.setAutoCommit(false) … conn.commit() / conn.rollback() (added: JDBC exposes BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK through Connection methods)
Hibernate / JPA (29)session.beginTransaction() / tx.commit() / tx.rollback(); JPA: em.getTransaction().begin()…
SpringOne annotation: @Transactional

What you'd write by hand in Hibernate:

Transaction tx = session.beginTransaction();
try {
    op1();
    op2();
    tx.commit();
} catch (Exception e) {
    tx.rollback();
    throw e;
}

How @Transactional works: an around advice on a proxy

This is the AOP from Lectures 23–25. Spring intercepts methods annotated with @Transactional and effectively wraps them in the code above, as an around advice: begin before proceed(), commit if it returns normally, roll back if it throws.

Under the hood (added): the advice is Spring's TransactionInterceptor. It delegates to a PlatformTransactionManager; with Spring Data JPA that's the auto-configured JpaTransactionManager, which opens the EntityManager and JDBC connection for the transaction.

The lecturer notes you could build the same thing yourself: an @Around advice matching a custom annotation, with Hibernate's begin/commit/rollback inside.

Correction: class-level @Transactional doesn't make the class "one transaction":
The lecture says putting it on a class makes "the whole class run inside one transaction". It actually applies the annotation to every public method of the class. Each call to each method gets its own transaction (unless one is already active and propagation joins it). A method-level annotation overrides the class-level one.

Worked example: transaction-demo project

Entities

  • Account (@Entity, Lombok @Getter @Setter @NoArgsConstructor):
    • Long id (@Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)), String name, BigDecimal balance.
    • debitAccount(BigDecimal amount) and creditAccount(BigDecimal amount), the domain operations with validation (below).
  • TransferRecord is the audit table: id, Long fromAccountId, Long toAccountId, BigDecimal amount, LocalDate transferredAt.
    • Why plain Long ids rather than @ManyToOne Account? The lecturer says it keeps the audit table simple, since nothing but the ids is needed.
    • Constructor: @AllArgsConstructor also included id ("Cannot resolve constructor"), so the lecturer generated a constructor without id in IntelliJ.
public void debitAccount(BigDecimal amount) {
    if (amount == null || amount.signum() <= 0) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
    }
    if (balance.compareTo(amount) < 0) {
        throw new RuntimeException("Insufficient balance");   // lecture: a custom exception would be better
    }
    balance = balance.subtract(amount);
}

public void creditAccount(BigDecimal amount) {
    if (amount == null || amount.signum() <= 0) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
    }
    balance = balance.add(amount);
}
Why signum(), compareTo() and subtract():
BigDecimal is an object, so <, - and + don't work on it. signum() gives −1/0/1; compareTo() compares values. Worth adding: never use equals() for money comparisons, because new BigDecimal("5.0").equals(new BigDecimal("5.00")) is false (the scales differ), while compareTo returns 0. And BigDecimal rather than double, because binary floating point can't represent 0.1 exactly.

Repositories and the transactional service

public interface AccountRepository  extends JpaRepository<Account, Long> {}
public interface TransferRepository extends JpaRepository<TransferRecord, Long> {}

@Service
public class TransferService {
    private final AccountRepository accountRepository;
    private final TransferRepository transferRepository;
    // constructor injection

    @Transactional
    public void transfer(Long fromAccountId, Long toAccountId, BigDecimal amount) {
        Account fromAccount = accountRepository.findById(fromAccountId)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new RuntimeException("Account not found"));
        Account toAccount = accountRepository.findById(toAccountId)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new RuntimeException("Account not found"));

        fromAccount.debitAccount(amount);
        toAccount.creditAccount(amount);

        transferRepository.save(
            new TransferRecord(fromAccountId, toAccountId, amount, LocalDate.now()));
    }
}
  • Three operations (debit, credit, audit record) inside one transaction: all three succeed or none do.
  • The lecture's first attempt failed to compile because the repositories were declared as raw JpaRepository. Fix: supply the generics <Account, Long> and <TransferRecord, Long>.
  • It also passed LocalDateTime.now() to a LocalDate field and switched to LocalDate.now().
  • The lecturer renamed the parameters from fromTransactionId to fromAccountId, the more accurate name.
  • Controllers:
    • AccountController: POST /api/account, body {name, balance} → AccountService.createAccount → accountRepository.save.
    • TransferController: POST /api/transfer, body {fromAccountId, toAccountId, amount} bound to a TransferRecord → transferService.transfer(…).
    • Both return "done". The lecture takes entities directly as request bodies, no DTOs.

Demo run

  1. Startup creates the account and transfer_record tables (MySQL, viewed in DBeaver).
  2. POST /api/account {"name": "Aditya", "balance": 15000} → done. {"name": "Rohit", "balance": 5000} → done.
  3. POST /api/transfer {"fromAccountId": 1, "toAccountId": 2, "amount": 10000} → done. Aditya 5,000, Rohit 15,000, and one row in transfer_record.

Anticipated question: "The balances changed, but we never called save on the accounts. Why?"

Dirty checking (Lecture 29). The transaction opens a persistence context; findById loads both accounts into it as managed entities. At commit, Hibernate flushes: it compares them with their snapshots, sees the changed balances, and issues the UPDATEs itself. No accountRepository.save(fromAccount) is needed.

Flush is not commit: demonstrating rollback

To show that data sent to the database can still be rolled back, the lecturer forces a flush after every step and throws at the end:

@Transactional
public void transfer(Long fromAccountId, Long toAccountId, BigDecimal amount) {
    // ... load both accounts ...
    fromAccount.debitAccount(amount);
    accountRepository.saveAndFlush(fromAccount);     // UPDATE sent to DB now
    toAccount.creditAccount(amount);
    accountRepository.saveAndFlush(toAccount);       // UPDATE sent to DB now
    transferRepository.save(new TransferRecord(fromAccountId, toAccountId, amount, LocalDate.now()));
    transferRepository.flush();                      // INSERT sent to DB now
    throw new RuntimeException("Some error occurred");
}
Rohit tries to send ₹10,000 back (from 2 to 1); starting state Aditya 5,000, Rohit 15,000
RunResult in DBWhy
With @TransactionalUnchanged: 5,000 / 15,000, no new recordFlushed SQL ran inside the open transaction; the exception caused a rollback of all of it
@Transactional commented outChanged: 15,000 / 5,000 and a new record, despite the exceptionNo surrounding transaction: each repository call ran and committed in its own transaction

Verified on Boot 4.1.0 + H2 with the same code: with the annotation the balances stayed at 5000/15000 with 1 record; without it they became 15000/5000 with 2 records.

The real failure mode without a transaction:
Here the exception came at the end, so everything had already been written. The lecturer points out the scarier case: if the exception hit after the debit but before the credit, the money would leave one account and never arrive. That's exactly the opening problem, and @Transactional is what prevents it.
Flush vs commit:
  • Flush sends pending SQL to the database, inside the current transaction. Other transactions can't see it yet (under normal isolation), and it can still be rolled back.
  • Commit ends the transaction and makes the changes permanent and visible (durability).

Anticipated question: "What if I catch the exception inside the method?"

Then the transaction commits. Rollback is triggered only when the exception propagates out of the @Transactional method through the proxy. If you swallow it with try/catch inside, the proxy sees a normal return. Verified: catching a RuntimeException inside the method committed the transfer. If you catch it, either rethrow or mark the transaction for rollback explicitly (TransactionAspectSupport.currentTransactionStatus().setRollbackOnly()).

Corrections & worth knowing

  • By default only unchecked exceptions roll back. Spring rolls back on RuntimeException and Error, but commits on checked exceptions (Exception subclasses that aren't runtime). Verified: a method throwing a checked exception after the debit and credit committed both. @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class) rolled back. The lecture only throws RuntimeExceptions, so it never hits this, but it's a classic interview question.
  • Self-invocation bypasses the transaction. Because it's proxy-based (same rule as AOP in Lecture 23), calling a @Transactional method from another method of the same class (this.transfer(…)) doesn't go through the proxy, so no transaction starts. Verified: a non-transactional selfCall() invoking transferFailTx() left the partial writes committed. Fixes: call it from another bean, restructure, or use TransactionTemplate.
  • Visibility: put @Transactional on public methods. Private methods are never proxied. Since Spring 6.0, protected and package-private methods work with class-based (CGLIB) proxies, but public is the safe convention.
  • Where to put it: on the service layer, around a whole use case (like transfer), not on controllers. Repository methods are already individually transactional (Lecture 32), which is why each call committed on its own in the no-annotation run.
  • Programmatic alternative: TransactionTemplate.execute(status -> { … }) gives explicit boundaries without annotations, useful for a transaction around part of a method.
  • Durability in practice: databases guarantee it with a write-ahead log (InnoDB redo log, PostgreSQL WAL), flushed to disk at commit. The data pages can be written later, because the log can replay them after a crash.
  • @Transactional(readOnly = true) for read-only use cases: Hibernate skips dirty checking and flushing, and some drivers/databases can optimise.
  • Use LocalDateTime/Instant for an audit timestamp. The lecture ends up with LocalDate, which records only the day. Or let the database fill it (@CreationTimestamp, or a column default CURRENT_TIMESTAMP), as the lecturer mentions.
  • No throws Throwable needed for orElseThrow(() -> new RuntimeException(…)). The lecture briefly added one to the signature; with a supplier of an unchecked exception nothing needs declaring.

Gaps worth raising in an interview

  • @Transactional alone doesn't stop the lost update. The lecture's transfer does read (findById) → modify in Java → write: exactly the T1/T2 pattern from the isolation example. Under MySQL's default REPEATABLE READ (or PostgreSQL's READ COMMITTED), two concurrent transfers from the same account can both read 15,000 and one debit is lost. Fixes:
    • Pessimistic lock: @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) on a repository finder, i.e. SELECT … FOR UPDATE.
    • Optimistic lock: a @Version column, with a retry on OptimisticLockException.
    • Atomic SQL: UPDATE account SET balance = balance - :amt WHERE id = :id AND balance >= :amt, checking the affected-row count.
  • Deadlocks. With row locks, transfer 1→2 and a concurrent 2→1 can each hold one lock and wait for the other. Always lock accounts in a consistent order (e.g. lower id first).
  • Missing validation: fromAccountId == toAccountId; the RuntimeException("Account not found") should be a custom exception mapped to 404 (Lecture 17), and "Insufficient balance" to 400/422.
  • Entities as request bodies: the client could send an id or transferredAt. Use a TransferRequest DTO with @NotNull/@Positive (Bean Validation).
  • Idempotency: a retried POST /api/transfer (client timeout) would transfer twice. Real payment APIs take an idempotency key.
  • Transactions across services/databases: one @Transactional covers one database. Cross-service transfers need patterns like saga or outbox, not a local transaction.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"account A decreases by ₹1,000" → ₹10,000.
"its balance wasn't 55,000" (durability example) → ₹5,000.
"Aditya ₹15,000 … ₹1,000" and later "Rohit has ₹1,000" → ₹15,000 in both places.
"the accounts updated because of dirty reads" → dirty checking. A dirty read is an isolation anomaly (reading another transaction's uncommitted data), a completely different thing.
"@Transaction" → @Transactional (org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional; jakarta.transaction.Transactional also works but lacks Spring-specific attributes such as readOnly and isolation).
"in JDBC we'd write the BEGIN/COMMIT SQL keywords" → JDBC does it through Connection.setAutoCommit(false), commit() and rollback().

Next lecture (announced): transaction propagation and isolation levels.

Lecture 34: @Transactional Deep Dive — rollbackFor, Propagation Levels and Isolation Levels

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #34 · 1h00m · Code Army · continues Lecture 33 (transactions, ACID)

The five attributes of @Transactional

Until now we wrote a bare @Transactional. The annotation takes attributes:

@Transactional(
    propagation = Propagation.REQUIRED,
    isolation   = Isolation.READ_COMMITTED,
    timeout     = 5,
    readOnly    = false,
    rollbackFor = IOException.class
)
public void createOrder(…) { … }
AttributeMeaningActual default (added)
propagationWhat happens when this transactional method is called from another method: join the caller's transaction, start a new one, run without one…REQUIRED
isolationHow much concurrent transactions may see of each other's changesIsolation.DEFAULT = the database's own default
timeoutSeconds after which the transaction should time out-1 = no timeout (database/driver default)
readOnlyRead-only or read-write transactionfalse
rollbackForWhich exception types trigger a rollbackEmpty: RuntimeException and Error only
Precision note (added):
The lecture says the values on its slide are the defaults. REQUIRED and readOnly = false are, but READ_COMMITTED and timeout = 5 are just example values. The real defaults are Isolation.DEFAULT and -1 (see table).

The most important three are propagation, isolation and rollbackFor.

rollbackFor: which exceptions roll back

  • Unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and subclasses, no try/catch required) roll the transaction back by default, whether or not you write rollbackFor.
  • Checked exceptions don't roll back by default: the transaction commits. (Verified in Lecture 33's notes.)
  • rollbackFor = SomeCheckedException.class makes that checked exception (and its subclasses) roll back too. A parent class works as well, e.g. rollbackFor = Exception.class.
Worth adding:
"Runtime exceptions always roll back, no matter what" is true only for the defaults. The opposite attribute, noRollbackFor = SomeRuntimeException.class, makes a runtime exception commit instead. Why checked exceptions commit by default: Spring follows the EJB convention that a checked exception is an expected business outcome the caller can handle, while an unchecked one signals an unexpected failure.

Setup: orders and payment audits

Project transaction-demo, reset for this lecture:

  • Order entity: id, productName, amount.
  • PaymentAudit entity: id, amount, orderId (acts as a foreign key to the order), and a new boolean success.
  • OrderController: POST /api/order → orderService.placeOrder(order) → "done". There's no controller for audits: nobody audits directly.
  • OrderRepository / PaymentAuditRepository extend JpaRepository<…, Long>.
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    private final PaymentAuditService paymentAuditService;
    // constructor injection

    @Transactional                                   // OUTER method
    public void placeOrder(Order order) {
        orderRepository.save(order);
        paymentAuditService.audit(order);            // calls into ANOTHER bean
    }
}

@Service
public class PaymentAuditService {
    private final PaymentAuditRepository paymentAuditRepository;

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRED)   // INNER method
    public void audit(Order order) {
        PaymentAudit paymentAudit = new PaymentAudit(order.getAmount(), order.getId(), true);
        paymentAuditRepository.save(paymentAudit);
    }
}
Transcript fixes from the setup:
  • Import the Spring annotation, org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional, not jakarta.transaction.Transactional. The Jakarta one works but has fewer attributes: no isolation, timeout or readOnly; its propagation (TxType) has no NESTED.
  • ORDER is a reserved word in SQL. The first startup failed with "You have an error in your SQL syntax … near 'order'", so the entity needs @Table(name = "orders").

What propagation means: outer and inner methods

placeOrder is the outer method; audit, which it calls, is the inner method. Propagation is always configured on the inner method and answers: when I'm called and a transaction may already exist, should I join it, start my own, run without one, or refuse?

We already saw one case of it. A @Transactional service calling a repository method makes the repository call join the service's transaction.

Physical transaction:
If placeOrder and audit run in the same database transaction, that's one physical transaction. Both methods share the same EntityManager and persistence context (Lecture 29), and if either rolls back, both roll back. Spring's term for each method's scope inside it is a logical transaction: several logical scopes can map to one physical transaction (added).

Propagation only applies when the call goes through the Spring proxy, i.e. to another bean, which is why the lecture puts audit in a separate PaymentAuditService. A this.audit() call inside the same class ignores the inner annotation (self-invocation, Lecture 33).

REQUIRED (default): join if one exists, else create

Rule:
If a transaction exists, use it; otherwise create a new one. Either way, the method requires a transaction.

Anticipated question: "If the inner method sets its own isolation/timeout, which wins?"

The outer. The lecture sets isolation = READ_COMMITTED, timeout = 30 on placeOrder and isolation = SERIALIZABLE, timeout = 5 on audit. Because audit joins the existing transaction, it inherits the existing transaction's settings, and its own are ignored.

Verified: an inner REQUIRED method annotated isolation = SERIALIZABLE, readOnly = true reported the outer's READ_COMMITTED and readOnly = false at runtime. Spring ignores the inner values silently. Setting validateExistingTransaction = true on the transaction manager makes it throw on such mismatches instead (added).

Demo run: four experiments with REQUIRED

#ScenarioResultWhy
1Happy path: POST {"productName": "iPhone 17 Pro Max", "amount": …}"done"; two INSERTs; rows in orders and payment_audit (success = 1)One physical transaction commits both
2Outer throws RuntimeException("Some error occurred") after audit() returns (Speaker, ₹2,000)Both INSERTs ran, but neither row existsRolling back the shared transaction undoes the audit too
3Inner throws RuntimeException("Something went wrong"), and inner catches it itself"done"; both rows savedThe exception never crossed the proxy, so to Spring nothing failed
4Inner throws, and outer catches it with an empty catch (Laptop, ₹50,000)Client gets an error; neither row savedUnexpectedRollbackException — see below

Experiment 4 explained: "silently rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only"

  1. audit() throws. The exception passes through audit's transactional proxy, and the inner scope sees a runtime exception.
  2. The inner scope doesn't own the physical transaction (it only joined it), so it can't roll back directly. It marks the shared transaction rollback-only.
  3. placeOrder catches the exception and returns normally, so its proxy tries to commit.
  4. The transaction manager sees the rollback-only flag, rolls back instead, and throws UnexpectedRollbackException so the caller isn't misled into thinking the commit happened.

Verified message: "Transaction silently rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only". Catching an inner exception doesn't save the joined transaction.

When to use REQUIRED:
When the inner work depends on the outer: an audit entry should exist only if the order exists. That's why it's the default: it's what you want most of the time. If the outer method has no transaction, audit simply creates its own.

REQUIRES_NEW: always a fresh, independent transaction

Rule:
No existing transaction → create one (like REQUIRED). Existing transaction → suspend it and create a new physical transaction, with a separate EntityManager, persistence context and (added) a separate JDBC connection.

Suspend doesn't mean commit or roll back; it means pause. The outer transaction waits while the inner one runs to completion, then resumes.

ScenarioResult (lecture demo; verified)
Normal flow (Laptop)Both rows saved; looks just like REQUIRED
Outer throws after audit() (Camera, ₹90,000)Audit row saved, order row gone. An inconsistent state: a payment audit for an order that doesn't exist.
Inner throws, outer catchesOrder saved, audit row gone, no UnexpectedRollbackException. The inner transaction rolled back on its own; the outer committed normally.
When to use REQUIRES_NEW (and when not):
Only when inner and outer are genuinely independent. For order + payment it's dangerous, as the Camera demo shows. Typical good uses (added):
  • Writing an audit/failure log that must survive even when the main operation rolls back.
  • Generating a sequence number.
  • Sending an outbox record that must persist.
Worth flagging (added):
  • A second connection. Each REQUIRES_NEW holds a second connection while the first is suspended. Under load, with a small HikariCP pool, all threads can hold one connection and wait for a second: pool exhaustion or deadlock.
  • A real foreign key would block. The inner transaction can't see the outer's uncommitted INSERT. The demo works only because orderId is a plain column; with a real FK the inner insert would wait on the outer's lock (or fail).

The remaining propagation levels

SUPPORTS: "a transaction is welcome, but not required"

  • Transaction exists → join it (behaves exactly like REQUIRED: shared rollback).
  • No transaction → run without one (a plain method call). Verified: isActualTransactionActive() was false.
  • Use: helper methods that have no opinion and should follow whatever the caller does. Rarely used.

MANDATORY: "I must be called inside a transaction"

  • Transaction exists → join it. No transaction → throw.
  • Demo: remove @Transactional from placeOrder and POST a "Bottle" (₹200). The result: IllegalTransactionStateException: No existing transaction found for transaction marked with propagation 'mandatory' (verified, same message).
  • Use: sensitive inner operations, like auditing a payment, that are only safe as part of a caller's transaction. The lecturer argues it fits this very use case better than REQUIRED: if the order service runs without a transaction, the audit refuses to run rather than risk an inconsistency nobody would notice.
Worth flagging (verified):
In that MANDATORY failure, the order row was still saved. With no outer transaction, orderRepository.save had already committed in its own repository-level transaction before audit() threw. MANDATORY stops the audit, but it can't undo what the non-transactional caller did. It's a guard that surfaces the bug (loudly), not a rollback mechanism.

NOT_SUPPORTED: "always run without a transaction"

  • Transaction exists → suspend it and run without one. None → just run.
  • Verified: inside a transactional caller, the inner method saw isActualTransactionActive() == false.
  • Use: operations that must not be part of a transaction.

NEVER: "a transaction must NOT exist"

  • Transaction exists → throw. None → run without one. Stricter than NOT_SUPPORTED, which suspends instead of complaining.
  • Verified: IllegalTransactionStateException: Existing transaction found for transaction marked with propagation 'never'.

NESTED: join, but with a savepoint

A savepoint is a marker inside a transaction you can roll back to without rolling back everything:

BEGIN;
op1; op2;
SAVEPOINT sp1;
op3; op4;
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1;   -- undoes op3, op4; op1, op2 survive; transaction still open
COMMIT;
  • NESTED: transaction exists → stay in the same physical transaction but set a savepoint when the inner method starts. None → create a new one (like REQUIRED).
  • If the inner method fails, only its work is rolled back (to the savepoint). The outer can catch the exception and still commit its own work.
  • If the outer rolls back, the inner work is rolled back too, because it's the same transaction. That's the difference from REQUIRES_NEW.
Correction (verified on Boot 4.1.0): NESTED doesn't work with Spring Data JPA out of the box:
With the auto-configured JpaTransactionManager, calling a NESTED method inside a transaction threw NestedTransactionNotSupportedException: Transaction manager does not allow nested transactions by default. After setting nestedTransactionAllowed = true it still failed: "JpaDialect does not support savepoints" (Hibernate's JPA dialect doesn't expose savepoints through Spring). The reason: a savepoint would roll back rows in the database but not the entities already cached in the persistence context. NESTED is for JDBC-based access (JdbcTemplate with DataSourceTransactionManager, Lecture 27), where savepoints work.
Propagation cheat-sheet
PropagationCaller HAS a transactionCaller has NO transactionTypical use
REQUIRED (default)Join itCreate newDependent work (order + audit)
REQUIRES_NEWSuspend it, create newCreate newIndependent work that must commit regardless (logs)
SUPPORTSJoin itRun withoutNeutral helpers
MANDATORYJoin itThrowMust only run inside a caller's transaction
NOT_SUPPORTEDSuspend it, run withoutRun withoutWork that must not be transactional
NEVERThrowRun withoutAssert "never call me inside a transaction"
NESTEDSame transaction + savepointCreate newPartial rollback (JDBC only)

REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW vs NESTED

QuestionREQUIREDREQUIRES_NEWNESTED
Physical transactionsOne (shared)Two (independent)One, with a savepoint
Inner fails, outer catchesEverything rolls back + UnexpectedRollbackExceptionInner rolled back, outer commitsInner rolled back to savepoint, outer commits
Outer fails after inner succeededBoth roll backInner stays committedBoth roll back
Inner's own isolation/timeoutIgnoredAppliedIgnored

Isolation: the three read anomalies

Isolation matters when several transactions run concurrently. First the three problems it's about, from most to least severe:

1. Dirty read: reading someone else's uncommitted change

TimeT1T2
1BEGIN
2UPDATE balance = 20,000 (was 10,000), not committed
3BEGIN; reads balance = 20,000
4ROLLBACK → balance back to 10,000Keeps working with 20,000, a value that never officially existed

2. Non-repeatable read: the same row, a different value

TimeT1T2
1BEGIN; reads balance = 10,000
2UPDATE balance = 8,000; COMMIT
3Reads the same row again → 8,000

The lecture's other example: row 1001, Aditya read at time 1 comes back as 1001, Rohit at time 2. Less severe than a dirty read, because the new value was committed.

Correction: why a non-repeatable read is a problem:
The lecture frames it as T1 possibly re-reading forever because others keep committing. The real issue: within one transaction, two reads of the same row disagree, so a decision based on the first read (e.g. "balance is 10,000, so allow a 9,000 withdrawal") may be wrong by the time T1 acts. Reports that read a row twice can contradict themselves.

3. Phantom read: the same query, a different set of rows

-- T1
SELECT * FROM employee WHERE salary > 100000;   -- A, B, C
-- T2: INSERT INTO employee (… salary 150000 …); COMMIT;
-- T1, same query again
SELECT * FROM employee WHERE salary > 100000;   -- A, B, C, D  ← a "phantom" row

Non-repeatable read = an existing row's value changed (UPDATE). Phantom read = the set/count of rows matching a condition changed (INSERT/DELETE).

The four isolation levels

isolation = Isolation.… is an enum, like Propagation. Each level decides which anomalies you accept, a trade-off between concurrency (how many transactions can proceed together) and consistency.

Stricter going down (SQL standard)
Isolation levelDirty readNon-repeatable readPhantom read
READ_UNCOMMITTEDPossiblePossiblePossible
READ_COMMITTEDPreventedPossiblePossible
REPEATABLE_READPreventedPreventedPossible (some DBs prevent it)
SERIALIZABLEPreventedPreventedPrevented
  • READ_UNCOMMITTED is the weakest: maximum concurrency, but even dirty reads happen. Not used in production.
  • READ_COMMITTED prevents dirty reads: "concurrency, but not so much that we read uncommitted data".
  • REPEATABLE_READ additionally prevents non-repeatable reads; only phantoms remain possible.
  • SERIALIZABLE prevents all three: the result is as if transactions ran one after another. The lecturer's nuance: that doesn't mean the database literally runs them one at a time. It may use locks so they overlap but never interfere in critical sections; they only look serial.
Why not always SERIALIZABLE:
Concurrency collapses: it starts to look like T1, then T2, then T3… The lecturer ties this to multithreading: if two transactions can safely run together, they should. Pick the weakest level whose anomalies your use case can tolerate. The lecture recommends READ_COMMITTED or REPEATABLE_READ.

Isolation.DEFAULT

The fifth enum value: use whatever the underlying database's default is.

  • MySQL (InnoDB): REPEATABLE_READ.
  • PostgreSQL: READ_COMMITTED.
  • (Added: Oracle and SQL Server also default to READ_COMMITTED.)

The lecture closes by setting isolation = Isolation.REPEATABLE_READ on audit, and repeats the REQUIRED rule: since audit joins placeOrder's transaction, that setting is ignored. If placeOrder sets no isolation, the database default applies. Put the isolation on the outer method.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • "Repeatable read is the most used" depends on the database. It's MySQL's default, so MySQL apps use it by default. READ_COMMITTED is the default, and therefore most common, level on PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server.
  • Real databases differ from the textbook table.
    • InnoDB REPEATABLE_READ uses MVCC snapshots, so plain SELECTs see no phantoms; locking reads use next-key (gap) locks to block inserts into the range.
    • PostgreSQL REPEATABLE_READ is snapshot isolation: no phantoms, but "write skew" is possible.
    • PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE (SSI) doesn't block; it aborts one transaction with a serialization failure, so the application must retry. MySQL's SERIALIZABLE uses shared locks.
  • Isolation levels don't fix the lost update by themselves (Lecture 33's read-modify-write transfer). At READ_COMMITTED the last writer silently wins. Use SELECT … FOR UPDATE (@Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)), @Version optimistic locking, or atomic UPDATEs. The four anomalies above are about reads.
  • readOnly = true is more than documentation. With Hibernate, Spring sets the session's flush mode to manual (no dirty checking or flush) and marks the JDBC connection read-only. PostgreSQL then rejects writes, and read replicas/routing data sources can use the flag.
  • timeout is in seconds. With JPA it's applied as a query timeout on statements, and checked when statements run. It doesn't interrupt pure Java code that's hanging. Exceeding it raises a TransactionTimedOutException/QueryTimeoutException and rolls back.
  • You can check the current state at runtime with TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive() / getCurrentTransactionIsolationLevel(), which is how the claims above were verified.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"the slide shows the default values" → only REQUIRED and readOnly=false are defaults (see table).
"@Transaction" → @Transactional.
"Propagation.REQUIRED_NEW" / "required new" → REQUIRES_NEW.
"payment order's audit" / "payment order service" → PaymentAuditService.
"non-repeatable read: balance ₹1,000" → ₹10,000.
"the inner method would implement without transaction" (SUPPORTS) → execute without a transaction.
"NESTED: the operations done so far won't be rolled back" → only the inner work after the savepoint is rolled back; if the outer fails, everything is (see NESTED).

Next (announced): transactions are done; the next topic is Spring Security.

Lecture 35: Spring Security Introduction — Security Vocabulary, the Authentication Object, Stateful vs Stateless and Boot's Default Security

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #35 · 1h19m · Code Army · first lecture of the Spring Security module

The problem: every endpoint is public

The starting project spring-security-demo has only spring-boot-starter-webmvc and one controller:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/students")
public class StudentController {
    @GetMapping
    public String getStudent() { return "Student retrieved successfully"; }
}

GET localhost:8080/api/students from Postman returns the message to anyone. Until now the mental model was just request → controller → service → repository → DB, and we never asked:

  • Is this caller allowed to make this call?
  • Is this a public endpoint?
  • Did we authenticate or authorize the user at all?

Anyone could fetch, create, update or delete data. The goal of the lecture: put a security layer in front, so the endpoint first demands a username/password.

Security vocabulary: assets, threats and trust boundaries

Assets: anything valuable

Asset typeExamples
DataUser email, password, username, bank details: any user data your app holds
OperationalThe operations your endpoints perform: create/delete a user, transfer money
SecuritySession IDs, JWT tokens: anything security-related
InfrastructureDatabase, application, servers
AvailabilityHow long the app stays up. If it's down, real users can't transact or store data.

Threat, vulnerability, attack

  • Threat — anyone or anything intending to harm an asset.
  • Vulnerability — a weak point in your application that can be exploited.
  • Attack — a threat exploiting a vulnerability.
One-liner from the lecture:
"Threat + vulnerability = attack."

Example: an attacker wants admin access (the threat) and opens /admin. The app allows unlimited password attempts (the vulnerability). A script (Python, say) tries password combinations until one works: a brute-force attack, and the application is compromised.

Trust boundary

Whenever data moves from one level to another, e.g. browser → internet → application → database, it crosses a trust boundary. Data crossing a boundary must not be trusted, because it may have been changed on the way.

Why the client can never be trusted:
Front-end code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) runs in the user's browser. Hiding an "Admin panel" button for non-admins isn't security: a user can edit the HTML/JS to reveal it. They don't even need the button, because it just calls /api/admin, which anyone can hit with curl or Postman. Access checks must happen on the server.

Authentication vs authorization

AuthenticationAuthorization
QuestionWho are you? Verify a claimed identity ("I am Aditya") using credentials (username + password)What may you do? Which endpoints/parts of the app you can access, typically based on your role (admin, user, manager)
Security-guard analogyThe guard checks your employee card before letting you into the buildingBeing inside doesn't let you walk into the CEO's room
Instagram analogyLogging inYou can delete your own posts, not a friend's
OrderFirstSecond: roles matter only after the claim is verified

Even a public API is an authorization decision: its access rule is "everyone". Every endpoint should have some access control, and you can tighten it later.

Authentication factors and MFA

FactorExamples
Something you knowPassword, PIN, security answer
Something you haveSmart card, authenticator app (Google/Microsoft Authenticator), cryptographic key, phone receiving an OTP
Something you areFingerprint, iris scan, face recognition
What makes MFA strong:
Multi-factor authentication means proofs from different factors: password + authenticator OTP, or password + fingerprint. Password + PIN is two things from the same factor, so it isn't real MFA.

Brute force vs honest mistakes

  • A real user may mistype a password, so allow a few retries; don't lock them out after one miss (bad UX).
  • But attempt after attempt after attempt is a pattern that suggests a brute-force attack. Unlimited attempts is exactly the vulnerability from the example above.
  • Don't reveal which part was wrong. Say "Invalid username or password", never "wrong password". Otherwise an attacker learns the username is valid, which makes brute force easier. You may log the exact reason internally; never send it to the client.

Worth adding: Spring Security doesn't lock accounts or rate-limit out of the box. Typical defences are rate limiting per IP/account, increasing back-off or temporary lockout, and CAPTCHA after N failures.

Spring Security's core terms

TermMeaning
IdentityAny entity whose actions the system must recognise: a human user, a customer, a scheduled job…
CredentialsProof offered for a claimed identity: username + password, OTP…
PrincipalThe identity currently being dealt with, i.e. the current user of this request
AuthoritiesPermissions/capabilities of the principal, e.g. COURSE_READ, USER_DELETE. In Spring each is a GrantedAuthority.
RolesA group term bundling authorities: ADMIN (may delete users), USER, MANAGER
PermissionsFiner-grained rights (which exact APIs); in practice treated the same as authorities
AuthenticationThe Spring Security interface holding principal, credentials, authorities and authenticated status
SecurityContextContainer holding the current Authentication
SecurityContextHolderGives you the current SecurityContext from anywhere
Identity isn't a database row:
It's tempting to think identity = the users row 1001, Aditya, 29. An account is one representation of an identity; one person can have several accounts. Identity is the conceptual claim ("I am Aditya") that you verify through credentials.
Precision note (added): roles are authorities with a prefix:
In Spring Security a role is just a GrantedAuthority whose name starts with ROLE_. hasRole("ADMIN") checks for the authority ROLE_ADMIN; hasAuthority("COURSE_READ") checks a plain authority.

The Authentication object: before and after login

The same interface represents both the login attempt and the verified user. The lecture calls these the "authentication request" and the "authentication principal":

FieldAuthentication request (before)Authentication principal (after)
principal"aditya": just the claimed nameThe full user details of Aditya, loaded from the DB
credentialsThe raw passwordnull: cleared, no longer needed
authoritiesEmpty: nothing proven yete.g. COURSE_READ, COURSE_UPDATE
authenticatedfalsetrue
 
public interface Authentication extends Principal, Serializable {
    Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> getAuthorities();
    Object getCredentials();
    Object getDetails();        // extra info: remote IP, session id…
    Object getPrincipal();
    boolean isAuthenticated();
    void setAuthenticated(boolean isAuthenticated);
    // getName() comes from java.security.Principal
}

Stored passwords are compared in hashed form (salt and pepper are promised for a later lecture).

Worth knowing (verified on Boot 4.1.0 / Spring Security 7):
  • The concrete class for username/password is UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken, with factory methods unauthenticated(principal, credentials) and authenticated(principal, credentials, authorities).
  • After a Basic-auth login the controller saw class UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken, principal of type User (a UserDetails), and credentials=null. ProviderManager erases credentials after successful authentication, exactly the "before/after" table.
  • Spring Security 7 also adds a factor authority (FACTOR_PASSWORD) recording how the user authenticated. This is part of its new built-in MFA support.

SecurityContext and SecurityContextHolder

"Context" in Spring always means a container:

  • ApplicationContext holds beans.
  • The persistence context holds entities.
  • SecurityContext holds the current Authentication.

Why a central container? Otherwise you'd pass the Authentication into every method. Instead, anyone who needs it asks the holder:

SecurityContext context = SecurityContextHolder.getContext();
Authentication authentication = context.getAuthentication();
Object principal = authentication.getPrincipal();
// also: getCredentials(), getAuthorities(), getDetails(), isAuthenticated(), getName()
How the holder works: ThreadLocal:
In a servlet app, one thread serves one request. The holder stores the SecurityContext in a ThreadLocal of that thread, so any code on that thread can read the current user. When the request finishes and the thread goes back to the pool, the context is cleared, so the next request served by the same thread (another user) can't inherit it. Added: ThreadLocal is the default strategy (MODE_THREADLOCAL). Code on other threads, e.g. @Async methods, doesn't see the context unless you propagate it (e.g. DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor or MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL).

HTTP is stateless: how does the server remember a login?

Each HTTP request carries no memory of previous ones. The user logs in with /login, then calls /getUser: how does the server know this second request comes from an authenticated user? Asking for the password on every like, comment or upload would be absurd UX. There are two architectures.

Stateful authentication (sessions)

  1. The browser sends /login?username=aditya&password=secret123 (for illustration only; never send passwords in a URL).
  2. The server authenticates, builds the Authentication object, and stores it server-side under a session ID.
  3. The response carries Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID=abc123, and the browser stores the cookie.
  4. Next request: GET /getUser with Cookie: JSESSIONID=abc123. The server looks up the stored authentication for abc123, sees authenticated=true, and allows the call if the authorities permit it.

Only the session ID lives in the browser; the session state lives on the server: in app memory, a DB, or a cache like Redis.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Authenticate once; later requests just look up the sessionStorage for every user's session
Full server control: invalidate any time (a bank app re-authenticating every 15 minutes), track last access timeScaling: with several replicas behind a load balancer, the session lives on only one of them
  • Problem: login landed on replica 1, which stored the session. The next request goes to replica 2, which knows nothing, so the user gets "please log in again".
  • Sticky sessions (hash the user/IP so they always hit the same replica) work, but break uniform load distribution. The lecturer calls this the wrong approach.
  • A central session store (distributed cache, e.g. Redis) that every replica queries is the standard fix. Added: in Spring this is Spring Session (spring-session-data-redis).
  • Session theft: anyone holding your session ID is you to the server, so the cookie must be well protected.
Correction: what session fixation actually is:
The lecture describes session fixation as "the session ID stays fixed to the authentication, so the user is never re-authenticated". The real attack: the attacker plants a session ID they know in the victim's browser before login (e.g. via a crafted link). The victim logs in, the server marks that same session as authenticated, and the attacker now uses it.
  • The real fix is the lecturer's second suggestion: issue a new session ID at login. Spring Security does this by default (the changeSessionId strategy).
  • Expiring sessions (the 24-hour invalidation) limits damage from theft but isn't the fixation fix.
  • Protect the cookie with the HttpOnly (no JS access), Secure (HTTPS only) and SameSite flags.

Stateless authentication (tokens)

The server stores nothing between requests. Every request carries a token, and the server builds a fresh Authentication from it each time and puts it in the SecurityContext for that request only. Any replica can handle any request; no shared session store is needed.

Self-contained (signed) tokenOpaque token
ContentsCarries everything: subject (user), authorities, issuer, expiry, plus a signature proving it wasn't tampered withA random identifier, e.g. x7Fq9LmP…, meaningless by itself
How the server gets the AuthenticationVerifies the signature and reads the claims; no external lookupAsks a token service (auth server) to resolve it: close to a session ID
ExampleJWT (its own lecture later)Many OAuth2 access tokens

Is an opaque token + token service really stateless? The lecturer admits it looks almost stateful. It's called stateless from the application's point of view when the token service is a separate system, whereas a Redis session store is part of your app. "It's a matter of definition."

The real distinction (lecture's key point):
Stateful vs stateless isn't about where the credential travels (cookie or header). A token can live in a cookie and still be stateless. It's about whether the server reuses a stored authentication (stateful) or recreates it from the request every time (stateless).

Bearer tokens

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi…: the user gets the token at login and must send it in a header on every request.

Correction: "bearer" means possession is enough, not proven ownership:
The lecture says a bearer token tells the server "the sender is the actual owner". It's the opposite. Bearer means whoever holds the token can use it, and the server can't tell a stolen token from the real owner's. That's why bearer tokens must travel only over HTTPS, have short lifetimes, and be stored carefully.
  • "Bearer" also doesn't imply self-contained: a bearer token can be a JWT or opaque.
  • Signed isn't encrypted: a JWT's payload is readable by anyone. The signature only prevents tampering.

Request lifecycles side by side

StepStateful (session)Stateless (token)
1POST /login with username/password; extract and authenticate credentialsGET /profile with Authorization: Bearer … (after an earlier login returned the token)
2Create Authentication, put it in SecurityContext, save the context in the HttpSession, return the session cookieExtract the token and create an Authentication from it
3Later GET /profile with Cookie: JSESSIONID=abc123 → load session → SecurityContext → holderPut it in a new SecurityContext → holder
4Authorization check → controller → service → repository
5Clear the SecurityContextHolder (the ThreadLocal)Clear the holder; nothing saved in any session. The next request repeats everything.

Authentication and authorization happen before the controller, so before the DispatcherServlet. That's the filter layer from the filters lecture.

Worked example: adding spring-boot-starter-security

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>   <!-- no version: managed by the starter parent -->

No classes written, nothing configured. Just the dependency and a Maven reload.

Demo run

  1. Startup logs: Using generated security password: 56… plus "This generated password is for development use only. Your security configuration must be updated before running your application in production." A new random password is printed on every restart.
  2. Postman GET /api/students → 401 Unauthorized.
  3. Postman → Authorization tab → Basic Auth, username user + the generated password → "Student retrieved successfully".
  4. Browser localhost:8080/api/students → redirected to a generated /login page. Sign in with the same credentials and you're sent back to the original URL, which shows the data.
  5. Every endpoint (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) is now protected.

Verified on Boot 4.1.0: no credentials → 401 with header WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="Realm". The same request with Accept: text/html (browser-like) → 302 to /login. Spring picks the entry point by request type.

Where Spring Security sits: the filter chain

Adding the starter puts classes on the classpath, and auto-configuration creates beans from them, including these filters. Two auto-configurations answer two questions:

Auto-configurationAnswersDefault
SecurityAutoConfiguration (+ the servlet web-security config)Which requests need authentication, and by which mechanism?All requests; form login for browsers, HTTP Basic for API clients like Postman
UserDetailsServiceAutoConfigurationWhich users exist, and where are they loaded from?One in-memory user user with a random password (no database needed)

The default filter chain bean is roughly:

@Bean
SecurityFilterChain defaultSecurityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http.authorizeHttpRequests(requests -> requests.anyRequest().authenticated());
    http.formLogin(withDefaults());
    http.httpBasic(withDefaults());
    return http.build();
}

The default user is built with InMemoryUserDetailsManager (username user, generated password, enabled). Both defaults back off: define your own SecurityFilterChain or user-details bean and Spring Boot stops creating its own (next lectures). The generated user exists only so you can test that security works.

Worth knowing (verified on Boot 4.1.0):
  • Class locations. In Boot 4 these classes live in the new spring-boot-security module (org.springframework.boot.security.autoconfigure…). The default chain is in ServletWebSecurityAutoConfiguration; in Boot 3 it was SpringBootWebSecurityConfiguration.
  • The debug log lists the default chain: SecurityContextHolderFilter, HeaderWriterFilter, CsrfFilter, LogoutFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, DefaultLoginPageGeneratingFilter, BasicAuthenticationFilter, …, AnonymousAuthenticationFilter, ExceptionTranslationFilter, AuthorizationFilter.
  • The lecture says the default user has ROLE_USER. Actually Boot's default user has no roles unless you set spring.security.user.roles.

Overriding the default user via properties

# application.properties
spring.security.user.name=aditya
spring.security.user.password=secret123
spring.security.user.roles=USER,ADMIN

After a restart, no password is generated. aditya/secret123 → 200; secret12 → 401. Verified: the authentication's authorities became ROLE_ADMIN, ROLE_USER (Spring adds the ROLE_ prefix to each role) plus the FACTOR_PASSWORD factor.

The CSRF surprise: correct credentials, still 401

The lecturer adds @PostMapping createStudent, @PutMapping updateStudent and @DeleteMapping deleteStudent. Without credentials they return 401, as expected. With the correct aditya/secret123, POST still returns 401. GET works.

The reason is CSRF protection (Cross-Site Request Forgery), covered in detail later. It's enabled by default and applies to state-changing methods (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE). GET is exempt because it shouldn't change anything.

The workaround in the lecture: an endpoint that hands out the token.

@GetMapping("/csrf")                       // own path: a second bare @GetMapping clashed at startup
public CsrfToken getToken(CsrfToken csrfToken) {
    return csrfToken;                      // Spring injects the current token
}
  1. GET /api/students/csrf (with Basic auth) returns {"headerName": "X-CSRF-TOKEN", "parameterName": "_csrf", "token": "…"}.
  2. Add the header X-CSRF-TOKEN: <token> to the POST/PUT/DELETE requests.
  3. Now they return "Student created / updated / deleted successfully".
Worth knowing (verified on Boot 4.1.0):
  • Why 401 and not 403. The debug log shows CsrfFilter: Invalid CSRF token found, i.e. an access-denied (403) decision. Spring then forwards to /error, which is itself secured; that error dispatch runs as anonymous, so the Basic entry point answers 401. The status is misleading; the real cause is the missing CSRF token.
  • The token is tied to the session. It's stored in the HttpSession (JSESSIONID cookie). Postman keeps cookies automatically, which is why the lecture's flow works. With the token but without the session cookie, the POST failed again (401).
  • The token changes on every read. Since Spring Security 6 it's XOR-masked (BREACH protection), so each value you receive differs, but all are valid for that session.
Correction: what CSRF really is:
The lecture describes it as "using another site's session ID on this site". The actual attack: you're logged in to bank.com (session cookie in your browser) and visit evil.com. Evil's page auto-submits a form to bank.com/transfer, and your browser automatically attaches bank.com's cookie, so the forged request runs as you. The CSRF token defeats this because evil.com can't read it.
  • The protection matters for credentials the browser sends automatically: cookies, and browser-cached Basic auth.
  • Stateless APIs that authenticate with an Authorization: Bearer header typically disable CSRF, a choice made later when writing our own security config.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • 401 vs 403. Despite its name, 401 Unauthorized means unauthenticated (no or invalid credentials; comes with WWW-Authenticate). 403 Forbidden means authenticated but not allowed. A classic interview question.
  • HTTP Basic is not a bearer token. In Postman's Authorization tab they're different options.
    • Basic sends Authorization: Basic base64(username:password) on every request. The lecture blurs "HTTP Basic" and "bearer token" together.
    • Bearer sends Authorization: Bearer <token>.
    • Base64 is encoding, not encryption, so Basic auth is only acceptable over HTTPS.
  • HTTPS = HTTP over TLS ("HTTP Secure"), not "secured transfer protocol".
  • Where the filters come from: the servlet container knows one filter, DelegatingFilterProxy. It delegates to Spring's FilterChainProxy, which picks the matching SecurityFilterChain (you can have several, e.g. one for /api/**, one for the web UI).
  • Stored passwords must be hashed with a slow, salted algorithm (BCrypt/Argon2 via PasswordEncoder), never encrypted or plain. The default in-memory user's password is stored with the {noop} (plain) prefix, which is another reason it's development-only.
  • JWT revocation is the price of statelessness. A self-contained token stays valid until it expires, so real systems pair short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens, or keep a deny-list, which is partly stateful again.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"grand authorities" → GrantedAuthority.
"Spring context is a container that stores the authentication" → SecurityContext.
"spring.security.username" → spring.security.user.name.
"update mapping" → @PutMapping (the lecturer corrects himself).
"HTTP Basics / bearer token are the same" → see Corrections.
"deployment use only" in the log message → "development use only" (the lecturer corrects himself).

Next (announced): our own security configuration and filters, and creating/authenticating our own users.

Lecture 36: Spring Security Hands-On (Part 1) — User/Role Entities, Password Hashing with BCrypt, Salt & Pepper, Registration

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #36 · 1h26m · Code Army · continues Lecture 35; login via Spring Security is promised for the next lecture

Goal and project setup

Store real users in a database and authenticate them by username/password, instead of Boot's generated user. New project (package in.strikes, "spring-practical-demo") from Spring Initializr with these dependencies:

  • Spring Data JPA
  • Spring Web
  • MySQL Driver
  • Spring Security
  • Lombok (added later)

application.properties gets the datasource URL/username/password, spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update, show-sql and format_sql. The first start failed without them, because a JPA starter on the classpath requires a datasource.

A test endpoint is added:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {
    @GetMapping("/hello")
    public String hello() { return "hello"; }
}

Calling it returns 401. With Basic auth user + the generated password it returns hello. So Spring already built a user details object in memory, stored its password, and matched the incoming password against it.

What authentication boils down to

  1. The client sends an identity claim (username, email or phone: anything unique, which is why you can't log in with just your name) plus a credential (password).
  2. Spring builds an unauthenticated Authentication (principal = "aditya", credentials = password, no authorities, authenticated=false).
  3. The app loads the stored password for that username (from a DB, memory, a third party…).
  4. It compares the stored password with the incoming password. On a match it builds an authenticated Authentication: principal = the user details, credentials = null, authorities = e.g. ROLE_USER, authenticated=true. This goes into the SecurityContext (Lecture 35).

Two Spring Security types sit behind the default in-memory user, and both are what we must plug our own users into:

  • UserDetails — an interface: Spring's view of "a user".
  • UserDetailsService — the service that loads a UserDetails by username.

Define your own user source and Boot's default backs off (next lecture).

The UserDetails contract

public interface UserDetails extends Serializable {
    Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> getAuthorities();
    String getPassword();
    String getUsername();
    default boolean isAccountNonExpired()     { return true; }
    default boolean isAccountNonLocked()      { return true; }
    default boolean isCredentialsNonExpired() { return true; }
    default boolean isEnabled()               { return true; }
}
FlagMeaning (lecture's examples)
isEnabled()Account disabled, not deleted, e.g. the user violated platform policies
isAccountNonLocked()Temporarily locked, e.g. too many wrong passwords ("locked for 30 minutes" in banking apps)
isAccountNonExpired()The account itself expires, e.g. all accounts expire on 31 December
isCredentialsNonExpired()The password expired, e.g. "change your password every month"

The flags are phrased negatively ("non-expired", "non-locked") so that true means "all good". The lecturer's rule: your entity can be anything (Customer, Student, User…) with any fields. It must have a unique login key and a password; the flags and authorities are optional, only if your app needs them. Spring Security works in terms of UserDetails, so your entity must be mapped/wrapped into a UserDetails, e.g. getUsername() → entity's username, getPassword() → entity's password. (Added, verified on Spring Security 7.1: the four flags are default methods returning true, so an implementation only needs the first three methods.)

Worked example: User and Role entities

Why not a role column in the user table? One user can have several roles (Aditya = USER + ADMIN, Rohit = MANAGER, Sohan = ADMIN + MANAGER), and one role belongs to many users: many-to-many. A role column would need the row 1, Aditya twice (once per role), which the primary key id forbids. So there's a separate role table plus a join table (Lecture 30).

@Entity @Getter @Setter @NoArgsConstructor
public class User {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)     // the identity claim must be unique
    private String username;

    @Column(nullable = false)                    // passwords may repeat, so no unique
    private String password;

    private boolean enabled = true;              // the only UserDetails flag this app needs

    @ManyToMany
    @JoinTable(name = "user_roles",
        joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "user_id"),
        inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "role_id"))
    private Set<Role> roles = new HashSet<>();
}

@Entity @Getter @Setter @NoArgsConstructor
public class Role {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
    private String name;                         // e.g. ROLE_USER, ROLE_ADMIN
}
  • Unidirectional: no Set<User> in Role. We always go from a user to their roles, never from a role to its users, and a bidirectional mapping would need both sides kept in sync.
  • Startup check: DBeaver shows three tables, role (id, name), user (id, enabled, password, username) and user_roles (user_id, role_id).
  • Import fix: the entity class was first named role, and @ManyToMany complained ("attribute value type should not be role"): IntelliJ had picked another Role class. Renaming to Role and importing our own fixed it.
Worth flagging (added):
  • @ManyToMany is LAZY by default. When Spring Security later calls getAuthorities() outside a transaction, the roles may throw LazyInitializationException. Login code commonly uses fetch = FetchType.EAGER for roles, or loads them with a fetch join / entity graph (Lecture 31).
  • user is a reserved word in PostgreSQL, H2 and SQL Server (it worked here on MySQL). Prefer @Table(name = "users"), just as order needed orders in Lecture 34.

Repositories

public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    Optional<User> findByUsername(String username);   // login always looks users up by username
}
public interface RoleRepository extends JpaRepository<Role, Long> {
    Optional<Role> findByName(String name);
}

The usual service layer between entity and repository will be Spring Security's UserDetailsService, covered next lecture.

Never store raw passwords: hash them

Storing aditya | secret123 means anyone with table access (or a leaked dump) can log in as Aditya.

EncryptionHashing
DirectionTwo-way: a key decrypts it backOne-way: you can't get from the hash back to the password
Key managementThe key must be stored somewhere, and it can leak tooNo key
Fits passwords?No: we never need the plain password backYes: store hash(password); at login hash the input and compare
The key insight:
We never need to know the password, only to check that the incoming one equals the stored one. Comparing hashes does that. Even the app's developers can't see users' passwords, provided you never log raw passwords.

Why a deliberately slow hash

SHA-256 is very fast, and for passwords that's exactly wrong.

  • How attackers guess: they keep huge lists (GBs, millions of entries) of commonly used passwords like password, aditya123, 12345. Humans pick weak, patterned passwords (name + @123, date of birth), so a bot tries every entry.
  • Why speed matters: with a fast hash, each guess costs nanoseconds. Make every hash cost milliseconds and the same list takes years, while a real user barely notices the extra wait at login.
  • The standard slow algorithm is BCrypt, which Spring Security uses.
Verified (Boot 4.1.0, this laptop):
One BCryptPasswordEncoder (default strength 10) hash took ~58 ms; strength 12 took ~242 ms (each +1 doubles the work). SHA-256 computed 100,000 hashes in ~75 ms, i.e. under 0.001 ms each. BCrypt is roughly 75,000× slower per guess, which is exactly the point.
Precision note (added): which attack slow hashing stops:
The lecture illustrates slow hashing with a bot hammering the login form. Online guessing through your login endpoint is mainly stopped by rate limiting / lockout (Lecture 35), since network latency already slows it. Slow hashing matters most for offline cracking: when the password table leaks, the attacker hashes guesses on their own GPUs at unlimited speed, and only a slow, salted hash makes that impractical.

Rainbow tables and salting

Hashing algorithms are public, and attackers know apps use BCrypt and a few others. So they can precompute a table: common password → its hash under each algorithm, e.g. secret123 → ER34@12…. If your hashed table leaks (a hack, an insider), a bot looks up each stored hash and gets the plain password back. Such a precomputed lookup table is a rainbow table.

  • Salt — a random string generated by the application (not the user), different for every password. It's appended to the password before hashing: hash("secret123" + "RE4567_…").
  • Why it defeats rainbow tables: the stored hash is of password + random salt, which no precomputed table contains.
  • Where the salt goes: it must be available at login to recompute the hash. BCrypt handles this for you.
  • Pepper — like salt but a fixed secret (the lecture uses qwerty), the same for all passwords: hash(password + salt + pepper). It isn't stored in the DB but in an environment variable or restricted file. It's a second line of defence: a DB leak alone isn't enough to crack hashes.
Worth knowing (verified): the salt lives inside the BCrypt string:
$2a$10$t7kovpeHrgy25SOC2iIkC.C9WDy7nyDYLXSNgKlPapI4QnIt9Z9BO (60 chars):
  • $2a$ — the BCrypt version.
  • 10$ — the cost: 210 rounds.
  • The next 22 characters are the salt: 16 random bytes, i.e. 128 bits. The lecture says "16-bit", which is off by a factor of eight.
  • The remaining 31 characters are the hash.
So no separate salt column is needed: matches() reads the salt and cost back out of the stored string. Spring's BCryptPasswordEncoder does not add a pepper; you'd implement that yourself (or use a keyed hash/HSM).

PasswordEncoder and BCryptPasswordEncoder

MethodDoes
String encode(CharSequence rawPassword)Salt + hash; use it when storing a password (registration, password change)
boolean matches(CharSequence rawPassword, String encodedPassword)Re-hash the raw input with the stored salt and compare; use it at login. Note the order: raw first, encoded second.
default boolean upgradeEncoding(String encoded)"Should this stored hash be re-hashed?", e.g. after raising the cost
 
@Configuration
public class SecurityConfig {
    @Bean
    public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
        return new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
    }
}

Demo run: same password, different hashes

  1. Print passwordEncoder.encode("secret123") twice: two different strings, identical only up to $2a$10$. The salt differs each time.
  2. passwordEncoder.matches("secret123", thatHash) printed true. Verified: true for secret123, false for aditya123.

Anticipated question: "Why did adding the PasswordEncoder bean make the generated password stop working?"

In the demo, as soon as the BCryptPasswordEncoder bean existed, Basic auth with user + generated password returned 401. The lecturer worked around it by commenting out the bean and writing new BCryptPasswordEncoder() inside the controller/service.

The actual reason (verified: the log shows "Encoded password does not look like BCrypt", and the request gets 401):

  • Boot's default user stores its generated password as plain text.
  • Without an encoder bean it's prefixed {noop}, meaning "compare as plain text".
  • Once you declare a PasswordEncoder bean, Spring Security uses your BCrypt encoder to check it, and a plain UUID isn't a BCrypt hash, so nothing matches.

The workaround is only for this interim demo. Hard-coding new BCryptPasswordEncoder() bypasses dependency injection. The proper fix, next lecture, is your own UserDetailsService whose users have BCrypt-hashed passwords, with the bean restored.

Worked example: the registration endpoint

Signing up sends POST /api/users/register with {"username": "aditya", "password": "secret123"}. The front end asks twice to confirm the password, but the back end receives it once. We use DTOs rather than the entity: the response must never include the password, even hashed.

@Getter @Setter
public class UserRegisterRequestDto { private String username; private String password; }

@Getter @Setter
public class UserRegisterResponseDto { private String username; private String message; }

@Service
public class AuthService {                     // named for its job; a controller can use several services
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    private final PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder;
    // constructor injection

    public UserRegisterResponseDto register(UserRegisterRequestDto dto) {
        User user = new User();
        user.setUsername(dto.getUsername());
        // NOT user.setPassword(dto.getPassword()) — that stores the raw password
        String encodedPassword = passwordEncoder.encode(dto.getPassword());
        user.setPassword(encodedPassword);
        user.setEnabled(true);
        // roles: left empty for now (a role service comes later)
        userRepository.save(user);

        UserRegisterResponseDto response = new UserRegisterResponseDto();
        response.setUsername(user.getUsername());
        response.setMessage("User saved successfully");
        return response;
    }
}

@PostMapping("/register")
public ResponseEntity<UserRegisterResponseDto> register(@RequestBody UserRegisterRequestDto dto) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(authService.register(dto));
}
  • Validation (@NotBlank, @Size(min = 8)…) could go on the DTO (Lecture 16).
  • Once encoded, the raw password is gone. No one can recover it unless it was logged or seen in a debugger.

Demo run

  1. POST /api/users/register → 401. Every endpoint is still protected, including sign-up: registration will need to be made public (next lecture).
  2. Added Basic auth with the generated user → still 401 because of CSRF (Lecture 35). Added the @GetMapping("/token") endpoint returning CsrfToken, fetched the token, and sent it as X-CSRF-TOKEN.
  3. Result: {"username": "aditya", "message": "User saved successfully"}. An INSERT appears in the log, and DBeaver shows aditya, enabled=1, and a long $2a$10$… hash instead of secret123.

The absurdity the lecturer points out: we had to log in as Boot's user to register. Fixing that means telling Spring Security which endpoints are public and plugging our users in (next lecture).

A hand-written login, and why we won't keep it

// AuthService — illustration only
public boolean login(UserRegisterRequestDto dto) {
    Optional<User> userOptional = userRepository.findByUsername(dto.getUsername());
    User user = userOptional.get();                          // assumes the user exists
    String encodedPassword = user.getPassword();
    return passwordEncoder.matches(dto.getPassword(), encodedPassword);
}

Demo: POST /api/users/login (Basic auth + a fresh CSRF token, because the old one was invalid after the restart) → true. With aditya123 → false.

Why hand-rolling login isn't enough:
This only answers "is the password right?" once. It doesn't remember the login, create a session or token, or check on every later request that the caller is logged in and allowed.
  • Spring Security's filter chain does all of that for every request.
  • Your job is just to register users and wrap your User in a UserDetails.
One-liner from the lecture:
"Focus on your business code." AOP takes the infrastructure code, validation takes validation code, exception handling takes exception code, and Spring Security says "leave the security code to me".

Gaps worth raising in an interview

  • Duplicate usernames: register doesn't check findByUsername first. The unique constraint then throws DataIntegrityViolationException, a 500. Check first and return 409 Conflict, but keep the constraint, because a check-then-insert race is still possible.
  • Optional.get() in login gives a 500 for unknown usernames and reveals which usernames exist. Return the same "invalid username or password" either way, and ideally spend similar time: run a dummy matches so timing doesn't enumerate users.
  • No roles are assigned at registration. New users should get ROLE_USER (looked up with roleRepository.findByName), seeded at startup.
  • Password policy: no minimum length or breached-password check. BCrypt only uses the first 72 bytes of the input, so very long passphrases are silently truncated.
  • Field injection (@Autowired private PasswordEncoder) and new BCryptPasswordEncoder() inside services were demo shortcuts. Use constructor injection of the single PasswordEncoder bean.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Prefer the delegating encoder for new apps. PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder() stores {bcrypt}$2a$10$… (verified). The {id} prefix lets you switch to Argon2/scrypt later while old hashes keep working, and upgradeEncoding tells you when to re-hash (verified: a strength-12 encoder reported true for a strength-10 hash).
  • Modern alternatives: OWASP now ranks Argon2id first, then scrypt, then BCrypt (cost ≥ 10). Spring provides Argon2PasswordEncoder and SCryptPasswordEncoder (these need Bouncy Castle), plus Pbkdf2PasswordEncoder. BCrypt remains a solid default.
  • Tune the cost so one hash takes roughly 100 ms or more on your server: new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12). Higher cost means more work per login, which is also a DoS consideration.
  • Lombok and boolean enabled: Lombok generates isEnabled(), which conveniently matches UserDetails.isEnabled() later.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"if you decrypt this password" (rainbow table) → you hash it; hashes aren't decrypted.
"SHA 256" read as "shar 256" → SHA-256.
"16-bit salt" → 16 bytes (128 bits).
"rest mapping" → @RequestMapping; "@Setter" said for @Service (the lecturer corrects himself).
"the user's sign-up happened" at the end of login matching → the user's login succeeded.
"getName()" on the DTO → getUsername() (Lombok getters were missing at first).

Next (announced): let Spring Security handle login. That means wrapping User in UserDetails, implementing UserDetailsService, and making /register public.

Lecture 37: Spring Security Hands-On (Part 2) — UserDetails, UserDetailsService, the Filter-Chain Architecture, AuthenticationManager & DaoAuthenticationProvider

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #37 · 1h32m · Code Army · continues the Lecture 36 project

Where we left off

  • The project so far:
    • UserController with /hello, /register, the /token CSRF helper, and the dummy /login.
    • Request/response DTOs, the User/Role entities and their repositories.
    • AuthService.register, which encodes the password with PasswordEncoder and sets enabled = true.
  • Today: delete the hand-written login from the service and controller. Spring Security will do login through its filters.
  • Missing piece: a new user gets no roles.

Assigning roles: never trust the client

The tempting shortcut is to accept "roles": ["ROLE_USER", "ROLE_ADMIN"] in the register body and call user.setRoles(…). That's wrong. A client can claim anything, and everyone would say "I'm an admin". Most users are plain users; admins and managers are a handful of internal people, and the application decides who they are. So the client sends only username + password, and the server attaches roles from the database.

Seeding roles through an internal endpoint

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/roles")
public class RoleController {
    private final RoleService roleService;
    // constructor injection
    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<String> addRole(@RequestBody Role role) {   // entity is tiny (just name), so no DTO
        roleService.addRole(role);
        return ResponseEntity.ok("done");
    }
}

@Service
public class RoleService {
    private final RoleRepository roleRepository;
    public void addRole(Role role) { roleRepository.save(role); }   // no validation, for now
}

This is meant as an internal/private API used from Postman, never by normal clients. Inserting rows directly in DBeaver would also work. Demo: after fetching a CSRF token and using Basic auth, POST /api/roles {"name": "ROLE_USER"} → "done". Then ROLE_ADMIN. Both rows now exist in role.

Registration now attaches ROLE_USER

// AuthService.register, before userRepository.save(user)
Role role = roleRepository.findByName("ROLE_USER").get();   // returns Optional; lecture assumes it exists
user.getRoles().add(role);

Every new user also gets a row in user_roles.

Wrapping our User in UserDetails

Spring Security speaks only UserDetails (its contract: username, password, authorities, four status flags). Our app has its own User entity. The bridge is a class that implements UserDetails and delegates to our User: an adapter/wrapper.

public class CustomUserDetails implements UserDetails {
    private final User user;
    public CustomUserDetails(User user) { this.user = user; }

    @Override public String getUsername() { return user.getUsername(); }
    @Override public String getPassword() { return user.getPassword(); }   // the BCrypt hash
    @Override public boolean isEnabled()  { return user.isEnabled(); }

    @Override
    public Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> getAuthorities() {
        return user.getRoles().stream()
                .map(role -> new SimpleGrantedAuthority(role.getName()))
                .toList();
    }
    // isAccountNonExpired / isAccountNonLocked / isCredentialsNonExpired:
    // not overridden — the interface defaults return true
}
  • GrantedAuthority is itself an interface. SimpleGrantedAuthority is the usual implementation, wrapping a string like "ROLE_USER".
  • The overrides: IntelliJ's "implement methods" offers the three abstract methods. We also override isEnabled(), the only flag our entity stores. (The lecture placed CustomUserDetails in the entity package.)

UserDetailsService: one method, despite the name

It sounds big, but it's a single-method (functional) interface: UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String username), meaning "given a username, give me a UserDetails".

@Service
public class CustomUserDetailsService implements UserDetailsService {
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    // constructor injection

    @Override
    public UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String username) throws UsernameNotFoundException {
        User user = userRepository.findByUsername(username)
