                .orElseThrow(() -> new UsernameNotFoundException("User not found"));
        return new CustomUserDetails(user);          // return the wrapper, not our entity
    }
}
  • UsernameNotFoundException is Spring Security's ready-made exception; Spring handles it and answers the client.
  • Alternative without a wrapper class: return Spring's own org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User, which also implements UserDetails, via its builder: User.withUsername(user.getUsername()).password(user.getPassword()).authorities(…).disabled(!user.isEnabled()).build(). The lecturer prefers the wrapper, so the method is just return new CustomUserDetails(user).

The missing piece: who does the actual checking?

We now have both halves: UserDetailsService → repository → UserDetails, and the PasswordEncoder bean. Something must receive the login attempt and connect them:

  1. Receive the incoming unauthenticated Authentication (username + raw password).
  2. Ask the UserDetailsService: loadUserByUsername(username) → UserDetails.
  3. Take the stored encoded password and call passwordEncoder.matches(rawPassword, encodedPassword).
  4. Check the account status flags (isEnabled, non-locked, non-expired, credentials non-expired).
  5. On success, return an authenticated Authentication (principal = UserDetails, credentials = null, authorities = roles). On failure, throw an exception that goes back to the client.

That class is DaoAuthenticationProvider. How a request gets there is the architecture below.

The Spring Security architecture: Tomcat to the filter chains

  • DelegatingFilterProxy is the only filter Tomcat knows about. It does nothing but forward the request into Spring.
  • FilterChainProxy holds several SecurityFilterChains and tries them in order, like an if / else-if ladder. The first whose matcher fits handles the request; the rest are skipped.
  • No chain matches (e.g. no catch-all /** chain)? Spring Security doesn't handle the request at all: it goes straight to the DispatcherServlet as before.
  • Boot's default, when you define none: one chain matching any request, which is why every endpoint needed a login.
public interface SecurityFilterChain {
    boolean matches(HttpServletRequest request);   // e.g. does the path match /api/**?
    List<Filter> getFilters();                      // the filters of this chain, called one after another
}

We never implement this by hand. HttpSecurity is a builder (Builder pattern) whose build() returns a SecurityFilterChain with the matcher and filters we configured.

Filter order inside a chain

#CategoryExamples
1Exploit protectionCsrfFilter, security headers
2AuthenticationUsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, BasicAuthenticationFilter
3Exception-handling boundaryExceptionTranslationFilter (turns security exceptions into 401/403 or a redirect)
4AuthorizationAuthorizationFilter

Authentication always runs before authorization. You don't memorise all the filter names; you learn the flow and a few important filters. Boot's default chain contains SecurityContextHolderFilter, CsrfFilter, LogoutFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, BasicAuthenticationFilter, AnonymousAuthenticationFilter, ExceptionTranslationFilter, AuthorizationFilter and others (the full list was verified in Lecture 35).

Authentication filters: form login vs HTTP Basic

Form loginHTTP Basic
ClientBrowser HTML form: username, password, SubmitAPI client such as Postman (Authorization tab → Basic Auth)
RequestPOST /login, Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded, body username=aditya&password=secret123Any request carrying Authorization: Basic base64(username:password)
FilterUsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilterBasicAuthenticationFilter
Enabled byhttp.formLogin(…)http.httpBasic(…)
What an authentication filter does, and doesn't do:
Its only job is to turn the incoming request into an unauthenticated Authentication object. For username/password that's a UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken: principal "aditya", credentials "secret123", no authorities, authenticated=false. Both filters above produce the same token type. The filter then hands it to the AuthenticationManager ("authenticate this") and doesn't verify anything itself.

AuthenticationManager, ProviderManager and providers

public interface AuthenticationManager {
    Authentication authenticate(Authentication authentication) throws AuthenticationException;
    // in: unauthenticated request token; out: authenticated token, or an exception
}

Different login styles need different checking logic:

  • Username/password — load the hash from the DB and compare.
  • JWT — verify the token and read its claims.
  • OTP — e.g. look the code up in Redis.

So the manager stays generic and delegates to providers, one per Authentication type:

  1. The filter calls authenticationManager.authenticate(token). The implementation is ProviderManager.
  2. ProviderManager asks each provider supports(token.getClass()). For UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken, DaoAuthenticationProvider says yes; the JWT and OTP providers say no.
  3. DaoAuthenticationProvider.authenticate(token) runs the five steps above, using our CustomUserDetailsService and the BCrypt PasswordEncoder.
  4. The authenticated Authentication goes into the SecurityContext, via SecurityContextHolder (Lecture 35).
Correction: providers don't "override" AuthenticationManager:
The lecture says DaoAuthenticationProvider, the JWT provider etc. "override/implement the AuthenticationManager". They implement a separate interface, AuthenticationProvider (authenticate + supports). Only ProviderManager implements AuthenticationManager, and it holds a list of providers (verified by javap on Spring Security 7.1). Also: JwtAuthenticationProvider exists in the OAuth2 resource-server module; an OTP provider would be your own class.

Worked example: SecurityConfig

@Configuration
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {             // re-enabled (Lecture 36 had it commented out)
        return new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
    }

    @Bean                                                  // optional: Spring would build this itself
    public DaoAuthenticationProvider authenticationProvider(CustomUserDetailsService userDetailsService,
                                                            PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder) {
        DaoAuthenticationProvider provider = new DaoAuthenticationProvider(userDetailsService);
        provider.setPasswordEncoder(passwordEncoder);
        return provider;
    }

    @Bean                                                  // replaces Boot's default "authenticate everything" chain
    public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http,
                                                   DaoAuthenticationProvider provider) throws Exception {
        http
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())                  // so POSTs work without the X-CSRF-TOKEN dance
            .authenticationProvider(provider)
            .formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())          // adds UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter
            .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())          // adds BasicAuthenticationFilter
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/api/users/register").permitAll()     // sign-up must be public
                // .requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")       // example: needs ROLE_ADMIN
                // .requestMatchers("/api/public/**").permitAll()       // e.g. contact page, public feed
                .anyRequest().authenticated());            // everything else requires login
        return http.build();                               // Builder pattern → SecurityFilterChain
    }
}
  • AuthService gets the PasswordEncoder via constructor injection again; the Lecture 36 hard-coded new BCryptPasswordEncoder() is removed.
  • Customizer.withDefaults() means "use the standard configuration", which is what you want almost always.
  • With CSRF disabled, the /token endpoint isn't needed any more. The controller keeps just /register and /hello.
  • No /login endpoint is written. Spring Security provides it. Unauthenticated browser access redirects there, and a front-end login page would POST to it.
  • The requestMatchers path must be the full path, /api/users/register. The lecture first wrote just /register and corrected it, since the controller is mapped under /api/users.

Demo run

  1. Startup: no generated password in the log any more.
  2. Delete the old Aditya row, restart. POST /api/users/register {"username": "aditya", "password": "secret123"} with No Auth → "User saved successfully". A user_roles row links the user to ROLE_USER.
  3. GET /api/users/hello without auth → 401. With Basic aditya/secret123 → still 401. The log shows LazyInitializationException: cannot lazily initialize a collection … roles … no session.
  4. Fix, then restart: Basic aditya/secret123 → hello.
  5. Unknown rohit → 401. Register rohit/secret1234, and now both users can call /hello.

Anticipated question: "Why the LazyInitializationException, and why an entity graph?"

@ManyToMany is LAZY by default. loadUserByUsername loads the User without its roles and returns. Later DaoAuthenticationProvider calls getAuthorities(), which touches user.getRoles(), but the persistence context is closed, so there's no session to lazy-load from. The lecturer's fix is an entity graph (Lecture 31), which fetches roles together with the user:

public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "roles")
    Optional<User> findByUsername(String username);
}

This is why knowing the internals pays off: you understand the error instead of pasting a fix from ChatGPT without knowing why it works.

Verified (Boot 4.1.0, H2, same classes):
  • Without the entity graph, Basic auth returned 401 and the log showed LazyInitializationException.
  • With it, 200, and the authorities were ROLE_USER (+ Spring Security 7's FACTOR_PASSWORD).
  • Wrong password and unknown user both returned 401.
  • Why open-in-view didn't prevent it (added): Boot's open-session-in-view is a Spring MVC interceptor, i.e. it starts after the security filters. During authentication there's no open persistence context.

The remaining flaw (as the lecturer sees it)

With Basic auth, every request must carry username + password, like Instagram asking for your password before every like or comment. The server doesn't remember the login yet. Sessions (stateful) or JWT (stateless) come in the next lectures.

Precision note (verified): form login already remembers you:
That's true for HTTP Basic: after a successful Basic request, a follow-up with only the cookie got 401, because Basic auth doesn't save the context in the session. Form login is stateful by default, though. POST /login (form-encoded) returned 302 to / with a JSESSIONID, and a follow-up with only that cookie got 200: the SecurityContext was stored in the HttpSession (Lecture 35's stateful flow).

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Filters aren't chosen by content type. The lecture says the request's content type decides between the form and Basic filters. Actually each filter checks what it handles:
    • UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter acts only on POST /login with form parameters. It doesn't read a JSON body; JSON login needs a custom filter or endpoint.
    • BasicAuthenticationFilter acts on any request with an Authorization: Basic header, not just /login.
  • Why the generated password disappeared: not because of CustomUserDetails (a plain class), but because a UserDetailsService bean (our @Service) now exists. Boot's UserDetailsServiceAutoConfiguration backs off when a UserDetailsService, AuthenticationProvider or AuthenticationManager bean is present.
  • The DaoAuthenticationProvider bean is optional. With exactly one UserDetailsService and one PasswordEncoder bean, Spring builds a DaoAuthenticationProvider itself; the lecturer writes it out only to show what happens.
  • Version note (verified on Spring Security 7.1): DaoAuthenticationProvider's only constructor takes the UserDetailsService. The old no-arg constructor + setUserDetailsService(…) (deprecated in 6.x) is gone, so tutorials using them won't compile on Boot 4.
  • Unknown user and wrong password look the same. By default DaoAuthenticationProvider hides UsernameNotFoundException and throws BadCredentialsException for both (the "don't reveal which part was wrong" advice from Lecture 35). It also runs a dummy password match for unknown users, to reduce timing differences.
  • Disabling CSRF is only safe for stateless APIs. This config enables form login with sessions, exactly the cookie-based setup CSRF attacks target (Lecture 35). Disabling it is fine for a Basic/JWT-only API, but a browser app with form login should keep it on.
  • /api/roles is a privilege-escalation hole. With anyRequest().authenticated(), any logged-in user can create roles. Protect it: .requestMatchers("/api/roles/**").hasRole("ADMIN"). Remember hasRole("ADMIN") checks the authority ROLE_ADMIN, which is why role names are stored with the prefix.
  • findByName("ROLE_USER").get() in register throws NoSuchElementException (a 500) if roles weren't seeded. Seed them at startup (a CommandLineRunner or a data.sql) or orElseThrow with a clear message.
  • Sessions store the principal. With form login, the CustomUserDetails (and the wrapped User entity) is saved in the HttpSession, so it should be Serializable if sessions are ever persisted or replicated (Spring Session/Redis). Also keep the password hash out of it, or let Spring erase credentials.
  • Where to put CustomUserDetails: a security package reads better than entity. It's an adapter, not a JPA entity.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"grand authority / simple grand authority" → GrantedAuthority / SimpleGrantedAuthority.
"DAO authentication filter" (when creating the bean) and "our DAO authentication filter calls getAuthorities" → DaoAuthenticationProvider.
"loadUserByUserName" / "load yuser by username" → loadUserByUsername.
"lazily initialise the roles" as the goal of the entity graph → the entity graph loads them eagerly for that query (the lecturer says both).
"Setter" for @Service (the lecturer corrects himself).

Next (announced): remembering the logged-in user across requests, with stateful sessions and then JWT.

Lecture 38: Sessions & JWT — Stateful Session Cookies, SessionCreationPolicy, Building JWT from First Principles, and Stateless Login with Spring Security

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #38 · 1h22m · Code Army · continues the Lecture 36–37 project; stateful/stateless theory from Lecture 35

Recap: the project and the problem

  • The project so far:
    • User–Role (many-to-many), RoleController, UserController (/register, /hello), AuthService.register (BCrypt + ROLE_USER).
    • CustomUserDetails/CustomUserDetailsService.
    • SecurityConfig: PasswordEncoder, DaoAuthenticationProvider, and a chain with /api/users/register permitted and everything else authenticated.
  • /hello now reports who's logged in. It takes an Authentication parameter and returns "Hello, you are logged in as " + authentication.getName(). Postman with Basic aditya/secret123 gives "Hello, you are logged in as aditya".
  • The problem: switch Postman to No Auth and the next call is 401. HTTP requests are stateless, so the server treats every request as brand new. It builds the unauthenticated Authentication, authenticates, builds the authenticated one (principal = user details, credentials = null, authorities = ROLE_USER, authenticated = true), serves the request, and forgets.

Stateful: the server already keeps sessions

The stateful idea (Lecture 35): store the authenticated object server-side under a random session ID, e.g. asdf123. Send that ID to the client in a cookie; the client sends it back on every request; the server looks the ID up and reuses the stored Authentication, with no login again.

Spring Security already does this by default; we just weren't using it:

  1. Postman's cookies for the Basic-auth request show a JSESSIONID.
  2. Browser demo: open localhost:8080/api/users/hello → redirected to the generated /login. Log in as aditya/secret123 → "Hello, you are logged in as aditya".
  3. Open the same URL in a new tab → no login asked. DevTools → Application → Cookies → localhost:8080 shows JSESSIONID, a random string that carries no information itself; the server maps it to the stored authentication.
  4. Delete that cookie and refresh → back to the login page. Log in again and a new JSESSIONID is issued.
  5. /logout (provided by Spring Security) → redirected to login. The old session is no longer valid, so you must log in again, which creates a fresh session.
Precision note (verified in Lecture 37): which logins actually use the session:
Form login saves the SecurityContext in the HttpSession, which is why the browser demo works. HTTP Basic doesn't (since Spring Security 6). The JSESSIONID Postman received for a Basic request holds no authentication; resending it alone still gives 401. (Postman normally resends stored cookies automatically, yet the No Auth call still failed.) The lecture's "we just weren't sending the session ID back" applies to form login, not Basic. After /logout the browser may still hold the old cookie; the server has invalidated the session behind it.

SessionCreationPolicy

http.sessionManagement(session ->
        session.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.IF_REQUIRED));   // the default
PolicyMeaning
IF_REQUIRED (default)Create a session when authentication needs one
ALWAYSAlways create one
NEVERSpring Security never creates a session (added: but uses one if the app created it)
STATELESSNever create and never use a session: the choice for JWT

The stateful downside is storing sessions. With several replicas, a session held by one server is unknown to the others (sticky sessions or a central store are needed, Lecture 35). The lecturer notes stateless isn't always better: stateful is fast, because the authentication isn't rebuilt on every request. Each has pros and cons.

Stateless: give the client a token that describes it

After login, the server builds the Authentication, gives the client a token containing everything needed to rebuild it (who you are, your roles…), and then discards the object. On each request the client sends the token in a header; the server recreates the Authentication from it and discards it again. Nothing is stored, so any replica can serve any request. The best-known token format is JWT, JSON Web Token.

Building JWT from first principles: why each naive idea fails

Say the server wants to hand the client this JSON and later rebuild the Authentication from it (principal = sub, authorities = role, authenticated = true):

{ "sub": "aditya", "role": "ROLE_USER" }
Attempt → how the client breaks it
#AttemptAttackResult
1Base64URL-encode the JSON into a compact, URL/header-safe string (qwe…)Encoding is reversible by anyone: decode, change ROLE_USER → ROLE_ADMIN, re-encode (wert456…)The server decodes it and believes the user is an admin. Broken.
2Send encoded.hash(json); the server re-hashes the decoded JSON and comparesHash algorithms are public and unkeyed: modify the JSON, re-encode and recompute the hash (try SHA-256 etc. until one matches)The hashes match, so the server is fooled. Broken.
3Encrypt with a server-held keyThe client can't read or change it without the keyWorks. This is JWE (JSON Web Encryption), but it's more than we need here.
4Sign with a server-held secret: encoded.signature(encoded, key)The client can still decode and edit the payload, but can't produce a valid signature without the keyThe server re-signs the received payload, sees a mismatch, and rejects it. Standard JWT.
The core idea:
Encoding gives no protection, and a plain hash gives none either, because anyone can recompute it. What stops forgery is a secret the client doesn't have. A signed JWT's payload is readable by anyone but tamper-evident. Added: the HS256 "signature" is technically an HMAC, a keyed hash. Attempt 2 fails and attempt 4 works for exactly that reason: the hash is now bound to a secret key.
Verified (Boot 4.1.0):
I took a real token, decoded the payload, changed authorities to ["ROLE_ADMIN"], re-encoded it, and kept the original signature. Calling /admin/panel returned 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token" … Signed JWT rejected: Invalid signature. The genuine ROLE_USER token got 403 there: authenticated, but not an admin.

Anatomy of a JWT

base64url(header) . base64url(payload) . base64url(signature): all three parts are Base64URL-encoded and joined by dots.

PartContents
Headeralg (e.g. HS256), typ (JWT), optionally kid (key ID)
Payload (claims)
  • Registered claims:
    • sub (subject, e.g. aditya), iss (issuer, e.g. coderarmy-api), aud (audience, e.g. course-api).
    • iat (issued at) and exp (expiry), both epoch seconds.
  • Custom claims, e.g. roles/authorities.
All optional. Never put passwords or sensitive data here: it's only encoded.
Signaturesign(base64url(header) + "." + base64url(payload), key) (the "signing input")

Symmetric vs asymmetric signing

Symmetric (e.g. HS256)Asymmetric (e.g. RS256, ES256)
KeysOne secret key signs and verifiesPrivate key signs; public key verifies
ProSimple, fastVerifiers can't forge tokens; the public key can be shared openly
RiskEvery service that verifies holds the secret. If one (say S3) is compromised, the attacker can mint valid tokens.Only the issuing service (S1) holds the private key
Typical useSingle app (this lecture)Microservices; most production systems

In microservices one service (e.g. S1) issues tokens and others (S2, S3) only verify them. With a symmetric key all of them could also sign, so asymmetric keys keep signing power in one place.

Worked example: stateless JWT login

Dependency and properties

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server</artifactId>
</dependency>   <!-- OAuth itself comes in a later lecture; this brings the JWT support -->

# application.properties
jwt.secret=<output of: openssl rand -base64 32>   # real apps: env var / secret manager, never committed
jwt.issuer=coderarmy-api
jwt.expiry=900                                    # seconds = 15 minutes

Beans

These beans are boilerplate that stays the same in every app. You need to know what each one is for, not memorise them.

@Bean
public SecretKey jwtSecretKey(@Value("${jwt.secret}") String secret) {
    byte[] decodedKey = Base64.getDecoder().decode(secret);
    return new SecretKeySpec(decodedKey, "HmacSHA256");
}

@Bean
public JwtEncoder jwtEncoder(SecretKey key) {        // signs tokens
    return new NimbusJwtEncoder(new ImmutableSecret<>(key));
}

@Bean
public JwtDecoder jwtDecoder(SecretKey key) {        // verifies signature + expiry, parses claims
    return NimbusJwtDecoder.withSecretKey(key).build();
}

@Bean
public AuthenticationManager authenticationManager(DaoAuthenticationProvider provider) {
    return new ProviderManager(provider);            // needed because we call authenticate() ourselves
}

@Bean
public JwtAuthenticationConverter jwtAuthenticationConverter() {
    JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter authorities = new JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter();
    authorities.setAuthoritiesClaimName("authorities");   // read roles from our claim
    authorities.setAuthorityPrefix("");                   // our values already start with ROLE_
    JwtAuthenticationConverter converter = new JwtAuthenticationConverter();
    converter.setJwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter(authorities);
    return converter;
}

The lecture's snippet for the AuthenticationManager bean isn't readable on screen. ProviderManager is one standard way; authenticationConfiguration.getAuthenticationManager() is another.

The filter chain

@Bean
public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http,
                                               JwtAuthenticationConverter converter) throws Exception {
    http
        .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())                                  // fine now: no cookies, Bearer header only
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers("/api/users/register", "/auth/login").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth.jwt(jwt -> jwt.jwtAuthenticationConverter(converter)));
    // formLogin / httpBasic / .authenticationProvider(...) removed: requests now authenticate via Bearer JWT
    return http.build();
}

Login endpoint and token service

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/auth")
public class AuthController {                        // separate from UserController for clarity
    // AuthenticationManager and JwtService injected

    @PostMapping("/login")
    public LoginResponseDto login(@RequestBody LoginRequestDto dto) {
        Authentication authenticationRequest =
            UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.unauthenticated(dto.getUsername(), dto.getPassword());
        Authentication authentication = authenticationManager.authenticate(authenticationRequest);
        String token = jwtService.generateToken(authentication);
        return new LoginResponseDto(token);          // { "accessToken": "…" }
    }
}

@Service
public class JwtService {
    // JwtEncoder injected; @Value("${jwt.issuer}") String issuer; @Value("${jwt.expiry}") long expiry;

    public String generateToken(Authentication authentication) {
        Instant now = Instant.now();
        List<String> authorities = authentication.getAuthorities().stream()
                .map(GrantedAuthority::getAuthority).toList();
        JwtClaimsSet claims = JwtClaimsSet.builder()
                .issuer(issuer)
                .issuedAt(now)
                .expiresAt(now.plusSeconds(expiry))
                .subject(authentication.getName())
                .claim("authorities", authorities)
                .build();
        JwsHeader header = JwsHeader.with(MacAlgorithm.HS256).build();   // see note below
        return jwtEncoder.encode(JwtEncoderParameters.from(header, claims)).getTokenValue();
    }
}
  • We write /auth/login ourselves, so we do by hand what Spring's form login did internally: build the unauthenticated token, ask the AuthenticationManager (which calls DaoAuthenticationProvider), then issue a JWT.
  • LoginRequestDto (username, password) is a separate class from UserRegisterRequestDto, for clearer naming. LoginResponseDto has accessToken plus @AllArgsConstructor.
Worth knowing (verified on Spring Security 7.1): specify HS256 when encoding:
The lecture says the algorithm was already given in the encoder bean. With new NimbusJwtEncoder(new ImmutableSecret<>(key)) and JwtEncoderParameters.from(claims) (no header), encoding failed: JwtEncodingException: … Failed to select a JWK signing key. The default header algorithm is RS256, which an HMAC secret can't satisfy. Pass JwsHeader.with(MacAlgorithm.HS256) as above. Spring Security 7 also offers a builder, NimbusJwtEncoder.withSecretKey(key).

Demo run

  1. POST /auth/login, No Auth, body {"username": "aditya", "password": "secret123"} → {"accessToken": "eyJ…"}. The endpoint is public.
  2. GET /api/users/hello with Postman Authorization → Bearer Token = that token → "Hello, you are logged in as aditya".
  3. Same result with a manual header Authorization: Bearer <token>. That's all Postman's Authorization tab does anyway.
  4. Any number of calls work without logging in again, until the token expires (15 minutes).
Verified (Boot 4.1.0, H2, same setup):
  • Decoded token: header {"alg": "HS256"}; payload {"iss": "coderarmy-api", "sub": "aditya", "exp": …, "iat": …, "authorities": ["ROLE_USER", "FACTOR_PASSWORD"]}.
  • /hello with the Bearer token → 200 with ROLE_USER, and no Set-Cookie in the response (STATELESS).
  • 401 cases: no token, a wrong password on /auth/login, and a forged token.

Anticipated question: "Why the JwtAuthenticationConverter?"

The lecture says that without it Spring would add its own prefix, turning ROLE_ADMIN into ROLE_ROLE_ADMIN. It's actually worse. The default JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter reads the scope/scp claim and prefixes values with SCOPE_; it never looks at a claim named authorities.

Verified: with a default converter, the user's authorities contained no ROLE_USER at all, just Spring Security 7's FACTOR_BEARER marker, so every hasRole(…) check would fail. Also verified: a JwtAuthenticationConverter bean is picked up automatically by oauth2ResourceServer().jwt(), even without passing it explicitly.

Session vs JWT

Session (stateful)JWT (stateless)
Client holdsOpaque JSESSIONID cookieSelf-contained signed token (usually a header)
Server holdsThe SecurityContext per sessionNothing but the key
Per requestLook up the sessionVerify the signature, rebuild Authentication
ScalingNeeds sticky sessions or a shared storeAny replica works
Logout / revokeEasy: invalidate the sessionHard: valid until exp
CSRFRelevant (cookies are sent automatically)Not with Authorization headers

Gaps worth raising in an interview

  • No revocation/logout. A stolen or old token works until exp. Keep access tokens short (5–15 min) and add refresh tokens (stored server-side, rotated, revocable). For true logout you need a deny-list, which is partly stateful again.
  • Where the client stores the token. localStorage is readable by any XSS script. An HttpOnly Secure cookie resists XSS but brings CSRF back. Pick deliberately.
  • Secret handling. The HMAC secret in application.properties (as in the lecture) must move to an environment variable or secret manager. Use at least 256 bits of randomness: openssl rand -base64 32 is 32 random bytes, not "a 32-bit integer". Support key rotation (the kid header).
  • Validate more claims. NimbusJwtDecoder checks signature and exp/nbf by default (with 60 s clock skew), but not iss/aud unless you add validators (e.g. JwtValidators.createDefaultWithIssuer(…)).
  • Stale authorities. Roles are baked into the token. If an admin demotes a user, the old token keeps the old roles until it expires.
  • Login errors. A wrong password makes authenticate() throw BadCredentialsException. It surfaced as 401 here, but map it explicitly (e.g. a @RestControllerAdvice) to a clean JSON error, and rate-limit /auth/login (Lecture 35's brute-force point).

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Base64URL is encoding, not encryption. The lecture says this correctly. Paste any JWT into a decoder and the payload is visible.
  • JWS vs JWE: a normal JWT is a JWS (signed). JWE (encrypted) hides the payload too; use it only when claims must be confidential.
  • Why "OAuth2 resource server": in OAuth2 terms our API is a resource server that accepts Bearer tokens. Here the same app also issues them (acting as its own authorization server). The next lecture covers OAuth.
  • Field injection (@Autowired private AuthenticationManager / JwtEncoder) was used only to save time, as the lecturer admits. Prefer constructor injection.
  • Where the FACTOR_PASSWORD claim comes from: copying getAuthorities() into the token also copies Spring Security 7's factor marker. Filter to ROLE_ authorities if you want a clean claim.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"sign up with JWT" → authenticate (log in) with JWT.
"JWT authentication token / JWT authentication provider are used here" → with the resource server, BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter + JwtAuthenticationProvider produce a JwtAuthenticationToken.
"SHA 256" read as "shar 256"; "HMAC SHA 256" → HmacSHA256.
"a 32-bit integer" → 32 random bytes.
"the client created this token" (in the hashing attempt) → the server creates it.

Next (announced): OAuth.

Lecture 39: OAuth 2.0 & OpenID Connect — Roles, Tokens, the Authorization Code Flow with PKCE, and "Sign in with Google" in Spring Boot

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #39 · 1h27m · Code Army · builds on sessions/JWT (Lectures 35 & 38)

The problem: login without owning the credentials

Until now our app handled authentication itself. The user registered with us, sent username + password to /login, and got back a session ID (stateful) or a JWT (stateless) to present on later requests. Two new situations don't fit that model:

  1. "Log in with Google" (authentication). The user doesn't want another password or to share details with every site; most browsers are already signed in to Google. The naive idea, POST /loginWithGoogle asking for the user's Google email and password, is absurd. With someone's Google password you could read their Drive, Photos and Calendar. Never ask for it, and no one should give it.
  2. Accessing Google data on the user's behalf (authorization). A Coder Army "Productivity App" wants to read the user's Google Calendar to plan their time. Again the app must not get the Google password; it needs limited access (read calendar only) that the user explicitly consents to.

So we need Google to authenticate users for us, and Google to authorize our app for a narrow set of data, both without the password ever reaching us. OAuth 2.0 solves authorization; OpenID Connect adds authentication on top.

OAuth 2.0: the idea and the four roles

Conceptual flow:

  1. The user tells Google "I allow Coder Army to read my calendar".
  2. Google gives the app a token.
  3. The app presents that token to the Calendar API.
RoleMeaningIn our example
Resource ownerOwns the protected dataThe user (owns their Google Calendar)
ClientThe application requesting access. It's not necessarily a browser: whoever makes the request is the client.Our Spring Boot app (Productivity App)
Authorization serverAuthenticates the user, collects consent, issues tokensGoogle's auth system
Resource serverHosts the protected data and accepts tokensGoogle Calendar API
  • Scope — what the client asks for, e.g. conceptually calendar.read (read, not write). Added: Google's real scope string is https://www.googleapis.com/auth/calendar.readonly.
  • Consent — the screen Google shows: "Productivity App wants permission to: read your Google Calendar, view your profile". The user can allow or deny. Deny, and the app simply gets no token.
  • The token the client receives is the access token. OAuth doesn't mandate a format: it may be a JWT (the resource server verifies the signature) or an opaque string (the resource server looks it up).

OpenID Connect: authentication on top of OAuth

One-liner from the lecture:
OAuth 2.0 answers "what can this application access?"; OpenID Connect answers "who logged in?"

Why not just use the access token for login? It describes permissions for a resource server, not the user's identity for the client. OIDC adds a second token for that: the ID token, a JWT the client decodes to learn who the user is.

// decoded ID token payload (illustrative)
{
  "iss": "https://accounts.google.com",   // issuer (the lecture writes "google.com")
  "sub": "1098765432101234567890",         // Google's stable, unique id for this user
  "aud": "<your client id>",              // the token is meant for YOUR app
  "name": "Aditya",
  "email": "aditya@gmail.com",
  "iat": 1790000000, "exp": 1790003600
}

"Sign in with Google" flow in the lecture's words:

  1. The user clicks the button on our site.
  2. We 302-redirect them to Google.
  3. They log in there, if not already.
  4. Google gives our app an ID token.
  5. We decode it and register or log them in with our own database.

No password ever touches our site.

The three tokens

TokenPurposeConsumed byLifetime / format
ID token (OIDC)Authentication: who the user isThe clientShort; always a JWT (OIDC spec)
Access token (OAuth)Authorization: permission to call an API within the granted scopesThe resource server (the client just carries it)Short (minutes to an hour); JWT or opaque (Google's are opaque)
Refresh tokenGet a new access token when the old one expires, without bothering the userThe authorization server (client sends it)Long-lived; kept secret by the client

Why refresh tokens: access tokens should expire quickly (a leaked one is valid only briefly). Without a refresh token, every expiry would mean sending the user back to Google for consent. With one, the client quietly calls the authorization server: refresh token in, fresh access token out. Only when the refresh token itself expires or is revoked must the user consent again.

Precision note (added):
  • Refresh-token lifetime varies by provider. The lecture's "1–2 days" is just an example. Google's refresh tokens typically live until revoked, and Google issues one only when the client requests offline access (access_type=offline).
  • Never send an ID token to an API as if it were an access token. Its aud is your client, not the API.

Why tokens must not travel through the browser

Suppose Google just redirected back with the token in the URL: 302 → our-app/callback?token=…. Everything in a redirect is visible in the browser: history, logs, extensions, anyone intercepting. A hacker who grabs that access token can call the Calendar API exactly like our app, and the resource server can't tell them apart (a bearer token, Lecture 35). Rule: tokens are exchanged over the back channel (server to server), never the front channel (browser redirects). Added: the "token in the redirect" design is the old implicit flow, now deprecated for this reason.

The Authorization Code flow, step by step

  1. Authorization request. Our app 302-redirects the user to Google with:
    • client_id — issued when you register the app with Google, along with a client_secret.
    • redirect_uri — where Google should send the user back.
    • scope.
    • response_type=code — "don't give me a token here, give me a code".
    • state — a random string Google echoes back, so we can match each callback to the request that started it.
  2. Google authenticates the user (email, password, possibly 2FA).
  3. Consent ("Coder Army wants access to …").
  4. Authorization code. Google redirects to redirect_uri?state=abc123&code=TAYFGV456…. The code is not a token, just a one-time random string. Spring Security's default callback path is /login/oauth2/code/google.
  5. Exchange code for tokens. Our back end calls Google's token endpoint with the code and gets the ID, access and refresh tokens. This happens server to server, never in the browser.

PKCE: Proof Key for Code Exchange

The lecturer's worry: the code travels through the browser, so a hacker could grab it and call the token endpoint themselves. PKCE ("pixie") binds the code to the party that started the flow:

  1. Before redirecting, the client creates a long random code_verifier and keeps it secret.
  2. It computes code_challenge = SHA-256(code_verifier) and sends only the challenge in step 1. Google remembers it with that request.
  3. At the token exchange (step 5) the client sends the code plus the code_verifier.
  4. Google hashes the verifier and compares it with the stored challenge. Tokens are issued only on a match.

A hacker who stole the code never saw the verifier (only its hash went through the browser, and a hash can't be reversed), so their exchange is rejected.

Precision note (added):
  • The client secret already protects confidential clients. For a server-side app like ours, the token request also carries the client_secret, which never leaves our server, so a stolen code alone is already useless there.
  • PKCE was designed for public clients (SPAs, mobile apps) that can't keep a secret. It also defends against code-injection attacks, and OAuth 2.1 recommends it for all clients.
  • Exact encoding: code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)) with code_challenge_method=S256; the verifier is 43–128 characters.
  • state's main security job is CSRF protection for the callback (no attacker can make your browser complete their login). For OIDC, a nonce also goes into the ID token to prevent replay.
Verified (Boot 4.1.0 / Spring Security 7, dummy Google client):
  • A browser-style GET /profile → 302 to /oauth2/authorization/google. With a single provider, Spring skips its login page and goes straight there.
  • That endpoint → 302 to https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth with response_type=code, client_id, scope=openid profile email, state, redirect_uri=http://localhost:8099/login/oauth2/code/google, nonce, code_challenge=… and code_challenge_method=S256.
  • So Spring does all of steps 1–5 (state, nonce and PKCE included) even for a client that has a secret.

Registering the app with Google

Google won't talk to an app it doesn't know. In Google Cloud Console you create an OAuth client (the lecturer's notes list the few steps) and receive a client ID and client secret. Added: you must also register the exact redirect URI, http://localhost:8080/login/oauth2/code/google, or Google refuses the flow with redirect_uri_mismatch.

Our app's plan:

  1. Google authenticates the user.
  2. Spring receives the ID token and gives us an OidcUser.
  3. Does this user exist in our DB? Yes → load/update them. No → create them.

Worked example: oauth-demo

Spring Initializr dependencies:

  • Spring Web, Spring Data JPA, MySQL Driver, Lombok (added later).
  • OAuth2 Client, which brings Spring Security with it. Not OAuth2 Resource Server or Authorization Server: our app is the client here.

Entity and repository

@Entity @Getter @Setter @NoArgsConstructor
public class User {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private String email;
    private String provider;          // "google"
    private String providerSubject;   // the ID token's "sub": Google's stable id for this user
    // no password field: users never log in with a password here
    public User(String name, String email, String provider, String providerSubject) { … }
}

public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    Optional<User> findByProviderAndProviderSubject(String provider, String providerSubject);
}

provider + providerSubject together identify a user uniquely: that's how we recognise the same Google account next time.

UserService: register or update

@Service
public class UserService {
    private final UserRepository userRepository;

    public User registerOrUpdate(String provider, OidcUser oidcUser) {
        String providerSubject = oidcUser.getSubject();
        String name  = oidcUser.getClaimAsString("name");
        String email = oidcUser.getClaimAsString("email");
        Optional<User> existingUser =
            userRepository.findByProviderAndProviderSubject(provider, providerSubject);
        if (existingUser.isPresent()) {             // known user: refresh details
            User user = existingUser.get();
            user.setName(name);
            user.setEmail(email);
            return user;                            // (see Gaps: needs a save/transaction to persist)
        }
        User newUser = new User(name, email, provider, providerSubject);
        return userRepository.save(newUser);        // first login: create
    }

    public Optional<User> findByProviderAndSubject(String provider, String subject) {
        return userRepository.findByProviderAndProviderSubject(provider, subject);
    }
}

CustomOidcUserService: hook into Spring's OIDC login

@Service
public class CustomOidcUserService implements OAuth2UserService<OidcUserRequest, OidcUser> {
    private final OidcUserService delegate = new OidcUserService();   // Spring's default implementation
    private final UserService userService;

    @Override
    public OidcUser loadUser(OidcUserRequest userRequest) throws OAuth2AuthenticationException {
        OidcUser oidcUser = delegate.loadUser(userRequest);           // "let Spring do the real OIDC work"
        String provider = userRequest.getClientRegistration().getRegistrationId();   // "google"
        userService.registerOrUpdate(provider, oidcUser);
        return oidcUser;
    }
}

By the time loadUser runs, Spring has already done everything in the sequence diagram (redirect, callback, state check, code + verifier exchange). delegate.loadUser validates the ID token (and may call Google's userinfo endpoint) and builds the OidcUser. We only add "persist the user". This delegate-then-customise pattern is what Spring's reference docs recommend.

Security config, controller, properties

@Configuration
public class SecurityConfig {
    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http,
                                                   CustomOidcUserService customOidcUserService) throws Exception {
        http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/").permitAll()          // exactly "/", not "everything starting with /"
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2Login(oauth -> oauth
                .userInfoEndpoint(u -> u.oidcUserService(customOidcUserService))
                .defaultSuccessUrl("/profile", true));
        return http.build();
    }
}

@RestController
public class UserController {
    @GetMapping("/")
    public String home() {
        return "Public home. Login using http://localhost:8080/oauth2/authorization/google";
    }

    @GetMapping("/profile")
    public Map<String, Object> profile(@AuthenticationPrincipal OidcUser oidcUser) {
        User user = userService.findByProviderAndSubject("google", oidcUser.getSubject()).orElseThrow();
        Map<String, Object> response = new HashMap<>();
        response.put("internalUserId", user.getId());           // our own primary key
        response.put("provider", user.getProvider());
        response.put("subject", oidcUser.getSubject());
        response.put("name", oidcUser.getClaimAsString("name"));
        response.put("email", oidcUser.getClaimAsString("email"));
        return response;
    }
}

# application.properties (Google's endpoints are pre-configured by Spring Boot)
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.google.client-id=${GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID}
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.google.client-secret=${GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET}
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.google.scope=openid,profile,email
  • /profile returns the OidcUser details to show what Google actually sends, rather than a plain string.
  • We never write the callback endpoint or the token call: Spring provides /oauth2/authorization/google and /login/oauth2/code/google.
  • The lecture hard-codes the ID and secret in application.properties for the demo and warns: never commit the client secret. Use environment variables (as above) or a secret manager. (application.yml is an alternative that reads better for these long keys.)

Demo run

  1. Startup creates the user table (id, email, name, provider, provider_subject).
  2. Postman GET / → the public message with the login URL.
  3. Browser localhost:8080/profile → redirected to accounts.google.com → choose an account → "Sign in to Coder Army OAuth Demo. Google will allow access to your name, profile picture, email" → Continue.
  4. Back at /profile, showing provider, subject, name, internal user ID and email.
  5. Open /profile again → no Google prompt. DevTools shows a JSESSIONID: after the OAuth dance, Spring keeps the login in a normal stateful session (Lecture 38). You could issue your own JWT instead to go stateless.
  6. Visiting /oauth2/authorization/google directly also starts the Google login.

Homework from the lecture: offer both options, your own username/password + JWT login (Lecture 38) and Sign in with Google.

OAuth 2.0 vs OpenID Connect

OAuth 2.0OpenID Connect
AnswersWhat may this app access?Who is the user?
Key tokenAccess token (+ refresh token)ID token (JWT), on top of OAuth
Token audienceResource server (API)Client (your app)
TriggerAny scopes, e.g. calendar.readonlyThe openid scope
Spring Boot useCall Google APIs using the OAuth2AuthorizedClient's access tokenoauth2Login() → OidcUser

Gaps worth raising in an interview

  • The update branch doesn't persist. registerOrUpdate sets name/email on the loaded user but never calls save and isn't @Transactional, so changes are lost (Lecture 33's dirty-checking rule). Add @Transactional or save(user).
  • Race on first login. Two simultaneous first logins can insert duplicates. Add a unique constraint on (provider, provider_subject) and handle the conflict.
  • Identify users by sub, not email. The lecture does this correctly: emails can change or be recycled. If you ever link accounts by email, check email_verified.
  • Hard-coded "google" in /profile: use the registration ID from the OAuth2AuthenticationToken if you add more providers (GitHub, Microsoft…).
  • Roles. Google users get only default OIDC authorities; map them to your own ROLE_* from the DB in loadUser (return an OidcUser with your authorities) to use hasRole.
  • Calendar-style access (the Productivity App) needs the Calendar scope, access_type=offline for a refresh token, and secure storage of that refresh token. The demo only does login.

Corrections & worth knowing

  • Refresh tokens are exchanged at the authorization server's token endpoint, not the resource server. The lecture draws this correctly.
  • Why the OAuth2 client starter (added): spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client gives oauth2Login(), client registrations and authorized-client management. The resource-server starter (Lecture 38) is for APIs that accept Bearer tokens. The authorization-server project is for issuing tokens yourself.
  • The "resource owner password" grant (the app collects the user's password and sends it to the provider) is exactly what OAuth exists to avoid, and it's removed in OAuth 2.1.
  • The session after login is Spring's. The Google tokens live in the OAuth2AuthorizedClientService (in memory by default). Logging out of your app doesn't log the user out of Google.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"the user sent us the token… sorry, the server" → the lecturer corrects himself: the server issues it.
"iss: google.com" → https://accounts.google.com.
"code_challenge = SHA-256 of the verifier" → Base64URL of the SHA-256 digest.
"request_uri" (in places) → redirect_uri.
"@RestController... I mean @RequestMapping" → the lecturer corrects himself.
"permit everything that starts with slash" → requestMatchers("/") permits only the root path.

Lecture 40: Unit Testing in Spring Boot — JUnit, Mockito, @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest (and Course Wrap-Up)

Source: Code Army Spring Boot series, video #40 · 1h22m · Code Army · final lecture of the Spring Framework series

The problem: "it works in Postman" isn't testing

The project spring-testing-demo has a Product entity (id, name, price, stock) and two operations:

  • ProductController — GET /api/product/{id} returns 200 with the product; POST /api/product returns 201 Created.
  • ProductService:
    • getProductById — findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new RuntimeException("Product not found " + id)).
    • createProduct — throws IllegalArgumentException("Product already exists") if existsByName(name), else save.
  • ProductRepository — JpaRepository plus boolean existsByName(String name).

Demo: POST {"name": "laptop", "price": 50000, "stock": 10} → 201, row in MySQL. POST it again → 500, and the log shows IllegalArgumentException: Product already exists, which is expected behaviour.

That's manual testing: hit an endpoint, eyeball the status. It covers one path, is repeated by hand after every change, and misses edge cases in real business logic. Your Spring knowledge is incomplete if you can't write unit tests; in industry you're expected to.

Motivating example: a PriceCalculator with edge cases

@Service
public class PriceCalculator {
    public double calculatePrice(double price, double discount) {
        if (price < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Price cannot be negative");
        if (discount < 0 || discount > 100)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Discount should be within 0 to 100");
        return price - (price * discount / 100);
    }
}

The happy path (1000 at 20% → 800) is obvious. Price 0, negative price, negative discount or a discount over 100 are the edge cases, as in DSA practice. The two guard clauses were only added after thinking those cases through. Automated tests check them every time:

  1. Start from a known input.
  2. Execute the function to get the actual output.
  3. Compare it with the expected result: equal means pass, otherwise fail.
Anatomy of a test case: Arrange, Act, Assert:
  • Arrange — initial conditions and inputs (price 1000, discount 20).
  • Act — call the method under test (calculatePrice).
  • Assert — check the actual result against the expected one (800).

Kinds of tests

LevelScopeExample
UnitOne unit (class/method) in isolation; the rest of the app doesn't matterPriceCalculator.calculatePrice, ProductService with its repository mocked
SliceBetween unit and integration: one layerThe web layer via @WebMvcTest, the JPA layer via @DataJpaTest
IntegrationSeveral components togetherRepository + Hibernate + database; controller → service → repository
End-to-endThe whole flow, front end to databaseButton click → filters/security → DispatcherServlet → controller → … → DB

These are like concentric circles, unit innermost and E2E outermost. As a developer you mostly write unit tests, and they should all pass before your feature branch is merged.

Precision note (added): what "slice" means in Spring:
Spring Boot's "test slices" are annotations that load part of the application context. The lecture's controller test with @WebMvcTest and the repository test with @DataJpaTest are exactly such slice tests, even though the lecture files them under unit testing.

What to test, and what not to

TestDon't test
  • Business logic
  • Conditional branches (if/else ladders, switch cases)
  • Validation rules
  • Exception handling (deliberate exceptions are behaviour too)
  • Security checks
  • Anything that could break in production
  • Library/framework code (already tested upstream)
  • Plain getters/setters
  • Built-in JPA methods
  • Code with no meaningful decision-making
AI-generated test suites often include these; review before pushing, as they only slow the build.

Where tests live and what you need

  • src/test/java mirrors src/main/java (Lecture 3), so tests are easy to find: service/PriceCalculator → src/test/java/…/service/PriceCalculatorTest.
  • Initializr already added the test starters, one per main starter: spring-boot-starter-data-jpa-test and spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test. They bring JUnit (writing and running tests) and Mockito (mocks). Nothing extra to download.
  • Run with mvn test (the Maven test phase), the IntelliJ Maven panel, or the green run icon next to a test.
    • Failures print "There are test failures"; details go to target/surefire-reports/.
    • A test failure fails the build.
Version note (verified on Boot 4.1.0):
  • Libraries: JUnit Jupiter 6.0.3 and Mockito 5.23.0.
  • Test starters: Boot 4's per-technology test starters (spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test, spring-boot-starter-data-jpa-test) replace Boot 3's single spring-boot-starter-test.
  • Slice annotations moved: org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure.WebMvcTest and org.springframework.boot.data.jpa.test.autoconfigure.DataJpaTest (Boot 3: org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet / …orm.jpa).

Worked example 1: testing PriceCalculator with plain JUnit

class PriceCalculatorTest {
    private PriceCalculator priceCalculator;

    @BeforeEach                                  // runs before every test
    void setUp() { priceCalculator = new PriceCalculator(); }   // plain `new`, no Spring, no @Autowired

    @Test
    void shouldApplyDiscountToPrice() {
        // Arrange
        double price = 1000;
        double discount = 20;
        // Act
        double actualPrice = priceCalculator.calculatePrice(price, discount);
        // Assert
        assertEquals(800, actualPrice);          // (expected, actual)
    }

    @Test
    void shouldRejectDiscountAbove100() {
        IllegalArgumentException exception = assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
                () -> priceCalculator.calculatePrice(1000, 120));
        assertEquals("Discount should be within 0 to 100", exception.getMessage());
    }
}
  • No Spring here, on purpose. Don't start the application context, Tomcat or a port just to test a Java method: keep the test phase fast. Think "plain Java", not "Spring Boot".
  • @Test (org.junit.jupiter.api) marks methods JUnit should run. They return void.
  • Name tests by behaviour (shouldApplyDiscountToPrice) rather than test1: long names are fine and help other developers.
  • One method can have many tests, one per edge case (above 100, below 0, negative price…).
  • Failure demo: expecting 700 fails with "expected: <700.0> but was: <800.0>". Removing "should" from the expected message also fails.
  • @AfterEach runs after every test, like a finally block, e.g. to release resources.
  • The lecture deletes the generated …ApplicationTests (an empty @SpringBootTest that just starts the context) so only its own tests run.
Common JUnit assertions (org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions)
AssertionPasses when
assertEquals(expected, actual) / assertNotEqualsValues are (not) equal
assertTrue(condition) / assertFalse(condition)The condition is true / false
assertNull(x) / assertNotNull(x)x is (not) null
assertThrows(Type.class, () -> …)The lambda throws that exception type; returns it for further checks
Worth knowing (verified): compare doubles with a tolerance:
assertEquals(800, actualPrice) passes because 800.0 is exactly representable. But assertEquals(0.3, 0.1 + 0.2) fails (0.30000000000000004), while assertEquals(0.3, 0.1 + 0.2, 1e-9) passes. Use the delta overload for computed doubles, or better, BigDecimal for money (Lecture 33).

Why the service test needs Mockito

new ProductService() doesn't compile: the constructor needs a ProductRepository. @Autowired-ing a real repository would pull in the application context, Hibernate and a real MySQL, just to test a service. The service depends on the repository, so we replace that dependency with a test double.

Test doubles
DoubleWhat it isExample
DummyPassed only to satisfy a signature; never actually usedPassing null as the repository. It crashes with an NPE as soon as the service calls it.
StubReturns predefined answersfindById(1) always returns Laptop / 50000 / 10
FakeA lightweight working implementationAn in-memory "database": a HashMap, or the H2 in-memory DB
MockConfigurable: can act as dummy, stub or fake, and lets you verify interactionsMockito's @Mock ProductRepository

Added: the fifth classic double is the spy (@Spy), a real object whose calls are recorded and can be partially stubbed. The textbook distinction: stubs support state verification (check the result), mocks support behaviour verification (check which calls happened).

Worked example 2: ProductService with @Mock and @InjectMocks

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)              // lets JUnit understand Mockito's annotations
class ProductServiceTest {

    @Mock                                        // fake repository, managed by Mockito, NOT a Spring bean
    private ProductRepository productRepository;

    @InjectMocks                                 // real ProductService built with the mock injected
    private ProductService productService;       // (conceptually: new ProductService(productRepository))

    @Test
    void shouldReturnProductWhenProductExists() {
        // Arrange: stub the repository call the service will make
        Product product = new Product(1L, "Laptop", 50000, 10);
        when(productRepository.findById(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(product));
        // Act
        Product actualResult = productService.getProductById(1L);
        // Assert
        assertEquals(1L, actualResult.getId());
        assertEquals("Laptop", actualResult.getName());
        verify(productRepository).findById(1L);  // the repository really was called (once) with 1
    }

    @Test
    void shouldThrowExceptionWhenProductDoesNotExist() {
        when(productRepository.findById(99L)).thenReturn(Optional.empty());
        RuntimeException exception = assertThrows(RuntimeException.class,
                () -> productService.getProductById(99L));
        assertEquals("Product not found 99", exception.getMessage());
        verify(productRepository).findById(99L);
    }

    @Test
    void shouldCreateProductWhenNameIsUnique() {
        Product request = new Product(null, "Keyboard", 200, 5);     // incoming: no id yet
        Product savedProduct = new Product(10L, "Keyboard", 200, 5); // what save() returns
        when(productRepository.existsByName("Keyboard")).thenReturn(false);
        when(productRepository.save(request)).thenReturn(savedProduct);
        Product result = productService.createProduct(request);
        assertEquals(10L, result.getId());
        assertEquals("Keyboard", result.getName());
        verify(productRepository).existsByName("Keyboard");
        verify(productRepository).save(request);
    }

    @Test
    void shouldRejectProductWhenNameAlreadyExists() {
        Product request = new Product(null, "Keyboard", 200, 5);
        when(productRepository.existsByName("Keyboard")).thenReturn(true);
        assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,               // act + assert in one step
                () -> productService.createProduct(request));
        verify(productRepository).existsByName("Keyboard");
        verify(productRepository, never()).save(any(Product.class)); // save must NOT be called, for any product
    }
}
  • when(…).thenReturn(…) reads naturally: "when the service internally calls findById(1), return this product". No real database is touched.
  • verify(mock).method(args) is optional but useful: it proves a call happened, e.g. which branch ran.
  • verify(mock, never()) with any(Product.class) means "never called with any product". Passing the specific request would only check that one object.
  • These particular tests mostly re-check a thin wrapper around JPA, which contradicts "don't test framework code". The lecturer admits this and uses them purely to teach the mechanics; real services would have mapping and validation logic worth testing.
Worth knowing (verified): Mockito's strict stubs:
With MockitoExtension, a stub your test never uses makes it fail with UnnecessaryStubbingException ("Please remove unnecessary stubbings or use 'lenient' strictness"). This catches copy-pasted setup that no longer matches the code. Remove the stub, or mark it lenient().when(…) if it's intentionally shared.

Worked example 3: the controller with @WebMvcTest and MockMvc

Why test controllers at all when the business logic is in the service? To check the web behaviour:

  • URL and HTTP-method mappings.
  • @PathVariable / @RequestParam / @RequestBody binding.
  • Jackson JSON (de)serialisation.
  • Status codes (200, 201…).

Calling the controller as a plain Java method would skip all of that, so the request must flow through the DispatcherServlet.

@WebMvcTest(ProductController.class)             // small context: MVC infrastructure + this controller only
class ProductControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    private MockMvc mockMvc;                     // perform HTTP requests without starting Tomcat or a port

    @MockitoBean                                 // a Mockito mock registered AS A BEAN in that context
    private ProductService productService;

    @Test
    void shouldReturnProductIfProductExists() throws Exception {
        // Arrange
        when(productService.getProductById(1L)).thenReturn(new Product(1L, "Laptop", 50000, 10));
        // Act + Assert
        mockMvc.perform(get("/api/product/{id}", 1L).accept(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON))
               .andExpect(status().isOk())
               .andExpect(content().contentTypeCompatibleWith(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON))
               .andExpect(jsonPath("$.id").value(1))
               .andExpect(jsonPath("$.name").value("Laptop"))
               .andExpect(jsonPath("$.price").value(50000.0))
               .andExpect(jsonPath("$.stock").value(10));
        verify(productService).getProductById(1L);
    }
}
  • @WebMvcTest starts a limited context: controllers, MVC infrastructure, Jackson, filters. No services, repositories or other beans.
  • MockMvc simulates the servlet request, which goes through the filter chain and DispatcherServlet to the handler method. Without it you'd need a running server.
  • Why @MockitoBean, not @Mock: the controller is a bean in that context and needs a ProductService bean. A plain @Mock lives outside the context, so startup would fail on the missing dependency. @MockitoBean puts the mock into the IoC container.
  • POST works the same way: post("/api/product").contentType(APPLICATION_JSON).content("{…}") + status().isCreated(). Verified: both GET and POST controller tests passed on Boot 4.1.
Correction: @MockBean is gone in Boot 4:
Older tutorials use Spring Boot's @MockBean. It was deprecated in Boot 3.4 and removed in Boot 4 (verified: no MockBean class in spring-boot-test 4.1.0). The replacement is Spring Framework's @MockitoBean (and @MockitoSpyBean) in org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito, available since Framework 6.2.

Secured endpoints: @WithMockUser

If Spring Security is on the classpath, @WebMvcTest applies it. Annotate a test with @WithMockUser(username = "aditya", roles = "ADMIN") (from spring-security-test, which comes with the security starter's test starter) to run the request as an authenticated user with those roles.

Worked example 4: the repository with @DataJpaTest

Repository tests only make sense for queries you wrote (derived queries, @Query, native SQL), not built-in JPA methods. They need a real database to store and read data. @DataJpaTest loads only the JPA slice (entity manager, Hibernate, DataSource, repositories), not controllers or services. With the H2 dependency on the test classpath, you get an in-memory SQL database with zero configuration.

@DataJpaTest
class ProductRepositoryTest {
    @Autowired private ProductRepository productRepository;

    @Test
    void existsByNameFindsSavedProduct() {
        productRepository.save(new Product(null, "Mouse", 500, 3));
        assertTrue(productRepository.existsByName("Mouse"));
        assertFalse(productRepository.existsByName("Monitor"));
    }
}

Verified on Boot 4.1 with H2: passes. Added: each @DataJpaTest test runs in a transaction that is rolled back afterwards, so tests don't leak data into each other. The lecturer notes teams rarely test repositories, because native SQL is usually tried and tested against the real server first.

Comparison: which tool for which test

TestSpring context?DependenciesKey annotationsSpeed
Plain unit (PriceCalculator)NoneCreate with new@Test, @BeforeEachMilliseconds
Unit with mocks (ProductService)NoneMockito mocks@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class), @Mock, @InjectMocksMilliseconds
Web slice (ProductController)MVC slice@MockitoBean beans@WebMvcTest, MockMvcSeconds
JPA slice (ProductRepository)JPA sliceEmbedded DB (H2)@DataJpaTestSeconds
Full integrationWhole appReal beans (DB via Testcontainers)@SpringBootTestSlowest

Corrections & worth knowing

  • @SpringBootTest needs everything the app needs. The generated contextLoads() test starts the full context, including the MySQL connection. It passed in the lecture only because MySQL was running; on a CI machine without the DB it fails. Use slices, an embedded DB, or Testcontainers (a real MySQL in Docker, added) for full-context tests.
  • H2 isn't MySQL. Dialect differences (reserved words, functions, native SQL) mean an H2-green query can still fail in production. Testcontainers gives real-database fidelity for repository tests.
  • The 500 for a duplicate product in the opening demo is an unhandled IllegalArgumentException. With a @RestControllerAdvice (Lecture 17) it should become 409 Conflict, which is exactly the kind of mapping a @WebMvcTest should assert.
  • double for price in the entity and calculator is a teaching simplification. Use BigDecimal for money (Lectures 33 and 36).
  • AssertJ (assertThat(actual).isEqualTo(800)) comes with Spring Boot's test starters and gives more readable failure messages. Many teams prefer it to JUnit's assertions.
  • Coverage isn't correctness. Tools like JaCoCo report which lines ran, not whether you asserted the right things. Aim for meaningful branch and edge-case tests, not a percentage.
Transcript slips to ignore:
"mock it bean" → @MockitoBean.
"@BeforeEach is like post-processing" → it runs before each test (setup); @AfterEach is the after-hook.
"@JpaTest" → @DataJpaTest (the lecturer corrects himself).
"2001 Created" → 201 Created.
"test the security layer with unit tests" → that's done with slice/integration tests plus @WithMockUser.
"the lecture is repeated" near the end: the closing advice is spoken twice.

Course wrap-up: what the series covered

The lecturer closes the series by revisiting the Lecture 1 module map: Spring Core, Spring Boot, MVC, Data (JDBC, JPA, Hibernate, Spring Data), AOP, Security and now testing. The advice: rewatch anything you missed, revise the notes, and build one project that uses everything:

  • Filters, interceptors and AOP.
  • Exception handling, DTOs and entities.
  • Spring Security.
  • Unit tests.

Microservices, API gateway and a full project with a front end are announced for the channel's members-only videos.
